unit.title: Reflection in Action & Reflection on Action
unit.unit_summary: This unit teaches reflective practice as a core component of effective coaching. Reflection in action means adapting during a session in real time, while reflection on action means reviewing a session or competition afterward to understand what happened, why it happened, and how future coaching should change. The media content frames self-reflection as the foundation of continuous improvement, helping coaches analyze decisions, behaviors, communication, emotional intelligence, and training environments. The unit closes with reflective questions coaches can use during and after coaching.

chunk.content: [0:00:00] Welcome coaches to module one, the coaching mindset. In this module my objective is to get you to look closely towards your mental outlook of coaching and then begin to explore the ways in which this course is going to develop and enhance your practice. Self-reflection is the foundation of continuous improvement in coaching. It enables coaches to critically analyze their [0:00:20] decisions, behaviors and interactions with athletes. By fostering a reflective mindset, coaches can identify their strengths, address weaknesses and develop strategies to enhance their coaching effectiveness. This ongoing process ensures that coaches remain adaptable [0:00:36] and responsive to the needs of their athletes, ultimately fostering a more effective and supportive training environment. Self-reflection is crucial for personal and professional growth. It allows coaches to assess whether their methods align with their coaching philosophy and the goals of their athletes. Through self-reflection, coaches can recognize biases, [0:00:57] improve communication strategies and refine their training plans. Additionally, it helps in developing emotional intelligence, enabling coaches to manage stress, empathize with athletes and create a positive team culture. Without self-reflection, coaching can become stagnant, [0:01:15] limiting both athlete and coach development. Furthermore, I introduce the concept of growth mindset that is equally overlooked when a coach establishes their position within a community of athletes. The ability to show receptiveness and hunger to learn new things and develop new [0:01:31] concepts for personal growth and development is key for great coaching. So let's dive in and begin exploring this module, the coaching mindset.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Reflection In Action & Reflection On Action
chunk.content:
High-quality coaching is dependent on a coach's ability to reflect on their experiences, develop knowledge, and adapt their behaviors to meet athlete needs (Côté & Gilbert, 2009). A coach who actively engages in reflective practice is more likely to foster an environment of trust, motivation, and high performance. Reflective practice is not only a tool for personal and professional development but also a mechanism for enhancing athlete outcomes. When coaches consistently reflect on their actions, decisions, and interactions, they gain deeper insights into the effectiveness of their methods and the individual needs of their athletes.
The great educator Donald Shön, renowned for his research on reflective practice, stated that the capacity to reflect on action as to engage in a process of continuous learning is one of the defining characteristics of professional practice. Reflective practice can be divided into two key forms: reflection in action and reflection on action.
### Reflection In Action
Reflection in action occurs during the coaching process. It involves real-time critical thinking, allowing the coach to adapt and respond to situations as they unfold. For example, during a HYROX-specific circuit, a coach might notice an athlete struggling with their sled pull technique. The coach may question his or her initial methodology of developing this skill that translated in the athlete not adhering to movement efficiency or standards. Therefore, the coach finds an appropriate moment within the session to adapt their coaching style to help the athlete form a new and improved approach with the workout station. This in turn aids the athlete's performance and therefore prevents injury throughout the remaining moments of the session.
### Reflection On Action
Reflection on action takes place after the coaching session or competition has concluded. It involves reviewing what happened, analyzing the reasons behind success or failure, and planning improvements for future sessions. An example of this might be a coach reviewing quantitative data of a race or training session and realizing that their strategy for pacing didn't fulfill the athlete's potential, which led to a reduced overall performance. As a result, the coach and athlete decide to redesign how the athlete will adjust their intensity, ensuring a newly agreed pace is adhered to from the start to achieve greater outcomes in performance.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Reflection In Action & Reflection On Action
chunk.content:
Moreover, coaches who model a reflective mindset encourage athletes to do the same. When athletes are taught to reflect on their own training considering what went well, what could improve, and how they felt they begin to take greater ownership of their development. This fosters qualities like resilience, autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Over time, athletes become more engaged in the training process and more adaptable to setbacks. Ultimately, reflective practice is not an add-on to coaching, it is a core component of effective coaching pedagogy. By continually engaging in reflection, both during and after action, coaches can optimize athlete performance, enhance engagement, and cultivate a high-performance culture built on trust and continuous improvement.
---

chunk.content:
To truly harness the power of reflective practice, coaches must actively question their own methods and decisions. Reflection should not be a passive review but a critical and honest evaluation of both successes and setbacks. To deepen this process, consider asking yourself the following reflective questions:
### Coaching Questions
#### Reflection in Action
Used during coaching to adapt in real time.
1. What am I noticing about the athlete's body language or effort right now? 2. Is my current approach helping or hindering performance? 3. Do I need to intervene immediately, or would stepping back be more beneficial? 4. How can I rephrase my coaching cue to make it clearer or more impactful? 5. Are the athletes still engaged, or do I need to modify the task to re-focus them?
#### Reflection on Action
Used after coaching to review, evaluate, and improve future sessions.
1. What went well in the session, and why? 2. Were there any moments where I could have supported an athlete better? 3. How did my planning align with the actual execution? 4. What feedback did I give, and how was it received? 5. What will I change in my next session based on today's experience?
Finish.

unit.title: Coaching and the Growth Mindset
unit.unit_summary: This unit teaches coaches how a growth mindset shapes coaching quality in HYROX. It contrasts fixed and growth mindsets, explains why HYROX coaches must remain curious in a developing sport, lists behaviors of growth-minded coaches, identifies common fixed mindset traps, and gives strategies such as reflection logs, peer learning, curiosity, mentorship, celebrating failures, and using Schön's reflection-in/on-action framework. The media content adds Dr. Carol Dweck's growth mindset framework and a triathlon coaching case study showing how adaptability and athlete-centered communication improve

chunk.section_title: Audio: Growth Mindset vs Fixed Mindset in Coaching
chunk.content: [0:00:00] In the ever-evolving world of sport, especially in emerging competitive formats like HYROX, the mindset of the coach can significantly shape athlete outcomes. One of the most transformative frameworks to emerge in psychology and education, and now in sport, is the concept of the growth mindset. [0:00:18] Introduced by Dr. Carol Dweck, a Stanford University psychologist. Dweck's work distinguishes between a fixed and a growth mindset. The former assumes that abilities and intelligence are static, while the latter believes they can be developed through dedication and hard work. [0:00:35] Carol Dweck's research began in the educational field, where she discovered that students who believed their abilities could be developed, a growth mindset, were more likely to persevere in the face of challenges, respond positively to feedback, and ultimately achieve higher academic success. [0:00:52] This theory quickly gained traction in the fields of business and performance psychology, and has been widely applied in sports settings, including elite coaching environments. In sports, Dweck's theory has informed great athletes' development programs, talent ID pathways, and the ways coaches frame effort, success, and failure, [0:01:13] examples such as Michael Jordan embracing failures as learning opportunities. Jurgen Klopp provides effort-based praise on his team's cohesion. Simone Biles openly discusses how she focuses on learning and development rather than pure outcomes. [0:01:31] Finally, Barcelona's youth development program promotes effort and persistence in young athletes. It is particularly relevant in long-term athlete development, LTAD, where psychological resilience and adaptability are critical. [0:01:47] A growth mindset supports athletes in embracing setbacks, using failure as a learning tool, and pushing their perceived limits. However, the real power of the growth mindset lies not just in how it's applied to athletes, but in how coaches themselves adopt and embody it. [0:02:04] Let's take a closer look into coaching and the growth mindset in HYROX.

chunk.content: [0:00:00] I want to share one experience from my time working with British triathlon Paralympic athletes that really shaped the way that I think about coaching. Going [0:00:20] into those sessions I was very intentional about my approach. I used a lot of questioning techniques asking athletes what they thought about applications of a drill, how they felt during an interval or what adjustments they believed might improve performance. My aim was to elicit meaning to help [0:00:40] them apply their knowledge and check their understanding rather than simply telling them what to do. For some athletes this approach really clicked. They thrived when challenged to reflect. They enjoyed engaging with the reasoning [0:00:56] behind a session and I could see how it deepens their ownership of training itself. Their confidence grew as they started to make decisions independently which for elite athletes is crucial when competing under unpredictable conditions. [0:01:12] But not everyone responded that way. A few athletes became frustrated with constant questioning. They didn't want to spend extra mental energy breaking things down. They just wanted direct instructions. Tell me what to do and [0:01:28] I'll do it. For them my coaching style was actually getting in the way of performance in training. This was a pivotal moment for me. I realized that I had assumed that because questioning is a powerful tool in coaching it would automatically be effective with every athlete. But coaching isn't about applying [0:01:48] one good behavior universally. It's about recognizing the individual in front of you, their learning preferences, their mindset on the day and even their emotional state. So I began to adapt with some athletes. I continued to use [0:02:05] questioning as a way of empowering them. With others I shifted to a more directive style providing clear instructions when that's what they needed to perform at their best. And sometimes it was about moving between those two styles within the same session depending on the moment, depending on the [0:02:22] athlete. In other cases it was best to pose a scenario that the athlete had to respond to and together we discussed the experience to elicit solutions for future races. That one particular experience taught me one of the most valuable lessons of my coaching career. Adaptability is key. It's not about [0:02:42] coach showcasing a particular style. It's about meeting athletes where they are and creating the conditions that allow them to succeed. Looking back I am grateful for those moments of frustration because they forced me to reflect and grow and ultimately they made me a more flexible, responsive and [0:03:00] athlete-centered coach. For coaches doing the HYROX Level 2 course I encourage you to to also be reflective and discover what growth mindset can do for your personal development. With the athletes you work with it is important to identify what coaching behaviors they are most receptive to and other [0:03:20] behaviors that they are ineffective with. Take a moment now to reflect and continue deepening your awareness of your coaching.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: Growth Mindset vs Fixed Mindset in Coaching
chunk.content:
### Full Transcript Text
In the ever-evolving world of sport, especially in emerging competitive formats like HYROX, the mindset of the coach can significantly shape athlete outcomes. One of the most transformative frameworks to emerge in psychology and education, and now in sport, is the concept of the growth mindset. Introduced by Dr. Carol Dweck, a Stanford University psychologist. Dweck's work distinguishes between a fixed and a growth mindset. The former assumes that abilities and intelligence are static, while the latter believes they can be developed through dedication and hard work. Carol Dweck's research began in the educational field, where she discovered that students who believed their abilities could be developed, a growth mindset, were more likely to persevere in the face of challenges, respond positively to feedback, and ultimately achieve higher academic success. This theory quickly gained traction in the fields of business and performance psychology, and has been widely applied in sports settings, including elite coaching environments. In sports, Dweck's theory has informed great athletes' development programs, talent ID pathways, and the ways coaches frame effort, success, and failure, examples such as Michael Jordan embracing failures as learning opportunities. Jurgen Klopp provides effort-based praise on his team's cohesion. Simone Biles openly discusses how she focuses on learning and development rather than pure outcomes. Finally, Barcelona's youth development program promotes effort and persistence in young athletes. It is particularly relevant in long-term athlete development, LTAD, where psychological resilience and adaptability are critical. A growth mindset supports athletes in embracing setbacks, using failure as a learning tool, and pushing their perceived limits. However, the real power of the growth mindset lies not just in how it's applied to athletes, but in how coaches themselves adopt and embody it. Let's take a closer look into coaching and the growth mindset in HYROX.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: Growth Mindset vs Fixed Mindset in Coaching
chunk.content: I want to share one experience from my time working with British triathlon Paralympic athletes that really shaped the way that I think about coaching. Going into those sessions I was very intentional about my approach. I used a lot of questioning techniques asking athletes what they thought about applications of a drill, how they felt during an interval or what adjustments they believed might improve performance. My aim was to elicit meaning to help them apply their knowledge and check their understanding rather than simply telling them what to do. For some athletes this approach really clicked. They thrived when challenged to reflect. They enjoyed engaging with the reasoning behind a session and I could see how it deepens their ownership of training itself. Their confidence grew as they started to make decisions independently which for elite athletes is crucial when competing under unpredictable conditions. But not everyone responded that way. A few athletes became frustrated with constant questioning. They didn't want to spend extra mental energy breaking things down. They just wanted direct instructions. Tell me what to do and I'll do it. For them my coaching style was actually getting in the way of performance in training. This was a pivotal moment for me. I realized that I had assumed that because questioning is a powerful tool in coaching it would automatically be effective with every athlete. But coaching isn't about applying one good behavior universally. It's about recognizing the individual in front of you, their learning preferences, their mindset on the day and even their emotional state. So I began to adapt with some athletes. I continued to use questioning as a way of empowering them. With others I shifted to a more directive style providing clear instructions when that's what they needed to perform at their best. And sometimes it was about moving between those two styles within the same session depending on the moment, depending on the athlete. In other cases it was best to pose a scenario that the athlete had to respond to and together we discussed the experience to elicit solutions for future races. That one particular experience taught me one of the most valuable lessons of my coaching career. Adaptability is key. It's not about coach showcasing a particular style. It's about meeting athletes where they are and creating the conditions that allow them to succeed. Looking back I am grateful for those moments of frustration because they forced me to reflect and grow and ultimately they made me a more flexible, responsive and athlete-centered coach. For coaches doing the HYROX Level 2 course I encourage you to to also be reflective and discover what growth mindset can do for your personal development. With the athletes you work with it is important to identify what coaching behaviors they are most receptive to and other behaviors that they are ineffective with. Take a moment now to reflect and continue deepening your awareness of your coaching.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Coaching and the Growth Mindset
chunk.content:
Coaching is no longer simply about technical delivery or planning sessions. It requires ongoing reflection, critical thinking, evidence-based decision-making, and the ability to adapt to new research, methodologies, and athlete needs. Adopting a growth mindset empowers coaches to continuously evolve, challenge their assumptions, and embrace lifelong learning.
### Coaches with a growth mindset are more likely to
- Seek feedback from peers and athletes. - Reflect on their coaching decisions and outcomes. - Adapt and trial new strategies or interventions. - Stay informed of evolving research in sport science. - Foster a psychologically safe environment where failure is part of learning.
In contrast, a fixed mindset in coaching may manifest in subtle yet detrimental ways: rigid session plans, reluctance to adjust methods, defensiveness toward feedback, or assumptions that "some athletes just don't have what it takes."
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 03: Growth Mindset and HYROX Coach Development
chunk.content:
HYROX, as a relatively new and growing sport, has a relatively new research base. Key performance indicators, biomechanical analysis of movements, physiological profiling, training periodization models, nutrition strategies, and specific recovery protocols are still being explored. This landscape requires coaches to embrace a growth mindset more than ever! Unlike established sports with decades of scientific literature and governing body frameworks, HYROX coaching is being shaped in real-time.
### Coaches who adopt a growth mindset will thrive in this environment by
- Viewing the current lack of evidence as an opportunity to experiment and contribute. - Reflecting consistently on what is working with their athletes and why. - Staying curious and collaborating with physiologists, nutritionists, sport medics, and biomechanics experts as new data emerges. - Adapting training approaches to suit diverse athletes across age groups, fitness backgrounds, and physiological profiles.
Critically, growth-minded coaches will accept that they don't have all the answers yet, and that's okay! What matters is a relentless commitment to getting better, staying reflective, and evolving alongside the sport.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 04: Characteristics of a Growth Mindset in Coaching
chunk.content:
A growth-minded coach is defined by behaviors and attitudes such as:
1. **Curiosity:** They ask questions and seek to understand "why" behind methods. 2. **Resilience:** They bounce back from unsuccessful sessions or seasons. 3. **Reflection:** They view each coaching interaction and intervention as a learning opportunity. 4. **Feedback Seeking:** They welcome athlete, peer, and mentor feedback-even when uncomfortable. 5. **Innovation:** They trial new ideas, monitor impact, and adjust without ego. 6. **Development Focused:** They prioritize long-term athlete development over short-term wins.
Consider which of these areas you as a coach already embody and which ones you may look to apply within your upcoming coaching interactions/interventions.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: Common Fixed Mindset Traps in Coaching and How to Avoid Them
chunk.content:
Even experienced coaches can fall into fixed mindset traps, often without realizing it. These are some examples of a few to watch out for:
| Fixed Mindset Trap | Growth-Oriented Response | | "They're just not talented enough." | Avoid this by focusing on effort, adaptation, and individualized programming. | | "This is how I've always coached." | Challenge this with Continuing Professional Development (CPD), reflection, and evidence-based practices. | | "My athletes aren't improving because they're not motivated." | Flip this by reflecting on your motivational climate and feedback style. | | "If I change my approach, I'll look unsure." | Realize that adaptability is a strength, not a weakness. | | "I can't keep up with all the new research." | Engage with digestible, applied resources and connect with professionals from related fields. |
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 06: Essential Strategies to Cultivate a Growth-Oriented Approach
chunk.content:
For HYROX coaches specifically, creating a growth mindset can be developed through deliberate strategies:
### Weekly Reflection Logs
Reflect on coaching decisions, session outcomes, and athlete responses.
### Peer Learning Circles
Create regular check-ins with other coaches to share learnings and challenges.
### Stay Curious
Set a goal to read one new study, podcast, or case report relevant to performance coaching each week.
### Mentorship
Seek out coaches in other disciplines (e.g., triathlon, CrossFit, rowing) and explore transferable insights.
### Celebrate "Failures"
Normalize and share things that didn't work-model this transparency for athletes.
### Use Reflective Practice Frameworks
Schön's Reflection-in/on-Action framework.
### Media Reference
- Video: Video media from this unit.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: Training for HYROX Promotes Disease Prevention and Longevity
chunk.content:
HYROX, at its core, blends endurance running with functional strength movements. This hybrid style of training also aligns closely with evidence-based practices for disease prevention and long-term health. The balance of aerobic and resistance training required for HYROX uniquely promotes adaptations across multiple physiological systems, making it a powerful model for improving both length and quality of life. While other forms of fitness or competition can create adaptations to promote health, HYROX is presented as especially strong in its ability to promote a balanced training style to improve health and longevity.
### How HYROX Training Promotes Longevity - Cardiovascular Fitness and Muscular Health
Aerobic exercise is well established in the literature as a primary protective factor against cardiovascular disease by improving high blood pressure, preventing arterial stiffness, and lowering resting heart rate (Booth et al., 2012). These adaptations lower the risk of coronary heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes.
A high VO₂ max is considered by many in the medical community to be the strongest predictor of longevity. Research shows that individuals with higher VO₂ max have significantly lower risks of all-cause mortality. This correlation is likely due to improved cardiovascular efficiency, enhanced mitochondrial function, and better metabolic regulation, all of which protect against chronic disease and promote healthy aging.
An equally important predictor of longevity and health is muscle mass and strength. The strength components of HYROX training can help build and maintain muscle mass and bone mineral density. Bone mineral density and muscle mass are best measured with a DEXA scan. These metrics become increasingly important for the aging athlete. Research shows that low muscle mass, also called sarcopenia, and reduced strength, particularly grip strength, are strongly associated with higher all-cause mortality.
Longevity experts frequently use grip strength as a marker for functional strength. As a recommended goal for health and longevity, not necessarily for HYROX performance, male individuals should be able to perform a farmer's carry with their own body weight divided across each hand for one minute. For example, an 80 kg male should be able to carry 40 kg in each hand for one minute. Females should target 75% of their body weight. Individuals who are able to complete this task have been shown to have improved lifespan and healthspan.
> To summarize, cardiovascular fitness, as measured by VO₂ max, and muscular strength are the two strongest predictors for longevity.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: How HYROX Training Improves Health and Prevents Disease
chunk.content:
As a coach, you understand how HYROX training can improve both functional strength and endurance for athletes. Beyond this, adapting a hybrid fitness program has been shown to be one of the most effective ways to improve overall health, both metabolic and mental, and protect against chronic diseases.
### Metabolic Health
Metabolic health benefits from a hybrid fitness approach. Metabolic health refers to one's ability to process and utilize food, thus maintaining healthy blood markers and body composition. It is characterized by optimizing the body's responses to food, avoiding unhealthy spikes in blood sugar, and reducing inflammation. Being metabolically healthy lowers the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and obesity.
Both endurance and strength training have been shown repeatedly to improve metabolic health and should be a key component of any individual's effort to improve it. Studies have shown that alternating between high-intensity efforts and strength tasks, as frequently done in HYROX training, improves insulin sensitivity and glucose regulation. This not only supports healthy body composition but also reduces the prevalence of metabolic syndrome, a key driver of chronic disease.
### Gaining Insight
To spark creativity, feed your brain material like you are cramming for a tough test. Then stop thinking about the problem you want to solve. Go surfing or take a leisurely walk. Research shows that letting your mind wander fosters creativity.
It is also found that meditation helps you spot and solve problems in creative ways. It promotes divergent thinking that gets novel ideas flowing. According to these studies, meditation also makes you more open to considering new solutions. Time to breathe.
Mental health outcomes also can improve via a hybrid training program. Similar to metabolic health, countless studies have shown the positive effect of exercise on improving mental health. Many studies have shown exercise to be more powerful than pharmaceuticals for improving neurologic and emotional health.
Specific to HYROX-style training sessions, exercise incorporating both physical exertion and skill-based challenges has been associated with improved cognitive function and reduced risk of neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.
Furthermore, the stress-reducing and mood-elevating effects of regular training contribute to mental well-being, a recognized factor in overall health outcomes.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 03: How HYROX Can Impact Global Health
chunk.content:
As HYROX continues to grow globally, more individuals are improving their health and fitness. HYROX is unique in the way that it enables all kinds of people to pursue fitness regardless of their experience with exercise. Training for and competing in HYROX often lays a foundation and establishes habits that can lead to a lifelong pursuit of healthy living. When extrapolated, HYROX is positioned as having the potential to make significant changes in global health outcomes.
Longevity experts and public health researchers have made estimates on what the global impact would be if the entire world engaged in regular strength and endurance training. The result would be unprecedented reductions in chronic disease and significant increases in global life expectancy. Such improvements would also lead to massive reductions in healthcare spending.
Highlights include:
- Analyses suggest that up to 5 million deaths per year could be avoided if the global population was meeting standard international physical activity recommendations. - Evidence supports that meeting the recommended aerobic exercise amounts is associated with somewhere between 20-30% reductions in all-cause mortality. - Regular resistance training also provides up to 25-30% lower mortality. - Multiple global analyses estimate that lack of physical activity directly costs the global health system between $27 and $54 billion USD.
As a coach, it is important to realize that the vast majority of these health benefits occur when individuals make the change from no activity to minimal activity. Therefore, it is important to gradually progress athletes from wherever they are starting. What may seem insignificant to an experienced athlete can literally be life changing for someone at the start of their fitness journey.
> HYROX training is more than preparing for competition. It also serves as a comprehensive, evidence-based training model that incorporates the primary pillars of disease prevention-cardiovascular fitness, musculoskeletal strength, metabolic regulation, and cognitive health. By targeting these systems simultaneously, HYROX helps individuals create a fitness foundation that will allow them to maintain independence, functionality, and vitality across the lifespan.
As a HYROX coach, you play a powerful role in helping athletes improve their health and longevity.

unit.title: Understanding Sports Injuries & Medical Red Flags & Referral Process
unit.unit_summary:
As a coach, it is important to understand the difference between an acute injury and a chronic (overuse) injury. ### Acute Injury
An acute injury happens suddenly, often due to a specific incident or trauma. #### Running Example
An athlete twists their ankle during an outdoor run when stepping on uneven pavement. The injury is immediate, with sharp pain and swelling right away.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: Acute vs. Chronic Injuries in HYROX
chunk.content:
As a coach, it is important to understand the difference between an acute injury and a chronic (overuse) injury.
### Acute Injury
An acute injury happens suddenly, often due to a specific incident or trauma.
#### Running Example
An athlete twists their ankle during an outdoor run when stepping on uneven pavement. The injury is immediate, with sharp pain and swelling right away. This could be a sprained ankle, muscle strain, or even a fracture.
#### Strength Training Example
An athlete is attempting a new personal best in the deadlift. Mid-lift, they feel a sharp snap in their lower back. This could be a lower back strain or herniated disc. The injury is immediate, painful, and clearly linked to that specific lift.
#### Other acute examples
- Tearing a bicep during a heavy deadlift - Achilles strain while training heavy sled push - Quad strain during a squat
### Chronic Injury
A chronic injury develops over time due to repetitive stress, overuse, or poor training habits.
#### Running Example
A marathon runner starts to feel persistent knee pain after months of training. This could be runner's knee (patellofemoral pain syndrome) or another type of tendinitis. There's no clear moment when it started - it just got progressively more painful.
#### Strength Training Example
A powerlifter trains heavy squats 4 days a week with minimal rest and mobility work. Over time, they start to feel a dull, aching pain in their knees. This is likely a case of patellar tendinitis (jumper's knee) - a classic overuse injury that worsens gradually.
#### Other chronic examples
- Elbow tendinitis from high volume on the SkiErgg - Plantar fasciitis from increasing running mileage too quickly - Lower back tightness from months of high-volume deadlifts
### Key Difference
- Acute = sudden and traumatic - Chronic = gradual and overuse-related
Acute injuries generally require prompt evaluation by a sports medicine physician or orthopedic surgeon. These types of injuries necessitate medical imaging (x-rays, ultrasound, or MRI) to obtain a diagnosis or rule out the need for surgical intervention.
Chronic injuries do not necessarily require urgent evaluation by a medical provider. Medical imaging is typically less useful for these types of injuries. The mainstay of treatment for chronic injuries is rest and adjustments to training regimens.
As a HYROX coach, you will mostly work with athletes that are dealing with chronic or overuse injuries, but it remains crucial to recognize and be familiar with acute injuries so you can help the athlete take the proper steps toward recovery.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Acute Injuries During HYROX Competition
chunk.content:
A recent survey-based research study was done to help characterize injuries and presentation to medical staff during HYROX competition. Here is a summary of the project:
### Methods
Surveys were conducted at a HYROX event in Anaheim, California, in December 2024. Participants presenting to on-site medical staff were surveyed. The survey included questions about demographics, training history, and injury details. Inclusion criteria required injuries directly related to HYROX participation.
### Results
Among the 3,784 contestants, 89 (2.4%) presented on-site medical care during the event. Of the 42 participants surveyed, 27 (64.3%) were male, with an average age of 38.5 years (range 26-60) and an average BMI of 27.6. Most injuries (78.6%) occurred during running, with 40 participants (95.2%) reporting lower extremity injuries, particularly calf/shin injuries (61.9%). Only 1 athlete presented with an acute traumatic injury (hand/finger injury). Cramping or electrolyte imbalance was the most commonly cited cause of injury (59.5%), followed by inadequate preparation (9.5%). Burpee broad jumps and sled pull resulted in more injuries than the other exercise stations. Eighty-eight percent of participants trained for the event. The average weekly training time was 6.0 hours, with 1.9 hours dedicated to running.
### Conclusion
Running-related musculoskeletal complaints, particularly in the calves and shins, were the most common reason HYROX participants sought medical attention.
### Summary
HYROX competitions are overall very safe and injury rates are low. Most athletes present to medical staff due to cramping concerns. Muscle cramping is not a true "injury", but rather due to a combination of inadequate training, fueling, and hydration.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 03: Acute Injuries During Training for HYROX
chunk.content:
Risk of acute injury during training for HYROX will be directly related to the type of training the athlete performs. As a coach, you play perhaps the most important role in helping reduce this risk. This is done by programming safe exercises that are not beyond the abilities or skill set of your athletes.
In general, exercises with heavy loads, high speeds, or explosive movements will increase the risk for an ACUTE injury. Examples of acute injuries that could occur during training for HYROX:
- Ankle sprain while running, especially on uneven surfaces - Pectoralis rupture during heavy bench press - Crashing while cycling for aerobic development - Hamstring strain during burpee broad jumps
For example, if you program olympic lifts for an athlete that does not have experience with these movements, this will dramatically increase the likelihood of an acute injury. Even if you feel this athlete would benefit from incorporating more explosive movements, it may not be worth the increased injury risk. It would be prudent to find safer alternatives that will generate the same stimulus while keeping injury risk low.
- Repeat chronic vs acute injuries - Usually we focus on overuse injuries, but acute injuries are truly devastating and often require surgery or significant time away from training
The exercises specific to a HYROX competition would generally be considered low impact. Despite the heavy load of a sled push or sled pull, when done properly, these exercises pose a relatively low injury risk. HYROX stations that include high volume or impact exercises like burpee broad jumps, walking lunges, and wall balls have relatively light weight loads, thus decreasing the risk for injury when practiced during training.
However, it is still crucial that you help all athletes develop proper form when performing these exercises. This will not only reduce their risk of acute injury, but improve their performance by making them more efficient in those movements.
HYROX movements are overall low risk, but you still need good form. It is also very important to understand that there is some inherent risk with any form of exercise. Injury risk varies depending on how the exercises are implemented. For example, doing high repetition sets of burpee broad jumps with the goal of maximizing jump distance would be higher risk due to the greater eccentric impact associated with a more explosive jump and landing. Similarly, overloading the weight on a sled push may place an athlete's tendons or ligaments under excessive stress leading to a potential acute soft tissue injury.
- Its all about risk reduction - Things like activation, warm up - Athlete age can be important - Err on the side of being safe
---

In general, exercises with heavy loads, high speeds, or explosive movements will increase the risk for an ACUTE injury.

chunk.content:
As a coach, you will surely encounter all kinds of different "aches and pains" from your athletes. Although it is not your role to diagnose, it is helpful to be familiar with the most common types of overuse injuries.
The vast majority of overuse injuries you will encounter working with athletes will come from running. Below is a table highlighting some of the most common overuse injuries caused by running.
| Injury | Primary Structures Involved | Key Symptoms | Common Contributing Factors | | Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome (Runner's Knee) | Patellofemoral joint, surrounding soft tissues | Anterior knee pain, worse with stairs, squatting, or prolonged sitting | Poor hip/glute control, overstriding, weak quadriceps, training errors | | Iliotibial Band Syndrome (ITBS) | Iliotibial band, lateral femoral condyle | Sharp lateral knee pain, especially after longer runs | Hip abductor weakness, excessive downhill running, rapid mileage increase | | Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome (Shin Splints) | Medial tibia, posterior tibialis muscle | Diffuse pain along medial shin during or after runs | Sudden mileage or intensity increase, overpronation, inadequate footwear | | Achilles Tendinopathy | Achilles tendon | Pain/stiffness in posterior heel or calf, worse in mornings or with push-off | Calf tightness, rapid training progression, poor eccentric strength | | Plantar Fasciitis | Plantar fascia at heel | Heel pain, worst with first steps in morning or after rest | Overpronation, weak foot intrinsics, high mileage on hard surfaces | | Hamstring Tendinopathy | Proximal hamstring tendon (ischial tuberosity) | Deep buttock pain with running, sitting, or uphill work | Weak glutes, poor pelvic stability, overstriding | | Stress Fractures | Tibia, metatarsals, femoral neck most common | Localized pain, worsens with loading, may persist at rest | Energy deficiency (RED-S), repetitive high loads, inadequate recovery, low BMD |
As with running, sudden or rapid increases in volume with any sort of repetitive movement will place the body at risk of injury, even if the activity is considered "low impact", as with the Ski and Row Erg.
Overuse injuries from the SkiErgg typically involve the shoulder, elbows, and low back. Injuries such as rotator cuff tendinopathy, shoulder impingement, medial or lateral epicondylitis (elbow), or lumbar back strain are the most likely to be encountered.
Overuse injuries from the row erg include lumbar strain, quadriceps tendinopathy, hamstring tendinopathy, and medial or lateral epicondylitis (elbow).

chunk.content:
As with any form of overuse injury, it is imperative to guide an athlete by referring back to the three pillars of injury prevention-training, recovery, and prevention. When pain is encountered, it is a sign that the training stimulus to the musculoskeletal system is greater than its ability to recover. In these circumstances, athletes should alter their training to allow their body to adequately recover.
Building training plans that gradually increase volume, even for low-impact activities, is the most important way to keep your athletes healthy in training.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: Injury Red Flags: When to Seek Medical Attention
chunk.content:
When should you recommend an athlete seek medical attention?
### Acute Injuries
If an athlete experiences an acute injury, it is recommended that they seek medical attention promptly. Signs and symptoms from an acute injury that would require more urgent medical evaluation include the following:
- Hearing a loud "pop" - Inability to bear weight - Rapid severe swelling or bruising - Suspected fracture or dislocation - New and severe numbness, tingling, weakness in the extremities that does not resolve
In addition to the acute musculoskeletal complaints listed above, it is important to know red flags that can present from other body systems.
### Cardiovascular & Respiratory
- Chest pain, pressure, or tightness, especially if radiating to arm, jaw, or back - Unexplained shortness of breath out of proportion to exertion - Palpitations, sudden rapid or irregular heartbeat, with lightheadedness - Syncope or near-syncope, fainting or almost fainting during or after exertion - Cyanosis, bluish lips or fingertips
### Neurological
- Sudden severe headache, "worst headache of life" - Confusion, disorientation, or unusual behavior - Seizure activity - Sudden weakness, numbness, vision changes, or difficulty speaking - Loss of consciousness - Heat-Related / Environmental, to be covered in more detail in next section
### Other Serious Concerns
- Persistent abdominal pain - Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)-swelling of face/tongue, difficulty breathing, hives, dizziness - Uncontrolled bleeding despite pressure
In short, any sudden onset of chest pain, breathing difficulty, neurological symptoms, heat illness, severe injury, or altered mental status should trigger immediate removal from activity and prompt medical evaluation. If you witness any individual collapse, lose consciousness and/or become unresponsive, you should contact emergency services immediately and follow your affiliation's procedures for AED and CPR.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 06: When should an athlete seek medical attention for a chronic or overuse injury?
chunk.content:
An athlete should seek medical attention for an overuse injury if they experience any of the following signs or symptoms:
### Persistent Pain
If the pain doesn't go away after rest or worsens with training. Persistent pain can indicate that the body isn't healing on its own and professional intervention may be necessary.
### Pain That Affects Form
If the pain alters the way you run, lift, or move (for example, changing your stride or posture to avoid pain), it could lead to further injuries.
### Swelling or Bruising
Visible swelling or bruising around a joint or muscle after running could signal a more significant injury, such as tendon or ligament damage.
### Sharp or Acute Pain
While overuse injuries tend to develop gradually, sudden sharp or stabbing pain during training is a red flag. This might indicate a more serious issue, such as a stress fracture or a severe muscle tear.
### Limited Range of Motion or Weakness
Difficulty moving the affected joint or muscle normally, or experiencing weakness, is a sign that an injury may have affected the function of muscles, tendons, or ligaments.
### Pain That Doesn't Improve With Rest
If the injury continues to cause pain or discomfort even after several days of rest, ice, and elevation, it may be time to consult a doctor. Overuse injuries that don't improve with basic self-care may require physical therapy, imaging (like X-rays or MRIs), or other interventions.
### Inability to Bear Weight or Walk Normally
If the pain is severe enough to prevent you from walking or bearing weight on the affected leg or foot, it's important to seek medical care.
### Numbness or Tingling
If you experience numbness, tingling, or a "pins and needles" sensation in the affected area, it could indicate nerve involvement, which requires medical evaluation to rule out nerve damage or compression.
### Difficulty Sleeping Due to Pain
If the pain from the injury is interfering with your ability to sleep, this is a sign the injury may be severe or not healing properly, and it's worth getting checked by a medical professional.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 07: Dealing With Heat: Training, Competing, and Red Flags
chunk.content:
Coaches need to understand the implications and potential consequences of training and competing in harsh conditions. Although HYROX events are typically held indoors, venue temperatures and humidity levels can become high enough that athletes may start experiencing signs of exertional heat illness. Understanding how heat impacts exercise is also important as you help your athletes train during warm weather.
### Exertional Heat Illnesses
As a coach, you should have a basic understanding of the medical manifestations caused by heat during training and competition. It is crucial to be able to recognize when an athlete may be experiencing heat stress and know when to escalate the incident to a medical professional.
> Any athlete who collapses or has mental status changes should undergo prompt evaluation by a medical professional!
Exertional heat illness includes a broad spectrum of injuries related to heat gains exceeding heat loss.
#### Exertional heat exhaustion
- How it presents: Inability to continue activity due to heat stress with profuse body sweat, nausea, and vomiting without neurologic or mental status changes - Cause: Widespread peripheral vascular dilation - Diagnosis (for reference only): Core temperature of less than 39°C (102.2°F) and an absence of neurologic dysfunction - Treatment: body cooling, oral rehydration, continued rest and monitoring until symptoms improve
#### Exertional heat stroke
- Overview: A rare, but potentially life threatening, medical emergency that results from failure of the heat-regulation mechanisms of the body that can cause end-organ damage - How it presents: Severe hyperthermia (core temperature > 40°C or 102.2°F). Athletes may present, though not always, with dry skin and the absence of sweat. However, the defining feature of heat stroke is the presence of neurologic or mental status changes from baseline. - If an athlete seems overheated and acts confused, altered, or is unresponsive - Treatment (on-site): Immediate whole-body cooling, ideally via cold water immersion, and immediate activation of local emergency response protocols
### Electrolyte imbalances
As athletes sweat, they lose both water and salt. The rate at which athletes lose sweat is highly variable and depends both on physiologic and environmental factors. Sweat rates can range from 0.5 to 2.5 L per hour, and sodium losses can range from 500mg to 6000mg per hour. Helping athletes identify their sweat rates and sodium loss during training in different environments is key to helping them optimize hydration, fueling, and recovery strategies.
Below are two examples of sweat and electrolyte associated conditions that are more likely to occur when training or competing in warm environments.
#### Exercise associated muscle cramps

chunk.content:
- Painful skeletal muscle spasm secondary to electrolyte imbalance - Affected muscles can be random, individual spasms usually lasts 1-3min - Treatment is stretching and oral rehydration with NaCl supplementation - This is the most common presenting complaint at the medical tent during HYROX competitions
#### Exercise associated hyponatremia
- A rare, but potentially life threatening condition caused by severe drop in serum sodium levels (<135 mg/dl) and mental status change - Caused by prolonged ingestion of fluid (water) without electrolyte replenishment - Usually presents after long endurance exercise bouts > 3 hours - Presents with mental status change, numbness and tingling, and extremity swelling - If suspected, contact emergency services
#### Exertional associated collapse
- Collapse of a conscious athlete with or without syncope after completion of an exercise - Caused by decreased blood flow back to the heart at the end of an exercise - Most common condition seen in a marathon medical tent and commonly seen at HYROX competitions - Athletes should remain flat, elevate legs, and begin oral hydration
#### Exertional rhabdomyolysis
- Acute condition of muscle destruction which leads to breakdown product leakage into the bloodstream - Presents with muscle pain, weakness and dark or brown urine (myoglobinuria) - If suspected, requires urgent medical evaluation

chunk.content:
### Heat acclimatization
Heat training should be thought of like any other training stimulus. New stimuli should be introduced gradually and progressively. Training bouts should be modified in high-risk environments. Coaches should generally avoid hosting or scripting high intensity or long duration workouts in dangerous conditions.
One concept to be familiar with is wet bulb temperature. This is the gold standard for assessing when heat or humidity reach dangerous levels for training. To obtain wet bulb temperature, read off a thermometer wrapped in a wet cloth (starting temperature of the cloth does not matter).
General recommendations for wet bulb temperature:
- 82 - 86 degrees: athletes should have a 1:1 practice to rest ratio - > 86 degrees: training or competition should be postponed
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 09: Collaboration With Sports Medicine Professionals
chunk.content:
### How does my role fit into the multidisciplinary approach of sports medicine for HYROX?
As a HYROX coach, you will NOT diagnose or treat injuries like medical professionals in sports medicine. Although you will not provide formal diagnoses or treatments for sports injuries, you will often act as the first line of help for an injured or at-risk athlete. Occasionally, it is appropriate for you to recommend a period of rest or alter a training program when an athlete experiences pain or a minor injury.
For example, if an athlete mentions she is experiencing some new soreness or mild pain in her foot after an intense running workout, you can recommend she take a couple days off running and replace running workouts with a form of non-impact cardio (cycling, ergs, swimming, etc.). These situations require close follow up and communication with your athletes as you adjust their training to prevent an injury from progressing.
### Collaboration with Sports Medicine Professionals
In a professional sports setting, a sports medicine team includes multiple personnel that work together to help athletes diagnose, treat, and rehabilitate from their injuries. This includes physicians, physical therapists, kinesthesiologists, performance coaches, athletic trainers, and others.
For most HYROX athletes, having a formally organized team of sports medicine professionals that meet and communicate regularly is not a reality. However, the principles of collaboration still apply.
One way you can contribute to the rehabilitation process is by providing detailed documentation via a training log. Athletes can share this information with their medical team, providing objective data from which they can give specific rehabilitation recommendations.
### Additional Structured Unit Content
Acute vs. Chronic Injuries in HYROX Acute Injuries During HYROX Competition Acute Injuries During Training for HYROX Common Overuse Injuries Injury Red Flags: When to Seek Medical Attention When should an athlete seek medical attention for a chronic or overuse injury? Dealing With Heat: Training, Competing, and Red Flags Prevention Collaboration With Sports Medicine Professionals Level 2 - Module 2 - 3. Understanding Sports Injuries & Medical Red Flags & Referral Process
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: Anti-Doping and Clean Sport in HYROX: Protecting Health, Performance, and Integrity
chunk.content:
HYROX has grown from 650 competitors in Hamburg in 2018 to more than 900,000 participants across five continents in 2025, supported by over 15,000 affiliate gyms. HYROX has gone from a fitness format to a genuine sport - one with Olympic aspirations and a defining promise: HYROX is a sport for everybody.
> That growth changes things. As HYROX professionalizes, the anti-doping standards that govern Olympic sport increasingly apply to us. Testing at major events, registered testing pools for elite athletes, and partnerships with national anti-doping organizations are already in place and taking shape.
For coaches, this is not abstract. Coaches sit at the frontline. They are technical experts, but also mentors and guardians of the sport's values. The culture built now, while HYROX is still young, will define its character for decades.
This module gives coaches the knowledge to protect athletes and help shape a sport whose achievements are authentic.
---

key_facts.fact: HYROX has grown from 650 competitors in Hamburg in 2018 to more than 900,000 participants across five continents in 2025, supported by over 15,000 affiliate gyms.
HYROX has gone from a fitness format to a genuine sport - one with Olympic aspirations and a defining promise: HYROX is a sport for everybody.
As HYROX professionalizes, the anti-doping standards that govern Olympic sport increasingly apply to us.
Testing at major events, registered testing pools for elite athletes, and partnerships with national anti-doping organizations are already in place and taking shape.
They are technical experts, but also mentors and guardians of the sport's values.
The culture built now, while HYROX is still young, will define its character for decades.
This module gives coaches the knowledge to protect athletes and help shape a sport whose achievements are authentic.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Not only an elite issue: PEDs in recreational and fitness sport
chunk.content:
It would be a mistake to think of doping as something that only concerns high-performance athletes, the Olympic Games, or formal doping tests. The reality is that the same performance-enhancing substances - anabolic steroids, SARMs, growth hormone, stimulants, "testosterone boosters" and fat burners - are widely used in recreational and fitness settings, commercial gyms, and the broader physique-and-aesthetics culture from which many HYROX participants come.
For most people in these settings there is no testing pool, no Doping Control Officer, and no risk of a four-year ban. But the absence of a test does not make these substances safe.
The health risks are not contingent on whether someone competes at a World Championship or simply trains for personal goals. The risks are inherent to the substances themselves. When these preparations are taken without medical supervision and without a genuine medical indication, they can be seriously harmful, carrying the same cardiovascular, hormonal, hepatic, renal and psychological consequences described later in this module, regardless of training level.
A recreational athlete or fitness client who self-administers these substances is exposed to the same dangers as an elite competitor, often with less monitoring, lower-quality products from unregulated sources, and poorer information.
> For these reasons, it can never be a HYROX coach's goal to gamble with the health of their athletes and clients by tolerating, encouraging or facilitating the use of such performance-enhancing substances.
The coach's responsibility is to protect the people who train with them, not to put them at risk in pursuit of faster times or a particular physique. At the same time, the coach carries a clear moral obligation to educate: to inform athletes and clients honestly about the role these substances play, how they work, and what their real effects and consequences are.
In the recreational and fitness world, misinformation is everywhere and access is easy. An informed, values-based conversation from a trusted coach is often the single most powerful protection a client has. Clean sport is not only a rule for the elite; it is a standard of care for everyone coaches work with.
---

key_facts.fact: It would be a mistake to think of doping as something that only concerns high-performance athletes, the Olympic Games, or formal doping tests.

The reality is that the same performance-enhancing substances - anabolic steroids, SARMs, growth hormone, stimulants, "testosterone boosters" and fat burners - are widely used in recreational and fitness settings, commercial gyms, and the broader phy
For most people in these settings there is no testing pool, no Doping Control Officer, and no risk of a four-year ban.
But the absence of a test does not make these substances safe.
The health risks are not contingent on whether someone competes at a World Championship or simply trains for personal goals.

When these preparations are taken without medical supervision and without a genuine medical indication, they can be seriously harmful, carrying the same cardiovascular, hormonal, hepatic, renal and psychological consequences described later in this m

A recreational athlete or fitness client who self-administers these substances is exposed to the same dangers as an elite competitor, often with less monitoring, lower-quality products from unregulated sources, and poorer information.

> For these reasons, it can never be a HYROX coach's goal to gamble with the health of their athletes and clients by tolerating, encouraging or facilitating the use of such performance-enhancing substances.
The coach's responsibility is to protect the people who train with them, not to put them at risk in pursuit of faster times or a particular physique.

At the same time, the coach carries a clear moral obligation to educate: to inform athletes and clients honestly about the role these substances play, how they work, and what their real effects and consequences are.

chunk.content:
The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) defines doping as the use of prohibited substances or methods to artificially enhance performance, but the definition is deliberately broader than that. It also covers possessing prohibited substances, trafficking them, administering them, refusing or evading testing, and tampering with the doping control process.
At its core, doping violates sport's essential premise: that competition tests natural human capability, enhanced only by training, nutrition, preparation and legitimate recovery.
HYROX is a hybrid sport - eight kilometers of running plus eight functional stations - so almost every category of performance-enhancing drug can seem tempting to someone.
### Performance-enhancing drug categories relevant to HYROX
- **Anabolic agents (steroids):** Synthetic derivatives of testosterone, such as stanozolol, nandrolone, and designer steroids like THG. They build muscle and speed recovery. Their appeal for HYROX is linked to strength stations such as sled push, sled pull and farmers carry, and the ability to train harder and more often. - **Peptide hormones and growth factors:** EPO stimulates red blood cell production, raising oxygen-carrying capacity and endurance, which is relevant to running. HGH and IGF-1 promote muscle growth and recovery and are hard to detect. - **Stimulants:** Amphetamines and similar substances increase alertness and reduce perceived fatigue across a 60-90 minute race. They are prohibited in competition and are a common hidden contaminant in supplements. - **Beta-2 agonists:** Asthma medications, such as salbutamol, are permitted within limits with documentation but prohibited when abused for performance. - **Diuretics and masking agents:** These do not enhance performance directly but are used to dilute samples or hide other substances. - **Blood doping:** Transfusion or EPO use to raise red blood cell count. This can create major endurance gains but carries severe risks. - **Gene doping:** Still largely theoretical, but WADA has banned it pre-emptively.
These substances work. If they did not, people would not risk using them. Pretending otherwise costs coaches credibility because athletes see through it.
> Our job isn't to deny the benefit; it's to make athletes understand that temporary gains come with permanent, often irreversible, costs.
---

At its core, doping violates sport's essential premise: that competition tests natural human capability, enhanced only by training, nutrition, preparation and legitimate recovery.

They are prohibited in competition and are a common hidden contaminant in supplements.

chunk.content:
Most athletes who dope are not bad people. They are usually making what feels like a calculated risk under pressure. Understanding that pressure helps coaches prevent it.
### Competitive pressure
When an athlete trains relentlessly and still falls short, especially if they suspect rivals are doping, the temptation to find an edge grows. The belief that "everyone at the top is doing it" is usually exaggerated, but powerful.
Part of the coach's job is helping athletes define success in ways that are not entirely about beating one specific competitor: personal improvement, consistency, longevity, and pride in authentic achievement.
### Financial incentives
As HYROX professionalizes and prize money grows, so do the financial stakes. This can create pressure on an athlete who could "go full-time if they just cracked the top ten."
### Identity and self-worth
For many athletes, sport is their identity. The fear of losing that identity through ageing or injury can drive desperate choices.
### Poor decisions under stress
Doping decisions are often made in moments of crisis: after a crushing defeat, after an injury, or when an athlete feels most vulnerable.
### A normalized environment
Where doping is openly discussed or facilitated, the psychological barrier drops. It stops feeling like cheating and starts feeling like "what you have to do." This is why culture matters.
### Misinformation
Athletes consistently underestimate the health risks and overestimate their chances of avoiding detection. With improving technology and ten-year sample storage, the odds of eventually being caught are far higher than they assume.
---

chunk.content:
### Health
This is where it gets serious fast.
Anabolic steroids damage the cardiovascular system. Consequences include left ventricular hypertrophy, abnormal thickening of the heart muscle, damaged cholesterol profiles, accelerated atherosclerosis, raised blood pressure, and increased clotting risk. Young users can develop cardiovascular systems resembling those of elderly patients, and much of the damage can persist after stopping.
EPO and blood doping thicken the blood. Multiple young cyclists in peak condition died in their sleep during the EPO era because their hearts could not move blood that had become dangerously viscous.
The endocrine system also suffers. External testosterone shuts down the body's own production, causing testicular atrophy, collapsing sperm counts, and natural production that may never fully recover. This can leave athletes dependent on testosterone replacement for life.
In women, steroids can cause virilization, including deepening of the voice, facial hair and male-pattern baldness, which is often permanent. Oral steroids are hepatotoxic and can cause liver damage up to peliosis hepatis and cancer. Kidneys can also be damaged through several mechanisms. Psychological effects include mood swings, paranoia, post-cycle depression and elevated suicide risk. Fertility damage in athletes who start in their twenties may be irreversible by the time they want children.
### Legal
Doping is not just a sporting rule violation. In many countries, it is a crime.
In the United States, anabolic steroids are Schedule III controlled substances. Possession without a prescription can mean up to a year in prison and a minimum $1,000 fine, with trafficking carrying up to five years and $250,000.
Competing for prize money while doping can constitute fraud. Marion Jones, sprinter and Olympic Champion 2000, served six months in federal prison, not for doping itself but for lying to investigators. Pro cyclist Lance Armstrong settled a federal False Claims Act suit for $5 million.
Coaches who supply, administer or encourage prohibited substances face sporting bans and potential criminal liability. Providing substances to minors can mean child-endangerment charges.
### Career
Under the World Anti-Doping Code, a first violation typically means a four-year suspension, reducible to two years with proof of no significant fault. For an athlete who peaks in their late twenties, four years can erase their entire prime.
A second violation means a lifetime ban. Results are voided, medals stripped, records erased, prize money returned and titles vacated.

Sponsors terminate contracts and reclaim payments. Future earning potential, speaking engagements and coaching opportunities largely disappear. Reputational damage is permanent. Lance Armstrong won seven Tour de France titles and raised hundreds of millions for cancer research, yet is remembered as a disgraced doper. Marion Jones has spent nearly two decades trying to rehabilitate her reputation and is still primarily known for cheating. There is no easy redemption.

chunk.content:
A few cases are worth knowing well because they make the consequences concrete.
### Lance Armstrong
Lance Armstrong was stripped of seven Tour de France titles, banned for life, and described by USADA as running one of the most sophisticated doping programs sport has seen. His trainer, Dr Michele Ferrari, also received a lifetime ban.
The case shows how doping can corrupt an entire organization and marginalize those who refuse.
### Russia's state-sponsored program
Russia's state-sponsored program was exposed around the 2014 Sochi Olympics, with samples swapped through a hole in a laboratory wall and intelligence services involved.
The result was partial Olympic bans and clean Russian athletes forced to compete as neutrals. Even state-level resources could not hide it forever.
---

chunk.content:
Anti-doping is a coordinated global system, not a patchwork of national efforts. At its center is WADA, established in 1999 after the 1998 Festina affair made clear that sport could no longer police itself.
WADA is governed by a Foundation Board split equally between the Olympic Movement and governments, funded equally by both, with headquarters in Montreal.
Its mission rests on harmonization, coordination, education, research and monitoring. The cornerstone is the World Anti-Doping Code, first adopted in 2003 and updated regularly, most recently in 2021, and now adopted by more than 700 organizations.
### Criteria for the Prohibited List
The Prohibited List is updated annually. To be listed, a substance must meet at least two of three criteria:
1. Performance enhancement 2. Health risk 3. Violation of the spirit of sport
### Prohibited categories
Some categories are always prohibited:
- Anabolic agents - Peptide hormones and growth factors - Beta-2 agonists above therapeutic doses - Hormone and metabolic modulators - Diuretics and masking agents - Blood manipulation - Gene and cell doping
Other categories are prohibited in competition only:
- Stimulants - Narcotics - Cannabinoids - Glucocorticoids
### National Anti-Doping Organizations
National Anti-Doping Organizations (NADOs) implement the Code within each country. Their responsibilities include testing programs, education, results management, TUE review and whereabouts management.
Examples include:
- USADA, which led the Armstrong investigation - UKAD - NADA Germany, founded in 2002 and conducting roughly 10,000 tests a year, particularly relevant because HYROX is headquartered in Germany - ASADA in Australia - RUSADA, which was declared non-compliant after Russia's state-sponsored program was exposed
WADA's ADAMS database coordinates whereabouts, testing, results and TUEs globally.
### Testing process
Testing is rigorous by design. After notification, an athlete is shadowed by a Doping Control Officer until they provide a sample. They select their own sealed vessel, then provide at least 90 ml of urine, or 5-10 ml of blood, under direct observation.
The sample is split into A and B samples, sealed, coded without the athlete's name, and transported under strict chain of custody to a WADA-accredited laboratory.
Samples can be stored for up to ten years for retrospective analysis. In-competition testing targets substances banned during competition. Out-of-competition testing can happen anywhere, anytime, and is crucial for catching substances used in training, such as EPO and steroids.
### Detection methods
Detection happens in 29 WADA-accredited laboratories worldwide, including Cologne, Los Angeles, London, Sydney, Tokyo and Montreal.
Detection tools include:
- Mass spectrometry, sensitive to parts per billion or trillion - Isotope ratio mass spectrometry, which distinguishes natural from synthetic testosterone - Athlete Biological Passport (ABP), introduced in 2009

chunk.content:
The ABP represents a shift from finding the substance to tracking an athlete's biological markers over time. It includes a haematological module for blood and a steroidal module for hormones. It flags abnormal deviations and is effective even against micro-dosing and designer drugs.
### Whereabouts requirements
Elite athletes in registered testing pools face whereabouts requirements. They must specify where they sleep and train, plus one 60-minute window each day, typically between 6am and 11pm, when they will be at a stated location.
Three whereabouts failures in 12 months count as a violation, with the same four-year sanction.
### Results management
When a violation is identified, results management follows a structured path:
1. Initial review 2. Notification and provisional suspension 3. Optional B-sample analysis 4. Hearing before an independent tribunal 5. Sanctions per the Code 6. Final appeals to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in Lausanne
Reductions are possible for no significant fault, contaminated products, or substantial assistance.
WADA also monitors compliance. Non-compliant bodies face public disclosure, loss of hosting rights, athlete exclusion and funding loss. Russia's case showed that the system has teeth.
---

chunk.content:
Well-intentioned athletes can get caught through supplements. In most countries, supplements are regulated as foods, not drugs. Under the US DSHEA of 1994, for example, supplements can be sold with no pre-market testing or approval. The result is a regulatory vacuum.
The evidence is sobering. The 2004 Cologne study tested 634 supplements from 215 suppliers across 13 countries and found that 14.8% contained anabolic steroids not declared on the label. Follow-up studies found similar or higher rates: around 25% in one 2007 study, 12% of online products in 2016, and 50-80% of sexual-enhancement products containing undeclared pharmaceuticals.
Contamination can happen through:
- Deliberate adulteration, so users credit the listed ingredients - Cross-contamination on shared equipment - Contaminated raw ingredients - Labelling errors
### Supplement risk categories
| Risk level | Product categories | | Highest-risk | Muscle-building and "testosterone booster" products | | Highest-risk | Weight-loss and fat-burner products, often spiked with stimulants | | Highest-risk | Pre-workouts, including DMAA and other prohibited stimulants | | Highest-risk | Anything sold as a "proprietary blend" | | Lower-risk | Single-ingredient products from reputable manufacturers, including protein, creatine monohydrate, vitamin D and omega-3 |
The single best protection is third-party certification. Useful certifications include:
- Informed Sport - NSF Certified for Sport, which screens for 270+ substances and verifies label claims - Informed Choice - BSCG
These certifications do not guarantee perfection because testing is batch-specific and has detection limits, but they dramatically reduce risk.
### Contaminated-supplement defense
The contaminated-supplement defense offers only limited protection. To succeed, an athlete must:
1. Identify the specific product 2. Test it to confirm contamination 3. Show that the amount is consistent with their sample 4. Demonstrate that they took reasonable precautions
Even then, sanctions are usually reduced, often to 6-12 months, not eliminated. Strict liability stands.
### Practical guidance for athletes
1. Default to food first; supplement only for genuine, documented nutritional needs. 2. If supplementing, use only third-party-certified products from reputable brands. 3. Choose simple, single-ingredient formulations; avoid proprietary blends and exotic claims. 4. Keep records: product names, batch numbers, purchase dates, label photos, and a retained sample of each batch. 5. Never use muscle-building or weight-loss products promising dramatic effects, and never accept supplements from others without verifying contents. 6. Check ingredients against the prohibited list using Global DRO, and be extra cautious with products bought abroad.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 09: A special note on young athletes
chunk.content:
If you coach anyone under 18, your responsibilities are heightened.
Young athletes are more vulnerable to pressure and less able to weigh long-term consequences. The power imbalance between an adult coach and a teenager is especially pronounced.
The health risks are also greater. PEDs during adolescence can prematurely close growth plates, ending height development, and permanently disrupt a still-developing hormonal system.
Coaches should be conservative with supplements and medications, involve parents and guardians in education, watch carefully for outside pressure, and understand mandatory-reporting obligations.
Providing PEDs to a minor can be a criminal offence.
---

Young athletes are more vulnerable to pressure and less able to weigh long-term consequences.

Coaches should be conservative with supplements and medications, involve parents and guardians in education, watch carefully for outside pressure, and understand mandatory-reporting obligations.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 10: HYROX's path forward - and your part in it
chunk.content:
Olympic recognition requires demonstrating that HYROX meets international anti-doping standards, and the infrastructure is already being built.
As a sport, HYROX must:
- Formally adopt the Code - Establish in- and out-of-competition testing - Create education programs - Register elite athletes in a testing pool with whereabouts requirements - Build fair results-management procedures - Partner with NADOs such as NADA Germany, UKAD and USADA
As these systems arrive, the coach's role expands. Coaches should prepare athletes for what testing actually involves so it does not intimidate them. Coaches should help elite athletes manage whereabouts requirements, which becomes part of performance management. They should guide athletes with genuine medical needs through the TUE process properly.
Coaches also need to stay current because the Prohibited List and detection methods change every year.
When other coaches or athletes question whether testing is necessary, coaches should explain why it protects clean athletes rather than threatening them.
The facts above are the reference toolkit. The next part - the podcast - is about what coaches do with them.
---
