chunk.content: Welcome, I'm Ralf Iwan, Global Head of HYROX Academy. You've just worked through the facts, what doping is, the health risks, the WADA System, the supplement minefield, all of that matters. But here's the truth I want you to sit with. You can memorize every rule on the prohibited list and still miss the most important part. Because anti-doping isn't ultimately about rules, it's about values, it's about what kind of sport we want HYROX to be. Let me give you some personal context. Before HYROX I spent many years coaching internationally in track and field, athletes at European Championships, World Championships, Commonwealth Games, Olympic Games. And across those years I dealt with anti-doping from every angle, educating athletes, walking them through testing, watching the pressures they faced at the very top. That experience taught me something I want to pass on directly. Engage with this topic, deeply, from the beginning, whatever level you coach at. Don't treat it as a box to tick, make it part of who you are as a coach. Because I saw both sides. I saw clean athletes achieve extraordinary things through dedication and intelligent training, and I saw careers destroyed, not just the bans and stripped medals, but the psychological damage, the broken relationships, the permanent stain. I don't want that for anyone in HYROX. And we have a rare chance here to build something different. Now here's something I want to say early, because I know what some of you are thinking. Ralph, that's all elite level stuff. My athletes aren't going to the Olympics. Half the people I coach just want to finish their first HYROX, or look better in the mirror. None of them will ever be tested. And you're right, most of them won't. But I need you to hear this clearly, that is exactly the trap. The substances we're talking about, steroids, growth hormone, SARMs, stimulants, the test boosters and fat burners sold in every gym, they're not confined to elite sport. They are everywhere in the fitness world. They're in the commercial gym down the road. They're one click away online. And a lot of the people who walk into your HYROX gym come from exactly that culture. So picture the client who's never going to race for a podium, who'll never see a doping control officer in their life. If that person starts taking these things, do you know what protects their health? Not a drug test? There isn't one. Not a ban? There isn't one. The only thing standing between them and a damaged heart, wrecked hormones or worse is information and the relationship they have with you. Because the damage doesn't care whether you're an Olympian or a weekend athlete. When these substances are taken without medical supervision and a real medical reason, the heart, the liver, the hormones, the mind, they take the hit just the same. Even worse for the recreational user because the products come from dodgy sources and nobody's monitoring anything. So let me be blunt about where we stand as coaches. It can never, never be our goal to gamble with a client's health for a faster split or a better physique. That's not coaching, that's the opposite of it. But staying silent isn't neutral either. We have a moral obligation here. Our clients are swimming in misinformation and access has never been easier. The honest, calm, values-based conversation you have with them about what these substances actually do. That might be the single most protective thing anyone ever gives them. Clean sport isn't just a rule book for the elite. It's a standard of care for every single person who trusts us with their training. So let's talk about it. What are we actually protecting? The Code calls it the spirit of sport. But what is that, really? Let me make it concrete. When I watch a HYROX athlete cross the line after 60-90 minutes of brutal effort, lungs burning, legs gone, having pushed through every station and every kilometre, that achievement means something. It represents real capability, built over months and years. But if that performance came from EPO and steroids, the meaning evaporates. It's no longer a test of what a human can do, it becomes a test of pharmaceutical access. And I'll tell you from experience. Even when doped athletes try to convince themselves otherwise, that knowledge eats at them. The result isn't really theirs. It belongs to the drugs. Think about fair competition. In a HYROX race, everyone runs the same distance, does the same stations, faces the same challenge. That's what gives your result meaning, but if some are using EPO for the run and steroids for the sled while you're clean, is that competition or a pharmaceutical arms race? In athletics, I watch clean athletes tortured by a single question. Am I just not good enough or am I racing people on drugs? That doubt is corrosive. It destroys the thing. Then there's respect for your opponents, for the rules, for your own body. Racing says, I care more about winning than about any of that. There's health. Sports should build stronger bodies over a lifetime and doping inverts that. Trading your health, sometimes your life, for a temporary edge. I've known athletes who developed heart problems and hormonal disorders in their 20s and 30s. And there's community, one of the most beautiful things we have in HYROX. That community runs on trust. You assume the person beside you is competing fairly, doping replaces trust with suspicion, and I watched exactly that poison happen in athletics. And here's one more, maybe the deepest, character. Sport builds discipline, perseverance, resilience, humility, grace in winning and losing. Those lessons follow people into their careers and their relationships for the rest of their lives. Many of my former athletes have told me years later that what sport taught them about handling pressure and setbacks mattered more than any result. So ask yourself, what does doping teach? That shortcuts are fine? That the ends justify the means? That deception is acceptable if it gets you what you want? Those are not lessons we want HYROX to be teaching anyone. So when we say we're protecting the spirit of sport, this is what we mean. Excellence through effort, fair competition, respect, health, community, character. Doping doesn't just break a rule, it dissolves the things that make sport worth doing. Your role is bigger than you think. When an athlete comes to you, yes, they want a faster time, more strength, better endurance. But they're also handing you their trust, their health, their development, sometimes their future. That trust creates responsibility. And there's a power imbalance here we have to be honest about. Athletes, especially younger or less experienced ones, defer to you. They assume you know best. That's exactly why a coach who encourages or facilitates doping commits such a catastrophic betrayal. Athletes will go along with it against their own instincts because they trust you. I saw this in the wider sport. Young athletes who didn't want to dope but felt they had no choice because a coach they respected implied this is just what you do at this level. So we owe athletes a duty of care. Protect their physical safety, including from prohibited substances. Protect their psychological well-being. Don't build environments where success requires compromising your values. And prioritize their long-term development over next month's result. In athletics, I always try to ask, where will this person be in five years, ten years? Will they be healthy? Will they look back on sport with good memories? That long view changes how you coach. It makes you more conservative about risk. And it makes you put the athlete ahead of the medal. And remember, you're not only a technical expert, you're an educator, a mentor, a moral guide. Athletes watch how you behave when you think no one's looking. If you cut corners elsewhere, why would they believe you on doping? Integrity is indivisible. You can't be ethical about anti-doping and loose about everything else, and expect anyone to take you seriously. Educating Athletes Beyond Don't Dope Real education has four layers - knowledge, the facts you just covered. But facts alone don't change behavior. So you also need skills. Basically walking an athlete through global DRO, practising checking their supplements together, describing exactly what a doping control feels like so it isn't terrifying when it happens. Then values - sitting down and talking about what they want sport to mean in their life, what they want to be able to say about their achievements when they look back. That builds internal motivation that goes far beyond fear of getting caught. And finally critical thinking, because you won't always be in the room. You want athletes who can recognize a problematic situation and make the right call on their own. What actually works? Ongoing dialogue, not a once a year lecture. Let anti-doping come up naturally, when you review nutrition, when someone asks about a supplement, when you plan for a competition. Make it normal. Use real cases. Talk about Armstrong, Marion Jones, the East German athletes, because stories stick where abstract rules slide off. And run scenarios. A teammate offers you a totally natural recovery supplement. What do you do? You need a prescription medication, but you're not sure it's allowed. What's your next step? Walk through the reasoning together, so they've rehearsed it before they ever need it. Culture eats individual willpower for breakfast. Athletes' choices don't happen in a vacuum. They're shaped by the environment around them, and you are the primary architect of that environment in your gym. A clean sport culture has a few signatures. Values are stated explicitly and often. Don't assume people know what you stand for. Say it. At the start of every season in athletics, I'd say plainly, we achieve excellence through legitimate means. That's who we are. It's non-negotiable. Clean athletes are made into heroes. You tell the story of the process that got them there, the years of consistency, so everyone can see that legitimate methods work. Communication is open, so athletes feel safe, asking, I'm not sure this is okay. Can we check? Without being treated as paranoid. Clean sport is framed as a collective commitment. Our responsibility, including yours. Not a burden you've dumped on the athletes. The thinking is long term. And when a violation happens, it's taken seriously. You don't make excuses or minimize, because how you respond tells everyone whether your commitment is real or just talk. Two of those deserve a little more. First, celebrate the process, not just the outcome. When an athlete has a breakthrough race, I'd spend more time talking about the months of training that led there than about the result itself. The consistency, the smart programming, the mental toughness. Because that's where the development actually happened. And when athletes understand how adaptation works, how the body responds to training stimulus and recovery, they're far less susceptible to anyone claiming they need a pharmaceutical shortcut. Second, build a way for athletes to raise concerns safely. Tell them, if you ever feel pressure to use something, if you see something that worries you, come to me. It stays between us and there's no downside to you for speaking up. In athletics, athletes did come to me with concerns about others. And that safe channel protected the whole group. The difficult conversations. Even in a great culture, athletes face pressure. You need to be ready. When an athlete asks you directly about PEDs, don't shame them. I can't believe you'd even ask that, might feel righteous. But it guarantees they never come to you again. And they'll get their information from somewhere worse. Instead, I'm glad you feel you can ask me. Let's talk it through honestly. Give them the truth. Acknowledge the substance works, then lay out the health risks, the ethics, the four-year ban and the fact that detection keeps improving. Explore why they're asking, plateaued, suspicious of competitors, approached by someone. Each needs a different response. Then reinforce your belief in them and redirect that competitive drive into legitimate gains. Programming changes, technical work, recovery, nutrition, realistic goals. When you suspect doping, sudden dramatic improvements, rapid physical changes, secrecy, questionable medical contacts, be direct but not accusatory. I've noticed some big changes and that's exciting, but I want to make sure we're building this in a healthy, sustainable way. Can we talk about what you're doing differently? Listen for evasiveness, reiterate your boundaries clearly, offer support, document your observations confidentially, and know your reporting obligations. And when an athlete discloses doping to you, current or past, how you respond is critical. Stay calm, they're trusting you, and a shocked reaction shuts them down. Thank you for trusting me with this. Let's figure out the best way forward. Gather the facts, make sure they get medical evaluation because stopping some substances abruptly is dangerous. Talk through the options, including voluntary disclosure to authorities, which can reduce sanctions. Be clear about your role. You'll support their well-being, you can't help them keep doping, and you have obligations. Then don't abandon them, they made a serious mistake, but they're still your athlete and they still need support. There's one argument you'll hear sooner or later, but everyone else is doping, I'm at a disadvantage if I stay clean. Don't pretend that doping gives no advantage, and don't pretend enforcement is perfect. Athletes know both. And denying reality wrecks your credibility. Instead, give perspective. The idea that everyone dopes is almost always exaggerated. Most athletes, even at the top, compete clean. The consequences of being caught are catastrophic, and aren't worth a temporary edge. Detection keeps improving and samples are stored for years, so escaping today doesn't mean escaping forever. And success built on doping is hollow and anxious. It never feels like yours. Then, help them reframe success. Personal bests, consistency, longevity, pride in authentic achievement. Some athletes may have to accept that without doping, they won't reach a particular level. And our job is to help them find real meaning in the sport anyway. One more lever that's easy to forget. Families. Parents, partners and spouses influence the decisions athletes make. Bring them into the conversation, help them understand the health risks and the career consequences and they become some of your strongest allies in protecting an athlete from a bad choice. Consider a short education session for families or simply share these resources with them. In athletics, whenever families understood what was actually at stake, they were a powerful protective force. Talking the talk, your own integrity. I want to say something that might feel uncomfortable. You cannot promote clean sport if your own behavior contradicts it. Athletes are incredibly observant. They notice how you treat other coaches when you think no one's watching. Whether you bend rules in other contexts, how you handle dilemmas that have nothing to do with doping. Integrity is indivisible. If you cut corners on safety, fudge your credentials, play favourites or talk down competitors, athletes learn that ethics are flexible and rules are suggestions. That's not the lesson we want to teach. So model it. Keep your word. When you don't know something, say, I don't know, but I'll find out. That's intellectual honesty and it's worth more than a confident guess. When you make a mistake in programming or judgment, own it. I got that wrong. Here's what I'll do differently. Treat every athlete with respect regardless of their level. Follow the rules, even when no one's looking. I made mistakes in athletics. I missed warning signs. I didn't always ask enough questions. And when I realized it, I owned it, sometimes to the athletes themselves. That accountability is strength, not weakness. And you'll face pressure to compromise, pressure to win, pressure from athletes who want shortcuts, pressure from people who want champions regardless of how they're produced. It's easy to talk about integrity when it costs nothing. The real test is when holding the line means a competitive or financial sacrifice. I faced that. I turned down approaches I couldn't support, and it wasn't free. But over time, that reputation for doing things right became my most valuable professional asset. Athletes wanted to work with me because they trusted I'd keep them safe. Parents trusted me with their kids. That's built through thousands of small choices, day after day, to do the right thing, even when a shortcut is sitting right there. The legacy we're building. HYROX is young. We started in 2018. The decisions we make right now will shape this sport's character for decades. And I know from athletics how this goes. Once doping becomes normal in a sports culture, it's almost impossible to root out. We get to choose. Do we want HYROX to become another sport haunted by scandal and cynicism, where every record is questioned, or a sport known for integrity, where for everyone includes clean sport for everyone, where achievements are celebrated as real, where the community trusts each other? Our accessibility is part of this. When you finish a HYROX, you've done the same race as our elite athletes. Same distances, same stations. That shared experience creates a genuine community. Doping would split it into real athletes and everyone else. That's not who we are. Think about your own legacy too. Years from now, your athletes may not remember their HYROX times, but they'll remember whether you taught them that integrity matters, that shortcuts aren't worth the cost, that genuine achievement comes through honest effort. I've had former athletes reach out years later to tell me the lessons about doing things right served them in their careers, their relationships, their lives, far beyond sport. That's the legacy that lasts. And I'll tell you honestly, it's far more satisfying than any medal. So here's my challenge to you. This week, go back to your gym and have a conversation with your athletes about clean sport. Not a lecture, a conversation. Ask what they know, ask what questions they have, ask what pressure they feel and how you can support them. Review the supplements they're using, check for third-party certification. If you coach competitive athletes, prepare them for what's coming. Testing, whereabouts, scrutiny. Make this part of your regular practice, not something separate and occasional. We're building something special in HYROX, accessible, competitive, with a real community and genuine Olympic potential. Let's build it right. Let's build it with integrity. Let's create a sport athletes can be proud of, not just for what they achieve, but for how they achieve it. Thank you for engaging with this fundamentally. Now go out there and build the sport we all want HYROX to be.

key_facts.fact: You've just worked through the facts, what doping is, the health risks, the WADA System, the supplement minefield, all of that matters.
You can memorize every rule on the prohibited list and still miss the most important part.
Because anti-doping isn't ultimately about rules, it's about values, it's about what kind of sport we want HYROX to be.
Before HYROX I spent many years coaching internationally in track and field, athletes at European Championships, World Championships, Commonwealth Games, Olympic Games.
And across those years I dealt with anti-doping from every angle, educating athletes, walking them through testing, watching the pressures they faced at the very top.
That experience taught me something I want to pass on directly.
Engage with this topic, deeply, from the beginning, whatever level you coach at.
Don't treat it as a box to tick, make it part of who you are as a coach.

chunk.content: Okay, so what you're looking at here on the screen is exactly the slides that I use in the elite athlete briefings. Here we can see it's the singles version to template, which is why you've got the Xs on the screen. But in fact, these are the slides from the World Championships in Stockholm this year. And these ultimately, as we go to the first slide, doping controls, I mean, they can become admissible, or they are evidential in court in the event that we impose sanctions on an athlete for providing an adverse analytical finding or a positive test. And we need to then be able to demonstrate every step we took in that whole process. And here, it starts with saying that we basically will have doping controls in place at this race, whichever race it is, carried out in accordance as per the HYROX anti-doping code, which in the end, we follow the WADA guidelines. We usually test up to five athletes for singles, and that's from each gender category. So if we do five from each for singles, that's 10 samples. If it's doubles, we do five pairs of athletes from each gender category, so that's 20. So we often are taking 30 samples at each elite race this season, and it will go up next season because we're introducing another division underneath elite 15. Okay, so really importantly, let's say I'm an elite athlete, I come running across the finish line, I get to celebrate and do all those things and look at the camera, maybe even do an interview. The second I cross that line, if I'm going to be selected for doping control, I'm under observation. And we ultimately assign a chaperone to any athlete who is going to be subject to doping controls. And as they typically either step off the stage or move away from the finish area, then it's as simple as one of our doping control officers will approach them and just say, Hi, my name's whatever it is, I'm from such and such agency, you've been selected for doping controls today. This is your chaperone. She's called Sarah, and you're required to stay with Sarah now for when you go and provide a sample. So really importantly, it's the athlete's responsibility to maintain continuity with their chaperone, not the other way around. So if they go sprinting off into the crowd because they've seen their mom, their dad, their wife, or whoever it might be, to celebrate what they've just achieved. If they lose continuity of the chaperone, that's a problem. Our chaperones will try and stay with them in the end, but the athletes have to understand it's their job to stay with the chaperone, not the other way around. Now, if contact with the chaperone is broken, that could be considered as a missed test, which would count as an adverse test, which is bad news. However, as I say to the athletes in the briefing, don't go into a tailspin if that happens, because on a case-by-case decision, the doping commission representative will determine whether the test can be continued, or in fact, it is going to be considered a missed test. So, there's a process to go through, and so we just encourage them not to go into a tailspin in the event that they do lose the chaperone somehow. That chaperone will stay with them all the way through to the doping control station, and will stay with them until they are officially handed over, the athletes officially handed over to the doping control officer, and that's again a formal process, it's time and date stamped, and there's a whole framework around that for sure. Really important, we say to the athlete, to the last point on this slide, is that it's not permitted to return to the wall walls from the finish area. So, even though it can be lovely if the last person coming across, who will come across the line is struggling, and it's lovely to see the athletes go and cheer them on, however, for doping control reasons, that's not permitted at elite level. We have to maintain continuity with the athletes and have them in a relatively controlled environment, which is the finish area in the end. Alright, so then we move on, and as you can see here on the next slide, we talk a little bit about what we provide and how it works. So, we provide sealed bottles of water and sealed cans of Red Bull in the elite 15 changing rooms, the elite lounge, and in the doping control suite. Nothing else, and we have had examples where well-intended local teams have put maybe local produce or sweets, lolly candy, whatever language you want to go with for the elites, but we have to take them out before the elites arrive, because there's a risk that they're contaminated. We haven't got continuity of those products, so they get removed immediately before the elite athletes enter that space. We do provide open cups of water in the rock zone, and what I guess most people wouldn't be aware is we use sealed bottles of water for that as well, and the person that opens those bottles of water and puts some water into those cups then stays with those cups until the conclusion of the race. They then throw them in the bin. Any that haven't been used, they dispose of them, and if we're talking about women's races occurred, then we have a gap and we go again with the men's, they will get rid of all of the women's cups of water, replace them all with new cups, open more sealed bottles of water, partially fill them up and stay with them again until the conclusion of that race. Athletes are allowed to stage their own hydration and nutrition. We provide a dedicated table close to the outarch for that. Really importantly, and I really do stress this point in the athlete briefing, is that that table is not supervised or monitored. There's no camera on it, there's no security, there's no member of staff there. So anything they leave on that table, they do so at their own risk. Now, we try and limit the amount of time they have product on there. So it's not a free-for-all, out on the race floor before a race. So we chaperone them. Those who want to stage hydration and nutrition, we chaperone them at an agreed time. We meet them at the warm-up area and we chaperone them via an agreed route. So there's no free run lap of the course, for example, and they put it on the table themselves. We don't touch it, and then we chaperone them, supervise them back to the warm-up area. At the end of that race, anything left on that table just gets put straight into a bin, clean table, fresh start for the next race, for sure. Really importantly, and that's why it's highlighted in white here, the athlete is responsible for whatever they consume, not HYROX. Black and white can't be more clear than that. And here, that last point, you can see we talk about, as I've just described, we agree a time at which they can go and be supervised to put their own hydration and nutrition out on that table. Now moving on to, as you can see here, it says mandatory, and it means exactly that. So if an athlete DNFs or does not finish for any reason, they can't just slink away and lick their wounds unless they're DNFing for medical reasons and they're with the medical team, in which case one of our team will be with them anyway. If they're DNF, they have to either, as you can see here, tell myself as the technical director for elite racing, or they have to go to any one of the nominated race directors on the race floor. So here you can see we've named them. And that's really important. We've got Pearl, of course, as the doping control liaison in the recovery area, who, for sure, all of the athletes are very familiar with. It's really important. And I always say, it's not just someone randomly wearing a HYROX t-shirt. It must be one of those named people there. And I get them to stand up in the room. They're always at the athlete briefings, including all of the elite head judges. The whole team is present at the briefings so that they've heard the briefing, they've heard the questions, they've heard the answers, seen the faces. And there's a little bit as well. I say, we're all in this together. Let's put on a show. And that's what a nice vibe to it. Really importantly, at the conclusion of the race, athletes must stay in the recovery air until technically the air quotes, end of the race. That's defined as 30 minutes after the last athlete crosses the line. And that fun fact behind the scenes, the second the last person does cross the line, an email is sent to elite's at inbox with down to the thousandth of a second when the last athlete finished. And it's in part for doping control reasons and in part for race result challenge reasons. And the reason we say all of that is even if you DNF or you finish the race, you may still be subject to doping controls. So for that reason, if you just disappear and we don't know where you are, we can't find you, A, we've lost continuity of you and B, that can be considered a missed test because you are required to stay, either notifies as a DNF or stay until 30 minutes after the last athlete crosses the line. I have to say, this is always backed up with a, does anyone have any questions? Does anyone not understand anything? Does anyone think not clear about what we've just discussed? And that's, again, all part of the, I guess, the evidential path. I'm able to say that I asked that question and no one had any questions or they had questions and they got answers. So that's, yeah, those are in the end, the slides extracted from the athlete briefings. And that's an insight into what we talk about.

unit.title: Guide to Analyzing Movement
unit.unit_summary: Coaches must develop observation skills and formulate technical models to identify errors and performance limitations in HYROX movements. Good technical analysis depends on clear, consistent video capture. The audio explains that the goal is to build confidence in analyzing all HYROX movements.

chunk.section_title: Audio: Practical guide to analysing movement
chunk.content: [0:00:00] In this section we will provide you with some tips on how to analyze technique starting with developing your observation skills and progressing into the formulation of a technical model. Ultimately you should develop the confidence to analyze all HYROX movements to identify errors and understand the limitations on performance.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Tips on how to capture good quality video
chunk.content:
We're living in an era where everyone has a video camera at their fingertips. High quality cameras in smartphones make video analysis both affordable and available for coaches and athletes, but simply pressing the record button does not guarantee good quality footage for technique analysis.
The primary objective is to be able to play the video back, pause it, and move it on frame by frame to discuss key body positions with the athlete. Video analysis applications can measure angles, quantify movement timings, and compare and time-synchronise two videos side by side. This is useful for seeing how an athlete's technique has changed.
To make accurate observations and comparisons, coaches need to be consistent in how video is recorded.
### The Camera
The default video camera setting on most smartphones is HD 30. A frame rate of 30 fps is insufficient to make meaningful observations during HYROX movements. The recommended setting is FHD 60, which gives better image clarity and twice the number of frames, making key positions of the movement more defined.
For example, when recording an athlete running at 6 m/s at 30 fps, the video may capture only about five frames of ground support. The instants of touchdown and toe-off are not as well-defined as they would be at 60 fps.
If body parts such as hands, arms, feet or legs appear blurred when the video is paused, coaches should try filming in high-speed or slow-motion mode at 120 or 240 fps. This may reduce video resolution, but body parts are easier to see clearly. After recording in slow-motion mode, the video can be edited down to 60 fps while retaining clarity of body positions.
Slow-motion filming is also recommended when quantifying timings such as foot contact time, flight time or swing time.
| Frame rate | Time interval between consecutive frames | | 30 fps | 0.033 s | | 60 fps | 0.0167 s | | 120 fps | 0.0083 s | | 240 fps | 0.0042 s |
### The Vantage Point
A consistent filming position is required to make accurate comparisons of an athlete's technique over time. To decide on the best filming position, coaches should consider the technical model of the HYROX movement and identify which plane or planes of movement contain the most important aspects of technique.
This usually means filming from either:
- The side, for the sagittal plane - The front or rear, for the frontal plane - Both angles in some cases

The figure demonstrates that perception and assessment of body or joint positions can be compromised depending on the position of the athlete relative to the camera. In this scenario, the first image gives the most accurate observation and measurement of the knee joint angle.
### How to Film?
It is recommended to use a tripod to improve filming quality and avoid unsteady images caused by holding the camera.
Once the camera is placed on the tripod, it can either be kept fixed or panned:
- A fixed camera captures a defined area. - A panning camera captures a wider range.
Coaches should consider the size of the athlete within the frame of view and the horizontal range of movement the athlete is likely to cover.
For SkiErgg, rowing, sled pull and wall balls, there is limited horizontal displacement of the body, so a fixed camera position is ideal.
For movements with greater horizontal displacement, coaches can either:
- Record the entire movement from start to finish by panning the camera - Preferably record a short 6 m segment with the camera set at the midpoint of the range using a fixed camera position
When filming over a wide movement distance, the coach and camera should typically be positioned at the midpoint and 5 m to 10 m back from the athlete's line of movement. The exact distance depends on whether the camera has a wide-angle view option.
The key point is to adopt the most appropriate position to accurately observe the athlete's movements and to stay consistent in field of view and frame rate. This allows valid comparisons, such as comparing one athlete with another who demonstrates good technique, or comparing the same athlete at different time points to show improvements.

### Analyzing Video
There are many mobile applications and computer software packages available for coaches to enhance their observation, replay, review and analysis process.
These applications allow video footage to be captured or uploaded from a gallery, replayed, paused, advanced frame by frame, and used to capture screenshots of key instants. They can also quantify movement features such as time, distances and angles.
Applications such as VisualEyes and myDartfish Express are free smartphone or tablet applications that allow users to compare and synchronise videos side by side. This is useful for highlighting differences or changes in body positions and timings.
These applications allow video to be captured at 60 fps, which is adequate for most HYROX workouts. For analyzing running gait, video recorded in slow-motion modes at 120 or 240 fps is better for quantifying contact time, flight time and swing time.
Video can also be analyzed on a laptop using the free download of Quintic Player.
### Visual Note: Comparison of two videos and hip-angle measurement
The figure shows two side-view rowing screenshots compared vertically in a video analysis app. Hip angles are marked on both athletes:
| Video comparison | Measured hip angle | | Upper image | 43.8° | | Lower image | 50.2° |
The visual demonstrates how video analysis can compare two athletes or two attempts and quantify positional differences using angle measurements.
### Developing Technical Models
A technical model is a reference framework that describes the ideal execution of a skill, underpinned by sound biomechanical principles. The technical model removes guesswork from movement correction, so changes to an athlete's body positions and movements should lead to better and safer execution.
The technical model also highlights key factors that may limit performance, helping coaches prescribe supplementary training exercises.
Sports skills can be broken down into key phases, each with a distinct purpose. Typically, these relate to:
- Initiation phase - Priming phase - Execution phase - Follow-through or recovery phase
### Initiation Phase
The initiation phase is about getting into the start position, setting stance and preparing mentally to start the movement.
Examples include football players setting themselves to take a free kick, or a long jumper or gymnast standing at the end of the runway before accelerating down the track.
In HYROX, this could mean getting into the right stance position for the SkiErgg or the initial push of the Sled.
### Priming Phase
The priming phase is about creating the best scenario for muscles to generate greater or more efficient force production.

It often involves joint movements flexing before extending, or the center of mass moving in the opposite direction to the execution phase. It often primes the muscles through eccentric loading to benefit from the stretch-shortening cycle in the extension phase.
### Execution Phase
The execution phase is where muscle contraction and joint movements act sequentially to create force against the ground or onto an object, such as a medicine ball, in the intended direction of movement.
The execution phase ends when the body stops applying force against the ground, for example at toe-off in running or jumping, or when the object has been released. After this, a follow-through occurs or the limb enters a recovery phase in preparation for the next repetition.
### Description of key positions and phases
Once the distinct phases of movement have been identified, coaches should describe the ideal positions that define the beginning and end of each phase, and the desired movements that take place within each phase.
To ensure the technical model is robust, these descriptions should be sense-checked against robust biomechanical movement principles from Level 1.
Associating physical attributes with successful execution of the technical model helps identify limiting factors that athletes can train to improve their ability to perform skills better and more efficiently.

chunk.content: The video camera default setting on most smartphones will be HD 30. A frame rate of 30 fps is insufficient to make any meaningful observations during HYROX movements. The recommended setting would be FHD 60, which will give you better image clarity and twice the number of frames which makes key positions of the movement more defined. For example, if recording an athlete running at 6m/s at 30fps you may get 5 frames of ground support and the instants of touchdown and toe-off would not be a well-defined as 60 fps. Sometimes, when pausing the video, parts of the body (hand, arms, feet and legs) may be blurred making it difficult to observe the athlete. If you have this issue, try filming in the high speed / slow motion mode which takes the frame rate to 120 or 240 fps. This may reduce the video resolution (the number of video pixels) but you will be able to see the body parts clearly. After recording in slow motion mode, you can always edit the video and reduce it down to 60fps, but the clarity of body positions will still be there. I would also recommend filming in slow motion mode if you want to quantify timings, e.g. foot contact time, flight time, swing time, giving greater precision. The time interval between consecutive frames when recorded at 30fps is 0.033s, at 60fps is 0.0167s, at 120fps is 0.0083s and 240fps is 0.0042s. chunk.content: Once we have identified the distinct phases of movement it is important that we describe the ideal positions that define the beginning and end of the phases, and the desired movements that take place within each phase. There is one caveat to these descriptions, in order to ensure that our technical model is robust we should sense check these against our robust biomechanical movement principles (from Level 1). Associating physical attributes to the successful execution of the technical model helps us to identify limiting factors that athletes can train to enhance the ability to perform the skills better and more efficiently.

unit.title: Technical Models & Physical Attributes
unit.unit_summary: The unit defines technical models and physical attributes for HYROX movements. Running, SkiErgg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Rowing Erg, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, and Wall Balls are covered. Tables and visual notes provide movement phases, descriptions, principles, and equations for coaching analysis.

chunk.content:
### Table 1: Running technical model
| Run phase | Description | Principles | | Late Swing | Extend knee partially and dorsiflex ankle; hip extends into contact to create active contact rather than blocking. | Ground reaction force is applied in the direction of movement. | | Contact and Braking | Trunk slightly inclined forwards; knee partially flexed and ready to absorb impact; smaller touchdown distance reduces braking; flat-foot contact reduces impact forces and loads the Achilles tendon sooner; minimize knee flexion to load quadriceps and patellar tendons sooner; extend the hip to pull the center of mass over the foot. | Work with gravity; reduce braking impulse; stretch phase of the stretch-shortening cycle. | | Propulsion and Toe-off | Extend hip, knee and ankle; avoid pushing too far behind the body and creating a large take-off distance; avoid excessive lateral force and rotation in the transverse plane; arms should not cross the midline. | Proximal-to-distal sequencing; shorten the stretch-shortening-cycle phase; avoid force production in directions other than forwards. | | Swing / Recovery | Initiate hip flexion and forward thigh motion immediately; flex knee to reduce moment of inertia; dorsiflex ankle; recovery thigh should be parallel to support leg thigh at contact; keep recovery path direct; avoid excessive medial or lateral foot deviation and arms crossing midline. | Speed = step length x step frequency; efficient step frequency; direct recovery path. |
### Visual Note: Gait cycle terminology
The gait cycle visual labels toe-off, touchdown, flight distance, touchdown distance, take-off distance, step length right-to-left, step length left-to-right, stride length, and center of mass. Step length is presented as the sum of take-off distance, flight distance, touchdown distance, and foot length.
### Visual Note: Ground reaction force graphs
| Contact type | Visual features | Coaching meaning | | More rigid contact | Distinct vertical impact spike; greater anterior-posterior braking force and impulse; longer contact time likely. | Heel contact, straighter or extending leg, and foot planted further in front of the center of mass require more propulsive impulse to maintain speed. | | Less rigid contact | Reduced anterior-posterior braking impulse; less required propulsive impulse. | Knee partially flexed, foot moving downward-backwards, and foot planted closer to the center of mass are more efficient. |

chunk.content:
Running forms the largest part of the HYROX event, accounting for around 50% of an athlete's race time, so if you can find ways to reduce 1km times and/or make an athlete's running gait more efficient they you should improve.
As a biomechanist I focus on how athletes move, how they interact with the ground, how those interactions affect loading in bone, muscle and tendons, and develop a technical model of how an athlete should run and develop physical attributes to make these ground interactions more efficient, carrying less risk. Whilst improving running speed is a desirable outcome, in the context of HYROX, I believe being more efficient and reducing energy expenditure during running can be equally if not more beneficial to the overall race performance, thereby saving energy for the 8 workout stations.
When looking at running performance we can quantify this as the time to complete the 1km distance, or we can determine an average speed by dividing the distance by the time to complete that
distance. Both these are good performance indicators, but we need to go into more detail to explore the movements in individual strides and quantify body positions at specific instants in time - we call this 'gait' analysis.
A gait cycle is the time interval between specific instants of movement from one step to the same instant on the next step. Typically, this could be time interval from the video frame when the foot first makes contact with the ground (which we would refer to as the instant of 'contact' or 'touchdown') through to the next video frame where the same foot makes contact again. Equally we could go from toe-off to toe-off of the same foot. We break the gait cycle down further into 2 main phases, contact and swing (or recovery). Within the swing phase the opposite leg will have a contact phase, and when neither foot is on the ground we call this the flight phase. Either way during one gait cycle you would have a contact phase of each foot and two flight phases, one from left to right and the other right to left (see figure 5). When looking at the video frame by frame we define the instant of touchdown as the first when where we see contact between the foot and surface and toe-off as the last frame of contact before it has clearly left the floor.

chunk.content:
We can also see in Figure 5 that the step length is the sum of 4 distances; take-off, flight and touchdown distances (which are related to the position of the center of mass) plus the length of the foot. The flight distance will form the largest of these distances and
there are implications for attempting to lengthen both the touchdown and take-off distances.
A gait cycle and terminology
Probing into the contact phase a little deeper we know that the initial contact creates a braking action. Biomechanists can quantify the braking force and impulse using force platforms embedded in the floor, or with force treadmills. Figure 6 shows typical graphs of the horizontal (anterior-posterior) and vertical ground reaction forces during a running step. The dotted vertical line denotes the transition from braking to propulsion.
Figure 6a - Ground reaction force-time graphs of a more rigid contact
Ground Reaction Force characteristics representative of athletes landing with a more rigid contact, e.g. heel contact, straighter (or extending) leg which is planted further in front of the center of mass. Creates a distinct vertical impact spike, greater anterior- posterior braking force (and impulse). Requires more propulsive impulse to maintain a constant running speed and contact times may be longer.
Figure 6b - a less rigid contact.
Ground Reaction Force characteristics when landing with less rigidity, e.g. knee partially flexed, foot on a downward-backwards trajectory, and foot planted closer to the center of mass. Reduces anterior-posterior braking impulse, requires less propulsive impulse to maintain a constant running speed = more efficient.
We see in figure 6 that every foot contact has a braking phase and a propulsion phase. We also know that in order to maintain the same running speed from the instant of foot contact to the instant
of toe-off, the amount of horizontal impulse lost in the braking phase must be generated in the propulsive phase. A more efficient athlete will be one who requires less muscular effort generating propulsive impulse to overcome a greater braking impulse. The braking phase is also associated with eccentric muscle actions which cause neuromuscular fatigue, which has implications on race performance and recovery.
Building on this line of thought we need to think about how we can reduce braking forces, braking time and the combination of both, braking impulse.

The flight distance will form the largest of these distances and
there are implications for attempting to lengthen both the touchdown and take-off distances.

The dotted vertical line denotes the transition from braking to propulsion.

Figure 6a - Ground reaction force-time graphs of a more rigid contact

heel contact, straighter (or extending) leg which is planted further in front of the center of mass.
Creates a distinct vertical impact spike, greater anterior- posterior braking force (and impulse).

chunk.content:
I'll start with braking time. The braking phase is governed by the length of time the center of mass is behind the center of pressure under the foot. A typical running action would be where the trunk (body) is upright, and the athlete plants the leg with an extended knee in front of the body. We call this the 'touchdown distance'. The greater the touchdown distance the longer the braking time. If the trunk was slightly inclined forwards and the knee was partially flexed at the instant of touchdown we now have a smaller touchdown distance and shorter braking time. So, slight forward trunk inclination and a partially flexed knee at the instant of contact are beneficial.
Now let's consider braking forces. Athletes are going to experience greater horizontal braking forces if they make a hard rigid contact,
typically associated with extended knees and heel contact. A partially flexed knee will put the shin in a more vertical position at contact and allow more flat-foot contacts. A flat foot contact also has the benefit of creating a stable base earlier than a heel contact meaning that horizontal and vertical eccentric loads can be accepted sooner. We can add vertical shin and flat foot contacts as desirable technical features for improving efficiency.
Another aspect of reducing braking forces is to consider the direction in which the foot makes contact with the ground, is it moving forwards or backwards relative to the body as the foot approaches ground contact? If it moves forwards, then the thigh may still be moving forwards or the knee extending in the late part of the swing phase. This is undesirable because it creates a blocking effect and leads to higher braking forces. Ideally we want to see the hip extending towards foot contact, moving the foot down and backwards relative to the body. This creates an 'active' contact and reduces the braking forces. In order to create an active contact, the athlete needs to get the thigh (and foot) through to the front of the body earlier in the swing / recovery phase.
Shifting our focus the instant of toe-off (figure 5) the classic images of a runner would show them in 'triple extension', (hip and knee extension and ankle plantar flexion). This positions the foot far behind the body creating a long 'take-off distance'. At the start of the recovery phase, the athlete would then lift the heel tightly

key_facts.fact: The braking phase is governed by the length of time the center of mass is behind the center of pressure under the foot.
A typical running action would be where the trunk (body) is upright, and the athlete plants the leg with an extended knee in front of the body.
The greater the touchdown distance the longer the braking time.
If the trunk was slightly inclined forwards and the knee was partially flexed at the instant of touchdown we now have a smaller touchdown distance and shorter braking time.

Athletes are going to experience greater horizontal braking forces if they make a hard rigid contact,
typically associated with extended knees and heel contact.
A partially flexed knee will put the shin in a more vertical position at contact and allow more flat-foot contacts.
A flat foot contact also has the benefit of creating a stable base earlier than a heel contact meaning that horizontal and vertical eccentric loads can be accepted sooner.
We can add vertical shin and flat foot contacts as desirable technical features for improving efficiency.
If it moves forwards, then the thigh may still be moving forwards or the knee extending in the late part of the swing phase.
This is undesirable because it creates a blocking effect and leads to higher braking forces.

chunk.content:
flexing the knee, before starting the forward movement of the thigh to the front side of the body. This delay in the forward rotation of the thigh means that the knee extends towards the instant of foot contact creating a 'blocking' action and higher braking forces. To create an 'active' contact we need to thigh to initiate forward rotation immediately after toe-off while concurrently flexing the knee. By the time the opposite foot makes contact with the ground both thighs should be parallel to each other. This preferred type of leg recovery is referred to as 'front side mechanics', with the focus on getting the thigh to the front of the body earlier to create this downward and back foot motion prior to contact. We can add hip and knee flexion immediately after toe-off into our running technical model to facilitate the active foot contact.
Now let's consider what happens to the support leg in the ground contact phase. Immediately after contact the knee will flex and the ankle dorsi-flex in response to the impact. Landing with flat foot and partially flexed knees mean that the tendon will be loaded earlier, and with the reduced braking time we get a shorter faster stretch-shortening cycle, making use of that elastic energy which contributes to the drive-off.
Another aspect of efficiency is avoiding unnecessary movements and force generation outside of the primary direction of movement. While pelvis and shoulder rotation in the transverse plane is important for energy transfer and extending range of motion of the
legs in the sagittal plane, we don't want to see the arms crossing the midline of the body during their swing. A foot that deviates medially across the midline or laterally may cause unnecessary strain on the hip and lower back.
These key movements that describe the technical model of efficient running are highlighted below in Table 1.
To make the running intervals more efficient consider the points made previously about a more optimal gait pattern:
- Slight forward trunk lean
- Plant a flat foot closer to the body with some flexion in the knee and the shin close to vertical. The foot should travel downwards and backwards towards contact to reduce the braking impulse.
- Utilize the SSC in the quadriceps/patella and achilles tendons to utilize elastic energy into each step
- Use front side recovery (heel up and thigh forwards concurrently) to effectively fall into each step (working with gravity)
- Avoid unwanted lateral force generation which can cause excessive transverse plane rotation, the hands crossing the midline and the recovery foot deviating medially or laterally
- Include eccentric strength training and plyometric drills in your training to develop your elastic qualities

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Performing your own Gait Analysis and assessing symmetry in step length, step frequency, contact time and swing time asymmetry
chunk.content:
Using similar software and applications to the ones mentioned previously, following these steps to review your video:
1 To analyze and compare your running gait from time to time it is important that you select the same treadmill and run at the same speed, so select a speed that is comfortable but not too easy. I would recommend selecting a speed that is a whole number, e.g. 10km/h, 12km/h, 14km/h etc
2 Remember, you need to be filming in high speed mode 120 or 240 fps to make it more accurate.
3 Find a part of the video when you've settled into your running stride.
4 Forward the video frame by frame to a frame where the right foot makes clear contact with the treadmill belt. Make a note of this frame number = Right Foot Contact (RFC)
5 Advance the video to the last frame where the foot is in contact with the treadmill belt. Make a note of this frame number = Right Foot Toe-Off (RFTO)
6 Calculate Right Foot Contact Time by finding the difference in frame numbers (RFTO - RFC) and dividing this by the frame frequency.
Example RFC = frame 100, RFTO = frame 160, Video frame rate = 240fps
RFCT = (160-100)/240 = 0.25
7 Now advance the video to the first frame where the Left foot makes contact with the treadmill belt = Left Foot Contact (LFC) and the last frame of foot contact = Left Foot Toe-off (LFTO)
Example LFC = frame 200, LFTO = 255
As above Left foot contact time LFCT = (255- 200)/240 = 0.229 s
8 The Flight time is from Right foot toe-off to Left foot contact is calculated as
Example LFC = 200, RFTO = 160
Flight time (Right to Left) = (200 - 160)/240 = 0.167s
9 The Step Length from Right foot toe-off to Left foot contact is the distance the treadmill belt travels during the one complete step (i.e. from Right foot toe-off to Left foot toe-off, or Right foot contact to left foot contact). Step distance is equal to the treadmill speed multiplied by the step time (We need to convert the treadmill speed in km/h into m/s before we do this calculation)
Example Treadmill Speed (14km/h) = 14 / 3.6 = 3.889 m/s
StepTime = (LFC - RFC) / 240 = (200 - 100)/240 = 100/240 = 0.417s
Step Length = Speed x Step Time = 3.889 x 0.417 = 1.62m
10 We calculate step frequency as 1 / step time = 1/0.417 = 2.4 Hz
11 We repeat these steps for further foot contacts to calculate flight time, step length and step frequency (left foot to right foot).

chunk.content:
When analyzing the ski action we need to consider when and how force is being applied to the handles, ensuring that large body movements have a direct translation of force and velocity into the handles. The skill has been broken down into Initiation, Overcoming Inertia, Arm Pull and Recovery phases, (see table 3).
Phase breakdown and technical description for the SkiErgg
Initiation
This is about getting yourself in a comfortable stable position with feet shoulder width apart, set back at a distance that allows the athlete to get full extension of the arms and legs. It goes without saying that the handles should be held correctly to rest the base of the hand on the lip of the handle to give it more contact area and support for generating force. This stance position should optimize the range on motion that the athlete can apply force. If the athlete is too close, then they'll struggle to utilize forward flexion of the trunk.
Overcoming Inertia
The start of each pull is often a source of inefficiency. The biggest asset an athlete has at the start of the pull is their body weight, and this can be used to overcome inertia in the flywheel. Athletes should feel some resistance in the cord before using gravity to drop into the stroke. Reviewing sagittal plane video footage of the skiing action we can check if the hip and knees have started to flex before the handles have completed their recovery.
If the center of mass has started to move downwards while the handles to move upwards (or the shoulders are still extending) then the ability to overcome inertia through the athlete's body weight has been lost. This is effectively 'leakage' where limbs have gone through some of their range with applying force to the handles. This ineffective aspect of technique may also mean that the athlete has to perform more strokes and/or use a lower resistance.
Checking for 'leakage' in the early phase of overcoming inertia.
Arm Pull
When the hands start their downward motion, we are looking for a smooth and connected path of movement that transfers energy from one body segment to another. This path of movement starts proximally (close to the center of mass) and follows a sequence through to the distal segment (the hand in the case of skiing). We would see a build-up in speed of joint centers starting from the hip to the shoulder, to the elbow, then to the wrist and hand.

chunk.content:
Effective transfer of force to the handles requires the shoulders, elbows and wrists to brace isometrically until they are required to extend. The pull should end when the hands are alongside the thighs rather extending behind the body, (as no addition force will be applied at this point and it prolongs the start of the recovery).
Recovery
The athlete should start to stand tall into the starting stance as the arms finish their pull. The arm recovery shouldn't be rushed, use it to breath and compose ready for the next pull. The recovery path of the arms should follow the shortest and most direct path, the butterfly action should be avoided as it places greater stress on the shoulders stabilizing muscles. It's imperative not to start the pull until the arms are fully recovered and some tension is felt in the cord.
In summary, key technical points for the 1000m Ski are:
- The start or set position should optimize the range in which you can pull and generate force. With the shoulders and elbows extended hold the handles and stand upright, this will dictate your foot position.
- To provide more stability adopt a shoulder-width stance.
- Initiate the pull through trunk/hip flexion and knee flexion, keeping shoulders and elbow fixed (utilizing gravity to overcome the flywheel inertia)
- As some momentum is generated, brace the core and pull down and backwards through shoulder flexion allowing a moderate amount of elbow flexion. As the upper arm approaches a vertical position extend the elbow to complete the pull. The wrist should stay firm throughout the entire pull to create an effective transfer of force. This proximal to distal movement sequence transfers energy from the large muscle of the trunk through to the shoulder, arm and wrist to create more force and velocity to the handle.
- Keep the recovery in the sagittal plane in the most direct route to the starting position (avoiding the 'butterfly') by reversing the order of the pull (elbow flexion, shoulder extension, hip extension and knee extension).
- For efficiency, set an appropriate resistance that allows you to find the balance between distance per stroke (force) and stroke rate (velocity). You should feel some initial resistance at the start of each pull.

chunk.content:
The sled push is the station that requires the most 'strength', requiring the athlete to push an object that is invariably heavier than themselves. The phase breakdown and technical description can be seen in table 4.
Technique Choice and Set Position There are 3 noticeable techniques that HYROX athletes adopt (figure 8), a) arms extended with only the hands contact the poles, b) with elbows highly flexed with hands and shoulders contacting the poles, and c) the 'wrap around' where the athlete leans over the sled, shoulders ahead of the poles, with a low hand grip and the forearms providing the contact against the poles. Whichever technique is adopted there are a few important considerations to make the movement efficient.
Sled push techniques
A solid contact must be made with the sled, but athletes should avoid 'resting' body weight or directing force downwards as this increases downward force and increases friction on the sled (figure 9a compared to 9b). Every joint from the ankle through to the wrists has to be firm to transfer all the muscular force into the ground and sled.
The arms extended technique has more scope for 'leakage' as the force vector from the ground (green arrow) will not pass through the point of contact with the sled. This technique also has the potential to place the foot ahead of the center of mass and this may cause a sticking point or 'dead zone' if the sled does not have enough momentum. This technique may not be conducive for taller athletes as their arms will inevitably be pointing downwards, directing force into the ground and increasing friction.
Force application vectors and friction forces in the sled push techniques.
Double Foot Contact and Drive
The objective is to keep the sled moving and avoid having to restart with a stationary sled. It is desirable therefore to have a greater percentage of time with double foot contact, as this reduces the maximal effort in single foot contact phases. Effectively this means shorter and more frequent steps.
It's imperative that the shoes have good grip as this dictates how horizontally inclined the athlete can get without slipping. It is important that the heel fits snugly in the shoe, as any slippage also affects the transfer of force into the sled. Athletes need to drive the sled forwards, but sufficient vertical force has to be applied to overcome the body weight resting on the sled.

chunk.content:
Single Foot Drive and Rear Foot Recovery To maintain momentum the recovery leg should be in the correct position to apply a pushing force upon contact with the ground, the ankle should be directly below or slightly behind the hip joint (figure 9c and d compared to 9a and b). If the athlete makes foot contact on the forefoot then the ankles need to be firm and not collapse to transfer the force generated through the hip and knee. We can see in figure 10 that as the athlete enters single foot stance the ankle dorsi flexes by 10 degrees as the knee extends by 11 degrees, thereby reducing the effectiveness of force generated through the knee joint and the sled only moving 7cm in the initial single leg push. Not surprisingly the force required by the calf muscles to
resist dorsi flexion is extremely large, so eccentric strength of the calf muscles and conditioning of the achilles tendon are important to avoid injury.
Single foot contact and 'leakage'
In summary, key considerations for the sled push:
- Resting body weight on the sled and directing force downwards increases the load of the sled and ultimately increases the friction force. This means you have to generate more horizontal pushing force to move the sled.
- Athletes should predominately push forwards but also upwards to offset the body weight that is being supported by resting on the sled.
- To maintain momentum the recovery leg should be in the correct position to apply a pushing force upon contact with the ground, the ankle should be directly below or slightly behind the hip joint.
- If the athlete makes forefoot contact then the ankles need to be firm. If the ankle dorsi-flexes while the knee and hips extend the transfer of force to the ground will be compromised. The calf muscles and the achilles tendon need to be conditioned through eccentric and plyometric exercises to condition them appropriately for this task.
- Shoes should give sufficient traction to avoid slipping when pushing. Greater traction gives the potential to generate higher horizontal force. The Shoe should also be a good fit with a heel support to prevent it from sliding out of the back.

chunk.content:
From an efficiency perspective the difference between the sled push and the sled pull is that the it is almost impossible to maintain momentum of the sled in the pull. Every repetition of the sled pull is from a stationary position. The only way to maintain momentum would be to pull with one arm at a time continuously which would require superior upper body and arm strength.
Given this constraint athletes opt for either a static technique where the feet remain fixed at the front of the box and pull the sled through repetitions of leaning back, leg drive and arm pull, or they adopt the pull and walk technique. The advantage of the pull and walk technique is that the sled is pulled further each repetition, and the athlete can maintain momentum for longer with less repetitions.
Both the static and the pull and walk techniques follow very similar movements and principles in the first two phases of the technical breakdown (Table 5 and figure 11), with the additional two phases for the pull and walk technique. The choice of the two techniques
resides on the athlete's upper and lower body strength and how fatigued they are entering this station.
Set Position In the set position the athlete should squat into a deep position and reach for the rope with dry hands (to prevent any slipping of the rope through them). It is important that the center of mass is behind the heels, which is achieved by ensuring the shins are vertical, not inclined forwards. With both feet firmly planted on the floor the athlete is in a favorable position to overcome the sled's inertia.
Overcome Inertia and Pull
The most efficient way to get the sled moving is for the athlete to use their body weight against the sled by leaning backwards, working with gravity. Bracing the knees to create stability and rotating the trunk backwards while keeping the arms extended creates movement in the sled. Momentum of the sled is increased by the athlete then driving upwards and backwards through knee and hip extension. The shoes must provide a high level of traction to allow the athlete to lean back and drive upwards without slipping.
Walk and Arm Pull The sleds momentum is maintained by keeping tension in the rope and walking backwards to the end of the box, with a final pull with the arms to maximize the pull distance.

Recovery Walking back to the front of the box to find new rope is an opportunity to breath before setting up and preparing for the next repetition. Figure 11 shows that for this athlete he pulls the sled 2.34m in one pull, meaning he would take almost 6 pulls to get the sled completely into the box.
Movements in the Sled Pull
One thing that is not often considered is that as the sled gets closer on each pull the angle of the rope at the start of the pull becomes more inclined. This means that the athlete can't direct as much force horizontally, so each pull progressively gets harder as the athlete gets more fatigued.
Rope inclination (and line of force application) as the sled is pulled closer.

chunk.content:
Before we examine the technical movements of the burpee broad jump it is useful to break the distance per repetition down its constituent parts and identify the relative contributions of each. Figure 13 breaks the burpee broad jump distance into 6 components.
Breakdown of the Burpee broad jump distance
We measure an athlete's broad jump distance from the toe line at take-off to the heel on landing, but in terms of distance covered on the ground per repetition we also need to add the length of the athlete's foot. The rules now state that athletes can place the palm of the hand 30cm in front of the toes and recover the feet after the burpee to the fingertips, so the maximum distance per repetition is:
BBBJ Distance = Broad Jump Distance + Foot Length + 30cm + Hand Length
The broad jump distance can be broken down into 3 separate distances, the take-off distance, flight distance and touchdown distance. Of these the flight distance is the largest, the take-off distance next and then the touchdown distance. The flight distance is governed by projectile motion, where horizontal speed, vertical speed and projection angle of the center of mass dictate that distance the center of mass travels during the flight phase (figure 14). Landing in crouched position places the center of mass at a lower height than at take-off and this can lengthen the flight distance.
The broad jump
The phase breakdown and technical description for the burpee broad jump is presented in table 6.
The broad jump
Start Position and Burpee
The rules are that the hands should be behind the start line and a burpee must be performed before the broad jump, making sure the chest touches the floor.
Recover into Start Position
After the burpee, the athlete needs to bring the toes up alongside the fingertips, if they do not, they are losing distance. The athlete in figure 14 has lost distance by only bringing the toes to the palm of the hand. Athletes can reduce this loss through good flexibility in the lower back, hips, knees and ankles. Some athletes find bringing one leg through to the fingertip at a time helpful to optimize their starting foot position. The two footed jump recovery may be quicker, but the reality is for most athletes they will not be sufficiently flexible to get both feet alongside the fingertips. The choice of which recovery to perform is then based on the trade-off between performing one or 2 more repetitions of sacrificing time in the single leg recovery.

chunk.content:
Following the foot recovery athletes should take advantage of already having a range of movement in which to extend and drive into the broad jump. Standing upright to then initiate a countermovement requires the athlete to shift the center of mass through a range working against gravity which has both time and energy costs. The start position for the broad jump should therefore be the low position where the trunk is inclined forwards and knees are flexed.
Countermovement (optional)
From the low starting/recovery position some athletes prefer to keep a rhythm by immediately driving forwards into the broad jump take-off. Other athletes prefer to make a small countermovement and retract their straightened arms and swing them forwards to load the muscles and tendons to initiate the stretch shorten cycle. Performing a countermovement will add time to the contact phase, but the trade-off may be slightly longer flight distance due to the increased force and impulse they can generate to increase the velocity at take-off. It is worth experimenting and comparing times and the 'feel' of the continuous movement versus the addition of a countermovement for individual athletes.
Drive and Leap
Rotating forwards to shift the center of mass ahead of the toes is a good way off using gravity to initiate the start of the drive into the leap. This rotation movement effectively puts the athlete off balance and prompts fast muscle contractions to extend. Horizontal and vertical impulse are generated through the coordinated sequence of proximal to distal movements from hips to knees and then ankles. The flight distance is governed by the horizontal and vertical velocities of the center of mass at the instant the toes leave the ground (projectile motion).
Taller athletes have the advantage of being able to naturally develop longer take-off distances providing they fully extend the body at take-off. This places the center of mass further in front of the toes. From a visual perspective we can consider the body inclination angle, the line drawn
from the toes through the shoulders (figure 15), and we would expect it to be close to 45 degrees. If the inclination angle is more vertical then both take-off distance and flight distance will be compromised. If the angle is more horizontal then the take-off distance will be increased but the flight distance will be compromised. Athletes should try to optimize their take- off distance for their height, but the main determinant of the broad jump distance is the flight distance.
Land and layout

key_facts.fact: Following the foot recovery athletes should take advantage of already having a range of movement in which to extend and drive into the broad jump.
Standing upright to then initiate a countermovement requires the athlete to shift the center of mass through a range working against gravity which has both time and energy costs.
The start position for the broad jump should therefore be the low position where the trunk is inclined forwards and knees are flexed.

Countermovement (optional)
From the low starting/recovery position some athletes prefer to keep a rhythm by immediately driving forwards into the broad jump take-off.
Other athletes prefer to make a small countermovement and retract their straightened arms and swing them forwards to load the muscles and tendons to initiate the stretch shorten cycle.

Performing a countermovement will add time to the contact phase, but the trade-off may be slightly longer flight distance due to the increased force and impulse they can generate to increase the velocity at take-off.
It is worth experimenting and comparing times and the 'feel' of the continuous movement versus the addition of a countermovement for individual athletes.

Drive and Leap
Rotating forwards to shift the center of mass ahead of the toes is a good way off using gravity to initiate the start of the drive into the leap.
This rotation movement effectively puts the athlete off balance and prompts fast muscle contractions to extend.
Horizontal and vertical impulse are generated through the coordinated sequence of proximal to distal movements from hips to knees and then ankles.

chunk.content:
Landing in a partially flexed position with trunk inclined forwards will extend the flight distance and position the hands closer to the ground ready for them to contact the ground 30cm in front of the toes.
Body inclination angle in the broad jump
In summary, for effective burpee broad jump execution
- The flight distance in the broad jump forms the largest component of the broad jump distance which is where athletes really express their power.
- Optimize the take-off distance with a body inclination angle of 45 degrees at the instant of take-off.
- Land in a partially flexed position, forward trunk lean and flexed knees which extends the flight distance and puts the hands closer to the ground for the hand plant and burpee.
- Maximize the 30cm tolerance for the hand plant.
- Minimize losses in the recovery from the burpee and get the toes as close to the fingertips as possible. This will require good flexibility in the hips and lower back.
- With respect to efficiency the objective is to develop rhythm and avoid the temptation to go for maximum distance in each jump. Use gravity to roll into the next jump following the recovery from the burpee.
- Experiment with the small countermovement and arm retraction to compare the potential benefits of a longer flight distance against a longer movement time.

The main consideration for the rowing stroke is force generation against the handle involves a push (leg drive) and a pull (arms) and these movements are connected through the torso. The more force applied to the handle equates to greater distance per stroke. All things equal taller athletes will have an advantage as they have a longer stroke length to apply force to the handle. We also need to remember that distance is still being accumulated when the flywheel is still turning during the recovery. This means that athletes can take their time in the recovery to breath, compose themselves and prepare for the next pull. The recovery time should be double the time of the pull, giving the fan time to slow down sufficiently for you to apply a high level of force at the onset of the next pull. Lower strokes rates (20 - 25) are preferable over high rates (>28) as athletes get a greater distance per pull and reserve energy for the rest of the race.
The phase breakdown and technical description of the rowing stroke is outlined in table 7.
Set Position / Catch
Adopting a highly flexed posture in the set position provides the range of movement and the firm base of support against the foot plates in which to develop a high level of force. Knees should be together and the elbows extended outside them. A lack of ankle flexibility can restrict the ability to get the shin vertical in the starting position and will reduce the length of the drive. Gently cupping the handle provides sufficient force to hold the handle without the additional muscular effort to grip the handle tightly. Gripping the handle tightly also has implications for blisters and lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow).
The catch position can cause lower back problems for some athletes with poor hip and pelvis mobility and tight hamstrings, as the pelvis rotates posteriorly causing excessive lumbar flexion. Athletes should aim to adopt a neutral pelvis to offset this risk.
Drive
