To apply high forces against the handle you have to generate a kinetic chain, building speed into the handle through a proximal to distal sequence, starting in the hips and knees, to the shoulders (through trunk extension) to the elbows through shoulder flexion and then to the wrists and hand through elbow flexion. This should be a continuous flow of movement which sequentially adds speed to the handles. We can see this visually in figure 16a, where the velocity of joints peak in a temporal sequence, getting larger from the proximal joints (hip) through to the distal joints (wrist). There is evidence of some lag in wrist speed for the athlete in figure 16a which could be due to elbow extension at the onset of the pull. The handle should follow a straight path from onset to the end of the pull into the upper abdomen.
In contrast figure 16b shows an uncoordinated movement pattern where the build-up in speed of the wrist is delayed in a disconnected movement. This is indicative of a common mistake where the knees extend and the seat moves backwards but the handle does not follow. This is effectively 'slipping' and is an ineffective use of the available range of knee extension that could be used to apply force to the handle. The legs must be the main force producer at the onset of the pull, the arms should be fully extended and the trunk has to engage to create the stable platform to impart the force on the handle. Forward flexion of the trunk and shoulder protraction are signs of leakage in early force application and will create a delay in the build-up of speed into the handle.
Coordinated (a) and uncoordinated (b) proximal to distal sequence and velocity generation to the handle.
Recovery

chunk.content:
A common mistake is that athletes are so eager to recover and start the next pull (with a high stroke rate, > 30) they do not utilize the full distance per stroke, remember that distance is still being accumulated when the fan is rotating. The recovery should take twice as long as the pull, so slowing the recovery down will also provide time for the athlete to breathe and compose themselves for the next stroke. They should aim to be at the catch position at the time the rotation of the fan has slowed down sufficiently for them to express their preferred level of force against the handle. Athletes should experiment with the damper levels and stroke frequency to be more purposeful in every stroke. The common error of lifting the handle over the knees can be solved easily with a slow recovery and performing to the stroke movements in reverse, extend the arms, lean forwards to pass the handle beyond the knee, then flex the knees. Avoiding unnecessary movements is more economical.
In summary, the main considerations for rowing are
- The rowing action involves both a push (leg drive) and a pull (arms). The trunk is required to provide a stable platform to transfer the leg drive to the handle. A leg drive that doesn't transmit to the handle is 'leakage' and an ineffective use of the leg muscles and results in the movement being more focused on the upper body.
- The aim is to transfer all the muscular effort into the handle, using a resistance level that strikes a balance between distance per stroke and stroke frequency.
- With the arms extended with a loose 'cupped' grip on the handle in the start position (trunk forward, knees flexed), the initial leg drive must be accompanied with the pull on the handle.
- Be mindful of the risk for lower back strain, adopt a neutral pelvis position at the catch position.

chunk.content:
The challenge with the farmers carry is to make this exercise as relaxed as possible while maintain a good grip on the kettlebell. This station requires significant muscular endurance in the wrist and forearms muscles and the movements made during walking should not make this burden worse. The phase breakdown and technical considerations are outlined in table 8.
Set position and hold
In order to reduce muscular effort through the shoulders and torso the kettlebells should be in horizontal alignment with the shoulders and hips, i.e. trunk upright, arms extended by the side. This reduces the turning effect of the kettlebells and the need to counteract their weight through muscular effort.
Single leg stance and recovery
When walking the time when both feet are in contact with the ground accounts for approximately 20% of the gait cycle, with left and right foot contacts accounting for 40% each. The time spent supporting the body weight and additional weight of the kettlebells is more challenging during single leg stance than when supported on both legs.
As the athlete begins to walk with kettlebells by the side of the body moving into single leg stance inevitably creates a turning moment around the hip joint of the support leg. This turning moment will have the tendency for the pelvis to drop on the opposite side. Greater eccentric hip abductor strength and strong postural are required to counteract the pelvic drop and attempt to keep the trunk upright. Whilst excessive lateral trunk flexion should be avoided, small lateral ranges of movement towards the side of support will shift the center of mass directly over the support foot and reduce the moment arm of this combined weight. This will reduce the muscular effort required of the hip abductors. Planting the foot more medially towards the midline of the body in a more adducted position would create a greater moment on the support leg hip joint, so maintaining a normal walking gait may be preferable.
Greater grip strength will be required if the kettlebells jolt in the hands due to heel impact when contacting the ground. This would be worse when running versus walking, so keeping steps lengths short and cushioning foot contacts will reduce the muscular strain holding the kettlebells.
If the athlete's grip strength, postural control and hip strength are good then fast walking, shuffling or running are very much an option. However shorter steps mean that double leg stance is more frequent which is preferable for weight distribution and creating more dynamic stability.
Turning moment about the hip in single leg stance.
Double leg stance

chunk.content:
The double leg stance phase provides the opportunity to shift the combined center of mass of the body and kettlebells slightly more laterally to the side of the next single leg support, to reduce its turning moment about the hip. This would be done by pushing laterally into the ground rather than actively flexing the trunk laterally.
In summary, when performing the farmer walk
- It is important to keep steps short, as placing the foot further in front or behind the center of mass places more demand on postural control and pelvic stability.
- If athletes want to walk faster, they should initially focus on step frequency as this places the feet closer to the body and reduces the time interval between periods of double foot support, creating more dynamic stability.
- Athletes with exceptional postural control, pelvic stability and grip strength can complete the 200m faster by increasing step frequency in walking, shuffling or running.

chunk.content:
The sandbag lunge presents a number of challenges including eccentric control in the quadriceps, stability and muscular endurance. The number of repetitions are typically between 100 to 150 repetitions dependent on the athletes height or leg length. In this section we will propose a method to determine an athletes minimal / optimal number of repetitions and reducing the challenges of overstriding.
The phase breakdown and technical description of the lunge is outlined in table 9.
Starting Position
It is important that the sandbag rest securely on the athletes' shoulders with good contact, making it easier to miminiZe any movement of this additional load on the body. In this way the center of mass of the sandbag remains in a constant position throughout the 100m.
Lean into the Lunge
Leaning forwards with the trunk to position the sandbag above the hips shifts the combined center of mass of the trunk and sandbag forwards ahead of the hips and closer to the toe. A small movement forwards then puts the athlete off balance and allows them to use gravity to fall into the contact.
Contact and control
The nature of the lunge movement means that the athlete will brake to zero velocity on every repetition, albeit it momentarily. As with running, ideally the athlete should aim to reduce the braking impulse and high impact forces by the way they connect with the ground. Overstriding with extended leg ang knee joint with a heel contact will elevate the impact force and braking force and require greater eccentric control of the quadriceps. It is also important to control any medial rotation of the knee, or valgus movement during this contact phase to avoid the risk of patellar-femoral pain.
Figure 18 presents the sandbag lunge 'S-O-S', highlighting the 'safe', 'optimal' and 'strong' options for step length. The 'optimal' step length is effectively the length of the thigh plus the length of the foot. It describes the position where the thigh of the lead leg is horizontal with the knee flexed to 90 degrees and the shin vertical, combined with the rear leg thigh adopting a vertical position. The legs form a rectangle shape with 90 degree angles. Measuring from the toe of the rear leg to the toe of the front leg in this position gives you the step length. Dividing the 100m by this step length will give you the suggested minimum number of lunges, half will be allocated to each leg. The rationale for this suggestion relates to the drive phase.
Rear leg drive

chunk.content:
From this midpoint in the lunge where velocity is momentarily zero the athlete has to drive upwards and forwards to an upright stance. This movement should be initiated from the rear foot plantar flexing followed by knee extension. Effectively this pushes the front knee into more flexion, raises and shifts the athletes center of mass forward, providing enough momentum to overcome inertia. A strong rear leg drive will rotate the center of mass over the foot of the front leg making it easier to perform a single leg squat to stand upright (figure 19a). Now consider the challenge of overstriding (in addition to the higher impact force and braking impulse).
If the athlete doesn't have enough strength in the rear leg to rotate the center of mass over the front foot, it will reside in the behind the heel which is more difficult to rise from when the rear foot has left the ground (figure 19b). The longer step length in figure 19b was 20% longer than the suggested 'optimal' of figure 19a, and is likely to be at the limit of the
athlete's comfort due to the center of mass residing behind the heel and the full range of extension he has gone through to the instant of rear foot take-off. If the center of mass was further behind the heel this would fall into the 'dead zone' which is difficult to raise from and be a sticking point that would affect the momentum of the athlete.
In summary, considerations for the sandbag lunge are:
- The lunge movement requires good eccentric control in the quadriceps and gluteal muscle to lower the rear knee to the ground
in a controlled manner and avoiding knee valgus and medial rotation of the lead leg knee.
- The 100m sandbag lunge time will be dependent on the step length and step frequency. An 'optimal' step length was suggested based on the avoidance of getting stuck in the 'dead zone'.
- Longer step lengths, typically 20% greater than the suggested optimal will require greater flexibility in the hips and greater strength and power to develop the momentum to get the center of mass over the front foot.

chunk.content:
The main objective of the wall balls is to impart the minimum amount of vertical velocity onto the medicine ball for it to hit the target. The minimum amount of vertical velocity is dependent on the height the medicine ball must travel from the height of release to the target. Taller athletes who have a greater reach height are at an advantage as the do not need to generate as much power and kinetic energy into the medicine ball as athletes with a lower reach height. They do however have to lift the medicine to a greater height, so the time per repetition may not be significantly different. The exercise has been broken down into 4 phases (table 10).
Hold In order to propel the medicine ball it is important to establish a firm hold in a position that facilitates a good transfer of force against it. Positioning the hands halfway between the center and bottom of the medicine ball satisfies these requirements.
Performing 100 repetitions of this exercise is demanding enough so avoiding any additional muscular effort in supporting the medicine ball is essential. Bringing the medicine ball close to the chest reduces the turning moment it produces in the lower back and supporting it through contact with the chest reduces the muscular effort in the arms and shoulders that would be required to hold it in front of the body.
Standing approximately 1.0m to 1.5m away from the target allows for some forward travel of the medicine ball and gives a better sighting of the target. The ball will drop in close proximity without the need to reach out for it, retrieve it if it drops to the ground, or land on the athlete's head if too close.
Countermovement With the medicine ball close to the chest athletes should drop into the squat which will initiate the stretch shorten cycle. Adopting a fast 'collapse and catch' approach will create greater eccentric loading stretch in the patellar, quadriceps and achilles tendons. The weight of the medicine ball will enhance the eccentric loading, so developing eccentric strength in the quadriceps in particular will be an asset. Although the rules insist on the hips being lower than the knee at the lowest point, the transition into the upwards movement has to be quick to benefit from the elastic rebound potential. This effect will be lost if the athlete holds the waits in the squat position and will not benefit from the increased force and power in the upwards concentric phase of the drive. Athletes prone to failed repetitions can increase their ankle dorsiflexion range of motion and adopt a wider stance.
Drive

chunk.content:
The drive upwards should follow an uninterrupted sequential path where vertical velocity is progressively built up into the medicine ball. We can see in figure 19 examples of a disconnected (repetition 1) and continuous (repetition 2) movement pattern. The drive phase is denoted from the lines representing maximum knee flexion (MKF) and release. In repetition 1 the wrist reached a velocity of 1.6m/s concurrently with the shoulder and elbow (which is good as they moved together). However the velocity of all the joints drop close to zero which indicates the athlete has reached the standing position. The velocity of the elbow and shoulder then start from close to zero to reach a peak velocity of over 3.2m/s at the point of release (aimed at the lower target), but all of the wrist velocity was achieved through a 'press' of the medicine ball.
In contrast repetition 2 shows a continuous movement without any break in the velocity of the wrist, there is a progressive build up in velocity from the proximal (hips - shoulder) to distal (elbow - wrist). The wrist reached a velocity of 3.7m/s by the point of release (aimed at the higher target). Given that the shoulder reached a peak speed of 1.9m/s the 'press' part of the movement accounted for 1.8m/s. Whilst this is not only more efficient for the shoulders and arms there is also performance advantage in the much lower movement time for the continuous repetition compared to the disconnected repetition. Overall wall ball performance time can therefore be reduced significantly by utilizing gravity to make use of the downward momentum of the medicine and improving
eccentric strength and plyometric ability to enhance the stretch- shorten cycle.
Coordinated and disconnected wall ball movement patterns on velocity
Release and Catch The release height and vertical velocity of the medicine will be different for athletes with different heights and arm lengths. Taller athletes with longer arms will have a higher release point, so they do not need to generate as much velocity onto the medicine ball to reach the target, (smaller flight range, figure 21). The closer proximity to the target will also have a benefit on the accuracy of
hitting the target. Shorter athletes have to apply greater impulse onto the medicine through a shorter range of movement to increase generate a higher vertical velocity for it to reach the target (longer flight range).
Carry and flight ranges in the Wall Balls.
The vertical velocity required to hit the target can be calculated using the equation:
Vertical Velocity of Medicine Ball = (2 x g x Flight Range) (where g = 9.81m/s2)

key_facts.fact: The drive upwards should follow an uninterrupted sequential path where vertical velocity is progressively built up into the medicine ball.
We can see in figure 19 examples of a disconnected (repetition 1) and continuous (repetition 2) movement pattern.
The drive phase is denoted from the lines representing maximum knee flexion (MKF) and release.
In repetition 1 the wrist reached a velocity of 1.6m/s concurrently with the shoulder and elbow (which is good as they moved together).
However the velocity of all the joints drop close to zero which indicates the athlete has reached the standing position.

The velocity of the elbow and shoulder then start from close to zero to reach a peak velocity of over 3.2m/s at the point of release (aimed at the lower target), but all of the wrist velocity was achieved through a 'press' of the medicine ball.

In contrast repetition 2 shows a continuous movement without any break in the velocity of the wrist, there is a progressive build up in velocity from the proximal (hips - shoulder) to distal (elbow - wrist).
The wrist reached a velocity of 3.7m/s by the point of release (aimed at the higher target).
Given that the shoulder reached a peak speed of 1.9m/s the 'press' part of the movement accounted for 1.8m/s.

Whilst this is not only more efficient for the shoulders and arms there is also performance advantage in the much lower movement time for the continuous repetition compared to the disconnected repetition.

chunk.content:
From this we can calculate the amount of kinetic energy that the athlete needs to impart onto the ball:
Kinetic Energy = 0.5 x mass of ball x Vertical Velocity2
We can see in table 11 that the cumulative effect of performing 100 repetitions can create a significant increase in the amount of kinetic energy required to perform this station, particularly in the men's pro division where the mass of the medicine ball is 9kg.
So, does this mean that taller athletes have an advantage? The downside to being taller is that more work has to be performed in lifting the medicine ball through a greater range:
Work Done in Lifting (Potential Energy) = (mass of ball x g x Carry Range)
If the additional range the taller athlete raises the medicine ball was equal to the differences in flight range then the Total
Mechanical Energy (sum of Potential Energy and Kinetic Energy) would be equal, meaning there would be no advantage. However, this would assume that the lowest point in the squat would be the same, where in reality the medicine ball would be at a slightly greater starting height at the bottom of the squat, (somewhere equivalent to the difference lower leg length, e.g. possibly 10cm. If we assume that our shorter athlete in table 11 has a carry range of 1.2m and the taller athlete 1.5m, then the overall difference in total mechanical energy for the 100 repetitions is significantly smaller than we may have thought.
The advice for athletes of shorter stature is therefore to become efficient holding the medicine ball in the right position, making use of the countermovement with eccentric strength and plyometric ability, and reducing the repetition movement time by a continuous proximal to distal movement in the drive phase.
Mechanical energy considerations in the Wall Balls for athletes of different stature, gender and open v pro weights
The later the medicine ball is caught on its downward decent the greater the velocity (and momentum) it will have. If it is caught well in front of the body this will require more muscular effort in the arms, shoulders and torso to control it. For this reason, the position where the athlete stands is critical to been able to catch the ball slightly above the head and close to the axis of the body, without the need to reach out. The athletes can cushion the medicine ball and carry its momentum through knee flexion as they go directly into the next repetition thereby saving time.

- Hold the medicine ball halfway between the center and bottom and close to the chest to establish a relaxed but firm grip and sufficient leverage to propel it without additional muscular effort holding it further in front of the body.
- Stand approximately 1 - 1.5m away from the base of the target
- Utilize gravity and the momentum of the medicine ball to generate greater eccentric loading in the countermovement that can be used to enhance the force and power in the drive phase (reducing the drive time through the stretch-shorten cycle)
- Do not dwell at the lowest point, otherwise the stretch-shorten effect will dissipate.
- The drive should be a continuous movement from develop velocity onto the medicine ball, transferring energy in a proximal to distal sequence.
- Develop eccentric strength and plyometric ability to be more efficient and reduce movement time per repetition.
- Avoid foul repetitions by improving dorsiflexion range of motion and adopting a wider stance.

unit.title: Assessment of Physical Attributes
unit.unit_summary: Testing identifies whether movement limitations are related to deficiencies in physical qualities. Relevance, validity, and repeatability determine whether test data are useful. HYROX activity demands should guide test selection.

chunk.content:
A limitation to an athlete's ability to execute a movement technically well may be partly due to a deficiency in physical attributes.
For some athletes, deficiencies may result from injury or chronic conditions that have led to asymmetries in joint ranges of movement, strength, power, or musculoskeletal misalignment.
The scope of this module is to provide fundamental principles for testing the physical qualities of athletes and to highlight when referral to appropriate medical professionals for a more detailed musculoskeletal assessment may be recommended.
---

key_facts.fact: A limitation to an athlete's ability to execute a movement technically well may be partly due to a deficiency in physical attributes.
For some athletes, deficiencies may result from injury or chronic conditions that have led to asymmetries in joint ranges of movement, strength, power, or musculoskeletal misalignment.

The scope of this module is to provide fundamental principles for testing the physical qualities of athletes and to highlight when referral to appropriate medical professionals for a more detailed musculoskeletal assessment may be recommended.

chunk.content:
Testing athletes has become something sports scientists and coaches use to monitor improvements in an athlete's capacity.
The data can be used to compare physical attributes before and after a focused training block, or to compare the same time point across previous years.
Testing results can provide useful insights to develop or revise training programs and provide a focus for discussion and reflection with athletes.
The quality of these discussions and their impact depends on several principles that may seem obvious but are not always followed.
---

chunk.content:
To get buy-in from athletes, it is useful to explain the benefit of a test and how the result will inform decision making.
Coaches are asking athletes to sacrifice training time and energy to perform tests, and sometimes to incur additional costs. The coach must therefore be accountable for the relevance of testing.
Testing should match the demands of the sport. Testing a swimmer's speed on a running track rather than in a swimming pool, or testing the aerobic capacity of a discus or hammer thrower, would not be relevant examples.
To ensure relevance, the starting point is generally to conduct a needs analysis. A needs analysis outlines the demands of the sport and identifies specific qualities required for success.
### Needs Analysis and proposed physical assessment test battery

chunk.content:
Validity relates to both the test and the technology used to measure an attribute.
With numerous technologies available, from force platforms to smartphone applications, it is easy to generate numbers. However, the foundation of test validity is often not questioned or critiqued.
Examples to be mindful of:
- The sit and reach test is often regarded as a test of hamstring flexibility, but the results reflect hamstring, lower back and gastrocnemius muscle tightness, as well as the length of the athlete's arms. - Hand-held dynamometers measure force. Typically, the tester holds the device by hand and provides a fixed resistance for the athlete to push against. The score can be compromised if the tester cannot resist the athlete's force, or exaggerated if the tester pushes too hard against the athlete. These devices can be effective if the dynamometer is fixed to apparatus rather than held by the tester. - The angle measured through a video analysis application depends on the alignment of the athlete's movement relative to the camera. - To measure force, the gold standard is technology that uses a force transducer. Other devices may claim to measure force, but estimate it using other technologies such as inertial measurement units (IMUs), displacement transducers or velocity transducers. More accessible or affordable devices should be checked for validity against studies comparing them to the gold standard.
---

The score can be compromised if the tester cannot resist the athlete's force, or exaggerated if the tester pushes too hard against the athlete.
These devices can be effective if the dynamometer is fixed to apparatus rather than held by the tester.
- The angle measured through a video analysis application depends on the alignment of the athlete's movement relative to the camera.
- To measure force, the gold standard is technology that uses a force transducer.
Other devices may claim to measure force, but estimate it using other technologies such as inertial measurement units (IMUs), displacement transducers or velocity transducers.

chunk.content:
Data is only useful if it is accurate, precise and repeatable.
If the same athlete were tested several times within a short duration, without the effects of fatigue, the result should be the same. If not, the data cannot be trusted to support meaningful changes in performance.
If the technology and test are valid, coaches must also consider how the test is conducted and what instructions are given to the athlete. Tests need to be controlled so that as many factors as possible remain the same from one testing session to another.
### Factors affecting repeatability
- **The athlete:** Wherever possible, ensure that on the day of testing the athlete is in a similar state as in the previous test. They should be fresh, ideally after one or two recovery days, perform tests at a similar time of day, have slept well, be hydrated and have eaten sufficiently to perform maximal effort tests. For females, testing within the same phase of the menstrual cycle can also be considered. - **Fatigue:** If multiple tests are performed on the same day, be consistent with the test order and recovery time between tests. After a gentle warm-up for physical and mental preparation, speed and power tests should typically be conducted first, followed by strength tests, with endurance tests at the end. - **Resistance:** Ensure the same load or settings are applied, such as resistance level on the Row Erg, SkiErgg and Strength Erg. - **Surfaces:** Where friction influences the test, such as sled push or pull, use the same sled with the same load, on the same surface and with the same shoes. This may mean performing tests in the same gym or HYROX Performance Center. - **Instructions:** Ensure that the starting position and the way the athlete should perform the test are clear and consistent.
### Additional Structured Unit Content
Principles of Testing Testing athletes has become a 'thing' that sports scientists and coaches do to monitor improvements (hopefully) in an athlete's capacity. The data is used to compare physical attributes before and after a focused training block, or for comparison to the same time point in the previous year(s). Testing results per se can provide good insights to develop / revise training programs and to provide a focus for discussion and reflection with athletes. The quality of these discussions and the impact that they can have depends on a few obvious but not always adhered to principles.

If the same athlete were tested several times within a short duration, without the effects of fatigue, the result should be the same.
If not, the data cannot be trusted to support meaningful changes in performance.
If the technology and test are valid, coaches must also consider how the test is conducted and what instructions are given to the athlete.
Tests need to be controlled so that as many factors as possible remain the same from one testing session to another.

### Factors affecting repeatability
- **The athlete:** Wherever possible, ensure that on the day of testing the athlete is in a similar state as in the previous test.
They should be fresh, ideally after one or two recovery days, perform tests at a similar time of day, have slept well, be hydrated and have eaten sufficiently to perform maximal effort tests.
For females, testing within the same phase of the menstrual cycle can also be considered.
- **Fatigue:** If multiple tests are performed on the same day, be consistent with the test order and recovery time between tests.
After a gentle warm-up for physical and mental preparation, speed and power tests should typically be conducted first, followed by strength tests, with endurance tests at the end.

unit.title: Defining the Terms
unit.unit_summary: The terms defined in this section are important background knowledge for any coach. Understanding what each term means helps coaches better understand what is being presented and discussed throughout the module. The definitions in this section relate to sport science and general fitness. The list is not comprehensive, but it can be used as a reference when a term is used in a way that may be unfamiliar.

The course warns that there is a lot of confusion and incorrect usage of threshold terminology in forums, blogs, and magazine articles.
Some people talk only about "the threshold" or incorrectly call the aerobic threshold the lactate threshold. This is incorrect in the terminology used here because the lactate threshold is typically defined as the same as the anaerobic threshold.
Coaches should understand the two types of threshold so they can deduce from context which threshold people are referring to.

unit.title: 5 Level System

chunk.content:
This framework helps athletes and coaches identify training needs and racing goals across five levels of HYROX readiness.
Each level progresses in gym and running experience, performance standards, and recommended race formats.
### HYROX Fitness Level Overview
| Level | Description | Gym experience | Running volume | Recommended HYROX race level | | 1 | Novice: needs fitness for health | <1 month | <5 km/week | None | | 2 | Beginner | 1-6 months | 10-20 km/week | Relay | | 3 | Open level athlete | 6 months-2 years | 30-45 km/week | Doubles or Open Solo | | 4 | Pro level athlete | 1+ years | 45-60 km/week | Pro Doubles or Pro Solo | | 5 | Elite level athlete | 3+ years | 65+ km/week | Pro Solo or Elite 15 Doubles |
### Performance Structure
Each level is evaluated in four categories:
| Category | Description | | Cardio Guidelines | Endurance and conditioning requirements for the level. | | Strength Guidelines | Strength requirements organized by movement pattern. | | HYROX Exercise Standards | HYROX-specific station standards and movement capacities. | | Time Guidelines | Race-format or division-specific time targets. |
---

The terms defined in this section are important background knowledge for coaches. These terms are used throughout the course and help coaches understand the sport science and general fitness concepts discussed in the module.
This is not a comprehensive list of all possible definitions, but it provides a reference for terms that may be used in ways coaches are not used to.
### Sport Science and Fitness Terms
| Term | Definition / Explanation | | Velocity at VO2Max | The maximum speed at which an athlete is running while at peak VO2Max. | | Aerobic threshold | In this course, the aerobic threshold measured in a blood lactate test is described as the same as ventilatory threshold I measured in an RER test. | | Lactate threshold / Anaerobic threshold | The lactate threshold or anaerobic threshold is described as the same as ventilatory threshold II and roughly the same as functional threshold. | | OBLA | Onset of blood lactate accumulation. The course describes it as essentially the same as the anaerobic threshold. | | MLSS | Maximum lactate steady state. The course describes it as essentially the same as the anaerobic threshold. | | Functional threshold | Described as roughly the same as the lactate threshold / anaerobic threshold. | | FATmax | The range of exercise intensity where fat oxidation is at its highest. It is not super low intensity, but not very high intensity either. Recent research is described as showing that FATmax correlates very well with the aerobic threshold. |
### Threshold Clarification
| Concept | Clarification | | Aerobic threshold vs. lactate threshold | The course warns that people may incorrectly call the aerobic threshold the lactate threshold. | | Lactate threshold usage | The lactate threshold is typically defined as being the same as the anaerobic threshold. | | Context matters | Coaches should understand both threshold types so they can deduce which threshold people mean from context. |

chunk.content:
Defining Terms The terms defined in this portion are important background knowledge for any coach to have. These are terms that will be used in this course and having an understanding of what each thing means will help you better to understand what is being presented and discussed throughout the module. The definitions in this section pertain to sport science and general fitness that coaches should know about. While this is by far, not a comprehensive list of all the definitions, you will be able to save this page to reference when a term might be used in a way you are not used to. Velocity at VO2Max - This is the maximum speed at which you are running while at your peak VO2Max. The aerobic threshold measured in a blood lactate test is the same as the ventilatory threshold I measured in an RER (respiratory exchange ratio) test.
The lactate threshold or anaerobic threshold is the same as the ventilatory threshold II. This is also roughly the same as the functional threshold. Other terms, like the onset of blood lactate accumulation (OBLA) and maximum lactate steady state (MLSS) are essentially the same as the anaerobic threshold One thing to keep in mind is that you will see a lot of confusion about and incorrect usage of these terms on forums, blogs, and even magazine articles. Some people will talk about just "the threshold", or call the "aerobic threshold" the "lactate threshold". This is incorrect, because the lactate threshold is typically defined as being the same as the anaerobic threshold. Make sure that you understand the two types of threshold, so you can deduce which threshold people are talking about from the context of that discussion. Another term to define is FATmax. This is the range of exercise intensity where your fat oxidation is at its highest. It's not a super low intensity but not a very high intensity either. Recent research shows

chunk.content: [0:00:00] Hello coaches and athletes. Welcome back to the level 2 module 4 section 4. This section is about safety, efficacy, and efficiency and how to make that flow for beginner to elite level athletes. Safety, efficacy, and efficiency is a pattern of how to effectively teach and progress athletes [0:00:22] along the scale. So you want to have high level movement quality when working with an athlete and you want to work with the natural biomechanics that their bodies use to produce strength and power and speed and it should be held paramount by any fitness program. And the way you do that [0:00:46] is that you first deal with athletes, understand that safety is the priority. So you want to deal with if you have an athlete that is having trouble getting fully deep into the squat, your first movement is to teach them to get as far as they can safely. And then [0:01:07] after the safety aspect, you keep working on that range of motion. Before you get into the efficacy, the efficacy would be are they meeting the movement standards, which is where you start to press how far they can get into that. So you worked on the mobility, and then you work on their efficacy. And then the last step is efficiency, where you work on how fast can you actually [0:01:28] move through that range of motion. So I'm here with Hidde Weersma. And Hidde, do you have anything to add on top of how safety, efficacy, and efficiency can be used with movement quality? Yeah, so I think the first thing I always mention is that those three things, especially safety, [0:01:46] is really important. Because one of the things you will hear every coach say is that consistency in training is very important. And you need these three things, especially safety, to be consistent [0:02:02] over time. So I think that's very important for coaches to understand why these things are so important. And another reason I think those three are very important is a lot of athletes, [0:02:18] they find training really fun because you can see progression in what you are doing. And therefore, when it's not safe and you get injured, it's of course very frustrating. But when you're not noticing that you are improving in the things that you actually want to improve on, then the fun can [0:02:39] also disappear a little bit. So I think those three things are very important for those reasons, to keep consistent, but to also have fun in training and to really achieve your goals. Yeah, I agree with that a lot. And I've always said this with our elite athletes too, is that the best ability an athlete can have is availability. [0:03:00] When you're available, you don't get injured, and you're consistent with it, exactly like you talked about. It allows you to be consistent. It lets you stack one day on top of another day, on top of another day, until you have a good week, followed by another good week, and then all of a sudden it's a good month, good month, to good month, to good year. [0:03:19] And then all of a sudden, before you know it, you have five years stacked on top of each other, and it really just lets you progress higher and higher. So by following these tenets of safety, efficacy, and efficiency, it really is like triage as well. If I have an athlete who [0:03:39] just wants to go fast, I have to slow them down to make sure they're safe first. If they have a broken piece in their chain of movements, then that's a liability for injury. I need to fix that. If they move safely through these movements, but they're not hitting the standards, [0:03:57] I need to fix them hitting the standards, because that's going to be the efficacy piece. Only after those first two things are fixed do I go into the efficiency. And efficiency is how quickly and what's the best way to move through that range of motion that we've defined. [0:04:14] So the coaches in this module need to understand how a body should move naturally with somebody's biomechanics. They need to be able to identify weaknesses in a chain of movements. They need to be able to assess the points of performance for any of the exercises that the [0:04:33] athletes will perform. They need to be able to identify common faults and how to correct them. And then to see how athletes move, if it will result in any like repetitive use injury or [0:04:50] something with that type of movement pattern they're using. So in the later sections, we'll go over those movement patterns, but is there anything you would add to that type of list of how a coach should address approaching these athletes? Yeah, definitely. So I think the [0:05:08] very important addition is maybe more practical takeaway. So the three questions I really like to ask myself with every change I make in a training program is to start, is this the safest way for the athlete to perform this at race intensity? Then the second one is, will this [0:05:29] adjustment actually make them faster or improve station execution? And the last one is, does this change reduce wasted effort or unnecessary fatigue? chunk.content:
Safety means minimizing the risk of injury or harm during exercise. This should be the primary focus of any coach. Coaches must ensure that the athletes under their care are not injured because of lack of care or neglect.
### Why Safety Matters
No fitness goal is worth pursuing if the method consistently results in injury or long-term health compromise.
A safe program ensures that athletes can train consistently over time. Consistency is the only path to sustainable results.
### Safety Examples
- Coaches should teach proper technique before adding load or intensity. - Coaches and athletes should scale movements to match the athlete's ability level. - Coaches should avoid movements or loading schemes known to cause frequent injuries when the athlete is unstable, lacks mobility to complete the exercise, or is ill-prepared to perform the movement.
---

key_facts.fact: Safety means minimizing the risk of injury or harm during exercise.
Coaches must ensure that the athletes under their care are not injured because of lack of care or neglect.

### Why Safety Matters
No fitness goal is worth pursuing if the method consistently results in injury or long-term health compromise.
A safe program ensures that athletes can train consistently over time.

### Safety Examples
- Coaches should teach proper technique before adding load or intensity.
- Coaches and athletes should scale movements to match the athlete's ability level.
- Coaches should avoid movements or loading schemes known to cause frequent injuries when the athlete is unstable, lacks mobility to complete the exercise, or is ill-prepared to perform the movement.

chunk.section_title: Safety in Coaching Movement for HYROX
chunk.content:
### Goal
Ensure the athlete can repeatedly complete race movements without breakdown or injury.
### How Safety Applies in HYROX
| HYROX safety factor | Coaching implication | | Repetitive volume | HYROX requires high reps under fatigue, such as 100 wall balls, 200 m farmers carry, and 8.7 km of running. Poor mechanics are exposed and compounded over time. | | Mixed surfaces | Athletes run on concrete, polished floors, or smooth tiles; push sleds on varying friction turf; and carry loads across different surfaces. Coaches must prepare joints and tissues for this variability. | | Fatigue-resilient form | Movements and exercises should be trained with a focus on posture, bracing, and stability under duress. |
### HYROX Safety Examples
- Teach athletes how to brace during sled push and sled pull to protect the spine and shoulders. - Progressively load wall balls and lunges while monitoring knee tracking, glute activation, and posture. - Reinforce controlled transitions into and out of the rower, burpee broad jumps, and similar movements to avoid ankle or wrist tweaks.
---

chunk.content:
Efficacy is the capacity to produce the intended result. The goal could be fat loss, strength gain, improved VO2 max, or sport performance.
Efficacy also extends to the ability to achieve the movement standards for any exercise. This comes after safety because once it is established that an athlete can safely get into the required positions without injury, the athlete should comply with the accepted standards for completing that movement.
For example, a wall ball requires a full squat where the hip crease descends below the horizontal plane made parallel to the floor at the height of the tallest point on the athlete's knee. Efficacy is the ability to meet this standard on every rep.
### Why Efficacy Matters
A program should actually work. Fancy movements or high effort do not always equal results.
Efficacy ensures that the program is aligned with, and produces measurable progress toward, the athlete's goal. Achieving movement standards is also a race requirement and supports better movement patterns in life, promoting health.
### Efficacy Examples
- Use progressive overload to build strength. - Run and re-run a HYROX race year over year to measure progress. - Program in a way that aligns with sport-specific demands, such as HYROX, triathlon, or weightlifting. - Squat below parallel every rep. - Ensure the chest, defined as the imaginary line bisecting the nipples, touches the ground on every burpee rep.
---

chunk.section_title: Efficacy in Coaching Movement for HYROX
chunk.content:
### Goal
Train and cue movement patterns that most directly translate to race-day performance outcomes.
### How Efficacy Applies in HYROX
| HYROX efficacy factor | Coaching implication | | Race-time contribution | Every movement must contribute to a faster overall race time and be in line with the athlete's biomechanics. | | Counted repetitions | Every rep is counted, so there should be no wasted energy expenditure or futile movement. | | Performance-impactful skills | Prioritize skills that strongly affect performance, such as transitions, pacing, sled strategy, and run economy. | | Individual physiology | Coach movement with the athlete's personal physiology in mind, including height, limb length, and background. |
### HYROX Efficacy Examples
- Use short but intense intervals to improve row or SkiErgg power per stroke, not just volume. - Find the most effective grip strategy for farmers carry, such as hook grip versus relaxed grip. - Customize the athlete's wall ball stance and cycle time to maximize reps without burning out. - Optimize time spent on certain race modalities within an easy or zone 2 effort to ensure the athlete has the requisite aerobic base.
---

chunk.content:
Efficiency means achieving results in the least amount of time and effort necessary, without sacrificing safety or efficacy.
Once it is established that an athlete can safely perform a movement, exercise, or program and reach the maximum range of motion required, or once the program leads the athlete toward their goals, intensity and finding the most efficient path to complete the exercise can become the main coaching objective.
### Why Efficiency Matters
Time is limited. Efficient programs respect the athlete's schedule while delivering results.
Efficiency prioritizes functional movements that give a high return on investment. Using the principles of minimum effective dose across exercises and modalities helps athletes achieve their goals within a specified time frame.
Understanding movement biomechanics helps athletes move efficiently so they do not waste energy getting into required positions, while still doing so safely.
### Efficiency Examples
- Choose compound lifts over isolation exercises when appropriate. - Combine strength and conditioning in one session when appropriate. - Improve running mechanics to reduce the energy cost of running, allowing the athlete to run faster or preserve more energy for other stations in a HYROX race.
---

chunk.section_title: Efficiency in Coaching Movement for HYROX
chunk.content:
### Goal
Move in a way that conserves energy and improves output over the entire race, thereby maximizing work with minimal waste.
### How Efficiency Applies in HYROX
| HYROX efficiency factor | Coaching implication | | Race duration and structure | Efficiency is crucial in a roughly 60-90 minute race with 8 stations and 8 runs, especially in transitions, also called the RoxZone. | | Movement economy | Movement economy is equivalent to free speed. Saving even 1-2% of energy per station can mean a minute saved at the end. | | RoxZone execution | Running through the RoxZone and not treating it as a rest area before the run can save 2-4 seconds per transition, which can become roughly 30-60 seconds across the race. | | Waste reduction | Eliminate extra steps, bounces, and unnecessary tension. Move with purpose and always move forward toward the finish line. |
### HYROX Efficiency Examples
- Optimize burpee broad jump rhythm and foot placement to reduce wasted motion. - Teach athletes to move in and out of sleds or ergs quickly without flailing or unnecessary standing. - Focus on breathing and pacing during lunges to conserve energy before the final run and wall balls.
---

chunk.content:
By applying the principles in the order of safety, efficacy, and efficiency, coaches can responsibly progress athletes toward their goals in the least amount of time with fast and efficient movement.
If a training method is safe, it allows for longevity. If it is effective, it delivers the desired result. If it is efficient, it respects time and maximizes return on investment.
### What the Framework Prevents
| Coaching extreme | Why the framework helps | | Overly cautious training that does not drive results | Efficacy ensures training still produces measurable progress. | | Dangerous methods that might be effective but are unsustainable | Safety remains the first filter before performance or intensity. | | Wasted time doing ineffective or inefficient exercises | Efficiency keeps focus on high-value work once safety and efficacy are satisfied. |
### Why This Matters
- Injury risk is high because of fatigue, high volume, and competition intensity. Safety-first coaching allows athletes to compete more frequently. - Every second counts. Movement that is effective, meaning fast and strong, and efficient, meaning energy-saving, can be the difference between podium and middle-of-pack. - Coaching should build toward repeatable execution, not just peak performance once, but consistent results across a full season.
---

chunk.content: So no, you won't be an elite marathoner and weightlifter at the same time-but you can be strong and fast. Think: 5-min mile + 500 lb squat 1:22 half-marathon + 750 lb powerlifting total (women) 2. How to Minimize the Interference Two types of interference: Acute: Fatigue from one session affects the next. Chronic: One session reduces adaptation from another. Smart training strategies: If doing both in a day, separate sessions by 6-8 hours. Do endurance first, then strength (endurance) without a focus on power OR strength first, then short/light endurance. Avoid training the same muscle groups back-to-back.

| Athlete profile | Training emphasis | | Already strong but slow | Focus on velocity and RFD | | Already fast but weak | Build more raw strength |
### How to Train These Qualities for HYROX
#### Build strength first
- Use squats, presses, and deadlifts with progressive overload. - Emphasize full range of motion, controlled eccentric work, and trunk stability.
#### Add power and RFD focus
- **French Contrast Method:** heavy lift plus plyometric combination, such as squats plus hurdle hops. - **Sprint-Lift Pairs:** EMOM structure with AirBike sprints plus power cleans. - **Odd-object and carry work:** sandbags, sleds, and yokes can build applied strength.
#### RFD-specific tips
- Keep repetitions explosive, not slow. - Use isometric pauses to build force production from a static start. - Use plyometrics and short ground-contact jumps to train rapid force expression.
In HYROX, athletes are not just required to be strong. They must express strength fast and repeatedly under fatigue. This is why strength, power, and especially RFD at the start of every effort matter.
### Additional Structured Unit Content
Power examples SkiErgggg & Rowing: Power across the full movement cycle ensures a high velocity, an efficient stroke and a consistent pace. Sled Push & Pull: After you used a high RFD to move it from a dead stop, power allows you to keep momentum and make sure the sleds keep moving with a high velocity Wall balls: Sustained power over the entire rep allows you to throw the ball at the correct height. 2. What Builds Strength, Power, and RFD? Strength is built through: Muscle hypertrophy (bigger fibers = more force potential) Greater motor unit recruitment (neurological adaptation) Progressive overload (gradual increase in demand) Power is developed by combining strength with speed:
Squats, presses, deadlifts, done with progressive overload Emphasize full range, controlled eccentric, and trunk stability Add Power + RFD Focus: French Contrast Method: Heavy lift + plyometric combo (e.g., squats + hurdle hops) Sprint-Lift Pairs: EMOM with AirBike sprints + power cleans Odd-object & carry work: Sandbags, sleds, yokes, which can build applied strength RFD-Specific Tips: Keep reps explosive, not slow Use isometric pauses to build force production off a "static start" Plyometrics and short ground-contact jumps train rapid force expression In HYROX, you're not just strong, you have to express that strength fast and repeatedly, under fatigue. That's why strength, power, and especially RFD at the start of every effort matter so much.

There is more or less a big spectrum, as I just referred to there, where there will be sort of in-between fibers or hybrid fibers, [0:05:46] which we will also talk about shortly. chunk.content: [0:00:00] Hello and welcome to this level 2 course of HYROX 365 and we're with me Dr. Dan Plews [0:00:16] and we are talking about thermoregulation and hydration. So I guess a good place to start with this is talking about the physiology of cooling. [0:00:34] To start off then it's worth noting that of course as we get hotter we do seem to have a greater stress imposed upon us as we exercise. So as you can see on this chart here we have exercising varying temperatures from 4 degrees [0:00:54] to 11 degrees, 21 degrees and 31 degrees and you can see if you just look at heart rate on the right there you can see that at those hotter temperatures especially the 31 is substantially [0:01:12] harder to exercise and we typically see increases in that heart rate as we are exercising at higher temperatures. But what we can see in this diagram is it shows us how a rise in environmental temperatures [0:01:33] sets off a chain reaction that directly affects performance. As ambient temperature increases which is very common in the indoor HYROX environment setting, we see a rise in skin temperature, that heat and that heat gets sensed by the [0:01:52] brain and contributes to an increased thermal perception. In other words we generally feel that little bit hotter and at the same time core body temperature rises triggering a little bit more cardiovascular strain and therefore more [0:02:08] blood is sent to the skin to offload heat which means less blood is then available for the working muscles. And what's important is that these two signals, the thermal perception and the cardiovascular strain come together to elevate perceived exertion. [0:02:26] So the same pace suddenly feels harder and this makes us instinctively reduce our exercise work rate. And that's why therefore it is advantageous to feel cool. And strategies that reduce our thermal perception even without changing core temperature such [0:02:44] as ice towels, menthol rinses or fans for example can preserve performance by keeping RPE lower and that thermal strain that little bit lower also. So in summary it's pretty advantageous to feel cool. [0:03:03] But when it comes to exercising in the heat, humans are actually incredibly well adapted for thermoregulation. So unlike many animals that rely on panting or have limited ability to evaporate heat, [0:03:19] we rely heavily on evaporation and convection to stay cool. And our ability to sweat across most of our body is one of our greatest evolutionary advantages allowing us to regulate temperature effectively even during prolonged intense endurance efforts, [0:03:37] just like we typically see in HYROX. So as we exercise, muscle contractions generate heat, increasing muscle blood flow and overall heat production. If that heat isn't dissipated, it leads to rising core temperatures and declines in performance. [0:03:55] Comparing that to animals like the antelope shown here, for example, their strategies involve panting, reflective fur and limited evaporation. And these mechanisms work well for short sprints, for example, but not for sustained high output [0:04:12] efforts in the heat like we typically would see in a human doing a marathon. But for humans, our advantage lies in being able to pump, in being able to dump heat via sweat evaporation, especially when there's airflow or wind to assist the convections. [0:04:30] So yes, humans are cool, quite literally, and this has unique adaptations. So you can see here, evaporation, convection leads to a nice bit of overall convection [0:04:51] in cooling, provided that heat is dissipated. But when we talk about heat loss during exercise, evaporation is the most effective mechanism available to humans, especially in hot environments. [0:05:08] And here is how it works. So sweat is secreted onto the skin surface, and then when it evaporates, it takes heat with it. But critically, it's not just the sweat sitting on your skin that cools you down. It's the phase change from liquid to vapor that drives heat loss. [0:05:26] And on this diagram here, we can see water molecules moving from the skin into the air. That transfer only happens effectively if the air is dry enough to allow evaporation. So in humid conditions, this process becomes much less efficient. [0:05:45] What you can also notice with the athlete is as they run, convection helps too. So air moving across the skin assists in evaporation by removing the humid air layer near the skin and replacing it with drier air. And this is why airflow from fans, for example, or the running movement, is critical for moving. [0:06:08] And in still air, if you're drenched in sweat, for example, the evaporation slows down dramatically. So in hot conditions, it's not just about how much you sweat, it's about how well that sweat evaporates. But what we do have is we have this competing demand. [0:06:30] And what's highlighted here is the critical challenge when exercising in the heat. And we have this competing blood flow demand between your muscles and your skin. So when you're racing or training hard, your working muscles are crying out for more blood. [0:06:47] And they need it. And they need it to deliver oxygen, clear byproducts and sustain performance. But at the same time when it's hot, your thermoregulatory system is also demanding blood, not for oxygen, but to move heat from your core to your skin surface, where it can be lost via evaporation [0:07:08] as we have just talked about. The problem is, there's only so much blood that can go around. So the blood is constantly juggling, trying to supply the muscles without letting core temperature rise too much. The balancing act increases cardiovascular strain and then can ultimately result in reduced [0:07:28] performance as your system starts to compromise. And the hotter it is, the tougher that compromise becomes. So as you can see, we have the competing demand between the muscles and then also the competing demand of the skin. [0:07:45] However, something really important to understand is human movement is actually also quite inefficient. When we break down nutrients and use that as energy to fuel exercise, only about 20 [0:08:02] to 25% of that energy goes into actual movement, what we call mechanical work. And the rest, well, that is lost as heat. And that means during intense exercise, especially in hot conditions, your body is generating [0:08:18] a massive amount of internal heat. For example, if you're producing about 300 watts of mechanical power on a bike, you're actually generating over 1,200 watts of total metabolic energy, with the majority of that being heat. [0:08:34] So when you're racing in the heat, it's not just the temperature outside that's the problem, it's the heat you're making inside your body that also has to be managed. And the internal load of that can be very, very vast. [0:08:54] But despite how challenging it can feel to race or train in the heat, humans have actually become some of the most advanced cooling animals in the world. But first, we have the ability to sweat from large surfaces almost our entire body, which

chunk.section_title: Audio: REDs A Useful Model, but an incomplete Picture
chunk.content: [0:00:00] A recent paper by Euchendrup et al. criticized the REDS model. It points out, most of the evidence comes from short-term studies, and most real-life athlete data relies on inaccurate energy intake-slash-expenditure measurements. [0:00:16] A big argument is that EA is hard to measure, as athletes under-report food intake by 20 to 60 percent, exercise energy expenditure devices are very inaccurate, fat-free mass FFM estimates vary, and EA fluctuates day-to-day and hour-to-hour. [0:00:39] It is also important to consider the symptoms related to REDS can also be caused by high training load-slash-overreaching, poor sleep, psychological stress or illness or infection, etc., and it doesn't necessarily mean it is caused by under-fueling. [0:01:00] But the authors also do not deny that LEA affects athletes. LEA can impair health and performance, short-term experimental studies clearly show endocrine and metabolic responses, and some athletes do under-fuel, intentionally or [0:01:20] unintentionally. Symptoms attributed to REDS are real, but their causes are multifactorial, and LEA is only one possible contributor. These behaviors and patterns often indicate low energy availability, LEA, or [0:01:39] emerging disordered eating patterns, fear of certain foods or food groups, especially carbohydrates, sudden drop in body weight or body fat, particularly without performance benefit, belief that leaner [0:01:56] equals better performance despite sport-specific demands, reliance on very high-volume, low-energy foods, for example, large amounts of vegetables, to feel full while minimizing calories, fear [0:02:12] of sugar, avoiding it even around training or competition despite its performance benefits. Coaches should stay within their scope of practice and refer athletes to qualified practitioners such as sports dieticians, psychologists, or physicians when assessment or [0:02:32] treatment is needed. Their most powerful role is creating an environment that reduces the risk of underfueling. This includes encouraging proper fueling before and after training, normalizing eating during [0:02:48] sessions and competitions, avoiding the glorification of grind culture or extreme leanness, supporting open judgment-free conversations around food and fueling. The REFUEL study provides evidence that low energy availability can directly [0:03:08] contribute to menstrual disturbances in exercising women. In this trial, athletes with menstrual dysfunction increased their caloric intake without altering training volume, and many subsequently experienced recovery of ovulatory function and normalization of menstrual patterns. In this [0:03:29] study, exercising women with menstrual disturbances increased their daily caloric intake by approximately plus 330 kilocalories per day over a 12-week period. This moderate rise in energy intake was sufficient to restore ovulatory function in many participants, providing strong [0:03:50] evidence that low energy availability is linked to menstrual dysfunction in exercising women.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: What it is and introduction
chunk.content:
Energy Availability is an important concept that can help coaches and athletes understand the long-term effects of underfueling in athletes.
It is especially relevant when athletes or coaches use concepts such as a low-carbohydrate diet or being "as light as possible" for the sport.
Energy Availability (EA) refers to the dietary energy remaining for essential physiological functions after subtracting the energy expended through exercise.
### Energy Availability formula
```text EA = (Energy Intake - Exercise Energy Expenditure) / Fat-Free Mass ```
| Formula element | Meaning | | Energy Intake | Dietary energy consumed by the athlete. | | Exercise Energy Expenditure | Energy expended through exercise. | | Fat-Free Mass | Body mass excluding fat mass. | | Energy Availability | Energy remaining for essential physiological functions after exercise expenditure is subtracted. |
### Visual Note: Daily Energy Balance vs Daily Energy Availability
The visual adapted from Areta et al. (2018) contrasts daily energy balance with daily energy availability.
| Concept | What the visual shows | Coaching interpretation | | Daily Energy Balance | Energy balance from a biological system while maintaining physiological function. The diagram shows daily energy intake compared against components such as RMR, DIT, NEAT, and EEE. | Energy balance describes total intake relative to total expenditure. It does not directly show what energy remains for physiological function after exercise. | | Daily Energy Availability | Energy available to a biological system for maintaining physiological function after subtracting exercise energy expenditure. | EA focuses on the energy left for health, metabolism, hormones, recovery, and adaptation after exercise cost is removed. |
### Energy Availability thresholds
Research indicates that optimal EA is approximately 45 kcal/kg FFM/day and is necessary to support an athlete's health, metabolism, hormonal balance, and training adaptations.
When EA is at or below 30 kcal/kg FFM/day, endocrine and metabolic disturbances begin to appear, including reductions in reproductive hormones, thyroid hormones, and growth-related factors.
Typical signs of Low Energy Availability (LEA) include missed periods for over 3 months, longer menstrual cycles in women over 35 days, and low bone mineral density that can lead to stress fractures.
### Visual Note: Energy availability thresholds for physically active females
The threshold visual states that EA should be calculated by subtracting exercise energy expenditure from energy intake and adjusting for fat-free mass.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: What it is and introduction
chunk.content:
| Energy availability range | Threshold | Interpretation | | Adequate EA | At least 188 kJ/kg FFM/day, equivalent to 45 kcal/kg FFM/day | Recommended to maintain adequate energy for all physiological functions. | | Reduced or sub-clinical EA | 125-188 kJ/kg FFM/day, equivalent to 30-45 kcal/kg FFM/day | Suggested as a tolerable short-term range for athletes aiming for weight loss as part of a well-constructed dietary and exercise regimen. | | Low EA | Less than 125 kJ/kg FFM/day, equivalent to less than 30 kcal/kg FFM/day | Defined as unsafe for optimal bodily function and may lead to unfavorable health outcomes and sport performance. |
Low Energy Availability is the root cause of the physiological disturbances described in RED-S, Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport.
LEA is linked to numerous physiological disruptions, including:
- Menstrual dysfunction - Impaired bone health - Metabolic and hormonal changes - Weakened immunity - Reduced cardiovascular function
Prolonged LEA negatively impacts performance through:
- Reduced glycogen stores - Increased injury risk - Decreased muscle strength - Poorer recovery
### Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport
Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) is a broader clinical condition resulting from chronic or severe low energy availability.
REDs includes a wide range of physiological impairments:
- Altered metabolism - Impaired reproductive function - Decreased bone health - Compromised immunity - Disrupted protein synthesis - Psychological effects
Unlike the Female Athlete Triad, which focused only on low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, and poor bone health, REDs includes both male and female athletes and expands to multiple body systems.
The updated 2023 IOC Consensus emphasizes that REDs is caused by "problematic LEA," meaning LEA that is severe, prolonged, or poorly tolerated due to moderating factors such as high training load, low carbohydrate availability, mental stress, or genetic susceptibility.
### Adaptable LEA vs Problematic LEA
| LEA type | Definition | Typical context | Risk level | | Adaptable LEA | A short-term drop in energy availability that the body can handle without harm. | Planned weight changes or short periods of intensified training. | Lower risk when short-term and reversible. | | Problematic LEA | LEA that lasts longer, is more severe, or happens repeatedly, causing noticeable and potentially long-lasting disruptions across body systems. | Chronic underfueling, repeated energy deficits, poorly tolerated low carbohydrate availability, high stress, poor sleep, or high training load. | Higher risk; more likely to cause symptoms, health problems, and performance impairment. |
Problematic LEA represents a maladaptive response. The degree of harm depends on how deep the energy deficit is, how long it lasts, and how often it occurs. It can differ from person to person and between body systems.

chunk.content:
Measuring Energy Availability in athletes is difficult because there are no standardized methods in the literature yet.
In real-world coaching, it is not easy to measure calories burned during exercise, and most athletes do not know their fat-free mass.
Nevertheless, the concept of EA provides a valuable starting point for coaches and athletes to educate themselves and talk about underfueling risk.
---

key_facts.fact: Measuring Energy Availability in athletes is difficult because there are no standardized methods in the literature yet.
In real-world coaching, it is not easy to measure calories burned during exercise, and most athletes do not know their fat-free mass.
Nevertheless, the concept of EA provides a valuable starting point for coaches and athletes to educate themselves and talk about underfueling risk.

### Health-related symptom table

chunk.section_title: Possible Symptoms of Low Energy Availability: Performance Related
chunk.content:
### Performance-related symptom table
| Performance category | Possible symptoms or impairments | | Reduced aerobic performance | Decreased time-to-exhaustion and overall stamina; lower maximal or sustainable training intensities such as tempo or threshold; impaired glycogen synthesis and carbohydrate availability | | Impaired recovery between sessions | Elevated fatigue across multi-session training days; higher injury incidence during high-volume blocks; reduced resting metabolic rate affecting adaptation to endurance load | | Cardiovascular and metabolic symptoms | Increased heart rate at submaximal workloads; reduced ability to utilize carbohydrates effectively during intensity; slower lactate clearance or reduced ability to repeat efforts |
### Mental health and REDs
Disordered eating behaviors and clinical eating disorders are common in at-risk athletes and frequently coexist with or precipitate REDs.
These behaviors can be aggravated by:
- Social media - Pervasive societal pressure - Specific coaching environments - Underlying body dissatisfaction
The psychological consequences directly stemming from problematic LEA and REDs can include:
- Mood disturbances - High cognitive dietary restraint - Strong drive for thinness - Poor sleep quality - Perfectionism - Depressive symptoms - Anxiety - Reduced overall well-being - Exercise addiction - Difficulty managing weight-related performance demands - Potential progression toward clinical eating disorders
Mental health responses vary widely among individual athletes. Further research is needed to clarify sex differences, competitive-level differences, and why some athletes show few noticeable symptoms in early stages.
### Performance Impairments and REDs
Athletes experiencing REDs can show multiple performance-related impairments.
| Performance impairment | Explanation | | Reduced athlete availability | REDs increases the risk of illness and injury, making athletes less able to train or compete consistently. | | Reduced training response | Athletes adapt less effectively to training stimuli, experience reduced training intensity, and may report low energy or fatigue. | | Impaired recovery | Recovery between sessions is slower, with poorer restoration of performance capacity. | | Reduced cognitive performance and skill execution | Athletes may experience reduced concentration, slower decision-making, and diminished neuromuscular coordination. | | Reduced motivation | Athletes may report reduced drive, increased emotional instability, and greater perceived effort for regular training loads. | | Reduced muscle strength | Muscle strength can decline due to reduced protein synthesis, impaired neuromuscular function, and decreased training quality. | | Reduced endurance performance | Endurance performance can fall due to reduced aerobic capacity, increased perceived exertion, and lower ability to sustain prolonged or high-intensity efforts. |

chunk.content:
The most important strategy for athletes suffering from LEA is to increase energy intake and/or reduce the gap between energy intake and energy expenditure.
### Nutritional strategy overview
| Strategy | Practical meaning | Intended effect | | Increase Total Energy Availability | Increase caloric intake and/or decrease training volume. | Restore adequate EA, menstrual function, metabolic hormones, and muscle protein synthesis. | | Improve Within-Day Energy Distribution | Eat regularly every 3-4 hours; include a small meal or snack before training and recovery nutrition after sessions. | Keep energy availability stable and reduce performance dips from low EA. | | Increase Carbohydrate Availability | Use higher-energy-density carbohydrate sources, liquid carbohydrates, and strategic sugar intake around training. | Boost total intake, support fueling, and support recovery. | | Reduce Excess Fiber Intake | Temporarily reduce very high fiber intake when it limits total energy intake. | Make higher-energy foods easier to consume and help restore EA. | | Use Energy-Dense Foods | Add small-volume, high-calorie foods and calorie-boosting meal components. | Increase intake without excessive food volume. | | Ensure Bone-Supporting Micronutrients | Ensure adequate calcium, vitamin D, protein, magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, and fluoride. | Support bone remodeling and reduce RED-S-related bone risk. | | Integrate Psychological Support | Address perfectionism, drive for thinness, restrictive thoughts, disordered eating, and eating disorders. | Reduce central REDs risk factors and support recovery capacity. |
### Increase Total Energy Availability
Coaches and athletes have two main options:
1. Increase caloric intake. 2. Decrease training volume.
Increasing EA alone through higher caloric intake, improved energy distribution, or reduced exercise load can restore menstrual function, normalize metabolic hormones, and increase muscle protein synthesis, even without major training modifications.
The time required for menstrual recovery varies widely between athletes, but restoring adequate EA remains the essential cornerstone of treatment.
### Improve Within-Day Energy Distribution
Eating regularly every 3-4 hours helps keep energy availability stable.
This supports better training adaptations and helps prevent dips in performance associated with low energy availability.
A small meal or snack before training and proper recovery nutrition after sessions help athletes stay fueled and reduce LEA risk.
### Increase Carbohydrate Availability
Carbohydrate availability can be improved by choosing higher-energy-density carbohydrate sources.
Examples include:
- Replacing chickpeas with rice - Swapping potatoes for pasta - Using fruit juice - Using sports drinks - Using smoothies
These options increase total intake without adding excessive food volume.
The unit emphasizes that sugar is not harmful in the athletic context. Strategically including sweets before, during, or after training is a valid and effective way to support fueling and recovery.
### Reduce Excess Fiber Intake
