chunk.content:
High fiber intake can unintentionally reduce total energy intake by increasing satiety and gastrointestinal discomfort.
This can worsen LEA.
Reducing fiber temporarily allows higher-energy foods to be consumed more easily, supporting restoration of EA.
Athletes who underfuel often compensate by eating large amounts of vegetables, which can reflect fear of overeating or consuming higher-energy foods.
### Visual Note: Use Energy-Dense Foods
The visual lists high-calorie, low-volume or energy-boosting foods across five categories.
| Category | Examples from visual | | Easy add-ons: small volume, big calories | Nut butters such as peanut, almond, cashew, and tahini; olive oil, pesto, chili oil, butter; honey, maple syrup, jam; seeds such as chia, hemp, pumpkin, sunflower; nuts and nut mixes | | High-energy snacks and sides | Trail mix with nuts, dried fruit, and chocolate; granola or muesli, including higher-calorie versions; energy bars, flapjacks, oat bars; dark chocolate and chocolate-covered nuts; dried fruit such as dates, mango, apricots, raisins | | Carb-dense staples | Pasta, rice, couscous; bagels, wraps, sourdough bread; oats prepared with milk plus toppings; potato dishes with added oil or cheese | | Dairy and dairy alternative: energy-boosting options | Full-fat Greek yogurt; cheese such as parmesan, cheddar, feta, mozzarella; whole milk; skyr plus energy add-ons such as cereal, honey, and nuts | | Meal components that add calories easily | Avocado; hummus and bean dips; coconut milk in sauces or curries; pesto pasta |
### Ensure Adequate Bone-Supporting Micronutrients
LEA independently suppresses bone formation.
Controlled trials show that even brief LEA periods of 5 days at 10-30 kcal/kg FFM/day can lead to a dose-dependent reduction in bone formation markers and an increase in bone resorption, even when menstrual function remains normal.
Adequate intake of bone-building micronutrients is critical in RED-S because insufficient consumption compromises bone remodeling independently of LEA.
| Bone-supporting nutrient | Role in this unit | | Calcium | Bone-building micronutrient required for bone remodeling. | | Vitamin D | Bone-supporting micronutrient relevant to RED-S risk management. | | Protein | Supports tissue and bone remodeling; also relevant to muscle protein synthesis. | | Magnesium | Bone-building micronutrient. | | Phosphorus | Bone-building micronutrient. | | Potassium | Bone-supporting micronutrient. | | Fluoride | Bone-supporting micronutrient. |
### Integrate Psychological Support and Address Disordered Eating
Psychological factors such as perfectionism, drive for thinness, and restrictive thought patterns are considered essential triggers for LEA and REDs.
They may also be caused by chronic undernutrition.
The IOC classifies eating disorders as a central risk factor and highlights that psychological strain can intensify hormonal disturbances and reduce recovery capacity.

chunk.content:
The idea behind low-carbohydrate nutrition is partly based on the belief that carbohydrates "make you fat" and partly on the assumption that fat metabolism is trained more effectively on a low-carbohydrate diet.
Many athletes also associate being thin with being faster and better.
Daily carbohydrate intake in low-carbohydrate approaches is usually below 2.5 g/kg body weight. In practice, the unit notes that coaches often see simply inadequate total carbohydrate intake for the athlete's overall caloric needs, where underfueling becomes the primary issue.
### Low-carbohydrate diet and performance
According to the unit, current scientific evidence indicates that a low-carbohydrate diet performs worse than a high-carbohydrate diet for high-intensity exercise because the body lacks enough glycogen to meet high energy demands.
Potential consequences include:
- Reduced performance - Impaired interval training performance - Negative effects on muscle hypertrophy - No clear demonstrated improvement in endurance performance - Higher susceptibility to infections - Mental and physical fatigue in real life - Poorer bone metabolism in female athletes, even when total energy availability is adequate
### Fasted training and fat metabolism
Many athletes believe fasted training enhances fat metabolism and therefore improves performance.
The unit states that the evidence does not support this claim clearly. So far, there are no clear findings that training with low or empty glycogen stores improves endurance performance.
Only 37% of 11 studies showed a performance benefit. The remaining studies reported either no improvement or a decrease in performance.
Strategies for training with low carbohydrate availability include "train low" and "sleep low".
Anyone who wants to try this type of training should perform these sessions at low intensity.
The unit states that the negative effects of low carbohydrate availability on performance and potential training adaptations outweigh the potential benefits in many cases, so any attempt to target fat metabolism should be carefully planned.
### Simple rule for carbohydrate availability
| Training intensity | Carbohydrate availability recommendation | | High-intensity training | Requires high carbohydrate availability. | | Low-intensity training | Does not necessarily require high carbohydrate availability; fasted training may be possible. |
### Train-low models
| No. | Train-low model | | 1 | Twice-a-Day Training | | 2 | Fasted Training | | 3 | Sleep Low, Train Low | | 4 | Recover Low | | 5 | High-fat feeding + low glycogen | | 6 | Mixed strategies: "fuel for the work required" |
Performance results from low-carbohydrate availability strategies are inconsistent. Only about one-third of studies show measurable performance improvements.
This lack of benefit is likely due to:
- Compromised training intensity - Elevated perceived effort - Impaired recovery - Difficulty isolating carbohydrate-specific effects from overall energy deficits in real-world elite training

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Key Principles of HYROX Race Day
chunk.content:
### Carbohydrates Are the Priority
On HYROX race day, carbohydrate intake through food and fluids should be the priority.
Carbohydrates can be readily used as fuel to provide energy for HYROX competition. They are stored in the body as glycogen, but only a limited amount can be stored as liver glycogen, and liver glycogen is significantly reduced overnight.
Because HYROX requires repeated running segments, high-intensity efforts, and quick powerful bursts of work such as sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jumps, and wall balls, carbohydrate stores should be fully topped up before the race begins.
Most HYROX athletes benefit from consuming 1-4 g carbohydrate per kg bodyweight in the 1-4 hours before the race.
The exact amount and timing should depend on:
- Race start time - Individual preferences - Gastrointestinal tolerance - Time available before the race
Where time allows, a larger meal can be consumed. If there is less time, a smaller meal may be better.
A carbohydrate-rich meal 1-2 hours before the start is ideal for many athletes. For athletes who experience stomach discomfort when eating close to exercise, a carbohydrate meal 3-4 hours before start time may be preferred.
Race-day nutrition should be practiced before training sessions. Athletes should not trial unfamiliar foods, fluids, or strategies on race day.
### Race-day carbohydrate timing table
| Timing before race | Carbohydrate target | Practical use | | 1-4 hours before race | 1-4 g carbohydrate/kg bodyweight | Main race-day carbohydrate intake window. | | 1-2 hours before race | Carbohydrate-rich meal if tolerated | Ideal for many athletes when stomach comfort is good. | | 3-4 hours before race | Carbohydrate-rich meal | Preferred for athletes who experience stomach discomfort when eating close to exercise. |
---

chunk.section_title: Moderate Protein, Low Fat and Fibre
chunk.content:
Protein, fat, and fiber slow gastric emptying. This can lead to:
- Bloating - Cramping - Gastrointestinal distress - Mid-race interruptions
On race day, athletes should focus on simple foods with high carbohydrate content, moderate protein, and minimal fat and fiber.
When fiber is ingested, it increases bowel movements and accelerates fluid loss. For athletes prone to gastrointestinal symptoms, a low-fiber diet on competition day, and even in the days leading up to competition, is important.
### Race-day food choice table
| Recommended | Avoid or limit | | White pasta | Wholegrain pasta | | White rice | Wholegrain rice | | Plain bagels | Wholegrain alternatives | | Simple high-carbohydrate foods | High-fat foods | | Moderate protein | High protein close to racing if it slows digestion | | Low-fiber foods | High quantities of fruit and vegetables | | Fluids with electrolytes where possible | High intakes of milk and milk products | | Familiar foods tested in training | Fructose-only foods if they increase GI risk |
---

Refill overnight-depleted glycogen with easily digested carbohydrates.

Low fiber reduces gut discomfort during high-impact running. | | Optional top-up, 30-45 minutes pre-race | Approximately 25-30 g carbohydrate | Medium banana; small carbohydrate bar; carbohydrate drink | Maintains blood glucose, especially if breakfast was light or eaten early. |

chunk.content:
Evening races require more careful planning because a long day can lead to unintentional under-fueling.
### Primary goal
Prevent energy depletion across the day without feeling heavy before the race.
### Evening meal structure
| Timing | Target | Examples | Rationale | | Breakfast | Based on early and middle-of-day recommendations | Overnight oats + banana + honey; bagel with jam; low-fat plain yogurt with fruit and honey; smoothie | Starts glycogen replenishment early. | | Lunch, minimum 4-5 hours pre-race | Main carbohydrate meal of the day; aim for 1-4 g carbohydrate/kg bodyweight across the race-day intake plan | Rice with lean chicken or tofu and vegetables; pasta with tomato sauce and vegetables; baked potato with baked beans or tomato sauce and vegetables; stir-fry with rice and minimal oil | Provides the core energy for the race but is eaten early enough not to sit heavy in the stomach. | | Pre-race meal, 2-3 hours pre-race | Light carbohydrate-focused meal | Bagel or toast with honey or jam; rice cakes + banana; small portion of pasta; small portion of white rice + soy sauce | Tops off glycogen and keeps the stomach light. Simple foods can reduce GI sensitivity when race nerves are present. | | Optional top-up, 30-45 minutes pre-race | About 25-30 g carbohydrate | Medium banana; small carbohydrate bar; carbohydrate drink; carbohydrate chews; carbohydrate gel | Provides a small glucose boost to increase energy availability for the start and prevent energy dips. |

### During the Race
Fluids, including water and electrolytes, can be beneficial during the race. Some HYROX athletes may also benefit from consuming carbohydrate fuel during the race.
### Optional in-race fuel table
| In-race option | When to use | Condition | | One gel, about 25 g carbohydrate | Halfway through the race if race time is above 60 minutes | Only if practiced. | | Small sips of sports drink | Between stations | Useful if an energy source is needed. |
The intensity of HYROX often means that mid-race eating is uncomfortable. If an energy source is needed, liquids may be better tolerated.

unit.unit_summary: Whilst it is generally accepted that a food first approach should be prioritized by athletes where possible, there are certain circumstances where individuals may choose to supplement their diet. chunk.content: [0:00:00] Whilst it is generally accepted that a food first approach should be prioritized by athletes where possible, there are certain circumstances where individuals may choose to supplement their diet. This could be in order to meet macronutrient requirements in and around [0:00:17] training and competition, to address specific deficiencies as a result of dietary restriction, or to utilize nutritional ergogenic aids to enhance performance capacity or recovery. It can be [0:00:33] difficult to decide whether an athlete should supplement or not, and it is important to understand the implications regarding permissibility, safety, and efficacy. Use of evidence. Before taking or [0:00:50] recommending any kind of dietary supplement or ergogenic aid, it is important to evaluate the available evidence regarding its safety and effectiveness. A number of supplements have a strong evidence base for performance enhancement, whilst there are others with very little evidentiary [0:01:09] support. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses, papers that pool findings and data from a number of studies to provide an overview of results, are often the strongest evidence regarding a product's effectiveness. Position stands or consensus statements can also provide insight [0:01:29] regarding the use of certain substances. Consulting a registered dietitian or sports nutritionist can also help you determine whether small changes to your habitual diet could ensure sufficiency to support your training and recovery, or whether you or your athletes would benefit [0:01:49] from incorporating additional dietary supplements. There are certain risks associated with the consumption of commercially produced supplements. An individual may experience unwanted side effects or products [0:02:05] may be contaminated with banned substances that would violate the HYROX anti-doping code. Legislation and batch testing. The World Anti-Doping Agency, WADA, was established in 1999 as an international independent agency whose primary aim is to drive the clean [0:02:27] sport movement. WADA develops and coordinates anti-doping policies across all sports and countries. Whilst WADA is responsible for monitoring compliance with the program, they also support research, education, [0:02:43] and the development of anti-doping capacity within national anti-doping organizations. HYROX introduced drug testing for athletes in February 2024 and this was expanded for the 25 slash 26 competitive season. Doping is defined as the violation of one or more of [0:03:05] the anti-doping rules which are outlined in the HYROX anti-doping code, available in full on the HYROX website. It is an athlete's individual responsibility and duty to ensure that they do not utilize prohibited substances or methods and it is not necessary for intent or knowing use [0:03:28] to be proven for a violation to be upheld. It is important for HYROX athletes and coaches to understand the anti-doping regulations and to minimize risk as far as possible. There are a number of steps that can be taken to minimize the risk of inadvertent doping. Firstly, you should [0:03:49] familiarize yourself with the list of banned substances and check regularly for updates. If you take any medications or over-the-counter medicines, you can use the Global Drug Reference Online, global DRO website, [0:04:06] to check whether they contain any substances on the banned list. If they do, it may be possible to source alternative options that would not put you at risk of a doping violation. Importantly, [0:04:22] formulations for the same medicines may differ between countries, so double-check before consuming medications purchased outside of your home country. In circumstances where you take a WADA-banned substance for legitimate medical reasons, for example, steroid-based [0:04:42] medications for asthma, and there is no suitable alternative available, you can apply for a Therapeutic Use Exemption, TUE, certificate. Without an exemption, an athlete cannot compete for [0:05:01] competitive results, podiums, World Championship qualification. However, they may be allowed to participate in the event for time. Regarding dietary supplements and ergogenic aids, whilst the [0:05:17] vast majority are not banned and are routinely used by athletes, there is always a small risk of inadvertent doping due to contamination. Sourcing products that have been tested by an independent third party can reduce this risk. Informed Sport is a global banned [0:05:38] substance testing and certification program that was developed with UK Anti-Doping, UKAD, and is recognized by numerous anti-doping organizations and sporting bodies worldwide. [0:05:54] Informed Sport certification is voluntary for supplement companies who wish to certify some or all of their products. Once certified, products can carry the Informed Sport logo or on-pack descriptor, making it easy for athletes to identify certified products. [0:06:17] Certification ensures that products have undergone rigorous testing, that no banned substances are present, and that they have been manufactured to high quality standards. Whilst Informed Sport tests for the presence of banned substances, it does not explicitly verify listed [0:06:39] ingredients and dosages. The Informed Sport website allows you to search directly by brand, product type, or batch code to check compliance. The HYROX anti-doping code stipulates that anti-doping [0:06:55] tests can be conducted on any athlete at any time, both in competition and out of competition. The testing program primarily targets elite competitors. For major events, majors, [0:07:11] regional championships, and world championships, five athletes are selected for testing. Athletes achieving podium finishes in the elite 15 races are mandatorily tested, and two other competitors [0:07:27] are selected from the field at random. Selected athletes are notified immediately upon finishing the race and are chaperoned until the test is completed. Unannounced out-of-competition testing can also occur at any time for licensed elite athletes. The penalties associated [0:07:49] with anti-doping violations vary based on individual circumstances but could lead to a ban of up to four years for a first offense. Where athletes are caught on multiple occasions, a lifetime ban may [0:08:06] be applied.

chunk.content:
Once a supplement has been identified as potentially beneficial, the next step is careful implementation and ongoing evaluation.
Introducing a new supplement should be planned and implemented carefully. Even when best-practice guidelines exist, individual responses can differ, so dosing strategies should be determined individually.
Athletes should trial any new supplement during training and never for the first time on race day.
### Supplement implementation framework
| Step | Coaching action | Purpose | | Identify potential benefit | Determine whether the supplement has a relevant purpose for the athlete. | Avoid unnecessary or unfocused supplementation. | | Plan implementation | Define dose, timing, and form. | Make supplement use deliberate and measurable. | | Trial during training | Practice before training sessions, not race day. | Observe response and reduce race-day risk. | | Monitor subjective response | Track energy, focus, and gastrointestinal comfort. | Identify whether the supplement is tolerated and useful. | | Monitor objective response | Track training output and recovery markers. | Evaluate whether the supplement improves performance or recovery. | | Individualize strategy | Account for physiology, training load, sex, habitual diet, and tolerance. | Match supplement use to the athlete rather than copying generic protocols. | | Re-evaluate regularly | Reassess supplement use across the season. | Keep use purposeful, safe, cost-effective, and aligned with current goals. |
### Why Re-Evaluation Matters
Supplement needs can change as:
- Training volume shifts - Nutritional status improves - Performance goals evolve - A structured diet begins to meet the same need a supplement previously filled
Periodic check-ins ensure supplement use remains:
| Evaluation criterion | Meaning | | Purposeful | The supplement still has a clear reason for use. | | Safe | The athlete tolerates it without unacceptable side effects. | | Cost-effective | The supplement provides enough benefit to justify use. | | Aligned with objectives | Use still matches the athlete's current performance and recovery goals. |
---

chunk.content:
Caffeine is a naturally occurring central nervous system stimulant.
It can increase wakefulness and delay fatigue. It works primarily by blocking adenosine from binding to receptors in the brain, which promotes alertness and improves cognitive function.
Caffeine occurs naturally in:
- Coffee - Tea - Chocolate
It is also available in concentrated form as caffeine anhydrous. Caffeine anhydrous is a processed, dehydrated form of caffeine and is commonly used in:
- Pre-workout formulations - Energy bars - Capsules - Chewing gum
A recent study of dietary habits among high-intensity functional training athletes found that 68% of supplement-using participants reported caffeine supplement intake, highlighting widespread use of caffeine as an ergogenic aid.
### Caffeine summary
| Topic | Detail | | Supplement type | Central nervous system stimulant / ergogenic aid | | Main mechanism | Blocks adenosine from binding to brain receptors | | Primary effects | Increased wakefulness, delayed fatigue, improved alertness and cognitive function | | Natural sources | Coffee, tea, chocolate | | Supplement form | Caffeine anhydrous | | Common supplement products | Pre-workouts, energy bars, capsules, chewing gum | | Reported use in HIFT athletes | 68% of supplement-using participants reported caffeine supplement intake |
### Caffeine efficacy and dose
Studies on caffeine and exercise performance consistently report improvements in:
- Aerobic endurance - Muscular strength - Power - Sport-specific skills
These improvements are reported after moderate doses of 3-6 mg/kg taken 30-60 minutes before exercise.
### Caffeine dosing guidance
| Variable | Recommendation / finding | | Moderate dose | 3-6 mg/kg | | Timing | 30-60 minutes before exercise | | Start point | Begin at the lowest end of the range when testing individually | | Higher doses | Little evidence suggests higher doses enhance effects | | Possible side effects | Jitteriness, anxiety, gastrointestinal distress, sleep disturbance |
### Factors affecting caffeine response
| Factor | Why it matters | | Genetics | Can influence individual sensitivity and performance response. | | Habitual caffeine intake | Regular intake may affect tolerance and perceived response. | | Training status | May influence how caffeine affects performance and fatigue. | | Gastrointestinal tolerance | Some athletes experience GI distress. | | Sleep sensitivity | Late or high caffeine intake can impair sleep. |
### Caffeine in high-intensity functional training
Research on caffeine in high-intensity functional training suggests that acute intake can modestly enhance:
| Potential benefit | Evidence note | | Anaerobic power | May improve modestly. | | Reaction time | May improve modestly. | | Repeated sprint ability | May improve modestly. | | Some sport-specific skills | May improve, but not across all measures. |

chunk.content:
Iron is a core component of haemoglobin and myoglobin, the oxygen-carrying proteins found in blood and muscle tissue.
Iron also plays a role in:
- Energy production and metabolism through the electron transport chain - Immune function - Muscle function - Organ function - DNA synthesis
Athletes need sufficient iron levels to support training and performance and to avoid anaemia.
### Iron function summary
| Function | Relevance for athletes | | Haemoglobin | Supports oxygen transport in the blood. | | Myoglobin | Supports oxygen handling in muscle tissue. | | Electron transport chain | Supports energy production and metabolism. | | Immune function | Supports health during training. | | Muscle and organ function | Supports normal physiological performance. | | DNA synthesis | Supports cellular processes. |
### Why athletes are at higher risk of iron deficiency
Athletes tend to have a higher risk of iron deficiency than the general population.
| Risk mechanism | Explanation | | Increased red blood cell demand | Regular intense exercise stimulates production of more red blood cells to meet oxygen demand. | | Erythropoietin and bone marrow stress | EPO release and physical stress on bone marrow signal red blood cell production. | | Increased iron demand | Iron is required for red blood cell creation, so demand increases. | | Exercise-induced inflammation | Exercise increases hepcidin, which temporarily blocks iron absorption in the gut. | | Sweat losses | Iron losses in sweat can become significant during periods of increased exercise intensity. | | Footstrike haemolysis | Endurance exercise can destroy red blood cells through repeated impacts. | | Gastrointestinal bleeding | Exercise-induced GI bleeding can contribute to iron loss. |
### Additional iron deficiency risk factors
| Risk factor | Explanation | | Sex | Females are at higher risk because of menstrual blood losses. | | Athlete populations | Iron deficiency prevalence can be up to 5 times greater in female athlete populations than in the general female population. | | Sport type | Endurance-heavy athletes have higher risk because of footstrike haemolysis, sweat losses, and GI bleeding. | | Habitual diet | Vegetarian and vegan diets may increase risk because plant-based iron is less readily absorbed. | | Age | Adolescents have higher iron requirements to support growth and maturation. |
Iron deficiency, even without anaemia, can impair athletic performance, reduce oxygen transport, increase fatigue, and affect mood states.
### Iron intake guidance

chunk.content:
Vitamin D3 is an essential nutrient that supports:
- Bone health - Muscle function - Immune function
Vitamin D3 aids calcium absorption, which is important for preventing stress fractures. It can also reduce the incidence of illnesses that could disrupt high-volume training schedules.
Vitamin D3 is naturally synthesized in the body through exposure to UVB radiation from sunlight.
To synthesize sufficient vitamin D3, athletes need safe summer sunlight exposure over most of the skin surface for approximately 30 minutes per day. This can be achieved through several shorter exposures to avoid skin damage.
### Vitamin D3 function summary
| Function | Relevance for HYROX athletes | | Bone health | Supports calcium absorption and helps reduce stress fracture risk. | | Muscle function | Supports training and performance capacity. | | Immune function | May reduce illness interruptions during high-volume training. | | Calcium absorption | Critical for skeletal health and injury risk management. |
### Vitamin D3 deficiency risk factors
| Risk factor | Explanation | | Darker skin | Longer sun exposure is required to produce the same amount of vitamin D3 compared with lighter skin. | | Limited sun exposure | Indoor training, night training, early-morning training, or skin-covering training kit can increase deficiency risk. | | Northern latitudes | Athletes living and training in northern latitudes are likely to be deficient during autumn and winter without supplements or fortified foods. | | Seasonal limitation | Autumn and winter reduce sunlight exposure and vitamin D3 synthesis. |
### Vitamin D3 intake guidance
| Guidance point | Recommendation | | Daily target for athletes | 25-50 micrograms/day | | Daily target in IU | 1,000-2,000 IU/day | | Particularly relevant period | Winter months | | Maximum daily intake | Do not exceed 100 micrograms/day | | Maximum daily intake in IU | Do not exceed 4,000 IU/day | | Supplement quality | Choose a third-party batch-tested product from a reputable company. | | Total intake caution | Include habitual diet, supplements, and multivitamins when calculating total intake. |
---

chunk.content:
Racing literacy in HYROX goes beyond having the fitness required to complete the course.
It reflects an athlete's ability to:
- Read the race as it unfolds - Interpret race constraints - Adapt performance behaviors in real time - Integrate perception, decision-making, and action under stress
### Academy Definition of Racing Literacy
> "The athlete's capacity to adjust pacing, movement execution, and tactical choices moment-to-moment to optimize performance within the dynamic, high-pressure HYROX environment."
### Racing Literacy Framework
| Component | Meaning in HYROX | | Perception | The athlete reads race conditions, fatigue, station demands, competitors, and environmental constraints. | | Interpretation | The athlete understands what those constraints mean for pacing, movement execution, and tactical choices. | | Adaptation | The athlete adjusts behavior in real time to optimize performance. | | Action under stress | The athlete executes decisions while fatigued and under race pressure. |
The module positions key principles that help coaches improve an athlete's racing literacy over time.
---

- Read the race as it unfolds - Interpret race constraints - Adapt performance behaviors in real time - Integrate perception, decision-making, and action under stress

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Categorization of Skills in HYROX Racing
chunk.content:
At its core, a skill is a specialized learned ability to complete a task that demands training and knowledge.
In sport, skill is often considered a cornerstone of performance, but this unit presents skill as more than a static attribute.
Drawing on Araújo and Davids (2011), skill is described as a dynamic interplay between:
| Skill factor | Meaning | | Environmental constraints | Race-day conditions, equipment variability, competition pressure, station layout, and event demands. | | Athlete resources | Fitness, technical capacity, awareness, fatigue state, decision-making ability, and adaptability. |
This view shifts skill away from isolated competencies and toward adaptable, context-driven behaviors.
In HYROX, this is important because athletes must constantly adjust to:
- Race-day conditions - Equipment variability - Physiological state - Fatigue - Competition pressure
The goal is not only technical proficiency, but also adaptability and awareness in real-world race scenarios.
### Three Fundamental Skill Categories
To improve HYROX performance, coaches should break down the sport's skill requirements into three fundamental categories.
| Skill category | Core purpose | Performance contribution | | Resilience of Movement Standards and Economy of Movement | Maintain legal, efficient movement under fatigue. | Helps athletes avoid penalties, reduce wasted energy, and sustain movement quality. | | Pacing Intensity | Regulate effort across running and workout stations. | Helps prevent early burnout while maintaining competitive output. | | Decision Making | Select and adjust strategy under race pressure. | Helps athletes manage transitions, respond to fatigue, and adapt to unexpected race events. |
Each category helps an athlete perform efficiently, sustain effort across all race components, and make critical race-day choices.
---

chunk.section_title: Chapter 03: Resilience of Movement Standards and Economy of Movement
chunk.content:
Movement standards refer to the technical execution of exercises and race components according to official rules.
Economy of movement means performing these movements with minimal energy wastage.
In HYROX, proper technique affects the athlete's ability to maintain speed and endurance throughout the race.
### Movement Standards and Economy Table
| Concept | Definition | HYROX relevance | | Movement standards | Technical execution according to official rules. | Required to avoid penalties, no-reps, or disqualification. | | Economy of movement | Performing movements with minimal energy wastage. | Helps conserve energy across eight stations and multiple running segments. | | Resilience of movement economy | Maintaining efficient movement even when fatigued. | Supports consistent form at race intensity. |
The running element and all workout stations require precise form to avoid unnecessary fatigue and meet competition standards.
Poor movement efficiency can lead to:
- Early exhaustion - Wasted energy - Accumulated fatigue across workout stations - Accumulated fatigue across running segments - Increased likelihood of penalties or disqualification
### Coaching Development Methods
| Coaching method | Purpose | | Structured drills | Develop mechanical efficiency and repeatable movement patterns. | | Mobility work | Improve positions and reduce compensations. | | Technique practice under fatigue | Ensure movement quality remains stable at race intensity. | | Regular video analysis | Help athletes identify inefficiencies and technical breakdown. | | Competition-standard reinforcement | Build consistent legal execution under pressure. |
Coaches should ensure that movement execution remains consistent at race intensity, reducing the likelihood of penalties, disqualification, or excess energy expenditure.
---

chunk.content:
Pacing intensity refers to an athlete's ability to regulate effort across different race segments.
HYROX combines running with functional workout stations, so pacing must be managed strategically.
A good pacing strategy should:
- Prevent early burnout - Preserve competitive performance - Account for the energy cost of each station - Account for thresholds where running becomes compromised - Adapt to fatigue and race conditions
### Pacing Risk Table
| Pacing error | Likely consequence | | Over-aggressive start | Excessive fatigue before key early stations such as the sled push. | | Too conservative early pacing | Untapped performance potential in later race stages. | | Poor understanding of station cost | Inaccurate effort distribution across the race. | | Failure to adjust dynamically | Reduced ability to respond to fatigue or changing race conditions. |
### Coaching Development Methods for Pacing
| Coaching method | Purpose | | Race-specific interval training | Teach athletes to regulate intensity across HYROX-like efforts. | | Race simulation workouts | Provide practice in realistic pacing demands. | | Biofeedback | Help athletes understand internal load and fatigue signals. | | Performance metrics | Allow athletes and coaches to reflect on pacing decisions. | | Dynamic effort adjustment | Teach athletes to change effort based on fatigue and race conditions. |
Teaching athletes to adjust their efforts dynamically is crucial for optimal HYROX performance.
---

chunk.content:
Decision making in HYROX means adapting to race conditions, selecting the right strategy under fatigue, and managing transitions efficiently.
Athletes must make split-second choices about:
- When to push harder - When to recover - How to approach each station - Whether to break reps strategically - How to minimize transition time - How to react to competitors - How to adjust to unexpected problems
### Decision-Making Examples
| Situation | Decision required | | Muscle fatigue during lunges | Decide whether to break reps strategically or push through. | | Transition between run and station | Choose a speed that saves time without causing technical breakdown. | | Race positioning | React tactically to competitors. | | Equipment malfunction | Adjust strategy without losing composure. | | No-rep penalties | Respond efficiently and avoid further errors. |
Optimal transition speed between running and workout stations can make a significant difference to overall time.
### Coaching Development Methods for Decision Making
| Coaching method | Purpose | | Race simulations | Expose athletes to realistic decision-making demands. | | Scenario-based workouts | Teach athletes to respond to specific race problems. | | Transition practice | Improve time efficiency and decision quality between race components. | | Race visualization | Help athletes rehearse likely scenarios before competition. | | Composure training | Improve decisions under pressure and fatigue. | | Self-awareness development | Help athletes understand their own fatigue, pacing, and technical limits. |
Developing self-awareness and adaptability helps athletes stay in control when facing adversity.
---

unit.unit_summary:

These concepts provide a perspective for developing skills and tactics within progressive training structures. Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development highlights the "sweet spot" for learning.

chunk.content:
Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development highlights the "sweet spot" for learning.
Learning takes place when the task or activity stretches the learner beyond what they can accomplish unassisted, but does not make the challenge so difficult that they cannot show progress.
### ZPD Learning Zones
| Zone | Meaning | Coaching implication | | Current understanding | The athlete can learn or perform unassisted. | The task may be too easy if the goal is development. | | Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) | The athlete can learn with specific assistance or scaffolding. | This is the ideal learning zone for guided development. | | Out of reach | The task is too difficult for the athlete's current ability, even with support. | The task may cause stagnation, frustration, or lack of progress. |
### ZPD in HYROX Coaching
In HYROX, identifying an athlete's ZPD means understanding their current technical and tactical capabilities, such as:
- Ability to execute efficient transitions between stations - Ability to manage pacing during compromised running phases - Ability to maintain movement standards under fatigue - Ability to make tactical decisions under pressure
Coaches should design interventions that challenge athletes just beyond their current capabilities while providing appropriate support.
### Coaching Supports Within the ZPD
| Coaching support | Purpose | | Feedback | Helps the athlete adjust execution and decision-making. | | Demonstrations | Shows the athlete what the target movement or tactical behavior should look like. | | Progressive drills | Builds skill in stages without overwhelming the athlete. | | Collaboration or guided support | Helps the athlete perform beyond what they could do alone. |
By finding the learning "sweet spot," athletes can develop the confidence and competence needed to perform consistently under competition pressure.
---

chunk.content:
Newcombe's Funnel of Variability introduces progressive variability and opportunities for action, also called affordances, into training environments.
The model demonstrates the dynamic nature of competition.
The funnel progresses from low variability and fewer affordances in drills or unopposed practice to high variability and many affordances in variable practice, contextual race experiences, and HYROX racing.
### Visual Note: Funnel of Variability
The visual shows a progression from the narrow, low-variability, technical end of the funnel toward the wide, high-variability, tactical end.
| Funnel stage | Variability level | Emphasis | Coaching meaning | | Drill | Low | Technical | Isolated skill introduction with little or no variable pressure. | | Unopposed Practice | Low to moderate | Technical | Skill is assessed without direct opposition. | | Opposed Practice | Moderate | Technical to tactical | Skill is performed against an opponent of similar ability, depending on the athlete's ZPD. | | Variable Practice | Moderate to high | Mixed | Athletes respond and adapt to changing tasks, conditions, and constraints. | | Low Context Simulation | High | Tactical | Practice becomes more race-linked but not yet fully race-like. | | High Context Simulation | Very high | Tactical | Race-day features and pressure are deliberately simulated. | | HYROX Race | Highest | Tactical | Full competition context with maximum variability, pressure, and affordances. |
The model aligns with how skills are developed, secured, and enhanced under pressure.
---

key_facts.fact: Newcombe's Funnel of Variability introduces progressive variability and opportunities for action, also called affordances, into training environments.

The funnel progresses from low variability and fewer affordances in drills or unopposed practice to high variability and many affordances in variable practice, contextual race experiences, and HYROX racing.

### Visual Note: Funnel of Variability
The visual shows a progression from the narrow, low-variability, technical end of the funnel toward the wide, high-variability, tactical end.
| Funnel stage | Variability level | Emphasis | Coaching meaning | | Drill | Low | Technical | Isolated skill introduction with little or no variable pressure.
| | Unopposed Practice | Low to moderate | Technical | Skill is assessed without direct opposition.
| | Opposed Practice | Moderate | Technical to tactical | Skill is performed against an opponent of similar ability, depending on the athlete's ZPD.
| | Variable Practice | Moderate to high | Mixed | Athletes respond and adapt to changing tasks, conditions, and constraints.
| | Low Context Simulation | High | Tactical | Practice becomes more race-linked but not yet fully race-like.
| | High Context Simulation | Very high | Tactical | Race-day features and pressure are deliberately simulated.
| | HYROX Race | Highest | Tactical | Full competition context with maximum variability, pressure, and affordances.

chunk.section_title: Applying the Funnel Across the Training Season
chunk.content:
Early training begins at the narrow end of the funnel with drills.
Drills introduce a skill by:
- Breaking down the movement - Slowing pacing intensity where needed - Using a sequential format - Allowing movement standards to be performed under little or no variable pressure
As training progresses, the skill can be assessed in unopposed practice and then differentiated into opposed practice against an opponent of similar ability, depending on the athlete's ZPD.
A simple example is an EMOM workout that includes the skill focus, accumulates fatigue, and identifies whether the athlete can maintain control.
Coaches can use these stages throughout the coaching process within the full macro-cycle of the season.
### Funnel Progression Table
| Training progression | Example from unit | Skill development purpose | | Drill stage | Break down movement, reduce pacing pressure, use sequential format. | Introduce and refine the skill under low pressure. | | Unopposed practice | Skill-focused training without opposition. | Assess whether the athlete can maintain control. | | Opposed practice | Similar-ability opponent introduced where appropriate. | Add pressure while keeping the challenge within the athlete's ZPD. | | Variable practice | Vary tasks, station conditions, or opposition starting positions. | Improve adaptation and decision-making. | | Low-context simulation | Competitive linked activities with conditioned environmental dynamics. | Expose athletes to unpredictable but controlled race-like moments. | | High-context simulation | Station transitions, compromised running at race intensity, opponent pressure, judges, penalties, course layout. | Embed skills under contextual race pressure. |
---

chunk.content:
As athletes develop confidence in skills, coaches may allow training to enter variable practice and low-context simulation segments.
These sessions can include activities that are competitively linked with other athletes.
Conditioned environmental dynamics force athletes to respond and adapt.
### Examples of Variable Constraints
| Constraint | Coaching purpose | | Varying the task | Prevents athletes from relying only on one fixed movement solution. | | Varying station conditions | Improves adaptability to race-day variation. | | Adjusting opposition starting positions | Creates tactical pressure and chase scenarios. | | Adding station judging | Exposes athletes to standards, no-reps, and judgment pressure. | | Introducing controversial no-reps | Tests emotional control, decision-making, and resilience. |
This stage enhances skill adaptability, decision-making under changing conditions, and resilience.

chunk.content:
As training variability progresses further, the funnel opens into competition-specific contexts.
In HYROX, high-context simulations may include:
- Station transitions - Paced compromised running at race intensity - Direct opposition - Psychological pressure - Physiological race demands - Skill testing under heightened arousal
Within these higher-variability stages, skills are tested, evaluated, and reflected upon rigorously to embed skills under contextual race pressure.
### High-Context HYROX Simulation Definition
| Item | Detail | | Definition | A full-spectrum race rehearsal simulating race-day complexity: physical, cognitive, environmental, and logistical. | | Purpose 1 | Develop decision-making and race management under pressure. | | Purpose 2 | Train mental readiness, distractions, and unpredictable elements. | | Purpose 3 | Simulate responses to judges, penalties, and transitions. |
### Setup Guidelines
| Guideline | Practical implementation | | Use full or condensed race format | Use full race format: 1 km + 8 stations, or a condensed version. | | Include race features | Add competition lanes, judge interaction, and course markings. | | Appoint judges | Use judges to create realistic standards pressure. | | Simulate crowd and noise | Use music, other athletes, countdown timers, or a start gun. |
### High-Context Variables to Include
| Variable | Implementation | | Roxzone Navigation | Athletes must enter and exit through marked arches; add penalties for skipping or error. | | Course Layout | Use lane ropes, signage, or cones to mimic real station transitions. | | Opposition Presence | Athletes start in seeded waves; add chase or pacing pressure. | | Judges | Use coaches or peers to judge reps, issue no-reps, or give feedback. | | Penalties | Add time penalties or rep penalties for rule breaches. | | Drink Station | Place a hydration station and assign a drinking rule. | | Time Feedback | Yell lap times, rank position, or station splits in real time. | | Warm-up Area Simulation | Athletes must have limited space and equipment to warm up in. | | Noise & Pressure | Play crowd or music noise; use countdown timers; simulate a start gun. | | Pre-Race Briefing | Deliver a real race briefing with course rules and layout before starting. |
---

chunk.content: [0:00:01] Okay we are in module 7.1 Skill Development and I'm joined by Rich Ryan. So Rich can I just ask you from your perspective up to this moment in time where you've had a lot of experience within the sport, what does skill mean to you? [0:00:19] So when thinking about skill when it pertains to HYROX or in any endeavor really for me it's about just being able to accomplish a task automatically. Like having the ability [0:00:35] just to turn something on and being able to do it and doing it with intent the way that you want it to be done. So it really kind of comes down to just like confidence and then also being able to just know that you can do the task at hand. How I kind of [0:00:51] differentiate from like fitness like when I think about fitness it's always it's a lot of like load, volume, intensity. Skill can be done without needing to be under incredible duress as well. So you can work on the skill pieces of how to do the movement, how it should feel, [0:01:08] thinking about how to do the movement and developing the skill to make it automatically not physically but also mentally. Could you give an example in the field of HYROX kind of like how you would view a moment of skill application? [0:01:24] Yeah absolutely. So what people really love about HYROX right and what kind of like the narrative around HYROX is that it is low skill and to a point that it's true. You can look at something and be like, I can push that sled for sure. But to do it efficiently [0:01:40] and effectively there might be a little bit of skill like how to position your body, how to get there quickly, how it should feel. I think about that with a sled pull a little bit more where it's like how to position your arms, making sure that they are in a position [0:01:56] and that your hips are also in a position to put you in a strong and you're taking the tension out of the rope without needing to kind of think about it without wasting any time and you're able to move as soon as you're moving the sleds moving. No position. There's no loss in intention. There's no loss in strength. It's moving while you're moving [0:02:15] and you automatically know how many steps it takes to fill that box. So if it's four, five, six steps, and then you know how many steps it takes to get to the front of the box. It should be like one, two, one, two, or three. And if you can just do that and just turn it on and you just [0:02:31] repeat, repeat, repeat. When you get to the race, you don't have to worry about what to do, how to get into position. And the more mental energy you can save, the more it's going to improve your performance long-term because the mental energy is a lot. The [0:02:47] brain takes up a lot of glucose, right? It takes some energy from your body. So the more we can just do this skill and make it automatic, the better it's going to be just for our energy levels and our performance. So you alluded to preparing for the race itself. I [0:03:04] wonder if you could just deep dive a little bit further in terms of your processes over the years of how you built up to become an elite athlete. So in the race itself, obviously you're under pressure, you're under time and opposition that are fighting for, of course, elite [0:03:20] 15 positions at the World Championships. So I guess my question to you is, how would you develop certain skills and stress test them well in training so that when it comes to the race, there's good, clear transfer? So the first thing with this that makes everything way easier and much more [0:03:40] manageable is committing to a longer timeline, right? There are a lot of skills to develop here. And if you try to do them all at once, it's going to be hard to be effective in any of them really. [0:03:56] And also trying to build fitness at the same time. So just knowing that it's going to take time and you don't need to get better at every single station right now. So really it's, for me, what I've been able to do is like, where's my limiter? What do I need to work on? And then focusing on that one single task. So say lunges, for example, it's [0:04:13] like, I need to get better at lunges. It's like, okay, what, what can I do? It's like, can I do, I could do more lunges? Can I do heavier lunges? Like, sure. But is it the actual lunge that is hurting my ability to like, perform well? And usually it's not like, what, what [0:04:30] for me in this example, the the barrier was my recoverability. I would do lunges, it wouldn't feel great. And I wouldn't want to do them, I would avoid them because of because of these like recoverability factors. So okay, why then then then I dig a little bit deeper to why is the recoverability a problem to go maybe my movements not great. Maybe my [0:04:50] tendons aren't strong. Maybe when I'm moving in the positions, I'm not in an advantageous positions during the actual movement. So it's hurting my recoverability. It's like, okay, how do I get that better to go? Okay, like, my tibia is like, not based right direction, and it needs to go forward that whole biomechanic thing. How do I fix that? And then just [0:05:07] drilling all the way down. And then at the very base of it all, then it can start building it back up. Really, for me, it's identifying limiters, working it all the way down to understand like what this skill is, what what the components of the movement, like physiologically, what they are, what my limiters could be, how to address those, and then start building [0:05:27] back up. And really, the end should be volume load intensity. But I think a lot of times, it's intuitive just to be the start to God, I'm bad at wall balls, I'm gonna do 100 every day. And it's like, so well, I'm bad at wall balls, because my my, whatever my hips [0:05:43] are so tight, that the depth is a problem. And like the actual motion is just like inefficient. So really needs to start at that point to develop the skill of the squat, to then layer on the load intensity and volume of the actual task. That's some really, really great insight. Thank you for that. That is the [0:06:36] work that most people won't do. And to get and to beat most people, you have to do the work that they won't do. If it was as easy as doing the 20 hours of roadwork work a week, a thousand wall balls a week, like people would do it. But that the hard work really is [0:06:56] understanding where you are, like what you need to do to improve and kind of digging deeper into that and understanding like that your individual units as a body is going to be different than everybody else's. So understanding what your background is, why you move the way you move, [0:07:12] how is that the appropriate way to move to get better at the task you want to improve on, and then just like diving in and figuring it out. And it's harder, it's harder to do that than just being like, oh, what's a good wall ball workout? Like, that's easy. That's easy [0:07:28] information to find. It's hard information to find, like, how do I get better at squats? How do I become more efficient? How do I make it hurt less? This builds postural control and major muscle engagement, both critical for transferring force effectively during the sled pull. [0:01:14] Next we isolate the sled pull mechanics. Integrate [0:03:19] the skill into a simple workout, like three rounds of twelve and a half meter burpee broad jump into twelve and a half meter sled pull. This brings the skill transfer under fatigue. chunk.content:
This unit explains how skill development should be periodized differently for novice and high performance HYROX athletes.
The central idea is that effective skill development must reflect the athlete's stage of development.
| Athlete type | Main development need | Coaching style | | Novice athlete | Build fundamental movement efficiency, pacing awareness, and basic decision-making. | Structured, prescriptive learning with frequent external feedback and progressive complexity. | | High performance athlete | Maintain movement quality, pacing, and tactical decisions under fatigue, variability, and race pressure. | Higher variability, self-regulation, internal cueing, and decision-making under stress. |
The unit links this approach to Newcombe's Funnel of Variability and Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD).
Coaches should gradually increase exposure to variability and race context while ensuring that the challenge remains matched to the athlete's current capability.

chunk.section_title: Movement Efficiency: Novice vs High Performance
chunk.content:
Movement efficiency is a major difference between novice and high performance HYROX athletes.
For novices, the focus is on refining basic biomechanical patterns to improve efficiency and reduce injury risk.
For high performance athletes, movement efficiency is refined through specific overload, race-like conditions, and robustness under fatigue and external stressors.
| Skill area | Novice athlete | High performance athlete | | Movement efficiency focus | Refine basic biomechanical patterns. | Maintain efficient technique under fatigue and external stressors. | | Main purpose | Improve efficiency and support injury prevention. | Preserve performance under race scenarios. | | Practice structure | Isolated drills before integration into race-paced conditions. | Highly specific overload and race-demand replication. | | Feedback style | Frequent external feedback such as explicit coach cues or video analysis. | More internal cueing and athlete self-regulation. | | Variability | Introduced progressively after fundamentals are secure. | Strategically introduced through altered conditions and race-like pressure. | | Example | Basic drills before race-paced integration. | Sled pushes against varied opponents or judged burpee broad jumps after maximal effort runs. |
---

chunk.section_title: Pacing Intensity: Novice vs High Performance
chunk.content:
Pacing intensity differs significantly across experience levels.
Novices often struggle to manage exertion because they lack physiological self-awareness and may have underdeveloped aerobic capacity.
A common novice mistake is front-loading effort early in the race, leading to rapid or exponential fatigue.
High performance athletes need more advanced race-optimization strategies. They must fine-tune compromised running and race-specific surging strategies.
| Skill area | Novice athlete | High performance athlete | | Pacing challenge | Difficulty managing exertion across the race. | Optimising race strategy and compromised running. | | Common issue | Front-loading effort too early, causing exponential fatigue. | Need to maintain running form and speed after accumulated station fatigue. | | Coaching method | Controlled progressive overload, structured interval training, and time trials. | Race simulations, strategic surging, heart-rate data, and lactate-threshold data. | | Pacing goal | Understand sustainable effort levels. | Operate in precise intensity zones for maximal performance. | | Key strategy | Negative splitting and effort control. | Strategic surging and race-optimized compromised running. |
---

High performance athletes need more advanced race-optimization strategies.
They must fine-tune compromised running and race-specific surging strategies.

| | Common issue | Front-loading effort too early, causing exponential fatigue.
| Need to maintain running form and speed after accumulated station fatigue.
| | Coaching method | Controlled progressive overload, structured interval training, and time trials.

chunk.content:
Decision-making is a key differentiator between novice and high performance HYROX athletes.
Novices are often reactive. They respond to fatigue and external stimuli without a structured cognitive strategy.
High performance athletes are more proactive. They anticipate race dynamics and adjust strategies in real time.
| Skill area | Novice athlete | High performance athlete | | Decision-making style | Reactive. | Proactive and anticipatory. | | Main limitation | Responds to fatigue and external stimuli without structured strategy. | Must make high-quality decisions under high intensity and pressure. | | Training emphasis | Pattern recognition and pre-planned responses to race scenarios. | Real-time strategic adjustment under pressure. | | Coaching method | Constraint-led approaches such as limiting rest between stations. | Stress exposure training and variable opponents in races or workouts. | | Race demands | Learn how to respond more fluently to expected scenarios. | Assess competitor pacing, modify work-rest ratios, execute tactical accelerations. | | Example | Reduced rest periods between stations to simulate race conditions. | Small roxzones negotiated at very high heart rates. |
---

They respond to fatigue and external stimuli without a structured cognitive strategy.
They anticipate race dynamics and adjust strategies in real time.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: Novice Athlete - Skill Development Sequence
chunk.content:
The novice sequence progresses from fundamental movement learning toward full HYROX simulation.
### Novice Skill Development Sequence
| Step | Stage | Coaching purpose | | 1 | Develop Fundamental Movement Patterns | Focus on basic biomechanics and injury prevention in low-intensity, controlled environments to learn functional movement patterns. | | 2 | Introduce Isolated Skill Drills | Apply functional movements through individual exercises that break down the movement for motor pattern recognition. | | 3 | Integrate Skills into Simple Workouts | Combine movements into short, structured workouts with adequate recovery within unopposed or semi-opposed practice. | | 4 | Introduce Basic Pacing Strategies | Teach negative splitting and effort control to prevent early fatigue within low-context race scenarios or intervals. | | 5 | Simulate Race Conditions with Reduced Intensity | Apply skills in low-pressure adapted simulations with intervals to improve skill execution during intensity after rest. | | 6 | Perform Full HYROX Simulations | Progress to near-race-intensity workouts with complete event execution to establish learned skills under accumulated fatigue. |

chunk.section_title: Chapter 03: High Performance Athlete - Skill Development Sequence
chunk.content:
The high performance sequence begins with maintaining movement efficiency under fatigue and progresses toward performance analysis after competition-level simulation.
### High Performance Skill Development Sequence
| Step | Stage | Coaching purpose | | 1 | Refine Movement Efficiency Under Fatigue | Ensure technique remains effective under ranges of intensity conditioning workouts. | | 2 | Incorporate Race-Specific Pacing Strategies | Use even pacing, strategic surging, and heart-rate-based training sessions for optimization. | | 3 | Introduce Higher-Variability Skill Training | Apply cognitive load training, proactive responses to scenarios or opponents, judge no-rep decisions, altered conditions, different judges, and varied opponents. | | 4 | Conduct Adapted or Full Race Simulations at Competition Intensity | Use event-specific racing with minimal modifications to match real race conditions and consolidate movement efficiency, pacing intensity, and decision-making execution. | | 5 | Analyze and Adjust Based on Performance Data | Use post-race analysis to fine-tune overall athlete skill execution. |
### Higher-Variability Training Examples
| Variable | Example from unit | Intended effect | | Cognitive load | Proactive response to scenarios or opponents within workouts. | Improve decision-making under pressure. | | Judging pressure | Judge no-rep decisions. | Improve standards resilience and emotional control. | | Altered equipment or surface | Sled push on different carpet surfaces. | Improve adaptability to race conditions. | | Different judges | Different people assessing movement standards. | Prepare athletes for variability in race judging. | | Varied opponents | Increased variability of opponents within workouts. | Improve tactical responsiveness. |

chunk.content:
The HYROX Academy Skills Assessment Framework gives coaches a clear, consistent, and adaptable method for evaluating athlete performance across the full spectrum of HYROX preparation.
It is built around two complementary components.
| Framework component | Score available | Assessment context | Purpose | | Skills Assessment in Training | 10 marks | Training settings such as drills, unopposed practice, opposed practice, variable practice, and low-context simulations. | Assess underlying movement capability, movement efficiency, pacing intensity, decision-making, and adaptability under progressive constraints. | | Skills Assessment in HYROX Racing Context | 15 marks | Representative race environments, full or partial HYROX simulations, and high-context race-prep sessions. | Assess whether skills transfer into chaotic, competitive, fatigue-laden race execution. | | Combined readiness score | 25 marks | Combined training and race-context assessment. | Provide a holistic measure of athlete readiness and identify strengths and development areas. |
The dual-lens approach helps coaches prioritize reflective conversations and targeted interventions that build technical resilience, race execution, and HYROX performance capacity.

### Assessment Overview
| Item | Detail | | Focus | Resilience of movement efficiency, pacing intensity, and decision-making under progressive constraints and pressure. | | Key principle | Skill is not just execution in isolation. It is the athlete's ability to self-organize, explore, exploit, and execute effective movement solutions under progressively changing constraints. | | Athlete evaluation grading | 10 marks available. |
### Marking Criteria: Skills Assessment in Training
| Mark range | Level | Description | | 9-10 | High Performance | Movement quality is highly efficient, stable, and adaptable under varying constraints. The athlete maintains technical integrity across progressing fatigue and intensity. They show excellent pacing awareness and execution in isolated and competitive tasks. They make rapid micro-adjustments based on varying dynamic environmental scenarios, showing strong decision-making and perception-action coupling. Very few errors occur in skill application. | | 7-8 | Securing | Movement is mostly efficient and consistent. Minor breakdown under fatigue is corrected quickly. The athlete shows good pacing control with small deterioration under more pressure. Decision-making is generally effective, with some delayed adjustments in progressively challenging scenarios. | | 5-6 | Developing | Movement is functional but inconsistent in efficiency, especially under fatigue. Pacing awareness is occasionally present and only moderately well-regulated or adapted under varying challenging situations. Decision-making is reactive to dynamic environmental stimuli rather than proactive, limiting consistent effectiveness. | | 3-4 | Emerging | Movement quality shows basic structural competence but lacks consistent efficiency. Technical execution frequently deteriorates when constraints or fatigue increase, and recovery of form is slow. Pacing judgment is poorly regulated, with clear over- or under-exertion disrupting rhythm. Adaptation to changing demands is limited, delayed, or ineffective. | | 1-2 | Limited | Movement is inefficient, unstable, and susceptible to breakdown even under minimal constraint. Technical integrity is rarely maintained, and errors accumulate without self-correction. No observable pacing strategy is present. Decision-making and adaptation are minimal or absent, with little connection between environmental cues and movement responses. | | 0 | No credit | No meaningful performance evidence of skills. |

chunk.section_title: Skills Assessment in HYROX Racing Context
chunk.content: | Mark range | Level | Description | | 13-15 | High Performing | The athlete demonstrates exceptional race literacy to explore, exploit, or execute resilient movement efficiency and consistent, adaptable pacing across all stations and runs. They show proactive decision-making in response to environmental and competitive constraints such as crowding, lane changes, equipment or surface variability, judging decisions, and pacing surges. They navigate the course competently while maintaining race-group position, maintain technical integrity under maximal fatigue and pressure, and make rapid micro-adjustments that preserve speed and race position. Decision-making is strategic and anticipatory, allowing exploitation of race opportunities such as drafting, overtaking, and station entry or exit timing. Performance is stable, controlled, and highly effective with minimal errors and clear intentional race strategy. Movement standards are high and rarely questioned by judges. | | 10-12 | Securing | The athlete shows competent race literacy with minor breakdowns in pacing or movement efficiency under fatigue. Transitions are generally smooth but sometimes delayed under pressure. Decision-making is good but sometimes slightly delayed in response to environmental and competitive constraints. Course navigation is solid. Pacing intensity is mostly effective, but the athlete does not always capitalise on opportunities to maintain race-group position. Technical form and pacing degrade slightly in later stages but are corrected quickly. Performance is solid and competitive with few significant errors. Movement standards occasionally lack quality. | | 7-9 | Developing | The athlete shows good but uneven race literacy, with clear capability but inconsistent performance across the full HYROX profile. Movement efficiency is generally adequate but fluctuates as fatigue accumulates. Technical breakdowns occur intermittently and take time to correct. Pacing strategy is present but only occasionally effective and may be disrupted by opposition pressure, misjudged effort, or course navigation issues. Transitions are mixed. Adaptation is mostly reactive and often later than ideal. Decision-making shows glimpses of clarity but lacks proactive control. Movement standards are met on most stations, though several require correction and occasional warnings, with rare penalties. | | 4-6 | Emerging | The athlete shows emerging but inconsistent race literacy. Race dynamics and the environment begin to deteriorate overall skill application. Movement efficiency starts strong but declines under fatigue, and recovery slows in later stages. Pacing strategy is initially present but not well-regulated due to opposition pressure, fatigue, or misjudged effort. Transitions vary, often becoming hesitant. Adaptation is reactive rather than proactive. Decision-making is inconsistent and often lacks clarity or intention. Movement standards are challenged across multiple stations but mostly corrected after warnings, although some penalties may occur. | | 1-3 | Limited | The athlete has major difficulties operating in race context. Pacing is absent or erratic, transitions are disorganised, and technical form deteriorates rapidly even under low fatigue. There is little to no adaptation to environmental constraints, and the athlete appears overwhelmed by race demands. Decision-making is minimal or ineffective, leading to repeated errors, inefficient movement patterns, and inability to sustain required intensity. Performance lacks structure, strategy, and resilience. Movement standards are not thoroughly understood or applied, causing regular penalties. | | 0 | No credit | No meaningful participation in context. |

chunk.content:
Together, the Skills Assessment in Training and HYROX Race Context create a unified framework from foundational movement quality through full race execution.
| Assessment lens | What it reveals | | Skills Assessment in Training | The athlete's underlying capacity to move efficiently, regulate pacing intensity, and adapt under pressure. | | HYROX Race Context | How well those same qualities transfer into unpredictable, fatigue-laden competition demands. | | Combined use | Helps coaches track progress, identify limiting factors, and tailor interventions with precision. |
The framework reinforces that HYROX performance is not built on isolated abilities alone, but on the athlete's capacity to integrate skills, strategy, and resilience across an evolving race landscape.

And they are certainly not alone with this circle motion. Again, go to YouTube and watch videos of your favorite running athletes. Not hierofascist athletes because I don't trust them with good running technique. And then you will find many good exam

However, it is important to point out that just because Kipchoge and Kiptum move the way they do with their hands, doesn't mean that the hands have to move in circles. This can be solved in a number of different ways, this little flick.

But as long as your athletes find the power diagonally through the body, everything is fine. And that is what's important. Does running like this require a little extra mobility? Well, most people have enough mobility to do this.

However, some runners may be a little bit too stiff for it to work in the best way. It should be remembered that the size of any movement is always proportional to how fast you run. Fast you run, the bigger the movements.
So if you don't run very fast, you don't need to move very much. But if you run faster, you need more mobility. And since my guess is that many people who hire a HYROX Level 2 coach probably have

the ambition to run relatively fast, this mobility becomes a little more important. The problem is that many people, especially men actually, and people with sanitary jobs sitting down in the office too much, have too little mobility, which makes it

difficult for them to run with a good and efficient kayak paddle hip. The great thing is that if you run and use the power of your core and hips in this way, you get a dynamic mobility training in return.

chunk.content:
Running faster Step 1 - Find the rotation in the hip Step 2 - Kayak Paddle Hips Up/Forward Step 3 - Shoulders are connected to the hip Summary Level 2 - Modul 7.2 - 2. Run faster and reducing the cost for HYROX Stations
Running Faster If there's one thing I've been fascinated by in my years as a running coach, it's how many people think that the best way to run as energy efficiently as possible is to keep all movements small because they think that small movements always cost less energy than big movements. And indeed, this is often true. If I lift my arm 2.5 centimeters, 1 inch, it obviously costs less energy than if I lift my arm 25 centimeters, 10 inches.
As a result, many runners try to minimize all movements. This is often combined with a belief that you should be still in the core and hip because it is a sign of core stability, which of course is always good. A third thing on the same theme that these people believe is that you run with your legs. Of course, you should also move your arms. But the power is generated mainly with the legs and possibly also the gluteus maximus. The problem is that none of what I wrote above is true. No, small movements do not always cost less energy than large movements. In running it can be just the opposite. No, the hip and core should absolutely under no circumstances be still. It's not a sign of good stability and something that is good for your running efficiency. No, you don't run with your legs. Well, maybe you do. But you run with your legs about as much as you punch a right hook in boxing or throw a discus with your arm alone or kick a football with your leg alone.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: Run Faster and Reducing the Cost for HYROX Stations
chunk.content: If you meet a coach in any of the three sports boxing, discus, football, they will say that power comes from the hip and core. You get power from the ground and find a drive through the hip which then moves the arm and leg respectively. If a discus thrower has the slightest tension in their arm they won't throw that far at all. And no boxer throws a hard right hook using only their arm while leaving their hip completely still. By the way, what about now, should you hold your racket very tight or very loose when serving in tennis? Yes, that's right, very loose. Because you really don't want to have any tension in your arm because then the serve won't be as hard. This is how you can go through sport after sport. Do you lift a barbell with your arms? No, mostly with the hips. Do you swim with your arms only or should you also have a hip rotation? Do you do a roundhouse kick in karate by having a still and stable hip and then focusing on moving your foot as fast as you can towards your opponent? No, you don't. So why should running be different from almost any other sport that requires dynamic power? Sprint runners practice a lot on finding power from the core/hip. But for some reason, many long- distance runners and HYROX athletes don't really understand how important the drive from the hip is when they run. And this lesson is to help them understand how they can unleash a lot more power in their running without costing more energy. It's like a discus thrower who has been standing completely still with their body and only moving their arm when throwing but suddenly learns that it's all in the hip/core. I would say that this is even more important for HYROX athletes than for runners. At several of the stations, you have to use your leg muscles a lot, for example, sled push and lunges. When you engage large, strong muscles from the center of your body and allow the power to propagate out into your legs, you save your thighs a lot, for example. And if you have to do 100 meters of lunges with a sandbag on your shoulders, it's good to have saved your thighs as much as possible before station seven comes up. How this works and how to teach it in a good way is best if I show. That's why you'll find most of the facts in the video that accompanies this lesson. However, here is a short summary that you can watch to quickly refresh your knowledge after watching the video. It is not intended that the instructions below can be easily understood without having seen the video lesson.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: Run Faster and Reducing the Cost for HYROX Stations
chunk.content:
Step 1 - Find the rotation in the hip This is about getting the athlete to release tension in their core that costs unnecessary energy by allowing their hip to rotate and follow their foot backwards. This is also an important part of how to get the feet up a little higher under the body (which saves energy), creates knee lift, reduces the risk of overstride and creates a little more power in their push off. It's also a way to get longer legs which gives a better leverage which gives more power which gives more speed. As I say in the video, you don't want to ski cross country with short slalom ski poles. You want longer poles for cross country skiing because they give you more power. And with this rotation in step 1 of the kayak paddle hip, you get longer ski poles, I mean legs. Most runners/athletes have no idea how much they are actually resisting movement in their hips during normal running. This may also be a reason why many runners feel like they get more flow in their running after maybe 15 minutes of running and sometimes even longer. Of course, there are many reasons why running feels easier once the body has warmed up. But many people find that after a while they can't really resist the forces that create the rotation when they have been running for a while, which means that they get an efficient running stride by not working against the body's natural movements. The increased fatigue in their core helps them to run more efficiently.
Step 2 - Kayak Paddle Hips Up/Forward This is where the actual kayak paddle movement is introduced. Step 1 is only to teach runners/athletes how important it is to find a relaxed, dynamic and harmonious movement. Letting the hip rotate backwards is not really something you need to think about to any great extent when you run, although you may sometimes give it half a thought. Because if you don't let your hip rotate backwards, there is a risk that the up/forward movement that we now add in step 2 will not be as relaxed and good as possible. The name 'kayak paddle hips' comes from how the hip movement should look. You lift one side of the hip up/forward which creates downward/backward force on the other side, ie just when you push a kayak paddle up/forward creates down/backward force on the other side which drives the kayak forward. This is obviously not a big movement, as you do with a paddle, but it should definitely be there. This kayak paddle hip movement does a lot of good things for running.
