chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: Run Faster and Reducing the Cost for HYROX Stations
chunk.content: Firstly, this movement helps to lift the foot upwards after toe off which makes it move a little higher above the ground on the way forward which makes the foot move closer to the hip, creating a shorter 'pendulum' which costs less energy than moving a long pendulum as it does when you have the foot close to the ground on the way forward. It is also via the lift up/forward in the hip that you create a good knee drive. Just like when the Thai boxer sends a knee straight forward into his opponent preferably not only has his hip completely still and only uses the hip flexors but also gets the power from the hip movement, it is the kayak paddle hip that sends the runners' knees up/forward. There is an American expression often used by sprint coaches that I think is very apt for this: "Whip from the hip". When you lift your hip up/forward on one side, the body is also better at creating stability in the hip on the side where you land. And a strong and stable hip is of course beneficial. If you drop your hip, you usually get longer contact time and not as much help from the stretch shortening cycle. In addition, a dropped hip is often associated with a higher risk of injury, even though the dropped hip may not be the direct cause, but more a symptom of poor running technique that can lead to an increased risk of injury. When the hip is driven up/forward, force is also created down/back on the other side, which in this case is the foot that is on the ground, which of course also generates speed.

chunk.content:
power, but that's the case regardless of how the increased power is created. But if several muscles and body parts work together to create a certain force, each part has to work much less than if you rely on just a few body parts. So even if each individual part works less, a greater overall force is created. It works much like a team competing in a tug of war. If the whole team is in place and pulling in time with each other, they will generate a lot of total force even if each person is not pulling that hard. However, if half the team goes to lunch, those left behind will have to generate more force per person even if the total force of the pull is the same as when the whole team is in place. By using more muscles working together in long chains through the body and also finding the dynamics of movement that generate the 'rubber band effect' in the stretch shortening cycle, each muscle has to work much less than if only a few muscles have to do the whole job. Most runners feel this clearly when you first teach them these three steps and then ask them to run 'as usual' which is usually without any kayak paddle hip with diagonal connection to the shoulders. Then almost everyone can feel how much heavier it gets and how much more they have to work with their quads. Summary In any sport that requires some type of dynamic force, it largely comes from the body's midsection, hip and core. This is true whether we're talking golf, weightlifting, javelin, swimming, karate or sprinting. And, of course, it also applies to the running in HYROX races. It's a chain reaction. A relaxed shoulder that moves in multiple directions and a sliding shoulder blade work in relaxed harmony with the hips and core, creating the "kayak paddle hip" that in turn controls the movements of the legs and feet and the power required to run fast and efficiently. If there is any disruption in this chain, everything falls apart. Lifting the chest to achieve "better posture" locks the shoulders and shoulder blades, which prevents the chain from getting started at all. A sitting running style prevents the hips from moving like a kayak paddle.
The knees should be very relaxed so that the feet come up quickly and relatively high immediately after toe-off. It is largely the upward/forward movement of the kayak paddle hip that brings the feet higher and increases knee lift, which often counteracts braking forces and overstride while making it easier to generate power to run fast.

chunk.content:
Unlock your Hip So what is this mobility I speak of? How do you train this? Summary Level 2 - Modul 7.2 - 3. Unlock your Hip
Unlock your Hip The mobility that few runners realise they need and that is necessary to harness the power of the kayak paddle hip.
A quick reminder from the video in chapter 1: you don't swim front crawl using your arms, shoulders, and pectoral muscles. Instead, the power comes mainly from your back (latissimus dorsi) and, above all, your hips, core, and body rotation when swimming. If you are also going to combine 8x1000 meters of swimming with, for example, 8x50 push-ups, it is practical to save the power in your pecs, shoulders, and arms during the swim so that you have energy left for the push-ups. The same applies in HYROX. It is important to run in a way that is not only energy efficient and can generate high speed, but also in a way that allows you to save the muscles in your legs for the stations. And that is why you learned about the "kayak paddle hip" in lesson 1. Unfortunately, however, many people lack the mobility required for the kayak paddle hip movement, which means that as a coach, you must ensure that your athletes are able to perform the movements required to save energy during the run to the station. And this is what you will learn here in lesson 2. As you have now learnt in lesson 1, using the kayak paddle hips is a very efficient way to get longer legs and find the power through the chain shoulders, core, hip. As with all adjustments, they should be done in moderation. And the size of a movement is obviously related to how fast you run. The faster the pace, the bigger the movement. This also means that athletes who don't run as fast in HYROX don't have the same mobility requirements as those who run really fast. The problem is that those who are fast often have adequate mobility, which is one of the reasons why they are fast, while those who are slower often do not have the required mobility even though they do not need to be as mobile as the fast ones. One type of mobility that relatively few runners/athletes know they need is inward and outward rotation of their femur relative to their hip. This is largely because they know nothing at all about kayak paddle hips and, as I said in lesson 1, often actively try to discourage movement in a misguided attempt to save energy.

To get a powerful push off and have an energy-efficient running technique, it is good if you have a good hip extension. To achieve this, the pelvis must rotate slightly backwards. If it doesn't rotate, the movement will be straight backwards. The femur cannot be moved back more than about 30 degrees in relation to your pelvis. That's not very much. You can see how little it is in the picture of double Olympic triathlon champion Alistair Brownlee. If the movement is more straight backwards, without the rotation of the hip, will create this movement that does not create a good push off at all and also risks bending the back with problems in the lower back as a result. Of course, you can also avoid getting longer legs and a stronger push off by neither bending your pelvis back nor by rotating, but it will not be very efficient. So what is this mobility I speak of?
For some people reading this, this will not come as a surprise at all as they have full awareness of the rotation of the femur. If you are more of a strength coach, it may not be as obvious, although of course you still know how important the rotation of the femur is when doing a deep squat, for example. The left leg has obviously not rotated together with the hip. The runners quads and knees are still facing forwards. This means that this leg is in an internally rotated position in relation to my pelvis. This means that the runner's right leg / femur is rotated outwards. have the same knowledge, here is my attempt to illustrate what I mean.

Now compare it with the picture of me with my 90 degrees. No wonder he had big problems with his running and with many and long lasting injuries. When he cannot rotate his femur, his hip cannot rotate either, which means that the backward movement of the foot after toe-off takes his femur backward, bending his pelvis into an anterior tilt, which compresses the lower back while making it difficult for him to find power from the hip and gluteus maximus via the kayak paddle hip, forcing him to compensate for the loss of power by working much harder with other muscles, which risks overload.
How do you train this? Many of the absolutely most common exercises for runners are focused on training this. Take, for example, the fact that over the last 100 years or so, runners have done various hurdle drills. When going over a hurdle, you first lift one leg straight ahead while the other is lifted over the hurdle by lifting the knee up and then lifting the foot so high that the lower leg is horizontal between foot and knee which is great for improving inward rotation. Picture 6 Picture 7 Just doing as shown in picture 7 is also good and can be used as a warm-up exercise. The same goes for the running drill, which is often called 'Karaoke' (picture 8). It is an excellent exercise to both train mobility and to practice creating drive with the core and hip as you do with the kayak paddle hips. In the video accompanying this lesson, I talk more about this exercise and how you can do it in different ways depending on what you are aiming for. In the video, you will also find more examples of good exercises for unlocking your athletes' hips. So there are lots of different types of exercises and running drills designed to improve the mobility of the hip-leg connection, even if runners are not always aware of it. However, I believe it is my job as a coach to explain exactly why a runner/athlete should do an exercise. Because the better they understand what it is for and how that part fits into the big picture of optimizing running technique, the better they will be at performing the exercise in the best way. This leads us to the question: 'But do elite runners really train intentionally to improve and maintain this mobility, the inward and outward rotation of the femur in relation to their pelvis'? The answer is: no and yes. 'No' because there are many runners who may not know exactly what they are doing when they go over hurdles or do other hurdle exercises or the "Karaoke" exercise or improve inward and outward rotation skills. Then you can't say that they are working on this
deliberately. But just because they don't know exactly why they are doing an exercise other than that their coach has said it is good and therefore must include it in their routine, you cannot say that they are not working on this mobility. Because they are, even if they are not always aware of exactly what they are affecting. In addition, virtually all good runners run with an efficient kayak paddle hip even if they are not aware of it. In fact, none of the national team runners I have helped with their running technique have been fully aware of how the kayak paddle hip works. They use it, but without being really aware of what they are doing. Just like you are not aware exactly how all the muscles work and relax when you walk even if you have no problem walking. But once you have created awareness of what is happening, you can also start to nuance it to find what is optimal for each individual runner. Because the good runners have the kayak paddle hips in place, they get dynamic mobility training every minute they run. Moreover, because they run fast and the size of all movements is proportional to the pace, they get full mobility training from this rotation just by running. This is in contrast to recreational runners who not only run slower and then make much smaller movements in the hip but also many times consciously, or unconsciously, counteract this natural movement in the belief that they should be still in this part of the body. So the elite runners already have adequate mobility and use this mobility a lot when they run, which they do a lot every week. Meanwhile, recreational runners are mostly sedentary in offices and Netflix sofas, they are stiff and immobile and don't use even the tiny amount of mobility they have. The result is that elite runners maintain and develop their mobility for many hours each week while recreational runners continue to run in a stiff and inefficient manner.

chunk.content: Summary In order to extract power from the kayak paddle hip, the athlete must have adequate inward and outward rotation of the femur in relation to the pelvis. Without adequate mobility, two things can happen: Reduced force from the hip in the push off while the backward movement via the stretch shortening cycle contributes to the up/forward movement of the kayak hip which is a strong contributor to a good knee lift which is important for running fast and efficiently. When the femur moves straight backwards, without rotation, there is a high risk that the pelvic bone will also bend backwards, which results in a sitting running style that is not very effective and also makes it difficult to get your kayak paddle hip going.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Problem With Some Running Drills
chunk.content:
The problem with some running drills B-Skip But maybe it's a circle after all Summary Level 2 - Modul 7.2 - 6. The problem with some running drills
The problem with some running drills The running drill "B-skip" and the idea that runners should have a good "paw back" or that the feet moves in a circle or like a wheel is not how running works.
All parts of HYROX will require less energy and be completed faster if your athletes can improve their technique. Using your triceps the most on the SkiErgg or doing the row with bent elbows is obviously not ideal if you want to perform at your best in a competition. One thing that distinguishes running from the stations in HYROX is that in running there are a large number of different running drills that are used by many to improve their running technique. To my knowledge, there are not nearly as many established exercises for improving technique in wall balls, burpees, SkiErgg, or any of the other stations. Of course, there are technique drills for wall balls, but if you search YouTube for "running drills," you will find more than you can watch in a lifetime. Therefore, it is likely that you too will recommend running drills to your athletes to improve their running, and I would therefore like to raise a few issues with them, as I believe that they are not a good tool for improving an athlete's running technique and that there are exercises that can actually impair your athletes' efficiency. And that is obviously not what we want. Various running drills are great to do, especially when warming up for hard intervals. However, there is a problem with runners believing that running drills are the way to run, that they are a way to achieve a better and more efficient movement pattern. But some running drills can actually cause runners to run in a way that makes them less efficient. I know, it sounds so logical. In order to run fast, you have to make sure that there is quite a lot of force pushing your body forwards. But how do we do that? Do we push the foot forwards? No, we don't. That would probably mostly create braking forces, right? Straight down? No. We don't want to push straight down, because we want to run forward, not straight up. Backwards? And now you are probably screaming silently inside your head: "YES, backwards. Because that's what pushes me forward."

chunk.content:
B-Skip And if that is what you should do, it would be great to make sure you push your foot backwards, so that it moves backwards in relation to the ground before it hits the ground. You know, like when you do the running drill 'B-skip' (picture 1) or when a trainer tells you that it's important to have a so-called 'Paw back' or that you should think that your feet are moving in a circle, like a wheel. The big problem with most of what I have written so far in this lesson is that it is not true. No, large horizontal forces pushing us forward are not important. On the contrary, it is actually the vertical forces that determine how fast you run. High vertical forces increase forward speed, not unnecessary up and down movement. And the idea that the foot should be pulled in under the body, as in the 'B-skip' or the 'Paw back' instruction, or that the foot moves in a circle, is also not at all how running works. But you already knew this if you completed lesson 3. There, I included an image that, although it is about sprinting, clearly shows that the vertical forces are much greater than the horizontal forces. So it's really important to produce vertical forces if you want to run a bit faster. If your athletes instead focus on pulling their foot backwards in relation to the ground, very little vertical force is created and in fact hardly any force at all. The more horizontally
their feet move when they hit the ground, the LESS vertical forces they produce. The fact that the muscles do not work so much to create horizontal forces becomes clear if you look at when your main running muscles are activated. I have met many runners and running coaches who believe that much of the muscle work comes in the second half of the time you have your foot on the ground. That it is in that last part before toe off that you should really try to find power from, for example, calves and glute max. Especially the importance of activating the glute max at the end of your push off is an extremely widespread 'truth'. But the activation of the glute max and calf muscles is absolutely greatest at midstance. The further away from midstance the foot moves on its way to toe off the less activation there is.

chunk.content:
I've said it before and I'll say it again: Running is a bounce, not like pushing a car. So why is it that almost all running coaches who instruct efficient running technique stand as shown in picture 3 to the right? They stand as in the picture with the foot slightly in front of them and show how it is pushed downwards backwards so that it ends up under the body. And in principle, it is absolutely true that the foot is first in the place it is in picture. And a short moment later, the foot is (hopefully) more under the body. It then looks like that the foot must move backwards in relation to the ground if it is to go between these two points. Unfortunately, what is easy to forget to explain to the runners and athletes you coach is that the body is not stationary when this movement is performed. Lets look at picture number 4. First the foot is at the starting point marked with number 1. From that position it should move relatively vertically down towards the ground to number 2 as shown by the arrow. But doesn't that result in an overstride, you might be thinking now. No, because the body moves forwards when you run. The body
moves from 1 to 2 so the foot is more under the body. It is not the foot that moves backwards in relation to the ground that makes you land without an overstride.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Problem With Some Running Drills
chunk.content: [No readable text visible on this page.] Although I often let my runners do running drills, I am very careful to point out that the B-skip exercise, when you first throw your foot forward and then pull it under your body is NOT something that should try to resemble how you move when you run. Because just as I have many times seen runners who get a significantly worse running technique when a coach stood still and showed how to pull the foot under the body, it is not uncommon for B-skip to have the same effect. Runners get the idea that B-skip is a way to train to improve the movement of the foot backwards as they believe that it is the horizontal force backwards that drives them forward. My advice is therefore: Feel free to do the running drill B-skip, but be sure to tell your athletes that it is an exercise for mobility, coordination and activation, not a way to try to implement a backward movement of the foot! Maybe you've already figured all this out. You are (soon) a Level 2 coach in HYROX and probably have a good experience to teach good running technique. However, as I so often see even experienced coaches showing how to avoid overstride by pulling the foot under the body, I want to point out here that your athletes probably haven't got this at all. They see how you instruct and do

Because just as I have many times seen runners who get a significantly worse running technique when a coach stood still and showed how to pull the foot under the body, it is not uncommon for B-skip to have the same effect.

My advice is therefore: Feel free to do the running drill B-skip, but be sure to tell your athletes that it is an exercise for mobility, coordination and activation, not a way to try to implement a backward movement of the foot!

Ask them to run and imagine that their feet are moving in a circle like a bicycle wheel and that they have the wheel straight under them, the red circle in the picture 6. Then ask them to move the wheel forwards a little (which will make it feel much worse as there will be more overstride). Then you ask them to move the wheel back underneath them followed by moving the wheel back a little before going back to having the wheel underneath them again, the green circle in picture. This way they get a pretty clear sense of the differences and even if they move their imaginary wheel very little, it will probably still feel like they have moved it a lot and actually reduced their overstride as well. However, a little warning is needed here. If you ask athletes to move their wheel backwards, it is very easy for the adjustment to be too large, which usually leads to a strong posterior tilt of their pelvis. But with small, small adjustments, it is still possible to use the analogy of a circle or a wheel. At least as long as your athletes don't make their feet move backwards in relation to the ground just before they land.
Summary Vertical force is important if you want to run fast and efficiently. But vertical power doesn't mean you bounce straight up. You land, the body makes a small compression in midstance that makes the whole rubber band effect in the stretch shortening cycle kicks in, your body moves slightly forward which means that when you get the recoil from the elastic parts that makes you move diagonally upwards forwards. If you try to pull your foot backwards, you get almost no vertical force at all. If you try to move your feet in a circle, like a wheel, to get this backward movement of the feet in a "paw back", you will increase the risk of overstride. And finally, no, the feet do not move backwards in relation to the ground. At least not so much that it has any significant impact on your running. The foot goes down while the body moves forward over the foot. If you still want to think of the feet as moving in a circle, despite the obvious problems with that, then it is better if your athletes think of the circle as being a little more behind them. unit.title: the Cause of Running Injuries
unit.unit_summary:
The cause of running injuries
The cause of running injuries Continuity is key. It doesn't matter if you want to learn origami or drive a Formula 1 car, become better at a foreign language or become a better HYROX athlete. Training continuously over a long period of time is the path to success. If you manage to train 3-4 sessions a week for a year, you will probably develop more regardless of how you train compared to if you have had to take several breaks.

The cause of running injuries Continuity is key. It doesn't matter if you want to learn origami or drive a Formula 1 car, become better at a foreign language or become a better HYROX athlete. Training continuously over a long period of time is the path to success. If you manage to train 3-4 sessions a week for a year, you will probably develop more regardless of how you train compared to if you have had to take several breaks. That is why it is so incredibly important to avoid interruptions due to injuries. And since running injuries are extremely common, here you will learn what causes running injuries so you can help your athletes achieve the continuity they need for optimal development and performance. Various types of injuries are very common among runners. This is largely due to the fact that running is a very repetitive sport with (almost) exactly the same movement all the time, and that there is a lot of strain from all the thousands of landings you make even in a short session. Obviously, the faster a runner runs, the greater the forces. This means that athletes who come to me and say they want to run really fast AND minimise the risk of injury are almost like saying: 'I want to turn right at the next junction, but also left'. Okay, maybe not quite that extreme, but not that far off. Because you can run more or less gently at a given pace. But running in an extremely gentle way for 3 min/km, 4.50 min/mile, will still expose the body to much greater forces and strain than if you run with relatively poor technique for 6.31 min/km, 10.30 min/mile. It's like they say when it comes to the risk of serious injury in road accidents: 'Speed kills'. Luckily, unlike cars, with the right training we can make our bodies withstand very high forces so we can do our 3 minute HYROX runs without breaking. And it's your job as a coach to make sure your athletes can do that, if they have the right genes and the ability to train and rest as much as required. Therefore, it is also good that you know where to start looking for what causes pain and other types of injuries that limit your athletes to reach their goals, which is the point of this text. When I am asked by runners what their running injuries are caused by, I sometimes ask them to quote a Taylor Swift song where she sings: 'It's me. I'm the problem. It's me'. It can be assumed that the injured runner has been running more and/or with too much intensity than their body could handle. It is their own eagerness to train more and harder in conjunction with insufficient recovery and not listening to their body that caused the injury. They, the athletes, are the problem. It is them. I'm joking, of course. But only a little. Making sure athletes don't increase volume and intensity too quickly is perhaps the most important task of a running coach. Because the best way to success is of course continuity. So it's better to take it a little slower with the progression and to get continuity than to get quick, short-term results that end in injuries and training breaks. Who gets injured can seem almost random. Some people never get injuries while others suffer a lot. For example, with my 3D cameras I can measure joint loading. That's an insane amount. All the power bars showed dark red. But that athlete is very rarely injured. He can simply take a huge beating. He was one of the world's elite in his sport, Adventure Racing where you compete for maybe 5-6 days at a time, and has a World Championship medal to his name. Of course, I helped him to put less strain on his body without compromising the speed he needs to still be able to run fast. But it still says a lot about how unfair it can be. How some, thanks to very good genes in combination with a lifetime of training can withstand and absorb lots of training and very high loads while others, who in my software may get the value 12/100 on their joint load, which is less than half of what is required to end up in the 'Light' category, can still have lots of different injury problems. Of course, this won't come as a surprise to you as a soon-to-be Level 2 coach, but you have to pay a huge amount of attention to who you're coaching to help them avoid injury and develop optimally. In simple terms, the risk of injury is U-shaped if you look at how experienced a runner is, see the picture. This means that beginners have a higher risk of injury but that the risk decreases the longer they have been running. However, the risk rises again when runners start to approach elite level as it requires much greater volume of running and also generates higher forces due to faster pace. Some people can almost be considered as 'beginners' even if they have been running for several years. I am thinking mainly of those who live in a country where it is dark and cold for part of the year and they therefore engage in exercise other than running during that time of year. They are more likely to experience problems when it gets lighter and warmer outside and they start running again compared to those who continue to run all year round. Those who take a break from running for part of the year are therefore more likely to be counted as beginners when they start running again, which moves them far to the left on the red curve in the illustration.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Cause of Running Injuries
chunk.content: Most common causes of running injuries Highest risk of getting a running-related injury: Previous injury Running injuries are a very complex subject and it is rare to be able to say that there is a single cause behind an injury. But statistically speaking, the single biggest risk factor for an athlete to suffer an injury is that he/she has had a previous injury. For example, if a runner has had problems with his/her Achilles tendons, the injury that the runner is most likely to get is exactly the same type of Achilles injury as before. Therefore, coaches should be very aware of previous injuries, even if they are a few years ago. Apart from previous injury, here are the five most common causes of injury in running. Note that they are listed in the order in which they affect the risk of injury, with the one that affects the risk the most coming first. 1. Frequency, volume and intensity of training

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Cause of Running Injuries
chunk.content: This may sound obvious but how much, how often and how hard you train is the cause of a powerful majority of all running injuries. However, it can be good to be reminded of this because it is so extremely common for recreational runners to make up a variety of reasons why they got an injury that are not at all linked to how they trained. It could be that they wore new shoes or ran on an unfamiliar surface or that they stretched too little or that they stretched too much or that they forgot to take their daily magnesium pill, or whatever. But a good training program that takes this into account is by far the best way to avoid sports injuries. There are three variables you can work with: Frequency, which is how many sessions a week you train. Volume, which is how long the sessions are and what total volume in minutes you reach during a week or month. Intensity, which is of course how hard each session is. When building an exercise programm with the intention of reducing injury risk, you should not increase frequency, volume and intensity at the same time. Increasing only two of them is usually not good either. If you increase the volume, it may be good to reduce the intensity for a while. And of course the other way round, if you increase the intensity both in terms of the individual sessions and the number of more intense sessions per week, you should probably also reduce the volume a little and make room for extra recovery. 2. Poor recovery As the old saying goes: 'It's not when you run your hardest intervals or do your heaviest deadlifts that you get fast and strong. It's when you're sitting at home on the sofa and, most importantly, when you're sleeping that development happens'. It may not be an old saying, but it's hard to overestimate the importance of rest. There are several different studies that show the importance of sleep in particular. A good example is a study done in the US on collage basketball players ("The Effects of Sleep Extension on the Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players" 2011, Cheri D Mah et al.). Now remember, if you play collage basketball in the US, you are very good. It is not comparable to what school basketball looks like in most other countries (like in Sweden where I live).

It could be that they wore new shoes or ran on an unfamiliar surface or that they stretched too little or that they stretched too much or that they forgot to take their daily magnesium pill, or whatever.

Volume, which is how long the sessions are and what total volume in minutes you reach during a week or month.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Cause of Running Injuries
chunk.content: They started by measuring the participants' accuracy and speed through penalty shots and 15-second sprints. After the tests, they had to sleep 10 hours a night for six weeks. But it's hard to dictate sleep. So instead, the rule was that they would lie in their beds and try to sleep for at least ten hours a night. That was the only thing that changed. After the six weeks, their shooting accuracy improved, with free throw percentage increasing by 9% and 3-point field goal percentage increasing by 9.2% and they were 4-5 percent faster. This was by sleeping/lying in their beds more. Not training more. Also, don't forget that it takes longer for a 60-year-old to recover from a tough workout than for a 25-year-old. To maximize recovery, nutrition is also very important. Yes, I get it, as a Levels 2 coach you know this. But I still want to remind (nag) that the body must have enough building blocks to build a stronger body and become a little stronger and faster than you were before. With insufficient rest/sleep and poor nutritional intake, the body will not have a chance to repair everything you have broken down during training, which will only be a downward spiral that can lead to overtraining and/or injury. The risk of colds/viral illnesses also increases as the immune system is weakened by insufficient rest and nutrition. Again, this part cannot be overestimated and recovery should be planned into an athlete's schedule just as much as the training itself. There is a great quote by Swedish runner Anders Gärderud that I think you should take with you. Anders Gärderud won Olympic gold and broke the world record in the 3000 meters steeplechase in 1976 and held the Swedish record in the 5000 meters from 1976 to 2022. In an interview, when asked how many sessions a day he trained when he was at his best, he replied: 'One, but it was 24 hours long'. He then elaborated on that answer, explaining that everything he did was part of his training. The running, the eating, the resting, the sleeping. Everything was planned for every hour of the day. Now, it's likely that none of the athletes you train are full-time HYROX professionals. But I like the mindset. How many hours a day I lie in bed trying to sleep is almost as important to have in the schedule as the number of kilometers/miles to be run or wall balls to do. 3. Tissue Tolerance The risk of a house being destroyed in a storm depends largely on how solidly it is built. The stronger and sturdier a house is built, the stronger the winds it can withstand. The same goes for your body and the risk of it breaking down when you storm with a lot of exercise. The better the tolerance to high forces, the less risk of injury. Tissue tolerance increases over time as you run more. At least, provided that running is kept at a reasonable level and that the body is given time to adapt to higher demands, i.e. that points 1 and 2 in this list are properly managed. A very good way to increase tissue tolerance is of course also strength training and then preferably with really heavy weights. Fewer repetitions with heavier weights are better for tissue tolerance than many repetitions with lighter weights. And tendons, such as the patellar tendon and the Achilles tendon, are usually best trained with really heavy isometric exercises. 4. Biomechanics

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Cause of Running Injuries
chunk.content: It goes without saying that the higher the forces produced, the greater the risk of injury. Lifting a pencil 30 times will not cause any major injury risk. Lifting a dumbbell weighing 50kg/110 pounds 30 times has a much higher risk of injury, for the simple reason that you have to produce much more force. Now, increased forces certainly don't always have to be bad. As you know, a higher vertical force can make you get more energy return from the stretch shortening cycle. But there are more directions of force than vertical, for example, lateral forces, braking forces and screwing forces in both the sagittal and frontal planes. A runner's biomechanics, i.e. how he/she moves, joint angles and muscle activation affect the risk of injury. Some coaches I meet are a bit surprised when I tell them that running technique is only fourth on the list when it comes to injury risk. They think I would put 'efficient running technique' at the top of a list like this, as that's what I work on and I'm happy to tell them how efficient it can be in avoiding injury. But it doesn't matter how good a running technique a person has if they go from not running at all to doing two hard interval sessions a day, seven days a week. Same thing if they combine it with sleeping 4 hours a night and have poor tissue tolerance. Then it may not help to have a really good technique. 4.1 LEVELS AND DIRECTIONS OF FORCES 4.2. HOW DIFFERENT BODY PARTS INTERACT IN THE BODY

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Cause of Running Injuries
chunk.content: It may be that if you reduce one of these force directions, another increases. For example, if a runner lands too far in front of their center of gravity, that is, has an excessive overstride, the vertical forces will most likely decrease while there is a risk that the lateral forces and braking forces will increase. Or, in simpler terms, the forces that can help you run fast will decrease while those that make you less efficient and potentially increase the risk of injury will increase. Unfortunately, it is not possible to say 'the higher the forces, the greater the risk of injury'. At least not on an individual level. As I mentioned earlier in this text, there are athletes who have very high loads in different directions of their knees and hips but never suffer injuries, while there are runners who have very low joint loads and measurably load their bodies very little, but still suffer one injury after another. Life is pretty unfair that way. How much a runner loads their body is actually largely self-regulating. A person who has trained crossfit at a high level will probably run in a way that puts much more strain on joints and muscles than a person who is new to training and may weigh more than is optimal for runners. Relative to their body weight, overweight athletes almost always put less strain on their bodies than those who are really strong and fit. At the individual level, it is therefore difficult to say 'You have load X on your body, therefore your risk of injury Y is high'. At the group level, it might be possible to say that a really high load increases the risk of injury and/or that the person has to work quite hard and therefore finds it more difficult to keep going for a longer period of time. 4.1 LEVELS AND DIRECTIONS OF FORCES 4.2. chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Cause of Running Injuries
chunk.content: Here we can once again use the analogy of a team competing in a tug-of- war. If everyone in the team is in place and working at the same pace, they will be able to produce a lot of power. But if two of them take a lunch break and one of those left behind doesn't work at the same pace as the others, it will be very difficult to produce as much power as before it became unrhythmic and some went to lunch. For example, when swimming the front crawl, much of the power should come from the rotation of the body and the large and strong back muscles latssimus dorsi. However, it is quite common for beginners in swimming to use more shoulders and chest muscles (Pectoralis major/minor) which of course will be harder than if they also use the lats. If we go back to the tug of war comparison, your latissimus dorsi has gone to lunch. You can then produce less force and the risk of overload in the muscles that are left to do all the work increases a lot. This is why it is so important to get runners to connect the long chains through the body as I described in the first chapter here in Level 2. 5. chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Cause of Running Injuries
chunk.content: start by reviewing your training load in terms of frequency, volume and intensity, not by buying new running shoes. Sure, shoes can affect the risk of injury to a certain extent. However, there is a big difference between runners. Some can run in almost anything on their feet without it affecting them much, while others are more sensitive to the model they use. The runners who are usually most affected by their choice of footwear are those who do not have good running technique but are more engaged in 'jogging' where they mostly move their legs, have their feet close to the ground, have non-existent kayak paddle hip and an overstride. Where and in what terrain you run can also change loading patterns. Runners who live outside cities and always run on the same side of a country road can have problems as the road surface always slopes from the center to the edge for rainwater to run off. This results in uneven loading, which can be associated with ITB syndrome. As a general rule, the greater the variety, the lower the risk of injury. Running in the forest usually carries a lower risk of injury (unless you tend to always trip on roots and stones or twist your ankle) compared to running on tarmac or concrete. This is partly because the ground is softer in the forest, but perhaps mostly because the

chunk.section_title: Chapter 01: the Cause of Running Injuries
chunk.content: ground always slopes a little here and there and there are small hills and rocks and roots that provide a much more varied movement pattern. Just as it is good to train in at least two different models of running shoes to get variation in terms of how you load the body, the varied terrain in the forest works in the same way, there will be less exactly the same steps that wear the body in a monotonous way. But even if a softer surface is more gentle, it should not be too soft. Running on a sandy beach, for example, puts a lot more strain on most things below the knee, such as the calves, tibia, Achilles tendons, ankles and feet. Anyone who has decided to go for a run along the beach every day on holiday, but then abandons the idea on the second or third day because of severe pain in the calves, knows this.. However, if you tear your calf while running on a sandy beach on holiday, you may wonder whether it was because of the surface, that is, this point on risk factors, or the first point on frequency, volume and intensity because the sand makes the intensity go up radically from running on soft, dry sand, or whether it is a question of tissue tolerance that makes your calves too weak. It would be great if it was easier for us coaches to figure out exactly what is behind an injury. But it wouldn´t have been as much fun. What to do when an injury occurs? It is, of course, impossible to give general advice to someone who has suffered a running injury or other injury that prevents them from running as much. It must be decided on a case-by-case basis, from person to person. But as you probably know, it is often good for athletes with injury problems to keep moving and not just lie on the couch and wait for it to heal. If a physical therapist or similar professional thinks it is okay, it may be beneficial to try to train in a movement that is as similar to running as possible, but without putting too much strain on the body. An example of this was mentioned in lesson 8, namely that the four-time Olympic gold medalist Mo Farah ran on a treadmill at the bottom of a pool when he experienced pain because he still wanted to continue training the movement you make when running, but in a very low-impact way. For the same reason, special anti-gravity treadmills, such as AlterG, can be used, where you can choose how much you want to "weigh." Because the runner is suspended, you can choose to weigh only half your normal body weight, or even much less. However, they are extremely expensive and rare. The company Lever has a cheaper solution (or should I say a slightly less expensive solution) that can be mounted on existing treadmills, where the runner is suspended in rubber bands. And I'm guessing there are a bunch of other companies selling similar solutions. Of course, you can find even cheaper and more practical ways to run. Like water running, where you wear a belt that floats around your waist and run in a pool or lake where you can't touch the bottom, with the water as your only resistance. Using a cross trainer, which you can find at many gyms, is also a great option. They are easy to use, are often already available at the gym, require no investment, and provide a running-like workout that is still gentle enough on the injured body part.

chunk.content:
Summary Always take an injury seriously. It is much better to have a short break with alternative training than a longer period without any training at all. Strength training, adequate mobility training and an effective running technique can prevent injuries. The most common causes of injury in descending order of most common cause first: Previous injury 1 Frequency, volume and intensity of training 2 Poor recovery 3 Tissue Tolerance 4 Biomechanics 5 Equipment and surfaces 6

chunk.section_title: Audio: Expert Opinion of Strength & Conditioning
chunk.content: [0:00:01] Now going into the skiing station, the athlete is relatively fresh but heart rate is obviously rising, neuromuscular fatigue hasn't quite set in yet so there is a real opportunity to set the rhythm without spiking your heart rate. Now if we briefly look at some key technique cues, athletes should be looking to [0:00:18] hinge at the hips as opposed to performing a squatting movement with every stroke. In addition, aiming for power per stroke as opposed to gunning for a high stroke rate is a great way to help you regulate your heart rate response. Lastly, you want to use your large muscle groups to drive the stroke. [0:00:35] So during the catch phase at the top, you should be using your lats and driving down with your hip hinge as opposed to trying to pull the handles in with your arms which will essentially blow your smaller muscle groups in your biceps and triceps. Now moving into it, when we look at our body, anterior chain endurance is critical [0:00:54] for success in SkiErgggg. chunk.content: [0:00:00] When we look at the HYROX SkiErgggg through a biomechanical lens we're really analyzing one of the most elegant expressions of coordinated full body force production in the entire race. The SkiErgggg rewards athletes who can synchronize [0:00:17] upper body power, trunk stiffness and lower body rhythm into a seamless cyclical pattern. At its core this station is about efficient force transfer, taking the energy generated proximally and delivering it distally into the handles with minimal leakage. [0:00:37] One of the primary biomechanical principles at play is proximal to distal sequencing. The movement begins with the lats, trunk flexors and hip hinge initiating the pull before the arms finish the stroke. When this sequence reverses [0:00:55] when athletes arm pull too early, efficiency drops dramatically. A second key principle is optimal length tension utilization. The lats and trunk flexors produce their highest force when the athlete begins in a tall elongated position [0:01:13] allowing the subsequent contraction to occur through a strong mid-range. A third principle is cyclical elastic recoil. Skilled athletes use the upward return not as rest but as a moment to preload [0:01:29] the posterior chain storing elastic energy that feeds into the next pull. From a safety and interaction standpoint two biomechanical points matter most. First, athletes must maintain neutral cervical alignment. [0:01:45] Excessive neck flexion, common when fatigue sets in, disrupts scapular mechanics and increases strain on the upper traps. Second, the hip hinge must remain dominant over lumbar flexion. When the spine rounds to reach for more range, [0:02:02] the athlete loses both power and spinal integrity. A clean hinge preserves force output and reduces cumulative loading on the lumbar discs. Somatotype differences significantly influence how athletes engage with the SkiErgggg. [0:02:19] A shorter mesomorph with a naturally compact lever system and strong trunk to limb ratio typically excels in producing high force per stroke. Their shorter range of motion allows for rapid cycle rates [0:02:35] and strong proximal power. They often benefit from emphasizing rhythm and maintaining stroke consistency rather than chasing maximal reach. A taller ectomorph by contrast has long levers that create a biomechanical advantage in stroke [0:02:53] length. They can generate more work per pull but only if they maintain trunk stiffness and avoid collapsing through the midline. Their challenge is controlling the increased moment arms acting on the spine and shoulders. For them, the priority is sequencing and stability [0:03:13] using their height as an asset rather than allowing it to become a mechanical liability.

chunk.content: [0:00:00] The sled pull is a unique blend of posterior chain strength, upper body pulling mechanics and strategic footwork. Biomechanically the defining principle is force redirection. Unlike the push where force is applied directly into the sled, the pull requires [0:00:19] the athlete to anchor their body and redirect force through the rope. This demands strong ground reaction force management as the feet must create backward traction while the upper body generates horizontal pull. [0:00:35] A second key principle is lat driven pulling mechanics. The most efficient athletes initiate the pull with the lats and trunk, not the arms. This allows the large proximal muscles to handle the majority of the load. A third principle is counterbalance positioning. [0:00:53] Leaning back creates a mechanical advantage by shifting the center of mass behind the base of support, increasing traction and reducing slippage. Safety wise, two points are essential. First, athletes must avoid excessive spinal flexion when leaning back. [0:01:12] A rounded spine under tension increases shear forces and reduces pulling efficiency. Second, the rope must be pulled with elbows tracking close to the body, maintaining shoulder integrity and reducing strain on the biceps tendon. [0:01:29] Latter type differences shape the strategy. A shorter mesomorph typically excels at traction and stability. Their lower center of mass allows them to lean back aggressively without losing balance, and their strong trunk-to-limb ratio supports powerful lat engagement. [0:01:47] Their challenge is maximizing rope length per pull. A taller ectomorph benefits from longer arms, enabling them to take larger rope segments per stroke. However, their longer levers increase the torque on the spine when leaning back. [0:02:04] They must prioritize trunk stiffness and controlled footwork to avoid over-reliance on the arms.

chunk.content:
HYROX is structured as eight 1-kilometer runs. Each run is followed by a functional workout station.
This fixed race format combines:
| Demand type | Description | HYROX relevance | | Endurance running | Continuous endurance work across repeated 1-kilometer runs. | Approximately half of total race time is typically spent running. | | High-intensity resistance-based work | Repeated functional workout stations after each run. | Athletes must intermittently produce near-maximal power outputs, especially on the sleds. | | Hybrid endurance-strength demand | Continuous running is combined with repeated resistance-based stations. | HYROX differs from traditional endurance or strength sports because both continuous and intermittent stressors are present. |
### Aerobic Demands
Approximately half of total HYROX race time is typically spent running.
Aerobic endurance is therefore a fundamental prerequisite for successful performance.
The running segments are primarily fueled by oxidative metabolism.
The unit states that no direct studies have quantified VO2max specifically in HYROX athletes. However, evidence from elite-level athletes in similar hybrid fitness competitions indicates the following values:
| Athlete group | VO2max value reported for similar hybrid fitness competitions | | Male athletes | 62.7 ± 3.4 mL/kg/min | | Female athletes | 55.7 ± 4.2 mL/kg/min |
These values align with those reported for high-level aerobic endurance athletes and are expected to increase as HYROX continues to evolve.
### Functional-Station Demands
The functional stations impose greater glycolytic demand than the runs.
Each functional station typically lasts 2-4 minutes and produces higher blood lactate concentrations and perceived exertion than running segments.
This indicates a high reliance on anaerobic glycolysis for energy production.
### Functional-Station Demand Table
| Feature | Description | Performance implication | | Typical station duration | 2-4 minutes | Creates repeated high-intensity work bouts. | | Lactate response | Higher blood lactate concentrations than the runs | Indicates strong glycolytic demand. | | RPE response | Higher perceived exertion than the runs | Stations are experienced as more intense than running sections. | | Energy-system reliance | High reliance on anaerobic glycolysis | Athletes must tolerate and clear repeated metabolic stress. | | Fatigue mechanism | Metabolite accumulation may impair muscle contractility | Can contribute to fatigue and reduced output. |
### Compromised Running
Repeated glycolytic stress can lead to substantial metabolite accumulation.
This may impair muscle contractility and contribute to fatigue.
The unit refers to this as **compromised running**: accumulated fatigue experienced during a run after a demanding functional station such as lunges or sleds.
### Compromised Running Table

### Blood-Flow Redistribution Challenge
HYROX repeatedly alternates between upper-body-dominant and lower-body-dominant tasks.
This creates repeated redistribution of blood flow.
The redistribution can compromise running mechanics and economy, especially when running occurs under local muscular fatigue and elevated lactate levels.

chunk.content:
Fitness is described as a multifaceted concept that includes an individual's ability to perform physical activity effectively.
In practical terms, fitness can be understood as the ability to meet the demand of a specific event or environment.
However, fitness must be developed for the particular requirement or output of effort.
### Fitness Definition Table
| Concept | Meaning | | Fitness | A multifaceted concept that encompasses an individual's ability to perform physical activity effectively. | | Practical interpretation | The ability to meet the demand of a specific event or environment. | | Training implication | Fitness must be developed for the specific requirement or output of effort. |
Training stimulus must be selected and applied thoughtfully so that athlete physiology adapts through the supercompensation effect.
When a specific training stimulus is applied, the athlete immediately enters fatigue. This reduces performance level.
Through individualized recovery, the athlete's physiological state can undergo supercompensation and create a new baseline level of performance.
### Supercompensation Process
| Stage | Description | Performance implication | | Training stimulus | A specific training load is applied. | Creates the adaptive trigger. | | Fatigue / acute response | The athlete enters fatigue and performance temporarily decreases. | Immediate performance level is reduced. | | Recovery | The athlete recovers at an individualized rate. | Performance returns toward baseline. | | Supercompensation / overcompensation | The athlete adapts above the previous baseline. | A new higher performance baseline may be created. | | Detraining / involution | If the adaptation window is missed or training is not maintained, performance can decline. | Readiness and performance may fall again. |
### Visual Note: The General Adaptation Syndrome
The figure titled **The General Adaptation Syndrome** shows a performance-level curve after a training stimulus.
| Figure label | Meaning | | Performance Level | Vertical axis showing performance state. | | Training stimulus | Initial trigger that starts the adaptation curve. | | Acute response / Fatigue | Performance drops below baseline immediately after training stimulus. | | Recovery | Performance rises back toward baseline after fatigue. | | Overcompensation / Supercompensation | Performance rises above baseline after sufficient recovery and adaptation. | | Detraining / Involution | Performance declines if the adaptation is not reinforced appropriately. | | Preparedness and performance | Final performance state after the training-recovery-adaptation sequence. |
---

chunk.content:
In HYROX coaching, effective training programming is underpinned by planning and periodization.
The General Adaptation Syndrome is described as being at the heart of day-to-day fitness development.
However, because athletes may complete many training sessions across a season, training must be structured and ordered so athletic fitness develops specifically to meet the demands of HYROX racing.
Periodization is described as the structural backbone that ensures athletes work in a deliberate, measurable way that aligns with:
- Competition demands - Long-term development - Specific performance goals
### Goals of Periodization
| No. | Goal | | 1 | Elevate an athlete's performance at predetermined time points. | | 2 | Maximise specific physiological and performance adaptations. | | 3 | Reduce overtraining potential. | | 4 | Provide for long-term athletic development. |
Before advanced models and individualization methods are applied, coaches and athletes need a shared language for periodized training.
Without clarity on terminology, the risk is:
| Risk | Consequence | | Miscommunication | Coach and athlete may understand training terms differently. | | Misinterpretation | Training phases, cycles, or targets may be applied incorrectly. | | Misalignment | Program intent and execution may not match. |
The unit introduces key terms from Bompa & Haff that serve as reference points for later periodization models.
---

chunk.content:
| Term | Definition | HYROX coaching implication | | Periodization | Systematic planning of training to optimize performance and reduce overtraining risk by varying intensity, volume, and specificity over time. It uses structured cycles such as macrocycles, mesocycles, and microcycles to develop adaptations while balancing recovery and peak performance. | Provides the organizing structure for HYROX race preparation. | | Macrocycle | The longest training cycle, typically lasting several months to a year. It includes all phases of periodization and guides development toward peak performance at a specific time. | Aligns the full season or major preparation block with race targets. | | Mesocycle | A medium-term training block within the macrocycle, usually lasting 2-6 weeks. Each mesocycle has a specific objective and consists of multiple microcycles that progressively manage training intensity and load. | Organizes focused blocks such as base development, specific preparation, or race preparation. | | Microcycle | The shortest training cycle, usually lasting 5-10 days and often structured as a week. It consists of individual training sessions aligned with the mesocycle's objectives, including planned intensity variation and recovery days. | Converts block goals into weekly or short-cycle training structure. | | General Preparation Phase (GPP) | Foundation phase focused on overall physical capacity, including endurance, strength, and mobility. It is characterized by high volume and low intensity to build a broad and resilient athletic base. | HYROX-specific movements should be scaled so they do not unintentionally drive intensity too high. | | Specific Preparation Phase (SPP) | Phase aimed at enhancing sport-specific skills and energy-system development. Training becomes more specialized, using movements and intensities that replicate competition demands. | HYROX-specific movements fit well here because their high-intensity nature aligns with sport-specific demands. | | Pre-Competition Phase (Pre-Comp) | Phase that transitions within certain training loads while refining sport-specific techniques and tactical execution. The goal is to peak while reducing unnecessary fatigue. | Refines race-specific execution and readiness. | | Competition Phase (Comp) | Phase focused on maintaining peak performance, refining tactics, and managing recovery. Volume is reduced while intensity remains relatively high. | Keeps athletes ready for events while limiting excess fatigue. | | Transition / Recovery Phase | Active recovery and regeneration phase after the competitive season. It reduces training intensity and volume to promote mental and physical recovery before the next cycle. | Supports recovery before the next macrocycle begins. |
### GPP Scaling Guidance for HYROX Movements
Many HYROX-specific tasks are inherently explosive and power-oriented. Examples include:
- Sled pushes - Burpee broad jumps - Walking lunges
During the General Preparation Phase, these tasks can unintentionally drive intensity too high.
To maintain the intended GPP stimulus, the unit recommends scaling these movements.

chunk.content: [0:00:00] Block periodisation offers HYROX coaches a structured way to manage the sports unique challenge, developing multiple, sometimes competing, physical qualities. Sequencing training into accumulation, transmutation and realisation blocks means coaches can prioritize [0:00:16] one adaptation at a time while maintaining others through residual effects. This concentrated approach reduces the interference effect often seen when endurance, strength and high intensity conditioning are all trained at similar loads simultaneously. The strengths of [0:00:33] block periodisation lie in its clarity and focus, as each block has a defined training emphasis that simplifies monitoring and reduces athlete overwhelm. By developing endurance, strength and power qualities sequentially rather than simultaneously, it minimises interference and [0:00:50] supports more robust adaptations. This model also enables better load management, allowing training stress to be strategically distributed to lower the risk of injury and burnout in a sport that is both high volume and high intensity. Finally, the realisation block [0:01:07] enhances competition readiness by ensuring athletes peak at the right time with race-specific simulations that closely replicate the fatigue and demands of HYROX competition. The weaknesses and limitations of block periodisation stem largely from its rigidity, as a fixed [0:01:23] block sequence may not align with the unpredictable HYROX competition calendar or the needs of athletes who race multiple times in a season. Short-term deconditioning can also occur since residual effects only maintain neglected qualities for a limited time, meaning [0:01:39] poorly timed blocks or athletes requiring longer maintenance doses may see declines in certain capacities. Individual variability further complicates the model, as less experienced athletes may not respond as effectively to concentrated training phases and may benefit from more frequent exposure to multiple modalities. There is a risk of specificity gaps if blocks focus too [0:01:59] heavily on isolated qualities such as aerobic base work. Without integrating high rock style combinations athletes may arrive physiologically prepared but under-trained for the unique demands of transitions and cumulative fatigue that define competition. Finally, [0:02:15] block periodisation does not inherently account for an athlete's individual strengths and weaknesses. For example, many HYROX participants come from a strength or high intensity functional fitness background. These athletes may benefit from dedicating multiple training phases, blocks, to [0:02:31] higher volume low intensity aerobic work to address their primary limiter and better match the demands of HYROX racing. Conversely, athletes with an endurance background may require earlier emphasis on strength and power development. The aforementioned training phases [0:02:47] are general patterns, but each athlete presents with unique needs and rigid block sequencing may overlook this individualisation. Practical applications. Coaches should remain flexible, adjusting block length 2-8 weeks to athlete needs and competition timing. Micro [0:03:07] doses of HYROX specific skills should be layered throughout all phases to ensure technical readiness is never lost. For athletes competing multiple times per season, a hybrid or compressed block approach may work better than strict long blocks.

chunk.content: [0:00:00] For HYROX coaches the challenge is less about avoiding concurrent training and more about managing it effectively. Some principles emerge from the literature. First, sequence matters. Where possible, schedule strength work before endurance or separate modalities across different sessions or days to reduce direct interference. [0:00:19] Second, endurance volume should be monitored, especially running, as excessive mileage can compromise lower body strength and recovery. This is particularly important in phases where maximal strength or power is a training priority. Third, specificity must guide [0:00:37] design. While laboratory studies test strength with isolated lifts and endurance with VO2max protocols, HYROX requires blended performance. Coaches should therefore integrate race-like simulations, mixed modality intervals and strength endurance sessions that mirror the [0:00:54] transitions and fatigue of competition. Finally, athlete profiling is essential. Novice HYROX athletes may tolerate a more blended approach without severe interference, while experienced competitors with higher baseline capacities may need stricter [0:01:10] management of load, sequencing and recovery. Sex differences, training history and injury risk should all be factored into program design. In summary, concurrent training is not just relevant for HYROX, it is the foundation of the sport. The evidence highlights [0:01:31] potential pitfalls, particularly for strength gains under high endurance volumes, but also offers clear strategies to mitigate them. For coaches, the key lies in sequencing, recovery and specificity, ensuring that training not only develops strength and endurance in isolation, but [0:01:47] also prepares athletes to express both qualities seamlessly in the race environment. By blending insights from the literature with the practical demands of HYROX, coaches can strike the right balance between theory and performance.

chunk.content: [0:00:00] The following section will present insight and critical evaluation of six established periodization models, exploring their theoretical underpinnings, practical applications and limitations within the context of hybrid competition. Periodization remains one of the most widely debated and studied aspects of [0:00:18] training science, offering structured frameworks for sequencing workload, intensity and recovery in pursuit of peak performance. Each presents distinct philosophies for organizing training stress. Basically comparing these models will allow you, as HYROX coaches and practitioners, [0:00:34] to move beyond theory and assess which strategies may be most effective when applied to HYROX that demands multiple, and often conflicting, physiological qualities. While extensive research exists across endurance, strength and team sport contexts, [0:00:51] far less is known about how these models translate to hybrid competitions such as HYROX. As such, the demands are broader and more complex than in single modality sports, requiring nuanced training approaches that manage interference effects and balance multiple adaptations within a single preparation macrocycle. [0:01:09] To address this gap, this following section will not only examine periodization models in light of established literature, but also appreciate where further research is required and the application of periodization principles in such a multi-faceted performance environment. A researcher in exercise physiology, John Keeley, once wrote that opposing [0:01:28] innovation is an appeal to the weight of history, to point to celebrated champions who scaled great heights using conventionally pervasive methodologies. Essentially, HYROX coaches need to appreciate the well-established principles of periodization, but be receptive to new and updating knowledge, both present and future, on how to [0:01:46] effectively order the application of stimuli across the season. So without further ado, let's dive in and explore the periodization models.

chunk.content: [0:00:00] The potential implications for HYROX training are intriguing though underexplored. HYROX, as a hybrid fitness race, demands not only aerobic endurance but also repeated bouts of high-intensity functional exercise under fatigue. Anecdotally, Elite 15 HYROX athletes within the 2025 HYROX World Championships [0:00:19] reported adopting polarised style structures within their running training, suggesting real-world practical transferability. A polarised approach could help athletes accumulate the large aerobic base required for the hour-long event while still eliciting the central and peripheral [0:00:36] adaptations needed for repeated high-output efforts. Furthermore, minimising tempo training may mitigate sympathetic stress and enhance recovery, particularly important given the multi-domain demands of training. However, limitations exist. Unlike traditional endurance sports, HYROX requires [0:00:53] strength, muscular endurance, and metabolic resilience under resistance-based tasks. Excessive focus on low-intensity training might reduce the time available for strength and skill-specific work. Similarly, high-intensity training in polarised research is primarily running or [0:01:09] rowing-based. Whether equivalent adaptations occur under loaded movements, for example sled pushes, remains uncertain. Current evidence is also almost entirely endurance-focused, making direct application to HYROX contexts somewhat speculative. [0:01:26] From Heldetal, 2024, the findings here suggest that reducing the volume of high-intensity training while increasing low-intensity work may preserve performance adaptations while easing total training stress. This is highly relevant given the fatigue, injury risk, and recovery demands often [0:01:45] observed during HYROX preparation. A polarised model could therefore serve as a practical strategy for maintaining competitiveness without overloading athletes. However, several limitations must be considered. The intervention lasted only six weeks, which may not capture long-term adaptations [0:02:03] or the cumulative fatigue of a full season. The test workout, Jacky, while metabolically demanding, is far simpler than a HYROX race, lacking key modalities such as sled pushes, carries, or wall balls, and therefore may not fully replicate race-specific accumulative fatigue. [0:02:23] Similarly, isolated strength tests do not reflect the performance of compound tasks under exhaustion, which are central to HYROX racing. Future research should therefore investigate how polarised interacts with overall strength and conditioning demands in HYROX racing. [0:02:40] Until then, its adoption in HYROX remains promising and should be considered by coaches with intensity distribution.

reported adopting polarised style structures within their running training, suggesting real-world practical transferability. A polarised approach could help athletes accumulate the large aerobic base required for the hour-long event while still elici

adaptations needed for repeated high-output efforts. Furthermore, minimising tempo training may mitigate sympathetic stress and enhance recovery, particularly important given the multi-domain demands of training. However, limitations exist. Unlike tr

strength, muscular endurance, and metabolic resilience under resistance-based tasks. Excessive focus on low-intensity training might reduce the time available for strength and skill-specific work. Similarly, high-intensity training in polarised resea

rowing-based. Whether equivalent adaptations occur under loaded movements, for example sled pushes, remains uncertain. Current evidence is also almost entirely endurance-focused, making direct application to HYROX contexts somewhat speculative.

From Heldetal, 2024, the findings here suggest that reducing the volume of high-intensity training while increasing low-intensity work may preserve performance adaptations while easing total training stress. This is highly relevant given the fatigue,

observed during HYROX preparation. A polarised model could therefore serve as a practical strategy for maintaining competitiveness without overloading athletes. However, several limitations must be considered. The intervention lasted only six weeks,

or the cumulative fatigue of a full season. The test workout, Jacky, while metabolically demanding, is far simpler than a HYROX race, lacking key modalities such as sled pushes, carries, or wall balls, and therefore may not fully replicate race-speci

Similarly, isolated strength tests do not reflect the performance of compound tasks under exhaustion, which are central to HYROX racing. Future research should therefore investigate how polarised interacts with overall strength and conditioning deman
Until then, its adoption in HYROX remains promising and should be considered by coaches with intensity distribution.

chunk.content: [0:00:00] Undulating periodization can be a useful strategy to drive strength and hypertrophy adaptations while maintaining variety and motivation, but it should always be combined with structured endurance training to reflect the mixed demands of HYROX. Coaches should adapt the approach to each athlete's background, prioritizing what [0:00:17] they need most, while ensuring progressive overload without creating excessive fatigue. In practice, this often means that strength training in HYROX is organized in an undulating fashion with frequent variation in intensity, load, and repetition schemes, whereas endurance training more commonly follows a block-periodized structure. [0:00:35] Here, training volume is built first, followed by intensity, and then specificity as competition approaches, creating a progression that ensures athletes arrive prepared for both the continuous running and the intermittent, high-power functional demands of race day.

chunk.content: [0:00:00] The evidence comparing traditional and reverse periodization suggests no consistent superiority of one approach over the other across key performance outcomes such as running economy, swimming, muscular endurance, maximal strength or VO2 max. For HYROX preparation, this means both models can be applied effectively, provided [0:00:19] the structure aligns with the athlete's individual needs, competition schedule and training history. Traditional linear periodization offers a more progressive build, gradually layering endurance and strength capacities toward peak performance. This can be especially valuable for athletes newer to structured training or those [0:00:38] who benefit from a steady, predictable increase in workload. Reverse periodization, by contrast, may better accommodate the hybrid demands of HYROX by emphasising high intensity and explosive work earlier in the cycle before consolidating aerobic and strength endurance qualities. [0:00:56] This structure can be advantageous when an athlete needs to sharpen speed, power and high intensity tolerance while still preserving sufficient endurance. In practice, HYROX athletes and coaches may consider blending aspects of both systems rather than adhering rigidly to one. [0:01:13] For example, incorporating reverse-style blocks that target explosive and anaerobic capacity while still maintaining the progressive endurance and strength development of traditional models. Ultimately, coaching decisions between both models for HYROX will come down to [0:01:29] individualization, accounting for baseline fitness, strengths and weaknesses, for example, running versus strength stations, recovery capacity and the timing of competition.

This chapter explains intensity domains, low-intensity and high-intensity adaptations, polarized training evidence, and how endurance and hybrid sport athletes may apply polarized intensity distributions.
