unit.title: Performing Under Pressure
unit.unit_summary: This unit explains how HYROX athletes can perform under pressure by understanding the body-mind loop, the brain's high-performance networks, and the threat system. It starts with the autonomic nervous system: sympathetic activation prepares the body for action, while parasympathetic activity helps the body recover and calm down. It then explains three key brain networks: the Salience Network detects important internal and external stimuli, the Default Mode Network supports inward reflection and self-related thinking, and the Central Executive Network supports focus, decision-making, and goal-d

chunk.content:
The Foundation The 3 Key Functions of the Brain in High Performance Zooming in on the Threat Function and Why it Might Trigger at a HYROX Event Understanding Potential Triggers ​Successfully Dealing with Performance Pressure Why an Acceptance (Rather Than Blocking/Ignoring) Approach Works 6 Tools to Soothe the Threat System Level 2 - Modul 9 - 6. Performing Under Pressure
The Foundation When it comes to performing under pressure, anxiety, fear, and nervousness are not just buzzwords - they're familiar companions for athletes and coaches alike. In this chapter, we'll take a closer look at what actually happens inside the body and the mind when athletes find themselves in high-pressure situations. You may remember the basics of the body's stress response from the Level 1 module, so here's a short refresher: When we encounter stress, the autonomic nervous system switches into sympathetic activation. This activation prepares the body for potential fight or flight by releasing adrenaline and noradrenaline, increasing heart rate, ramping up muscle tension, and sharpening our sensory systems. The result? Faster reaction times, heightened visual and auditory acuity, increased force production, and even the ability to buffer fatigue in the short term. Balancing this response is the parasympathetic nervous system, which steps in to bring the body back down from high alert. It reduces muscle tension and heart rate, redirects blood flow to
digestive organs, lowers stress hormones, and boosts immune and repair functions - our classic rest & digest mode that lets us recover and calm down. Now, none of these physical reactions are inherently "good" or "bad." They're simply data signals showing that the body is preparing for something that is important to us or needed by our body. What we make of this data is shaped by the mind. The mind
and body are in a constant two-way loop: the brain interprets the physical sensations it receives, and at the same time, our thoughts and interpretations actively influence those sensations. Because of this continual back-and-forth, we must always look at performance through both a physical and a cognitive lens. Every athlete has a unique sweet spot of physical activation and emotional state that allows them to perform at their peak. While a certain level of adrenaline improves performance, too much adrenaline can impair it by making us shaky and nervous. The Yerkes- Dodson Law (very simplified) and the IZOF (Individual Zones of Optimal Functioning) or the Catastrophe Theory (Hardy, 1987-1990s) model all speak to this idea of optimal performance zones. Understanding how to identify and intentionally reach that optimal performance zone on a consistent basis is a topic of its own that can fill an entire module.
### Visual Note: Autonomic Nervous System Diagram

chunk.section_title: Chapter 02: The 3 Key Functions of the Brain in High Performance
chunk.content:
The 3 Key Functions of the Brain in High Performance When it comes to peak performance, the brain plays just as big a role as the body. So let's take a closer look at what's actually happening "up top" when athletes train, perform, and push their limits. At the psychological level, three major brain networks work together to control how we notice, think, and respond in high- pressure moments. Salience Network The first is the Salience Network - the brain's internal threat detector. It is crucial for detecting, integrating, and filtering internal or external information. It identifies salience by deciding what is, in the moment, the most important interoceptive or external stimulus that needs our attention in order to initiate an adequate response (by activating other brain networks). The amygdala, which you may have heard of, is an example of a brain region within the Salience Network that is involved in detecting emotional salience, such as threat. But the Salience Network also detects positive salience, like potential rewards, which is highly connected to motivation
and learning. Its job is to filter everything coming from inside the body and from the outside world and decide, in real time, what matters most. Whether it's a spike in heart rate, an opponent making a move, or a sudden change, the Salience Network tags meaningful information and alerts the rest of the brain & body. It's important to note that salience is highly individual: What captures one athlete's attention may be irrelevant to another. Default Mode Network Next is the Default Mode Network (DMN) - the system that turns on when the mind goes inward. It is associated with thinking about past or future events, helping us reflect, plan ahead and integrate past experiences, and make sense of who we are as athletes and people. Because it serves reflection, it is mainly suppressed when executing a concrete task - too much DMN activity can pull us into overthinking or self-judgment at the wrong moment. Central Executive Network When it's time to execute, the Central Executive Network (CEN) takes over. This is the brain's problem-solving and decision-making hub. It helps us stay focused, think clearly under pressure, and respond purposefully to whatever the Salience Network flagged as important. In high-demand moments, the CEN activates while the DMN steps back - allowing sharp, goal-directed action.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 03: Zooming in on the Threat Function and Why it Might Trigger at a HYROX Event
chunk.content:
Zooming in on the Threat Function and Why it Might Trigger at a HYROX Event What happens when the brain's Salience Network (especially the amygdala) becomes hyper-activated? Its job is to detect and prioritize potential danger - both physical and psychological. When this network fires up, attention automatically narrows onto anything that feels risky, uncertain, or evaluative. One literally "zooms in" on the threat cue - a burning muscle, a faster competitor, a missed split, an elevated heart rate... - and thereby lose access to broader situational awareness, calm, and strategic control - in other words, your central executive network is being suppressed because your body is in high alert mode for danger. This mechanism is evolutionary: In order to properly respond to potential danger, the brain has to detect danger first and think second. In sport, that same function can misfire - labeling performance situations as threats rather than challenges.
Why it might trigger at a HYROX event HYROX is a perfect storm for the salience network. Here are two major reasons: There are a lot of stimuli that are deviations from our regular surroundings and therefore quickly activate our salience network. 1 Whenever we care about something, we are extra aware of potential threats. 2 Those two factors can leave athletes hyper alert for detecting potential danger. Which can cause the brain's threat system (Salience Network) to hijack the focus and physiology, narrowing attention to danger cues and blocking access to our trained skills. It's important to note that when the brain "zooms in on the threat", it's responding to perceived danger, not necessarily real danger. What is considered perceived danger is again highly individual.

When this network fires up, attention automatically narrows onto anything that feels risky, uncertain, or evaluative.

Why it might trigger at a HYROX event HYROX is a perfect storm for the salience network.
Here are two major reasons: There are a lot of stimuli that are deviations from our regular surroundings and therefore quickly activate our salience network.

2 Those two factors can leave athletes hyper alert for detecting potential danger.

chunk.content:
Understanding Potential Triggers Let's have a closer look at some examples that can trigger our salience network and be perceived as potential danger by an athlete. We differentiate between 3 potential triggers: 1. Environmental Triggers What they are: Everything that's happening around the athlete. HYROX environments are noisy, chaotic, and intense. Common environmental triggers include: • Loud music & sudden noises • Crowds & spectators • Competitors overtaking or catching up • Transition zones/station entry • Judges, no-reps, or unclear signals
2. Physiological triggers What they are: What's happening inside the athlete's body. HYROX is a high-intensity endurance-strength hybrid. The body produces strong internal sensations that the SN continuously monitors e.g.: • Elevated heart rate • Burning legs, heavy breathing • Accumulating fatigue • Lactate buildup/muscle failure sensations • Breathlessness/chest tightness • Unexpected physiological shifts like cramps, etc. 3. Psychological Triggers What they are: What's happening in the athlete's mind. HYROX is mentally taxing. Psychological triggers can activate SN even when the body is fine e.g.: • Fear of failing or not hitting a time
### Trigger Interpretation Examples
| Phase | Trigger | Why the brain interprets it as "threat" | | Pre-race (anticipation) | Crowds, noise, comparison with others | The brain reads social evaluation ("others will judge me") as a potential threat to status and belonging. | | Start line | Adrenaline surge, heart racing, pre-race arousal | Physiological arousal feels similar to fear and can be misinterpreted as danger ("something's wrong"). | | Mid-race | Unexpected fatigue, pain, sled push feels heavier | Mismatch between expectation and reality activates the amygdala, creating a threat flag. | | During transitions | Losing rhythm, competitors overtaking | The amygdala might interpret this as loss of control or ego threat ("I'm failing"). | | Final stage | Near exhaustion, time pressure | The system over-predicts catastrophe ("I can't make it"), leading to tunnel vision and rigid behavior. |

Environmental Triggers What they are: Everything that's happening around the athlete.

2.
Physiological triggers What they are: What's happening inside the athlete's body.

The body produces strong internal sensations that the SN continuously monitors e.g.: • Elevated heart rate • Burning legs, heavy breathing • Accumulating fatigue • Lactate buildup/muscle failure sensations • Breathlessness/chest tightness • Unexpecte
Psychological Triggers What they are: What's happening in the athlete's mind.

Psychological triggers can activate SN even when the body is fine e.g.: • Fear of failing or not hitting a time
### Trigger Interpretation Examples
| Phase | Trigger | Why the brain interprets it as "threat" | | Pre-race (anticipation) | Crowds, no
| | Start line | Adrenaline surge, heart racing, pre-race arousal | Physiological arousal feels similar to fear and can be misinterpreted as danger ("something's wrong").
| | Mid-race | Unexpected fatigue, pain, sled push feels heavier | Mismatch between expectation and reality activates the amygdala, creating a threat flag.
| | During transitions | Losing rhythm, competitors overtaking | The amygdala might interpret this as loss of control or ego threat ("I'm failing").

chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: Successfully Dealing with Performance Pressure
chunk.content:
​Successfully Dealing with Performance Pressure A lot is happening at and around a HYROX event. The question is: How can athletes successfully deal with all of it mentally? First, it's important to understand that the emotions and thoughts that show up during training or competition are not random and not signs of weakness. They are part of a system that has developed over time, and that serves a purpose: To keep us safe - they have a job to fulfill. We therefore don't differentiate between 'good' or 'bad' thoughts or emotions, but between 'helpful' and 'unhelpful' ones in the moment. It's not about getting rid of the 'unhelpful' ones - instead, it's about learning to deal with them in a performance- enhancing way. For example: When your heart is pounding rapidly at the start line, your body is preparing you for the upcoming challenge. That physical sensation doesn't automatically mean you're nervous. A fast heartbeat can just as well signal readiness, activation, or excitement. What matters is the meaning your mind assigns to it. If
you label the sensation as nervousness and give it all your attention, it can become unhelpful and pull you into worry. But if you label it as "excitement" or "readiness" as your body is gearing up to perform - e.g.: "this is my system preparing me" - you are cognitively reframing the same sensation, and it becomes a resource instead of a threat. Another example: Feeling fear before a race. By feeling fear, your mind is trying to protect you from potential danger or failure. By default, this is not a bad thing. Quite the opposite, it's a good protective reaction. If we accept it for what it is, it can be helpful to us by making us aware of potential threats and prepping us emotionally for possible outcomes, like failure. If we give it too much weight, it can take our focus away from things that matter in the moment, hijack our attention, control our emotions, and impair our performance and well-being. Understanding the purpose behind these reactions - both physical and psychological - could fill an entire chapter on its own. For now, here are the two key takeaways: These reactions are learned over time and serve a protective purpose. 1 The goal is not to get rid of them, but to learn how to accept and work with them and see them as 2
data we can use - to support performance instead of hindering it.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 06: Why an Acceptance (Rather Than Blocking/Ignoring) Approach Works
chunk.content:
Why an Acceptance (Rather Than Blocking/Ignoring) Approach Works In this section, we'll explore three empirical reasons why an accepting approach is far more effective than trying to ignore, block, or suppress thoughts and feelings. 1. Ironic Thought Process (Wegner, 1994) Wegner's Ironic Process Theory shows that when we try to suppress a thought ("Don't be nervous", "Stop thinking about the pain", "Don't mess up"), the brain must first search for the unwanted thought in order to suppress it - which ironically makes it more active and more intrusive. In sport, this means: Trying to "push away" nervousness makes you more nervous. Trying not to think about the pain makes you more aware of it.
Trying not to panic increases panic. Quick Exercise: Close your eyes and with all your power, try NOT to think of an HYROX Sled. Notice: Even though the instruction was clear, to NOT think of a HYROX sled, you probably did see a sled in front of your inner eye. Hence proving the point that your brain can not deal with the "not" instruction. Therefore it is not about trying "not" to think of negative or performance-impairing thought - instead we have to replace the thought with one that is performance enhancing. E.g. "Don't panic" → "Stay calm" ; "Don't be scared" → "Believe in yourself".... Key takeaway: The more you try not to think or feel something, the stronger it becomes.
2. Acceptance Calms the Amygdala (SN) - Kober et al. (2019) Research by Kober and colleagues (2019) shows that when we practice acceptance ("I feel nervous - and that's okay," "This is discomfort - and I can allow it"), the brain stops treating the emotion as a threat. Instead of highly activating the amygdala - the region that triggers fear, alarm, and fight-or-flight - acceptance engages the prefrontal cortex, the system responsible for clarity, control, and decision- making. By allowing a feeling to be present instead of fighting it, the brain shifts from "danger mode" to "regulation mode," reducing emotional intensity and restoring cognitive control. Key takeaway: Acceptance calms the threat system. 3. Cognitive Defusion (Pilecki et al., 2022)

chunk.section_title: Chapter 06: Why an Acceptance (Rather Than Blocking/Ignoring) Approach Works
chunk.content:
Cognitive defusion helps athletes create space between themselves and their thoughts. Instead of treating a thought as a fact ("I'm failing," "I can't keep this pace," "Everyone is faster"), defusion teaches the brain to see it as a mental event - something passing through the mind, not a command. Neuroscience shows that this shift reduces the emotional "tagging" of the thought in the Salience Network, quiets the brain areas involved in overthinking and self-criticism, and reopens access to the Executive System responsible for focus, problem-solving, and steady decision-making under pressure. By shifting from "this is true" to "this is a passing thought," the brain becomes less reactive and more stable. For example: Instead of "I'm failing," an athlete learns to see: → "I'm having the thought that I'm failing." This breaks the fusion between thought and identity, lowering reactivity and restoring control.
Quick Exercise Key takeaway: Defusion doesn't remove thoughts - it removes their grip. This allows athletes to stay present, choose effective actions, and remain in their performance lane. Cognitive defusion is a powerful tool for mastering self-talk and forms the foundation for working effectively with inner dialogue. Learning to distance oneself from unhelpful thoughts and develop constructive, performance-supportive self-talk that enables us to reach our full potential and break our records and achieve peak performance is a skill that requires time and deliberate practice. Sport psychology offers a range of evidence-based methods to train this
Summing it up: Athletes don't need fewer thoughts or emotions - they need a better relationship with them. Our self-talk is not random, it's a system that can be understood, trained, and shaped. It has a powerful impact on both performance and well-being, and when mastered, it can become a strong motor driving long-term success and incredible performance. Modern sport psychology offers a wide range of evidence-based tools to deliberately change and master self-talk... which could fill an entire module by its own! ability - exploring them in depth, however, would go beyond the scope of this module.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 07: 6 Tools to Soothe the Threat System
chunk.content:
6 Tools to Soothe the Threat System Let's take a look at some tools that can be helpful for athletes when it comes to dealing with pressure in the moment. Again, the aim is not to suppress threat activation, but to recognize it and see it for what it is: data that we can work with. When the threat system (SN) is over-activated, the goal is to shift control back to the Central Executive Network (CEN). As mentioned previously, elite athletes take the mental component seriously - just like any other skill, since these skills have to be trained and take time to master. They have to be integrated into practice and trained deliberately to work when really needed.
Box Breathing / Slow Exhale Why It Works Stimulates vagus nerve, the main activator of the parasympathetic nervous system, thus lowers arousal, reduces adrenaline level, and stabilizes focus by activating CEN. Coach Application Box-breathing (e.g. 4-4-4-4) 4 sec inhale 4 sec hold 4 sec exhale 4 sec hold repeat HYROX Example Athlete approaches the sled push with rising heart rate → takes two slow exhales to settle the system before grabbing the handles. Hence actively regulating the parasympathetic nervous system and gaining active control over heart rate and sympathetic activation. Tool 1
Guiding Notes It's not about the exact breathing pattern that matters most - every athlete has to find what works for them in a given moment. It could be as simple as slow exhales. Box breathing is just one example. Athletes should be encouraged to find what works for them in a given movement. Again, mastering this takes PRACTICE.
Grounding Why It Works Anchors attention in the present moment, interrupting fight-or-flight spirals and reducing DMN overthinking. Coach Application Use sensory cues (feet on the ground, grip, breath, visual anchor) to bring athletes back into the present moment. HYROX Example During burpee broad jumps → athlete focuses on "feet-hands-forward" to break panic and regain rhythm. Guiding Notes One bigger example is: 5-4-3-2-1 Technique 5 - things you can see 4 - things you can touch 3 - things you can hear 2 - things you can smell Tool 2
1 - thing you can taste It all works the same way: Activating the CEN by consciously bringing myself in the present moment by bringing my attention to what I am doing right now. Shift focus from future thoughts to present actions.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 07: 6 Tools to Soothe the Threat System
chunk.content:
Focusing on Metrics That Matter Why It Works Redirects attention from threat cues to task cues, activating the Central Executive Network (precision, clarity, decision-making). Coach Application Identify 1-2 controllable performance metrics per station (cadence, stroke length, posture). HYROX Example On the SkiErgg → athlete focuses on "long pulls, calm breath" instead of competitors next to them. Guiding Notes What matters to an athlete is highly individual. It's about identifying patterns first to then find cues that work to set the focus on what is performance enhancing instead of impairing. Tool 3
Acceptance & Reframing Why It Works Reduces emotional resistance, lowers amygdala activation, and prevents the threat system from escalating. Coach Application Encourage athletes to find 'THE GOOD' in distracting thoughts / sensations. Doing so helps accepting them in and interpreting / reframing them positively. HYROX Example Physical sensational example: Legs burning on lunges → athlete reframes sensation as "my body doing its job, I'm pushing" reducing panic and tension. Guiding Notes Encourage athletes to find the good in the things that are on their mind. Finding 'The Good' in things helps shift the focus from negative to Tool 4
something positive and shift the mind away from a feeling of threat that needs constant attention. It helps accept what is happening.
Cognitive Defusion Why It Works Creates mental distance from unhelpful thoughts, reducing salience tagging and restoring cognitive control. Coach Application Use the phrase: "I'm having the thought that..." to unhook from intrusive thoughts mid-race. HYROX Example Athlete thinks "I'm blowing up" → shifts to "I'm having the thought that I'm blowing up," refocusing on cadence. Guiding Notes Allows athletes to see not just pink and black, but the thought for what it is, just a thought, not the ultimate truth. (s. exercise hand in front of face).
Tool 5
Control Mapping (W.I.N.) Why It Works Shifts attention from uncontrollable stressors to controllable actions, reducing Salience Network activation. Coach Application Coach asks: "What's Important Now?" → redirect to the next actionable step. HYROX Example 1. Competitor passes the athlete → they refocus on their own pacing plan: "Relax shoulders. Keep your line." 2. Sled push is not going as fast as planned. W.I.N. (What's Important Now?) → right now it's important that I pace myself. There is no benefit in fully burning my legs now. It's important that I pace now and stay calm to preserve my energy for later (creates an actionable next step) Guiding Notes Tool 6

chunk.section_title: Chapter 07: 6 Tools to Soothe the Threat System
chunk.content:
Winning happens by focusing on the right thing at the right time. Often athletes get distracted by things that are not in their control. By asking W.I.N. (What's Important Now?), athletes are encouraged to focus on what they can do in the moment to get closer to their goal.
Summing it up These tools work through different pathways - some regulate the nervous system, others shift attention, and others reduce the emotional weight of thoughts - but all serve one purpose: helping athletes regain control in real time and setting the focus on what is in their control. Not every tool will work the same way for every athlete, which is why it's essential to experiment during training and identify what helps in specific situations. None of this is a magic pill. These skills require repetition and practice, just like physical training. Elite performers don't avoid pressure; they learn to notice it, name it, work with it, and are able to quickly redirect their attention back to what matters most. One common challenge in mental skills training is overload: athletes hear many tools, understand them intellectually but don't create a plan to try them out. When talking to athletes about the above-mentioned sport- psychological tools, encourage athletes to pick ONE tool and think about how it can help them in their next training session and how they want to use it. Hence, encouraging them to move from theory to practice.
Reflection Exercise Pick one tool from the list that you believe would be most helpful for your athletes right now. Then reflect on the following questions: Which tool did you choose, and why this one? (What situation, athlete, or challenge made you choose it?) How will you introduce or cue this tool during training? (For example: a verbal reminder, a pause before a station, a question like "What's Important Now?") What goal are you trying to achieve with this tool? (e.g. calmer starts, better focus in transitions, reduced panic under fatigue) What challenges might come up when applying this tool? (Resistance, forgetting, time pressure, skepticism.) How will you respond when those challenges appear? (Reinforcement, normalization, simplifying the cue, revisiting it later.) Mental skills are learned the same way physical skills are: through repetition, guidance, and patience.
---

unit.title: Simulating Pressure in Training
unit.unit_summary: This unit explains that true HYROX simulation is not just copying the full race order under fatigue. A full station-and-run workout in a familiar gym may train physical capacity, but it does not necessarily train mental adaptability because race day includes unfamiliar environments, increased personal stakes, and heightened Salience Network activation. The unit teaches coaches to use simulations and regular training sessions to prepare the athlete's mind as well as the body. Pre-training, coaches should brief the mind by normalizing nerves, framing the workout as a challenge, and activating in

chunk.content:
Why "Simulation" Is Often Misunderstood Pre-Training: Prepping the Mind During Simulation - Coaching in the Heat of the Moment Debriefing: Post-Simulation Level 2 - Modul 9 - 7. Simulating Pressure in Training
Why "Simulation" Is Often Misunderstood When coaches talk about "doing a HYROX simulation," they often mean running through all eight stations and the 8 x 1 km runs in competition order. Physically, that's demanding. But mentally, it's often still a very safe, familiar environment for the athletes. Same gym, same layout, same equipment, same people, ... That's usually not what an actual HYROX event feels like to the athlete. On race day, the Salience Network (SN) is on high alert. The brain is scanning everything for what's important, unusual, or potentially threatening. Quick Reminder: Two big factors make HYROX competition very different from training: Deviations from the usual environment New arena, new sounds, different lighting, changing layouts, ... Stations are not exactly where they are in your gym. Athletes have to deal with questions like: "Where do I go next? Where is my lane? Where is my judge? Am I at the right spot? What is my competition doing?" 1
These changes alone are enough to activate the SN and tilt the system toward threat mode if the athlete isn't used to mentally dealing with variability. We care more on race day Qualification spots, PBs, rankings, friends watching, social media, goals, expectations, ... The more it matters, the more the brain looks for potential danger: "What if I blow up? What if I'm not as fit as I thought? What if I fail?" 2 So, if we only "simulate" by copying the workout structure in a controlled, familiar gym, we are mostly training physical capacity, not mental adaptability. In order to use simulation for holistic preparation, we also have to prep athletes for the mental challenges they will face at a HYROX event and expose them to variability and teach them how to respond mentally to chaos and variability with calm, clarity, and intention, rather than being hijacked by automatic threat reactions. In other words: It's not about tougher workouts - it's about smarter minds.

chunk.content: We're not just building fitness; we want to build confidence, adaptability, and the ability to keep a mental edge when it really counts. Hence, your job as a HYROX coach is to design sessions that not only load the muscles and lungs, but also train the athlete's mind to notice and effectively deal with pressure, stay in a challenge (not threat) state, use their tools (breathing, grounding, reframing, acceptance, defusion...), and keep the Central Executive Network (CEN) online so they can make good decisions under fatigue. This does not necessarily require a whole HYROX race simulation with all its stations. Regular training sessions can and should also be used to help the athletes prep not only physically for their upcoming races but also mentally. For that, let's take a look at the mental component during three phases: 1. Pre-Training 2. During Training 3. Post-Training

Hence, your job as a HYROX coach is to design sessions that not only load the muscles and lungs, but also train the athlete's mind to notice and effectively deal with pressure, stay in a challenge (not threat) state, use their tools (breathing, groun

Regular training sessions can and should also be used to help the athletes prep not only physically for their upcoming races but also mentally.
For that, let's take a look at the mental component during three phases: 1.

chunk.content:
Pre-Training: Prepping the Mind
Most coaches are good at briefing the body ("This is going to be hard"). Fewer coaches deliberately brief the athlete's mind. Before a pressure-focused training session or HYROX-style simulation, take 5 minutes for a mental pre-brief. The goal is not to remove nerves, but to: Normalize them, Frame the workout as a challenge, not a threat, Activate inner resources before the athlete is in the thick of it. There are two great ways to do this, depending on the setting and your coaching style: 1. An interactive mental pre-brief 2. An individual guided journaling ritual Both options work. You can use one or the other - or blend them. Option 1: Interactive Mental Pre-Brief
This can be done in a group setting or 1:1 with an athlete. It can happen as an open discussion or more quietly by simply giving prompts and allowing athlete(s) to reflect individually for a moment - whatever you and your athlete(s) feel comfortable with. Either way, the structure is the same: Name the goal clearly For example: "Today's session is designed to mimic mid-race fatigue and decision-making under pressure." "The goal is not just to survive - it's to stay composed and stay with your pacing and cues when it gets uncomfortable." This gives athletes clarity on the purpose of the session giving them an idea for what is about to happen. Invite athletes to recognize the mental challenge For example, ask:
"What kind of thoughts might show up for you today when it gets hard?" "What emotions are likely to appear? Nervousness, frustration, doubt?" This gives athletes permission to expect these reactions instead of being surprised by them. Plan the response For example, ask: "When those thoughts or emotions show up, how do you want to respond?" "Which tools will you use - e.g. breathing, cues, acceptance, defusion, W.I.N. (What's Important Now), cognitive reframing...?" You're essentially telling the athlete: "We expect your brain to react. That's normal. Your job today is to practice how you meet those reactions."

chunk.content:
You can facilitate this mental pre-brief in whatever way feels authentic and comfortable for you as a coach. For example as a full conversation, or as a short prompt you verbally introduce before warm-up and encourage athletes to reflect individually, or as a simple reminder: e.g. "Take 2 minutes and think about how you want to respond when it gets uncomfortable today." The Power of a Group When you are coaching a group of athletes, doing an interactive mental brief together as a group pre-training has several powerful effects. Here are 4 big ones: 1. It normalizes and reinforces the mental aspect: "Prep your mind like your body." 2. Athletes see they are not alone; others experience similar thoughts and emotions. 3. They learn from each other's coping strategies and understand that successful coping looks different across different people - hence, they are encouraged to find what works for them individually.
4. It strengthens group bonds, trust, and accountability - athletes can remind each other of their intentions during the session. Coaching the Mind - Within Your Lane This approach is not about doing something you don't feel confident with: You are not expected to become a sport psychologist or guide deep emotional processes. Your role is simply to create space and structure for reflection. You decide what you feel comfortable with. Whether that means facilitating an open group conversation or simply giving the prompts and letting athletes think for themselves instead. Think of it this way: You don't need to provide the answers but you can create room for reflection and structured mental preparation. Reflection Exercise: Ask: If you ever see an athlete struggling beyond what you can support, referring them to a sport psychologist or mental performance professional is not only appropriate - it's responsible.
What will your mental brief look like for your athletes for your next training? What is the goal of the session? What mental challenges might come up? How can you encourage a performance-enhancing response? Option 2: An individual guided journaling ritual When a group discussion isn't possible for example if you coach individual athletes remotely, or when athletes prefer privacy - individual guided journaling is a powerful alternative. A simple and effective tool is: The "1-1-3 Prep" to set intentions. Ask athletes to take a couple of minutes before a session to follow the following prompt: One mental goal for this session (1) 1

key_facts.fact: You can facilitate this mental pre-brief in whatever way feels authentic and comfortable for you as a coach.
For example as a full conversation, or as a short prompt you verbally introduce before warm-up and encourage athletes to reflect individually, or as a simple reminder: e.g.

"Take 2 minutes and think about how you want to respond when it gets uncomfortable today." The Power of a Group When you are coaching a group of athletes, doing an interactive mental brief together as a group pre-training has several powerful effects
It normalizes and reinforces the mental aspect: "Prep your mind like your body." 2.
Athletes see they are not alone; others experience similar thoughts and emotions.
They learn from each other's coping strategies and understand that successful coping looks different across different people - hence, they are encouraged to find what works for them individually.
It strengthens group bonds, trust, and accountability - athletes can remind each other of their intentions during the session.
Coaching the Mind - Within Your Lane This approach is not about doing something you don't feel confident with: You are not expected to become a sport psychologist or guide deep emotional processes.
Your role is simply to create space and structure for reflection.
Whether that means facilitating an open group conversation or simply giving the prompts and letting athletes think for themselves instead.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 03: During Simulation - Coaching in the Heat of the Moment
chunk.content:
During Simulation - Coaching in the Heat of the Moment Once the session starts, the goal is not to shield athletes from discomfort, but to help them build a better relationship with it. Your role in the session Remind them of their intention "Remember your mental goal for today - what are you focusing on right now?" Reconnect them with their cue "Back to your cue: 'Calm breath, long pull.' Stay with it for the next 10 strokes." Normalize the discomfort "This is the exact kind of fatigue you'll feel at station 6-7 in HYROX. This is not danger - this is effort."
Some coaching phrases you can use "Notice the thought, then come back to your task." "You don't have to like this sensation - you just have to work with it." "Yes, your legs are screaming. That's your body doing its job. What's important now?" "Can you stay curious instead of reactive for the next 30 seconds?" Encourage athletes to practice: Acceptance "This is tough, and I can allow it." Cognitive defusion "I'm having the thought that I can't keep this pace." Focus on controllables breath, cadence, posture, line If you occasionally add small unpredictable elements to the session - e.g. changing the order of stations, slightly altering distances, giving them a last-minute pacing change - you are
gently training their brain to stay flexible and composed when the plan shifts. This again should be done with a prior briefing and debriefing to avoid frustration and a feeling of uncertainty within the athletes. Exercise Take a look at what you wrote down for your mental brief for the next training session and think of 3 ways you can coach the mental aspect in the heat of the moment and support your athletes in becoming mentally stronger.

chunk.content:
Debriefing: Post-Simulation A simulation session isn't "complete" when the clock stops. The way you close the session is just as important for mental training as the way you start it. We can divide the post-simulation phase into two parts: 1. Immediate Decompression (Nervous System) Right after a hard effort, the nervous system is still in high activation. Before jumping onto phones, chatting, or rushing into the next task, give athletes 2-3 minutes to actively down-regulate. Options include: Box breathing (e.g. 4-4-4-4) or any slow exhale-focused pattern. Sitting or lying down, simply noticing the breath and feeling the body "drop" out of high alert. Brief body scan: "Feet, legs, trunk, shoulders, jaw - let each area soften 5-10%."
The message: "We push the system hard - and we also teach it how to come back down." This helps: Shift from sympathetic to parasympathetic activation, Calm the Salience Network, Prepare the brain for more objective reflection instead of emotional reactivity. Exercise: Have coaches take 3-4 minutes to actively down regulate their nervous system. Simply being in the moment and noticing the body to calm down. Not judging thoughts, but letting them come and go, seeing them simply as mental events, passing through. No judgment - just being. This could be done with a guided meditation, that focuses on box breathing (rhythm pattern) & audio for a progressive body relaxation and thought guidance. Listen to the Example:
Example of Meditation Audio 2. Cognitive Reflection (Teaching the Brain When to Review) Athletes will always replay their performance. The question is when and how. If they constantly analyze mid-workout or mid-race ("That was terrible, you messed that up!"), attention gets hijacked and performance suffers. We want to teach the mind: "We don't ignore mistakes - we just review them later." You can use a simple reflection protocol as a habit after key sessions:
Timing Wait 15-60 minutes post-training. Then set a timer for max. 10 minutes. Use a journal - not just thinking in your head. Writing creates distance and clarity.
Step 1 - Emotion Dump (2-3 minutes) Write freely about thoughts and feelings from the session. No editing, no polishing. Use phrases like: "Right now I feel..." "When X happened, I experienced..." The aim is not to analyze yet, but to empty the pressure tank slightly, so reflection can be calmer and more constructive.

chunk.content:
Step 2 - Well / Better / Learned Then guide athletes through three short lists: 1. Well - 3 things that went well "Held my planned pace on the runs." "Stayed with my cue during the sled push." "Didn't give up when I wanted to." 2. Better - 3 things I want to do better next time "Start slightly more conservative." "Use my breathing tool earlier." "Avoid looking at other lanes so much." 3. Learned - 3 things I learned from today's performance "I can still move well even when my legs are burning hard." "My mind gets loud after no-reps - that's a key moment for me." "If I prepare my cue beforehand, I can access it under pressure."
Finally, ask them to Commit to 1 thing to improve Choose ONE item from the "Better" list to improve next time. "Next session, I will... [specific behavior]." This keeps reflection actionable and future-oriented instead of ruminative and self-critical. REFLECTION EXERCISE This module is made to help you become a better coach. Reflect on how you have taken advantage of this opportunity. Use the well / better / learned reflection: 1. What did you do well while engaging in today's module? --> Name 3 things 2. What do you want to do better when engaging in the next module? --> Name 3 things 3. What did you learn? --> Name 3 things
4. Commit to Improvement --> Choose ONE thing from the "Better" list to improve next time. "Next session, I will... [specific behavior]." Summing it up Simulating HYROX is not just about physically copying the race order under fatigue. True simulation means training how the mind responds to pressure, variability, and unpredictability. Pre-simulation: We brief the mind, not just the body. We set a mental goal, define cues, and activate reasons to trust ourselves. During simulation: We help athletes build a relationship with discomfort, practice acceptance and defusion, and bring attention back to controllables. Post-simulation: We calm the nervous system and use structured reflection to learn and grow, rather than letting unstructured inner commentary run the show. Athletes tend to listen differently to their inner voice, emotions, and sensations on competition day. If they've never paid attention to that
voice, emotions, and sensations in training, they won't have the tools or experience to work with it when it really counts. By turning simulations into mental training sessions and not just physical ones, you help athletes show up on race day not just fitter, but mentally prepared, adaptable, and confident in their ability to stay in their performance zone - no matter what the arena throws at them.
---

unit.title: Coaching the Junior Athlete
unit.unit_summary: This unit introduces Module 10, Coaching the Junior Athlete, and defines the junior HYROX athlete as a 16-18-year-old transitioning toward adulthood rather than a scaled-down adult. It positions youth development through evidence-based models: Long-Term Athlete Development (LTAD), which provides a staged long-term roadmap, and the Youth Physical Development Model (YPDM), which individualizes physical emphasis around maturity markers such as Peak Height Velocity and Peak Weight Velocity. The unit warns that the 16-18 transition is often misread as a reason to tighten technical control, increase

chunk.content: [0:00:00] Welcome to the course The Junior Athlete. As coaches within HYROX, we are privileged to be part of a sport that inspires people to discover what they're capable of. Increasingly, that inspiration is reaching a new youth audience. Whilst Young Stars targets 8-15, the junior athlete can be defined as 16-18 year [0:00:17] olds who are enthusiastic, curious, and motivated to stay in the sport. They want to run, lift, compete, and most importantly, belong. But coaching junior athletes isn't simply a scaled down version of coaching adults. They are transitioning to adulthood. It is a fundamentally different responsibility, and one that requires a different [0:00:35] perspective. When a young athlete walks into your gym, they are not just there to improve their fitness. They are in the process of developing their confidence, their identity, and their relationship with long-term physical literacy. The experiences they have now will shape whether they see sport and fitness as something they love for life or something they leave behind. [0:00:53] Your role therefore extends far beyond sets, reps, and splits. You are not just building fitness, you are building people. In HYROX, we often talk about preparing athletes for the demands of racing. But with junior athletes, performance must be viewed through a wider lens. [0:01:09] Success is an athlete who leaves your session more confident than when they arrived. An athlete who feels capable. An athlete who feels seen, supported, and motivated to return. In this course, you will also explore how to develop their movement skills and racing literacy through coaching pedagogical strategies that move beyond simply telling [0:01:25] athletes what to do, and instead focus on designing learning environments that encourage exploration, decision-making, and adaptability. You'll learn how to help young athletes not only run, lift, and complete stations, but to understand how to race, how to regulate effort, and how to respond to [0:01:42] fatigue and changing conditions. Alongside this, we'll look at how you, as a coach, can create environments that support not only their physical development, but also their enjoyment, motivation, and long-term fulfillment. Our next generation of HYROX athletes are keen, excited, and full of potential. [0:01:59] The environment you create will shape who they become. So let's begin.

Introduction Youth Racing Transition Nonlinear Pedagogy Reframing the Junior Athlete Coaching Approach Environment Design Principles The Coach as the Environmental Architect Level 2 - Modul 10 - 1. Coaching the Junior Athlete
Introduction
The Junior Athlete Learning Objectives To analyse key youth development models within the HYROX Youngstars framework and how they guide age-appropriate training 1 Positioning specific coaching pedagogy to impact the future approaches of HYROX Youngstars coaching 2 The development of junior athletes (16-18 year olds) within HYROX must be guided by evidence-based frameworks that prioritize long- term engagement, enjoyment, and holistic growth, rather than
short-term performance outcomes. Junior athletes are not simply preparing for the next adult level race. They are building the foundations for future performance, health, confidence, and lifelong participation in physical activity. To support this, the HYROX Academy critically appraises two complementary models as the backbone of its youth philosophy for physical development: the Long-Term Athlete Development (LTAD) model and the Youth Physical Development Model (YPDM). The LTAD model, originally developed by Balyi et al (2013), emphasizes progressive, age-appropriate stages of development and reinforces a critical message for youth sport: children are not miniature adults. LTAD (figure 1) outlines 7 stages: Active Start, FUNdamentals, Learn to Train, Train to Train, Learning to Compete, Train to Compete and Training to Win. Each stage has a distinct developmental priority. Early stages focus on physical literacy, movement variety, confidence, and enjoyment, while later stages gradually introduce more structured training and competitive demands. This staged progression helps reduce the risks associated with early specialization, overuse injuries, and psychological burnout, while promoting a positive and sustainable relationship with sport.
Figure 1: Balyi et al. (2013) LTAD Model Within HYROX, LTAD translates into adapting traditional race elements into developmentally appropriate formats. For younger athletes, this means playful, exploratory versions of running, jumping, throwing, and carrying that emphasize agility, balance, coordination, and speed rather than load or volume. As athletes mature, these experiences evolve toward more technical execution, greater fatigue tolerance, and increased competition specificity. The intention is not to delay performance, but to build it on robust foundations that support long-term progression.

chunk.content:
While LTAD provides a valuable overarching pathway, its reliance on chronological age can limit its responsiveness to individual differences in growth and maturation. This is where the Youth Physical Development Model, developed by Lloyd and Oliver (2012), becomes a vital complementary consideration. Within the YPDM, physical qualities are not switched on or off at fixed ages. Instead, they are always trainable, but emphasized differently depending on maturation status. In the original YPDM visuals (figure 2+3), this is communicated through small text, bold text, and color coding, which signal relative emphasis rather than exclusivity. Smaller text indicates qualities that should still be exposed and maintained, while bold text highlights periods where adaptation potential is heightened and therefore deserves greater programming consideration. Colour coding further reinforces how emphasis evolves as young athletes progress through childhood and adolescence. Figure 2 Lloyd and Oliver (2012) Youth Physical Development Model Figure 3 Lloyd and Oliver (2012) Youth Physical Development Model
A defining strength of Lloyd and Oliver (2012) YPDM is the explicit recognition of Peak Height Velocity (PHV) and Peak Weight Velocity (PWV) as key maturational markers. Around PHV (when rapid increases in stature occur), coordination, balance, and movement efficiency can temporarily fluctuate. During this phase, YPDM places stronger emphasis on movement competency, strength foundations, and technical control, while managing load carefully to account for changing limb lengths and neuromuscular control. Importantly, speed, agility, and skill qualities never disappear from the model. They remain present, reinforcing the principle that well- rounded athleticism must be continuously nurtured. By aligning physical emphasis, skill development with biological readiness rather than chronological age, YPDM enables coaches to individualize training, optimize adaptation windows, and support long-term athlete development without sacrificing robustness or confidence during sensitive phases of growth. For HYROX Junior athletes aged 16 to 18, YPDM supports individualization in program design. Two athletes of the same age and sex may require very different training emphases

Using YPDM principles, coaches are encouraged to adjust workloads, intensities, and expectations so sessions remain physically challenging yet cognitively and emotionally appropriate. Importantly, success is framed around effort, learning, adaptability, and teamwork, rather than solely on race outcomes or rankings. Once evaluated, LTAD and YPDM form a powerful dual framework for HYROX Youngstars and the Junior Athlete. LTAD provides the long-term roadmap and trajectory, while YPDM ensures that the journey remains mindful of physical development to the individual athlete. Lastly, it is important to note that as the Junior athlete enters the final stages of teenage years, the models inherently demonstrate a need to increase structure and skill level orientated around the sport in focus. This can often lead to mixed coaching assumptions about what happens next? Therefore, the question every coach really wants to answer is: "how can the training process lead to a junior athlete's success in the adult arena?"

The LTAD figure presents a staged progression from **Physical Literacy** to **Active for Life**. The stages shown are **Active Start**, **FUNdamentals**, **Learning to Train**, **Training to Train**, **Learning to Compete**, **Training to Compete**, and **Training to Win**. The model links early stages to fundamental movement and sport skills, then progresses toward building physical and mental capability, performance sport, and active-for-life participation. It also visually shows that later stages vary by biological sex and approximate age bands.

The YPDM figures show separate male and female youth physical development models. They communicate that qualities such as **mobility**, **agility**, **speed**, **power**, **strength**, and **hypertrophy** can be trained across development, but with different emphasis depending on maturity status. The visuals use size, boldness, and color coding to show relative training emphasis, not fixed inclusion or exclusion.

chunk.content:
Youth Racing Transition Most HYROX coaches working with 16-18-year-old athletes do so with genuinely good intentions. At this stage of development, Junior athletes are stronger, fitter, and more physically robust than early teenage years. They can generally tolerate higher training loads, competition feels meaningful, and races now carry real consequences. Qualification pathways exist, comparison with peers becomes unavoidable, and ambition grows. As a result, coaching environments naturally begin to resemble adult performance programs. Sessions become more structured, exercises are prescribed with tighter rules, and there is an increasing focus on "doing movements correctly." On the surface, this feels like progress. However, this stage is also where many youth athletes quietly begin to struggle. Not necessarily physically, but application of skill within the context of racing. Despite doing more training, performance can often be observed to plateau. Skills that look stable in controlled sessions break down in races. Confidence fluctuates, and athletes may either become overly dependent on
the coach for feedback or disengage entirely. Long-Term Athlete Development and the Youth Physical Development Model do not oppose the move toward performance preparation at this age. In fact, they support it. But there is more to the story of youth athlete development with regards to the influence of coaching pedagogical practice. The critical global coaching assumption The ages of 16-18 represent a transition phase from youth sport toward adult level competition. This transition is frequently misunderstood. Many coaches interpret it as a signal to tighten the grip on technical control of specific movements in tasks increase training load to build capacity of tasks reduce variation of all-round physical literacy The assumption is: 'if the sport, and athlete, are becoming more serious, the athlete's movement must therefore focus purely on
Figure 4 - Coach led Task programming to enhance athlete performance becoming more precise and be able to achieve greater capacity for work'. This assumption has, and will continue to, create success within HYROX. Yet the junior athlete transition is not a switch that flips at a certain age, it is not linear, and it is not achieved simply by increasing emphasis on programming prescription of specificity and progressive overload. In essence, traditional coaching provides (figure 4) direction through pure periodization of the movement effectiveness and overall physical capacity of the performer to increase overall speed of the task (the HYROX race format).

chunk.content:
Figure 5 - Gullich et al. (2025) - Consequences of early specialization and gradual early progress. The belief that demonstrating correct technique, instructing, programming task based workouts alone, and correcting errors early will guarantee improved performance feels intuitive and has shaped generations of practice. Yet modern day research (Gullich, Barth, Hambrick & Macnamara, 2025) shows that early specialization of physical abilities and skills lead to plateauing of long term progression and performance (figure 5).
Skill is not installed through instruction alone, technique does not stabilize under pressure through repetition in isolation, and performance breaks down when athletes have not learned to adapt in changing conditions. Many youth athletes can look technically excellent in warm-ups, drills, or isolated workouts, yet when fatigue accumulates, pressure from opposition rises, and the environment becomes chaotic, the skills of an athlete can deteriorate. HYROX demands intensive functional movement under situational and environmental constraints, navigating race routes, running under fatigue, noise, heat, emotional stress, and making pacing tactical decisions in real time relative to opposition dynamics. No amount of perfect rehearsal and capacity building in calm conditions guarantees performance when the constraints of the performer, task and environment collide. This is not a failure of effort or discipline, it is a failure of learning and transfer design. Athletes who have only learned what to do and given pre-set coaching answers for race scenarios, rather than how to self-organize and adapt, end up becoming less able performers in the long term. This is where nonlinear coaching pedagogy (NLP) becomes essential. The HYROX academy recognizes that NLP reframes how learning can progress.
### Visual Note: Figure 4 - Coach-Led Task Programming to Enhance Athlete Performance
The figure shows two yellow arrows pointing toward each other: **Athlete** on the left and **Task** on the right. The athlete side includes **Profiling & Build Capacity (Tolerance/Output Expression)**. The task side includes **Physical & Technical Programming**. The figure represents a traditional coach-led approach that links athlete profiling and capacity with task-based physical and technical programming.
### Visual Note: Figure 5 - Gullich et al. (2025), Consequences of Early Specialization and Gradual Early Progress
The figure plots **Human Performance** against **Age**. A dashed line labelled **Just Below** rises quickly during early years through intensive discipline-specific practices and then plateaus. A yellow line labelled **World Class** rises more gradually through extensive multidisciplinary practice and continues toward higher peak performance age. The figure supports the point that accelerated early progress through specialization can plateau, whereas gradual early progress can support higher long-term performance.

key_facts.fact: (2025) - Consequences of early specialization and gradual early progress.

The belief that demonstrating correct technique, instructing, programming task based workouts alone, and correcting errors early will guarantee improved performance feels intuitive and has shaped generations of practice.

Yet modern day research (Gullich, Barth, Hambrick & Macnamara, 2025) shows that early specialization of physical abilities and skills lead to plateauing of long term progression and performance (figure 5).

Skill is not installed through instruction alone, technique does not stabilize under pressure through repetition in isolation, and performance breaks down when athletes have not learned to adapt in changing conditions.

Many youth athletes can look technically excellent in warm-ups, drills, or isolated workouts, yet when fatigue accumulates, pressure from opposition rises, and the environment becomes chaotic, the skills of an athlete can deteriorate.

HYROX demands intensive functional movement under situational and environmental constraints, navigating race routes, running under fatigue, noise, heat, emotional stress, and making pacing tactical decisions in real time relative to opposition dynami
No amount of perfect rehearsal and capacity building in calm conditions guarantees performance when the constraints of the performer, task and environment collide.
This is not a failure of effort or discipline, it is a failure of learning and transfer design.
Athletes who have only learned what to do and given pre-set coaching answers for race scenarios, rather than how to self-organize and adapt, end up becoming less able performers in the long term.
This is where nonlinear coaching pedagogy (NLP) becomes essential.

chunk.content:
Nonlinear Pedagogy Nonlinear Pedagogy (NLP) is a learner-centered approach to teaching and coaching that recognizes skill learning as a non- linear, adaptive process emerging from the continuous interaction between the athlete, the task, and the environment (Rudd et al., 2021). This perspective is grounded in the understanding that athletes are complex, adaptive systems whose movement behaviors evolve over time in response to changing constraints. Rather than assuming that learning progresses in a predictable, step-by-step sequence, NLP acknowledges that learning is dynamic and often unpredictable. Within this framework, several key principles are recognized: Learning is variable: Variability is not viewed as error or noise, but as a functional and necessary component of learning. Through experiencing different movement outcomes, athletes develop adaptability and flexibility in their performance.
Progress includes fluctuations and regressions: Improvements in performance are rarely linear. Periods of apparent regression, inconsistency, or instability are considered normal and can reflect important exploration processes that ultimately support more robust skill development. Skill emerges through exploration, not repetition of an ideal model: Rather than reproducing a single "correct" technique, athletes learn by exploring a range of movement possibilities and discovering solutions that are effective for their individual characteristics and the specific performance context. As a result, NLP recognizes that development is adaptive, individual, variable, and context-dependent, rather than smooth and linear. Each athlete's movement solutions are shaped by their unique physical capacities, perceptions, experiences, and the specific demands of the performance environment. Consequently, within Nonlinear Pedagogy, coaches do not attempt to install skills or funnel athletes toward a single idealized technique. Instead, the coach's role shifts toward the design and manipulation of practice environments that encourage exploration and problem-solving. By adjusting task constraints, environmental

chunk.content: constraint. This process leads athletes to investigate and refine movement solutions that are individually effective and context-specific. A second example is the sled pull. If a junior athlete shows a tendency not to maximize the total distance of each sled box, a coach can manipulate the box length within semi-competitive or time-based activities to observe how the athlete adapts. Through coach-guided questioning, the athlete can explore which movement actions, between the front and rear of the box, enable greater distance or decreased time spent with each pull. These discoveries can then transfer to more effective and adaptable movement solutions in a range of race situations. A junior athlete may demonstrate a tendency to misjudge pacing during running segments, often starting too fast and struggling to sustain performance later in the race. To address this, a coach could design a running challenge for a group of junior athletes that encourages exploration and self-regulation of pace. As part of the warm-up, the group completes 3 × 300 m runs, each separated by 45 seconds of recovery. The first repetition is performed at a perceived effort of 5 out of 10, the second at 7 out of 10, and the third at 9 out of 10. After each repetition, the coach provides time-based feedback, allowing athletes to associate their internal perception of effort with an external performance outcome. This exposes each athlete to a range of three distinct "gears" that they can later draw upon. The main challenge is then introduced: athletes must complete 6 × 300 m with a reduced recovery of 30 seconds. Before starting, each athlete selects a target pace they believe is sustainably high and repeatable across all six repetitions. The task requires them to HYROX STATION EXAMPLES HYROX RUNNING EXAMPLE

chunk.section_title: Chapter 04: Reframing the Junior Athlete Coaching Approach
chunk.content:
Reframing the Junior Athlete Coaching Approach The key reframe for HYROX Youth coaches is this: the coach's role is not primarily to set or correct movement, but to design learning environments. Well-designed environments allow athletes to self- organize solutions, experience errors as feedback rather than failure, and develop robust skills that transfer to competition. For youth athletes aged 16-18, this matters more than ever. They do not need perfect technique. They need adaptable movement skills that hold up under fatigue, pressure, and change. This introduction module, sets the foundation for why this pedagogical approach, not instruction-heavy coaching, should guide how HYROX coaches support youth athletes as they move toward competition. Environment, therefore, is the new focus point that coaches should turn toward to unlock the coaching strategies of the future within HYROX. If coaches default to coach-led approaches of the task to exclusively build the performer, they will limit the athlete's relationship with the contextual race environment. The module is not suggesting that coaches ignore their extensive experience and
Interpretation of Non-Linear Pedagogy for Junior Athlete Learning and Skill Development understanding of task design and periodization. As Dr. Gommaar D'Hulst and I presented in Module 8: the frontline of task periodization for HYROX performance! This introduction module to the junior athlete presents the case that Performer and Task are part of the big equation. To emphasize, NLP recognizes that skill emerges from the ongoing and continuous interaction between the athlete, the task, and the environment.

chunk.content:
Environment Design Principles As discussed, NLP is a learning framework that shifts coaching focus away from a coach-led approach by prescribing ideal techniques and programming tasks. Instead, Junior Athlete coaching can begin to lean toward designing environments that allow skill to emerge from the athlete themselves. The coaches' role can be viewed as shifting toward a guiding and facilitating one. Central to this approach are environmental design principles (EDP), outlined clearly by Newcombe et al. (2019). These principles guide coaches in shaping practice so that junior athletes learn to adapt, self-organize, and perform under realistic constraints rather than simply repeating rehearsed patterns. In fitness racing like HYROX, where fatigue, pacing disruption, and environmental unpredictability are inevitable, EDPs are critical for developing adaptable, resilient, transferable performance. There are 4 key pillars that underpin the EDP: Session Aim and Performance Targets
In NLP, the aim is not defined by how the movement should look, but by what the junior athlete is trying to achieve. Clear intentions set by the athlete and coach together can be framed by the three E's: Explore dynamics and test new solution, Exploit strengths/weaknesses or situational cues, and Execute a known or targeted strategy. Targets should reflect race-relevant outcomes rather than technical checklists. The three E's allow athletes to develop different movement solutions while still working toward a shared performance goal. Constrain to Afford This sits at the heart of nonlinear learning. Constraints act as informational limits that invite, afford, or restrict certain actions, allowing skill to emerge through exploration, not repetition of an ideal form. They fall into three interacting categories: task constraints (e.g. distance, pace demands, recovery, rules), environmental constraints (e.g. surface, space, presence of others, temperature, judges), and individual constraints (e.g. fatigue, strengths, weaknesses, psychological state). In NLP, constraints are not limitations to avoid but tools to afford specific behaviors. By carefully manipulating constraints, coaches invite athletes toward certain movement or pacing solutions without explicitly instructing them how to move. Learning emerges as athletes perceive information, act, and adapt in response. Representative Learning Design (RLD) For learning to transfer to competition, practice must contain the key informational variables of the performance environment. If athletes never experience pace disruption, spatial negotiation and limits, or decision- making under fatigue in training, those skills will not reliably appear in

races. Representative sessions preserve the perception-action couplings present in competition, even if the task is simplified. This ensures that learning remains functionally relevant rather than context-specific. Repetition Without Repetition While repetition of a stimulus is essential for physiological adaptation, NLP recognizes that repeating the same pre-set movement solution limits contextual adaptability. Instead, NLP proposes that athletes face varying problems while self-organizing solutions across different situations. This variability strengthens perception, decision-making, and robustness, allowing athletes to maintain the intended physical stimulus but increase the performance under pressure despite changing internal and external conditions. The outcome may look less "neat" in training, but it produces more durable skill. Let's now explore practical examples of how coaches could shift a youth athlete session to more learner centered.
Running Specific Applied Example: Same Task, Two Learning Designs
Session Task 6 × 1 km run at, or above intended race pace 75-second recovery is awarded after each repetition
Traditional Session An athlete performs the session alone on a treadmill, holding the same prescribed pace for all six repetitions. The environment is stable, the task is tightly controlled, and pacing feedback is dictated primarily by the treadmill. While this may develop physical capacity and threshold development, opportunities for perception-action coupling, decision- making, and movement adaptation are minimal. Variability is suppressed, and learning to improve race performance under contextual pressure is limited. Learning Outcome The athlete learns to reproduce a known pace solution under fatigue. Physiological load is high, but perceptual and decision-making demands are low during running segments that replicate similar speeds as race pace.
Environmental Design Principles Session Two athletes complete the same 6 x 1km efforts on a track or running path but with a desired time window to complete each repetition. On odd- numbered reps, Athlete A inserts two random 20-meter surges at self- selected points before returning to the original speed; on even-numbered reps, Athlete B does the same. Every surge must be targeted at different distance points from the preceding repetitions and consequences are handed out to athletes that fail to complete their role. Pace is disrupted unpredictably, athletes must respond in real time, and fatigue accumulates differently across repetitions. Informational Constraints Present Opponent behavior provides continuous visual information to respond to Unstable pacing constraints causing tactical decision-making External judgment of performance consequences Time pressure and competitive stress to explore, exploit or execute Fatigue directly alters perception-action choices Learning Outcome

This design preserves the environmental informational constraint that every run section within a HYROX race looks different due to the changing dynamics of the opposition. Athletes are encouraged to employ adaptable pacing strategies, decision-making, self-regulation and resilience under changing conditions. The task remains very similar, but the environment leans more to a representation of race demands as informational constraints invite athletes to create a range of actions.
HYROX Specific Applied Example: Same Task, Two Learning Designs
Session Task 4 rounds 1 km run 35 wall balls 2.5 minutes recovery between rounds
Traditional Session One athlete completes all rounds alone, either on a treadmill, track or a quiet running route. The 1 km runs are completed at a pre-determined, even pace, guided by smartwatch or treadmill feedback. The athlete knows exactly how fast to run and aims to replicate the same pacing profile in each round, regardless of accumulating fatigue. This is in effort to build physiological capacity and physical tolerance to lactate build up prior to the muscular wall ball effort. On completion of each run, the athlete moves immediately to 35 wall balls. No judging is applied beyond basic self-monitoring. Repetitions are counted by the athlete with depth being self-assessed and a random spot on a wall is self-picked for the athlete to hit and there are no external consequences for borderline no-repetitions. The athlete paces the wall balls in a familiar, repeatable way. Learning Outcome The athlete learns to reproduce limited known solutions under fatigue. Physiological load is high, but perceptual and decision-making demands are low. The athlete practices control, consistency and execution. However adaptability, emotional regulation, and competitive behaviors are largely absent.

chunk.content:
Environmental Design Principles Session Two or more athletes complete the same number of rounds, but the coach staggers the start of the 1 km run in each round by a matter of seconds. The stagger changes between rounds, meaning the athlete who starts first is not always the same. The explicit objective for the task is clear: win the round. Athletes must decide whether to push early, chase, hold back, or surge late based on what they perceive from their opponent(s). A time cut off is also placed for athletes to arrive in after each round with burpee consequences given if not met. Pacing is no longer prescribed. The opponent becomes a moving informational constraint, constantly shaping decisions during the run. Fatigue from previous rounds alters what actions feel possible, and pacing strategies naturally evolve. On arrival at the wall ball station, the competitive layer intensifies. The coach actively judges every repetition and has placed a small target for athletes to hit. Any no-rep (due to depth, target miss-hit, or loss of wall ball control) results in one further immediate penalty burpee before the proceeding wall ball. This introduces consequence, pressure, and risk. Athletes must now solve the problem of decreasing the time taken per rep to get to the finish before the opposition (just like in the race). All whilst maintaining movement standards and hitting a specific target. For extra challenges, coaches may change the weight of the ball without the athlete knowing, forcing them to adapt timing and coordination of the catch with
the weight. Fatigue, opposition dynamics, and athlete decision making all influence the outcome. Informational Constraints Present Unstable staggered start, differing wall ball weight and opponent pacing demands causing tactical decision-making External judgment and performance consequences Time pressure and competitive stress Fatigue directly also impacts perception and action choices Every repetition appears different and unpredictable in nature Learning Outcome The athlete learns to adapt under pressure. Movement solutions reorganise as fatigue, competition, and consequence interact. Pacing, transition speed, and wall ball strategy become emergent rather than pre- planned. The athlete practices managing emotion, attention, and technique when outcomes matter, mirroring real HYROX race conditions. The session intention is to not simply allow the athlete to execute a pre- planned tactic every round. Exploration of options and exploiting the dynamics of the opponent(s) is also at play here. The coach uses guided questioning after the session to harness the learning from the experience.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 06: The Coach as the Environmental Architect
chunk.content:
The Coach as the Environmental Architect Newcombe et al. (2021) makes the compelling case that, to enhance learning, the coach should consider themselves not simply as an instructor of technique, but as an architect of the environment in which learning emerges. This represents a fundamental shift in coaching philosophy: away from prescribing exact movements and toward shaping the conditions that allow athletes to discover effective solutions themselves. In this view, skill is not something directly transferred from coach to athlete, but something that develops through the athlete's interaction with carefully designed constraints, challenges, and opportunities. Within HYROX, this concept is particularly powerful because the sport is defined by variability, fatigue, and the constant interaction between running and functional work. No two race experiences feel the same. Athletes must continuously adapt their movement strategies based on their physiological state, pacing decisions, competitive pressure, and environmental conditions. A coaching approach that over-emphasizes perfect technique in sterile, predictable settings fails to prepare athletes for this reality. The
Environmental Design Principles reposition the coach as a designer of learning experiences rather than a controller of movement. Instead of asking, "How do I get the athlete to replicate the perfect sled push technique?" the environmental architect asks, "How do I design conditions that encourage the athlete to discover effective sled push solutions under fatigue, pressure, and uncertainty?" This might involve manipulating load, distance, rest intervals, competitive scenarios, or cognitive demands so that athletes learn to self-organize and adapt. This approach has several important benefits for youth athletes in particular. First, it enhances adaptability. When athletes are exposed to varied and representative environments, they develop movement solutions that are flexible rather than rigid. These solutions are more robust when fatigue accumulates, when pacing errors occur, or when unexpected challenges arise during competition. 1 Second, it improves perception-action coupling. Athletes learn to read their bodies, the task, and the environment more effectively. Rather than relying on constant external instruction, they 2
develop the ability to make better decisions independently. Third, it supports long-term engagement and development. Environments that encourage exploration, problem-solving, and autonomy are more intrinsically motivating for youth athletes. This fosters confidence, creativity, and ownership of their development, rather than dependence on coach feedback. 3 Ultimately, the environmental architect recognizes that their primary role is not to produce perfect training performances, but to prepare adaptable performers. In HYROX, where success depends on sustaining performance across prolonged fatigue and constantly changing demands, this adaptability is the defining characteristic of expertise. 4 By designing representative, challenging, and supportive learning environments, coaches help youth athletes build skills that are not only technically sound, but resilient, transferable, and competition- ready.
