Instead of asking, "How do I get the athlete to replicate the perfect sled push technique?" the environmental architect asks, "How do I design conditions that encourage the athlete to discover effective sled push solutions under fatigue, pressure, an
This approach has several important benefits for youth athletes in particular.
When athletes are exposed to varied and representative environments, they develop movement solutions that are flexible rather than rigid.

chunk.content:
Communication, Safety & Coaching Practice Why communication is critical Female athletes consistently report that their ability to discuss topics such as menstrual health, breast health, body image, and pelvic floor function influences how they train, recover and compete. Many athletes self-manage symptoms or uncertainty due to embarrassment, fear of negative judgment, or previous unhelpful experiences. Normalising these conversations as part of everyday coaching practice enables earlier discussion, appropriate support, and greater training continuity. Creating a safe and open environment A safe HYROX coaching environment is one where female athletes can raise questions or discuss experiences without embarrassment or negative consequences. Conversations should be athlete-led, voluntary, and free from pressure.
| Environment feature | What this looks like in practice | | Clear, neutral language | Coaches use direct, nonjudgmental terms such as bleeding, cycle, pelvic floor, leaking, and breast pain rather than euphemisms or humor. | | Female health integrated into performance | Female-specific factors are treated alongside sleep, training load, nutrition, and recovery, not as separate or exceptional issues. | | Respect for privacy | Athletes are offered one-to-one conversations when preferred, rather than being required to disclose information in group settings. | | Visible signals of inclusion | Evidence-informed resources, infographics, and a stocked female health kit signal that female health is expected and supported. | | Non-assumptive communication | Coaches avoid dismissive or reductive language such as "she's hormonal" or attributing performance changes to hormones without athlete input. | | Early expectation setting | Coaches state clearly during onboarding that conversations about female health are welcome and relevant to training quality. | | Routine check-ins | Simple questions are included in regular check-ins, for example symptom patterns, comfort with kit, and changes across the cycle. | | Consistent monitoring | Menstrual characteristics and symptoms are tracked in the same way as other training data, where the athlete chooses to share. | | Accessible hygiene support | Athletes have access to essential hygiene items and, where possible, private breastfeeding or pumping spaces. | | Flexible participation models | Where appropriate, female-only sessions or mother-and-child classes are offered to support training continuity. | Coach-athlete dynamics may influence disclosure. Some athletes may feel less comfortable discussing female-health with a male coach, and some coaches may feel uncertain initiating these conversations. Where appropriate, ensure athletes have more than one trusted support route, while maintaining privacy, choice, and athlete autonomy.

chunk.content: Cultural Considerations Attitudes to female health vary widely across cultures and communities. Some athletes may avoid specific movements while bleeding; others may face cultural or religious expectations around modesty, bodily privacy, or contraception. In some contexts, hormonal contraception is viewed as appropriate only within marriage, while in others, menstruating athletes may avoid certain recovery modalities for cultural reasons. As a coach, you can: Avoid assumptions about what an athlete "should" feel comfortable discussing Use open, respectful questions and allow athletes to determine what they disclose Additional visible paragraph in this section: The shift from self-focused concentration to team-focused concentration is one of the biggest differences between singles and doubles racing. Knowing how to keep the pair's engagement on the task in hand is the true essence of concentration.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 03: Menstrual Health & the Menstrual Cycle
chunk.content:
Menstrual Health & the Menstrual Cycle Menstrual health is a core female-specific health domain relevant to HYROX participation across the lifespan. Females menstruate for approximately 37 years, experience around 450 menstrual cycles, and bleed for the equivalent of approx. 6 years in total. Typical menstrual characteristics A typical healthy menstrual cycle commonly presents with the following characteristics: Cycle length: 21-35 days (average approx. 28 days) Bleeding duration: 3-7 days (average approx. 5 days) Luteal phase length: 11-17 days (typically approx. 12-14 days) Blood loss: approx. 30-60 ml per cycle (approx.2-3 tablespoons)
Ovulation: one egg released per cycle Some variability from cycle to cycle is normal. Menstrual characteristics may fluctuate in response to factors such as training load, travel, stress, illness, or changes in energy availability. A schematic figure highlighting the impracticality of planning greater training volume in one versus another phase of a woman's menstrual cycle based on data showing the extraordinary variability of the timing of ovulation in women-for example: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9473716/
Variation in menstrual cycle and phase length, and ovulation (@Colenso- Semple et al., 2023).
Female athletes may present with different menstrual patterns, including: • Anovulatory cycles • Luteal phase deficiency • Hormonal contraception-induced bleeding patterns Bleeding alone does not always reflect underlying menstrual health. Common terms and patterns that may indicate concern Common terms athletes may use include: Dysmenorrhea: painful menstruation in the absence of pelvic pathology
Premenstrual syndrome (PMS): physical, emotional, cognitive, or behavioral symptoms in the days leading up to bleeding Patterns that may warrant attention and possible referral include: Primary amenorrhea: no first period by age 15 Secondary amenorrhea: absence of menstruation for >=3 months (not pregnant) Oligomenorrhea: cycles >35 days Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia): >=80 ml blood loss per cycle Luteal phase deficiency: luteal phase <10 days Anovulation: no ovulation during the cycle
The ovarian hormone profile of a eumenorrheic cycle (A)... @Elliot-Sale (2025) Why We Must Stop Assuming and Estimating Menstrual Cycle Phases in Laboratory and Field-Based Sport Related Research...luteal phase deficient cycle (B), anovulatory cycle (C), and ovulatory and anovulatory oligomenorrheic cycles (D and E). @Elliot-Sale (2025) Why We Must Stop Assuming and Estimating Menstrual Cycle Phases in Laboratory and Field-Based Sport Related Research Clinical conditions that may affect symptoms and training tolerance include:
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS): an endocrine disorder characterized by ovarian dysfunction and hyperandrogenism
Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD): a severe depressive disorder with cyclic symptoms
Endometriosis: a chronic inflammatory condition defined by the presence of endometrial- like tissue outside the uterine cavity
Adenomyosis: a uterine disorder characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue within the myometrium
Uterine fibroids: benign smooth-muscle tumors of the uterus
Endometrial polyps: localized overgrowths of endometrial tissue within the uterine cavity

chunk.content:
These patterns and conditions are included to support awareness and informed conversation. Coaches are not expected to diagnose or manage menstrual patterns or clinical conditions. At Level 2, the coach's role is to recognize terminology, acknowledge athlete-reported experiences, and encourage appropriate referral when concerns are raised. When Referral Is Appropriate Referral to a qualified healthcare professional is appropriate when an athlete reports or presents with: Primary amenorrhea (no period by age 15) Secondary amenorrhea (>=3 months without menstruation, not pregnant) Cycles consistently <21 days or >35 days Very heavy bleeding (>=80 ml per cycle or bleeding that interferes with daily activity) Severe or worsening menstrual pain Symptoms consistent with PCOS, PMDD and endometriosis
Mood symptoms causing functional impairment Suspected low energy availability or relative energy deficiency in sport (see next Chapter) Hormonal Contraception Awareness A substantial proportion of female athletes use hormonal contraception. Key points for coaches include: Hormonal contraception alters natural ovarian hormone patterns Bleeding is usually a withdrawal bleed, not menstruation Hormone levels are more stable, but symptoms may persist Some athletes use continuous dosing to avoid bleeding around competition Some methods reduce bleeding; others increase it Hormonal contraception can mask menstrual dysfunction linked to low energy availability Athletes using hormonal contraception should be supported as individuals, without assumptions about symptoms, performance, or training response.
Key Take-Homes for Coaches Menstrual health is a normal component of female athlete health Coach priorities are recognition, nonjudgmental communication, and referral when indicated

The figure plots a eumenorrheic cycle with estrogen, progesterone, and luteinizing hormone (LH). It labels phases including early follicular, late follicular, ovulatory, and mid-luteal. The hormone curves illustrate that bleeding patterns can coexist with different underlying hormone profiles; bleeding alone does not confirm normal menstrual health.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 04: Energy Availability, Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) & Eating Disorders
chunk.content:
Energy Availability, Relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) & Eating Disorders Energy availability underpins adaptation, performance, recovery, and long-term athlete health. In HYROX, high training density combined with work, travel, and life demands can increase the risk of inadequate fueling. Core definitions Several related but distinct terms are important for coaches to know.
Low energy availability (LEA) Energy availability reflects the amount of energy remaining for basic physiological function after the energy cost of training and daily activity is accounted for.
LEA occurs when energy intake is insufficient relative to total energy expenditure It can be intentional (e.g., weight-loss attempts) or unintentional (e.g., poor appetite, busy schedules, high training density)
Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) is a syndrome that develops when problematic LEA is prolonged and/or severe, resulting in impaired physiological and psychological function across multiple body systems.
Eating disorders Eating disorders are clinical psychiatric conditions that require specialist diagnosis and treatment. An athlete may experience REDs without an eating disorder, and an eating disorder may be present even when performance appears normal.
Common eating disorders include: Anorexia nervosa Bulimia nervosa Binge eating disorder Other specified feeding or eating disorders (OSFED) How risk may present in HYROX contexts Risk may develop gradually and may be associated with: • Increased training volume without parallel increases in fueling • High session density combined with limited recovery time • Busy lifestyles that disrupt regular meals • Appetite suppression after hard or late sessions • Pressure around leanness or appearance
• Endurance-influenced beliefs that lighter always equals faster Why these matters for HYROX performance Chronic LEA can reduce training quality, impair recovery, and increase injury or illness risk. Athletes may continue to train and compete, but performance consistency and adaptation decline over time. Warning patterns coaches should recognize LEA, REDs and disordered eating are often missed because affected athletes may appear disciplined, committed, and highly motivated. Coaches should focus on clusters and patterns, not isolated observations.
Common warning patterns include:

| Warning pattern | Warning pattern | Warning pattern | | Declining or stalled performance despite increased training | Menstrual disruption or loss of ovulatory function | Guilt or distress when training is reduced | | Persistent fatigue or low energy | Frequent illness or poor recovery | Difficulty resting or stepping back when unwell | | Reduced "pop" or sharpness in key sessions | Disrupted sleep | Body checking or distress around body changes | | Recurrent injuries, particularly bone or tendon issues | Rigid food rules or anxiety around fueling | Avoidance of eating in social settings |
A particularly relevant red-flag cluster in female athletes is: fatigue + performance decline + menstrual disruption. Coach scope and referral Coaches do not diagnose or treat LEA, REDs, or eating disorders.
Referral is appropriate when an athlete presents with:
Rapid or unexplained weight loss Persistent fatigue and declining performance Missing periods or significant cycle disruption Recurrent bone stress injuries Marked food rigidity or fear-based eating Bingeing, purging, or compensatory behaviors Distress around body image affecting daily life
Anxiety around rest or inability to reduce training Key Take-Homes for Coaches LEA, REDs, and eating disorders are related but distinct Early recognition and referral protect health and performance continuity

chunk.content:
Pelvic Floor Health Pelvic floor symptoms occur across ages and performance levels, including young and nulliparous athletes. Symptoms are not a marker of weakness, poor fitness, or training failure. What coaches need to understand The pelvic floor is part of the body's support and pressure-management system. It is exposed to repeated load and fatigue during running, lifting, and high-impact tasks. Symptoms may be influenced by impact exposure, fatigue, breathing patterns, and cumulative training load. Common symptoms athletes may report Symptoms that athletes may report include: • Urinary leakage during running or jumping • Urgency or increased frequency • Pelvic pain or discomfort • A sensation of heaviness or pressure • Avoidance or modification of high-impact tasks
Symptoms often emerge under fatigue, during longer sessions, or periods of high training density. Why pelvic floor health matters for HYROX Pelvic floor symptoms can affect: • Willingness to push intensity • Comfort during high impact movements • Hydration behaviors • Confidence and focus Athletes may self-manage quietly, which can reduce training consistency over time. Factors associated with increased symptom likelihood Pelvic floor symptoms are influenced by multiple factors rather than a single cause. Factors associated with increased likelihood include: • High-impact running volume • High training density or fatigue accumulation • LEA or REDs (Section 3) • Pregnancy, postpartum, or menopause (Sections 6 and 7) • Chronic constipation or breath-holding When referral is appropriate
Coaches do not assess or treat pelvic floor dysfunction. The coaching role is to support disclosure, avoid normalizing symptoms as inevitable, and refer when needed. Referral to a pelvic health physiotherapist or appropriate clinician is indicated when an athlete reports: • Persistent or worsening leakage • Pelvic pain or discomfort • A sensation of bulging or heaviness • Symptoms that limit training, confidence or participation • Concerns during pregnancy, postpartum, or menopause Key Take-Homes for Coaches Pelvic floor health is relevant to all female HYROX athletes Pelvic floor symptoms are common and often underreported Coach priorities are supportive communication and timely referral

chunk.content:
Breast Health & Sports Bras Breast health is a performance-relevant but frequently overlooked component of female athlete support. Breast-related issues are common across female athletes of all ages, sizes, and competitive levels. Many athletes value how they look and feel in training and competition. Confidence in kit can support motivation and identity. However, sports bras that prioritize appearance over support may not meet the mechanical demands of HYROX. Why breast support matters for HYROX performance Breasts do not have intrinsic muscular support. During running and jumping, they move independently of the torso and are exposed to repeated impact and fatigue. Inadequate support is commonly associated with: • Breast pain or discomfort • Altered running mechanics or arm swing • Disrupted breathing rhythm
• Increased perceived effort Breast pain and movement: What coaches should recognize Exercise-related breast pain is common and reported across sports and ability levels. While more prevalent in larger cup sizes, it can occur in athletes of any size when support is insufficient. Athletes may respond by:
• Reducing running intensity • Holding or bracing the chest • Shortening stride length • Avoiding warm-ups or high-impact drills • Altering posture or breathing Sports bras as performance equipment Sports bras are performance equipment, not optional apparel. Appropriate support reduces breast movement, improves comfort, and supports efficient movement and breathing. Coaches should be aware of three broad bra types:
| Sports bra type | Support mechanism | Typical use case | | Encapsulation bras | Support each breast individually. | Often suitable for larger cup sizes. | | Compression bras | Compress tissue against the chest wall. | Typically appropriate for lower-impact activity or smaller cup sizes. | | Combination or hybrid bras | Use both encapsulation and compression mechanisms. | Generally most appropriate for high-impact hybrid sports such as HYROX. |
Common bra fit issues that athletes may report Common issues include: • Loose underbands that reduce primary support • Incomplete breast containment • Straps that dig in or slip • Worn-out bras with reduced elasticity • Chafing When referral is appropriate Referral to a clinician or physiotherapist is appropriate when athletes report: • Persistent breast pain despite adequate support • Unilateral pain, swelling, or tissue changes • Skin changes such as redness or dimpling
• Pain that limits movement or bracing • Significant distress related to breast discomfort Key Take-Homes for Coaches Breast support is performance-relevant and modifiable Inadequate support can affect running, breathing, and confidence Coach priorities are normalization, recognition, and referral when indicated
### Visual Note: Breast Anatomy Diagram

chunk.content:
Perimenopause & Menopause Perimenopause is the transition phase leading up to menopause. It commonly involves increased variability in cycle regularity and symptoms. Menopause is defined retrospectively as 12 consecutive months without menstruation (not due to pregnancy, hormonal contraception effects, or medical conditions). Typical experiences athletes may report Responses are highly individual. Some athletes report minimal disruption. Others experience symptoms that affect sleep, comfort, and perceived recovery. Athletes may report: • Greater variability in day-to-day readiness and recovery perception • Changes in heat sensitivity or hot flushes, particularly in indoor settings • Disrupted sleep • Changes in body composition
• Mood changes These experiences can fluctuate with stress, travel, illness, and training density. What may indicate concern and warrant referral Referral to a GP or appropriate clinician should be encouraged when athletes report: • Severe or persistent symptoms that meaningfully affect training or well-being • Significant sleep disruption • Persistent fatigue • Significant mood disturbance • Bleeding after menopause • New or unusual pelvic pain • Recurrent injuries suggestive of compromised bone health • Unexplained and sustained performance decline Key Take-Homes for Coaches Perimenopause and menopause are normal and do not imply reduced training or performance potential Coach priorities are symptom recognition, supportive communication, and timely referral

chunk.content:
Pregnancy & Postpartum Pregnancy and the postpartum period are normal physiological states. Many female HYROX athletes remain physically active during pregnancy and return to structured training postpartum. What coaches should understand Training tolerance may change across pregnancy and postpartum. Symptoms and day-to-day readiness are often more informative than timelines or trimester labels. Experiences are individual. Common experiences athletes may report During pregnancy, athletes may report: • Increased fatigue • Changes in breathing comfort • Increased heat sensitivity • Greater need for hydration and fueling consistency • Pelvic or low-back discomfort
• Changes in pressure or continence symptoms Postpartum athletes may report: • Sleep disruption • Increased fatigue • Pelvic floor symptoms • Discomfort with impact • Variable recovery capacity These experiences are common and not inherently problematic but may influence how training is tolerated. When referral is required During pregnancy, refer if the athlete reports: • Heavy, persistent, or worsening vaginal bleeding • Dizziness, fainting, or syncope • Chest pain or marked shortness of breath at rest or with minimal exertion • Calf pain, redness, or unilateral swelling • Severe or persistent headache, visual disturbance, or sudden swelling • Persistent pelvic, abdominal, or lower back pain not relieved with rest • Reduced or absent fetal movement once previously established • Sudden or concerning symptom change
Exercise should not continue until medical review if these symptoms are present. During postpartum, refer if the athlete reports: • Vaginal bleeding that increases with activity or does not progressively reduce • Persistent pelvic pain, pressure, or heaviness • New or worsening pelvic floor symptoms that affect daily life or training • Pain that escalates with loading or impact • Symptoms of postnatal depression, anxiety, or emotional distress • Marked fatigue, poor recovery, or dizziness not improving with rest and fueling • Uncertainty about readiness to resume higher-impact or higher- intensity training Postpartum progression should pause if symptoms worsen rather than stabilise or improve. Across both pregnancy and postpartum: • Coaches do not provide medical clearance • If symptoms are changing, escalating, or unclear - refer • When in doubt - refer Coach scope At Level 2, the coach's role is to:

key_facts.fact: Pregnancy & Postpartum Pregnancy and the postpartum period are normal physiological states.
Many female HYROX athletes remain physically active during pregnancy and return to structured training postpartum.
What coaches should understand Training tolerance may change across pregnancy and postpartum.
Symptoms and day-to-day readiness are often more informative than timelines or trimester labels.

Summary This Level 2 module reinforces three coaching fundamentals for female HYROX athletes: Female athletes follow the same training principles as male athletes 1 Female-specific health domains and life stages may influence comfort, readiness, recovery perception, and training continuity. However, every athlete is unique. 2 Effective coaching relies on awareness, clear communication, and early referral, not assumptions or clinical management 3 Across the module, you have been introduced to key female- specific health domains relevant to HYROX participation across the lifespan, including menstrual health, LEA, REDs and eating disorders, pelvic floor health, breast health and support,
perimenopause and menopause, and pregnancy and postpartum considerations. Your role is to recognize what is typically considered healthy within these domains, identify patterns that may indicate concern, and respond within scope. Learning Objective 1 You should be able to identify the key female-specific health domains relevant to HYROX participation across the lifespan. Learning Objective 2 You should be able to recognize typical or healthy patterns within these domains versus signs or symptoms that may indicate concern. Learning Objective 3 You should understand the coach's role in creating a safe, inclusive environment and know when referral is required. What good Level 2 practice looks like: Use clear, neutral language Invite athlete-led disclosure without pressure
Avoid attributing performance changes to "hormones" or life stage without the athlete's input Notice patterns over time rather than single days Refer early when symptoms are persistent, severe, or outside expected ranges, or when an athlete expresses concern Together, these principles support consistent, confident coaching across diverse female athlete contexts. By focusing on awareness, communication, and appropriate referral, coaches can help female HYROX athletes train safely, remain engaged, and progress across the lifespan without unnecessary limitation or assumption.

unit.title: Introduction to the Masters athlete
unit.unit_summary: This unit introduces the Masters athlete in HYROX through Dr. Dan Plews. The video defines the Masters athlete category broadly around older competitive athletes, noting that definitions vary across sports and that age 35 is often used because cardiovascular issues become a greater consideration, while Dr. Plews aligns more closely with the idea that the category typically becomes meaningful from around 40 years old. The unit explains why Masters categories matter: aging brings declines in strength and cardiovascular fitness, but competition also promotes active lifestyles, community, camarade

chunk.content: Hello and welcome to this HYROX 365 Level 2 course where we are talking about the Masters athlete with me Dr. Dan Plews. Some things we're going to go through in this module is we're going to talk about the definitions of what a Masters athlete actually is. We're then going to look at the determinants of strength performance and what the decrements of what happens with strength with aging. And then number three we're going to do the same with endurance performance so we're going to look at what are the determinants of endurance performance and what are the decrements with aging. We're going to talk a little bit about injury risk for the Masters athletes which is of critical consideration and then finally finishing off with some take-home points and conclusions. So what is a Masters athlete? So a Masters athlete is defined by older than 35 years of age as this is the age at which cardiovascular issues tend to become a greater cause of mobility who either trains for or takes part in athletic competitions or often specifically designed for older participants. But the age range of Masters athletes it actually varies across a number of sports and I always found it quite funny that swimming for example you're actually classed as a Masters athlete in swimming at the age of 25 years old and at rowing you're classed as 27 years old you're actually classified as a Masters athlete which seems very very young. There's a very famous physio who specializes in the Masters athlete named Rich Willy and he recommends or says that really you're a Masters athlete when you get over 40 years old and I have to tend to generally agree with that I would say that that is pretty much where the Masters athlete category typically lies and where most people think about the Masters athlete. So why do we even need a Masters Category? Well we decline physically with age in strength and cardiovascular fitness and this also promotes active lifestyles as we age and what's really important and often not a consideration is that it does allow for camaraderie and a sense of purpose which is really important for the aging athlete as well. Particularly if you can do things in groups like running groups, HYROX groups, whatever it might be, this is really important for us as we age because we know that community is really, really important. And this figure here it actually just shows what happens to performance as we age and it's quite interesting and typically we see bigger drops off in more of the sprint performances than we do in the longer distances for example. So if we just focus on this, this is the swimming performance as a percentage of respective world records and if you look at the 50 meter men versus the 1500 meter men, you can see that there's a percentage, we see a very big drop off in terms of the 50 meter quite quickly whereas the 1500 it does hold for quite a long time, in fact from around 25 to 40 there's not much change but then once we get over 40 we do tend to see this really big drop off. Marathon however, not so much, now it's the opposite way because this is marathon running time so as we go up it gets slower, you can say actually 30 to 40 there's not really that much difference in terms of men's and age but once we get over 40 especially into 50 we typically see this increase in or decrease in marathon running speeds and an increase in marathon running time but what we do tend to know is that the sprint explosive performances is going down quicker as we age rather than the pure endurance which is why we see a lot of older athletes doing things like Ironman and marathon running and still doing very well in those categories. So first up let's talk about the determinants of strength and the decrements with aging. So what determines us being strong? So first muscle cross sectional area, larger muscles generate more force due to greater contractile protein content. Muscle fiber type also plays a role here so fast twitch fibers high force fatigue quickly but they do produce more strength whereas the slow twitch fibers lower force but they are more fatigue resistant. Motor unit recruitment is also a factor and activation of more motor units and high threshold units enhances strength output neuromuscular coordination so things like improved synchronization within and between muscles it boosts efficiency and strength and also tendon stiffness so stiffer tendons improve force transmission from the muscle to the bone and as you'll find out that is one of the things that we do lose as we do get that little bit older. So what we typically see in the Masters athlete is strength does decline and masters athletes see slower decline rates typically around 5-10% per decade depending on the intensity and the consistency of their training. However sedentary athletes we see much bigger decreases with 10-15% per decade after the age of 30 and up to 30% per decade after 60. So we are seeing bigger increases quicker as we get older but we obviously also we will see big differences within people or between individuals as well. So some people might decline faster, some people may decline a little bit slower. But this is a nice picture of the muscle cross sectional area of some individuals. So you can see here, here is a 40 year old triathlete, here is a 74 year old sedentary man and here is a 70 year old triathlete and you can see that the 40 year old triathlete versus the 70 year old triathlete there is really not much difference. So if you look at the sedentary 74 year old compared to the active 70 year old, we're talking that he's very, very lean, very little adipose tissue which is the white and his quadricep muscle is in very good health. So sedentary, 3-5% of muscle mass loss per year per decade after 30. But we can preserve this with the right activity but the activity must be strenuous. And hormones do play a role here, testosterone, estrogen, growth hormone, and insulin-like growth factor are important and diminish with age. So the more we can keep these up with various types of activity, that's really important. But these are all anabolic exercises and upregulate with exercise, particularly strength training. So we know that those anabolic hormones like testosterone, insulin-like growth factor are very much upregulated with strength training, so important to do as we age. Research would also show that motor recruitment plays a critical role, but it is also very trainable. And motor unit loss becomes more pronounced after around 70 years old, but this also coincides with substantial losses in muscle loss as well, so strength loss. So maintaining size, tension, and the quality of muscle fibers can offset any motor unit loss, which goes back to the prior slide where we talked a little bit about the importance of doing strength training as we age. And then neuromuscular coordination. So we do see a loss of motor units as we get older, so we do have a reduction in fine control. We also see slower motor unit firing rates, which weaken the contraction. And we then get an impaired recruitment of fast twitch fibers, and then for a decrease in strength. So typically with worse neuromuscular coordination, we see a big reduction in things like our box jumps and our explosive power. So if you think about in the context of HYROX, burpees would be something that does require quite a lot of neuromuscular coordination. So we would expect older athletes to be really having a decline in the burpee broad jumps compared to the younger athletes. But of course, use it or lose it. So we can do exercises to help maintain this as best we can. So regular training does preserve motor unit and firing rates and enhances coordination and improves the synergy between muscles and reduces the inefficiencies. Also the training for the Masters athletes means better proprioception, which maintains balance and movement precision and functional strength. So doing those functional strength movements that we are typical in HYROX, see age-related declines are significantly slowed. And then lastly, we want to talk about tendon stiffness. So we do see age-related declines in tendon stiffness as well, and tendons do lose elasticity as we age, reducing their ability to store and release energy efficiently, which is really important for running, and that decreased tendon stiffness leads to slower force transmission from the muscle to the bone, and it also does increase the risk of injury during high-impact activities. But with regular training in the Masters athlete, we can maintain or even improve tendon stiffness, offsetting age-related decline, which has been shown in this paper in 2025. But strength and plyometric training, which we also talked about, becomes a critical piece of the master's training, the Masters athlete's training, because it promotes collagen remodeling and it increases tendon stiffness, enhancing force transmission. And that improved performance with stiffer tendons allows more efficient energy transfer, therefore supporting athletic performance. So we've talked a little bit about strength there. Now let's talk more about the endurance side. So what are the determinants of endurance performance? So there are a few things that we always mention when we talk about endurance. We talk about the heart, so maximal cardiac output, which is heart rate times stroke volume. We talk about VO2 max, or maximal oxygen consumption. A really important one is the ability to train consistently, maintaining high training volume with adequate intensity. That's also really key. Exercise economy, and then finally, those lactate and ventilatory thresholds. This is a nice little schematic that was shown by Tanaka in 2008 that nicely pulls together what actually happens with aging with various different areas of exercise physiology. So as we age, we do tend to see a reduction in training intensity and volume. This obviously coincides and helps or aids the reduction in various other markers. We typically see mainly differences in those maximal areas, so maximal heart rate, maximal stroke volume, and maximal a-vO2 difference, so our ability to extract that oxygen from the air and our VO2 max. So these all typically go down with aging. However, what we tend to not see too much of a decrease in as we age is our economy stays the same and our thresholds can stay the same. But with all that taken into account, all this goes into a maximal oxygen consumption, so our VO2 goes down, our VO2 max comes down, which reduces our overall exercise performance. And if you think about it, that's why we tend to see bigger reductions in sports that require higher VO2 max rather than sports that require good economy and threshold values. So a sport like a six-minute row, we see big reductions with aging in that performance. But something like an Ironman that is very exercise economy dependent, for example, lactate threshold dependent, we don't see as big a difference. So first off, let's talk about VO2 max. So in sedentary individuals, VO2 max declines by about 10% per decade at the age of 30. But in active individuals, VO2 max declines at around 5% to 7% per decade after age. For highly trained athletes, VO2 max declines at around 3% to 5% per decade after the age of 30. For Masters athletes, VO2 max may decline as little as 2% to 3% per decade until around 50, after which the rate of decline tends to accelerate slightly, even with continued training. Personally, I'm a 40-year-old athlete, and what I've found is my VO2 max to this point, I'm now 43, hasn't changed that much, and I can still maintain it in the low 70s. But I think I have had to do more and more high-intensity training to try and maintain that. And the strength training definitely helps on top of that. So when we talk about VO2 max and its decline with aging, endurance performer doesn't decline as steeply with age as VO2 max does. So this means other aspects, like muscular power, capillary density, may decline more slowly, which helps offset that drop in VO2 max. But VO2 max also declines in a curvilinear way, with a faster drop as age advances forwards. And this suggests that VO2 max reduction is the main driver behind decreased endurance in older athletes. The VO2 max reductions are more of a driver of decreased endurance performance once older than 50 years old. So we tend to be pretty free until we get to 50, and then we do tend to see bigger differences in VO2 max. But of course, VO2 max is also multifaceted, and the results of both central and peripheral factors. So we mentioned central and peripheral factors, but let's talk about heart rate, stroke volume, and cardiac output, which are central factors. So central factors, maximal cardiac output, which is the maximal amount of blood the heart can pump per minute. This generally declines with age, and studies have suggested it may maintain it, but you can maintain it with training. So maximal cardiac output decreases in healthy, sedentary adults as they age, aligning with a decrease in maximal oxygen uptake. But the maximal cardiac output is mainly a reduction, a result of reduced stroke volume. So remember, maximal cardiac output is a property of both heart rate and the amount of blood pumped per beat, and what the research tends to suggest is that we see mainly a reduction in the amount of heart blood pumped per beat. But maximal heart rate reduction is a primary factor in age-related declines in maximal cardiac output and VO2 max, especially in endurance-trained athletes. It begins in early adulthood, decreasing by about 0.2 beats per minute per year in adults. But the mechanisms of the decline are slower conductive velocity, we see reductions in the responsiveness of the sinoatrial node, and a decrease in intrinsic heart rate with age. So going into maximal stroke volume, so older endurance athletes have a maximal stroke volume reduced to 80% to 90% of that in younger athletes. But limited research on how age-related changes in preload, afterload, and contractility contribute to reduced stroke volume. So we don't really know much about why we're actually seeing these changes. But what we can assume is that with the preload, the age does not significantly affect the left ventricle end diastolic dimension, area, or volume in relatively active adults, suggesting no major impact on the left ventricular filling. Looking at the blood volume, total blood volume does remain preserved in older endurance athletes, which helps sustain the stroke volume. So the blood volume doesn't seem to be a major factor. But the cardiac preload factors in the left ventricle end diastolic pressure, diastolic filling time, and venomotor tone, mitochondrial compliance could contribute to a reduced stroke volume. So it seems most likely that it's due to the cardiac preload factors, less likely the preload in the blood volume, but we do need a little bit more research in this area. So the afterload does see some arterial stiffening, and age leads to increased aortic stiffness and vascular afterload, making the blood ejection during exercise more challenging, which reduces the stroke volume. So in endurance training, this attenuates arterial stiffening compared to sedentary adults, but stiffness still does increase with age in athletes. And the left ventricular afterload may contribute to this reduced stroke volume via the increased aortic impedance. But the contractility and the challenges in measuring is difficult to assess left ventricular contractility independently of preload and afterload in humans. However, what we do know is that in some of the animal studies, they do show a similar decline in contractility with age in both endurance trained and sedentary rats. And from human observations, older sedentary and endurance trained athletes show lower ejection fractions at maximal exercise, which is actually consistent with the animal findings. So to summarize, the change in maximal stroke volume is most likely coming from that afterload factor. Okay, we talked about those central factors. Let's talk a little bit about the peripheral factors. So when we look at the peripheral factors, we're now looking at more of the muscle rather than the heart. So the peripheral factors, it does reflect the ability of the muscles to extract and use oxygen from the blood for ATP production during intense exercise. And we know that this declines with age in both sedentary and endurance trained adults. And we do tend to see a significant reduction in the capillary density and mitochondrial enzyme activities in age-related declines with sedentary adults, which that leads to lower oxygen extraction and VO2 max with aging. However, with endurance trained athletes, we see more of a modest decline. And the arterial venous O2 difference, so that ability to extract the oxygen, it's around five to 10% over 30 years. And that's likely due to reduced oxygen delivery, so how much oxygen is getting to the muscle rather than the extraction capacity. So it's difficult to pull the two apart, but it's believed that it's more of a central theme rather than a peripheral feat. So oxygen delivery versus oxygen extraction. So older endurance trained athletes have similar muscle oxygen extraction abilities and lung oxygenation compared to young athletes, but reductions in oxygen delivery, not extraction, are likely the main factor to the decline. But muscle mass will play a very big role here. And muscle mass loss with age may contribute to a reduced VO2 max, but even after adjusting for muscle mass, VO2 max is still lower in older athletes. And fat-free mass influences VO2 max by affecting blood volume, stroke volume, and cardiac output. So let's talk, we'll talk a little bit now about thresholds and how they change with the Masters athlete. So there's a really good study by Lepers that was entitled, Masters athletes are extending the limits of human performance. And what's been found is previously suggested the decline in maximum lactation consumption is the primary factor driving reduced performance with age, and additionally diminished capacity to sustain a high percentage of VO2 max as assessed by blood lactate threshold and submaximal exercise economy may also play a role, but not as big a role as the reductions in likely stroke volume exercise economy. So we do know that muscle efficiency declines, muscle fibers changes, and loss of muscle mass increases in energy costs for movement, and we do get reduced mitochondrial efficiency which impairs oxygen use, which also slightly decreases economy. We have already talked a little bit about tendon stiffness, and I mentioned already that the tendon stiffness plays a critical role in economy, because stiffer tendons and joints reduce, stiffer tendons and joints reduce the ability to store and release energy efficiently. So we get changes in gait, changes in stride or posture, which makes movements less efficient. And then finally, when we look at the cardiovascular and respiratory factors, decreased oxygen delivery and a more effort for breathing contribute to higher overall energy expenditure. In terms of cardiovascular and respiratory factors, a decreased oxygen delivery and more effort for breathing contribute to higher energy expenditure. We also do get a decline in those neuromuscular factors. We also talked about the neuromuscular factors when we mentioned the strength components, but these also transfer over to the exercise economy, which is why doing plyometrics as we age can be multifaceted because it's actually going to be helping us with our running and exercise economy as well. We get a decline in motor unit coordination, which increases energy costs for movement, and a reduced proprioception affects movement precision and efficiency. But the good news is that regular training reduces age-related declines in all of these factors, which is why it's important to keep as active as we possibly can as we age. And what you can see here, there's a great paper that was done by Beck that shows older runners retain youthful running despite biomechanical differences. And you can see that there is the leg stiffness here of the younger athletes versus the older athletes. Of course, there is a bit of a difference at different speeds, but it's quite nicely maintained and it's only at the upper end that we see those differences. We see the bigger, sorry, the younger athletes tend to maintain at higher speeds, whereas the older athletes do lose a bit of stiffness as we run a little bit quicker. But what's quite interesting in this is that when you look at the younger versus older athletes, typically we're seeing just an increase in stride frequency when we are getting a little bit older. You can see here, 1.34, 1.38, 1.37, 1.45, 1.46, so very small differences, which is a very, I think this is almost like a small effect size up here. Coming up to small. So we tend to get, as we get older, we tend to increase our stride frequency. So what we're doing is because we are losing a bit of stride length, most likely due to a reduction in tendon stiffness, we are therefore increasing the stride frequency. So that's why you see older athletes doing this typical shuffle, which tends to work well because we're compensating for the reduction in tendon stiffness. So here are some take-home points for strength and endurance. Strain ability, use it or lose it. That's the most important thing. You've got to keep going. You've got to keep those systems firing to keep them tuned up. And it seems that higher intensity performance, VT1 and above, that is lost more than some maximal performances. In endurance, we see losses in VO2 max, which is largely due to reduction in central factors, stroke volume, max heart rate, and heart compliance. Peripheral changes as we get older seem to be modest. And then in strength, we see losses mainly due to size and tendon stiffness. Motor unit and neuromuscular factors can be reasonably maintained with the correct training until an older age. However, once you get over 70, this does become increasingly difficult. So one of the things that I really wanted to talk about that's really key for the Masters athlete is injury risk and the management of injury with master's athletes. Because as we talked about at the start, it's really important for master's athletes to continue to train consistently. And that's likely one of the reasons as to why we see reductions in performance simply because athletes could no longer train as hard once we get that little bit older. So let's have a look at the injury comparisons of master's versus younger athletes. So Masters athletes, there's a 49% reported an injury in the last year, 30% with multiple athletes, and you're seeing a little bit of an increase in younger athletes. So 45% reported in younger athletes with 24% with multiple injuries. But younger athletes are generally more knee, lower leg injuries, such as iliotibial band, so IT band syndrome and medial tibial stress syndrome. And with master's athletes, we tend to see a higher prevalence of muscular and tendinitis injuries, hamstrings, plantar flexors, Achilles tendons, I know all about that myself. Then we also see a little bit of osteoarthritis, which is reasonably rare among master's athletes due to the protective nature of running, which conditions joint cartilage and maintains similar cumulative load during loading as walking. So why do we see an increase in tendinopathy with lower limb injuries in master's athletes? Well, the most common injury in the Masters athlete, mainly runners, is often caused by training loads exceeding the tendon's capacity, leading to pain and pathology, which reduce strength and posteriorly stiffened foot pressure increases susceptibility. Reduced Achilles tendon stiffness increases calf strain during plantar flexor force transmission, raising the risk of microtrauma and Achilles tendinopathy, and running on soft surfaces like sand amplifies the risk, while harder surfaces like asphalt reduce it significantly. So contrary to belief, you actually want to run on harder surfaces to maintain that Achilles tendon. And to finish off this little section on injury risk, the reason that we are seeing these increases in injury risk as the Master's athlete ages is because we are mainly getting these differences in calf volume. So we see reductions in calf muscle volume, reductions in tendon stiffness, reductions in ankle power and propulsive force, reductions in knee and ankle excursion, and reductions in leg stiffness. So we already talked about many of these cardiovascular factors earlier on in this presentation, but these biomechanical factors are one of the biggest reasons why we are seeing an increase in injury risk, particularly in running. In the context of HYROX, of course, these will all transfer into many of the modalities of your sled push, your burpee, broad jumps, your wall balls, because you will always be in more of a compromised position. And as a result, there's an increased risk of Achilles tendinopathy and an increased risk in calf strains. Now, with this, the devil is in the detail of how we can do various exercises as part of our weekly routines to ensure that we are going to be minimizing that injury risk. So that's the end of this short lecture. One of the things that we didn't really talk about here is the, what can we do about this? Because now we know where those reductions occur. So we know that we are seeing reductions in muscle mass when we age. We know that we are seeing reductions in maximal stroke volume and VO2 max as we age. And we're also seeing those changes in biomechanical factors. Now the real question is, is we've talked about something that's interesting. We really want to get into the useful. So what can we do and what kind of training regimes and what sort of prescription can we be applying to our masters athletes to ensure these reductions are minimized as we age?

unit.title: Introduction to the High Performance Athlete
unit.unit_summary: This unit introduces the high-performance HYROX athlete and the role of the complete high-performance coach. It frames coaching through three pillars: Programming/Science, Empathy, and Expert in the Sport. Programming and science include evidence-based training, lactate threshold, vVO2max, Critical Power, volume building, strength training, and movement development through strength/volume, capacity, and intensity. Empathy emphasizes that athletes are not robots; coaches must connect, listen, adapt, avoid becoming an added stressor, and know when the athlete may need a different coaching relati

chunk.content: [0:00:00] Welcome to the High Performance Athlete Unit, a cornerstone for Level 2 HYROX coaches aiming to build athletes from the ground up. The expertise behind this unit comes from Anthony Parasini, whose broad athletic and coaching background includes wrestling, crossfit, weightlifting, marathon running, and short [0:00:16] distance triathlons. The objective is to give a general overview of how a HYROX Level 2 coach can address the programming, coaching, and needs of an elite level athlete. chunk.content:
Programming and science are important, but they are only one third of what the total elite coach should be able to provide. Coaches often spend a lot of time looking for an edge through perfectly planned, progressive, and polarized training. They may look for small percentages in how the human body functions by applying science into practice. Data and testing are valuable, but the best-made program will not matter if the athlete cannot complete it, if it does not fit the athlete's training schedule, or if it is inconsistently followed.
Programming should not only be what a coach can write on paper. Many coaches can write hard workouts and develop sound training plans. What sets an elite coach apart is understanding the athlete's time constraints, ability level, areas of strength, areas needing improvement, and recovery capacity. Knowing how much time the athlete can devote to recovery is vital for optimizing the balance between training and recovery.
Structured, evidence-based training is vital to progress. Coaches should continually learn and keep up with current science-based research. They should have a clear training philosophy while leaving room to adapt as they grow and learn. Scientific testing can help increase important parameters, but those parameters are not the main goal of training. The main goal is improved HYROX race performance.
Coaches should not get too bogged down in science data. The point of increasing fitness is to help athletes get better at HYROX racing. The most important parameter is race improvement or improvement in specific aspects within the race. Coaches should train to improve race results, not directly to improve isolated parameters such as VO2max. They must understand the difference between correlation and causation.
Movement development is also part of this pillar and is framed as:
- Strength/Volume - Capacity - Intensity
Knowing how much volume to apply, what level of strength is needed, how much capacity an athlete has in a movement, and the intensity at which they can perform those movements are all part of the science and programming side of coaching.
### Lactate Threshold
Blood lactate is measured, usually in lab settings, but it can also be done at home with specialized equipment. The test measures lactate accumulation in the athlete's blood at specific exercise intensities.
| Term | Meaning | | LT1 | The body's first shift in lactate accumulation above resting levels; the first point where slow, steady accumulation begins. | | LT2 | The exercise intensity at which lactate begins accumulating faster than it can be cleared, indicating a shift toward rapid fatigue. LT2 reflects the maximum sustainable pace for high-intensity anaerobic-aerobic hybrid endurance. |

chunk.content:
Higher lactate thresholds correlate with faster and longer efforts, making LT2 a key endurance performance metric. The standalone high-performance athlete course will go deeper into measuring blood lactate, interpreting results, and integrating lactate data into training. It will also cover double threshold training, threshold singles structures, use of these concepts in running, machine work, and HYROX movements, and whether FTP testing should be used in elite HYROX training.
### Velocity at VO2max
vVO2max is the speed at which the body reaches its maximum oxygen consumption capacity. It combines VO2max with running economy, making it a strong predictor of aerobic endurance.
The standalone course will cover the significance of vVO2max, how to test it, and how to use it with an elite athlete. The unit also emphasizes that coaches should not train solely to increase one parameter. Instead, the race itself - HYROX - should be treated like the key metric that is constantly tested. At certain elite levels, measures such as VO2max may not predict performance strongly. An athlete with a VO2max of 70 will likely beat a similar athlete with a VO2max of 50, but when values are within roughly +/- 8 points, the correlation between VO2max and performance is not strong.
### Critical Power
Critical Power is the highest sustainable metabolic rate or power output an athlete can maintain without entering rapid fatigue. It is the dividing line between heavy and severe exercise intensities and typically lasts 30-40 minutes. It can be an often more accurate alternative to FTP for guiding training, pacing, and measuring metabolic capacity.
Critical Power is generally just above the intensity elite HYROX athletes would want to train at. Understanding this level helps coaches keep training just below it within a comprehensive coaching protocol. Critical Power is paired with W-prime, a finite anaerobic battery of energy that can be spent on efforts above critical power. The standalone course will explain how Critical Power can be tested, translated into training, and interpreted.
### Building Volume
For elite athletes, the best ability is availability. Building aerobic capacity without risking injury requires precise loading waves and careful increases in total work volume. Smart loading builds an athlete who can withstand the amount of training required, even when the training model is lower volume and higher intensity.
The athlete should first identify the current starting point in weekly training hours. Then the athlete can increase that amount by about 30-60 minutes for 3-4 consecutive weeks before taking a slight deload and building up again until the desired volume is reached. Once volume is established, the athlete can focus on increasing the percentage of that volume performed at intensity.
### Movement Development: Strength/Volume - Capacity - Intensity

chunk.content:
Movement quality is paramount for athletes to learn and practice. For movement development, an athlete first needs good movement quality, then must progress along the spectrum from ability/strength, to capacity, to intensity.
A coach must identify the issues or weaknesses an athlete has in specific movements. For example, if an athlete can perform a weighted lunge but cannot do more than a few repetitions, the issue lies in capacity or because the load is too high a percentage of the athlete's one-rep max. The coach should increase the volume of reps the athlete can perform and the total weight the athlete can lift in the lunge. At that stage, intensity - such as adding the component of time - is not yet the priority.
Once the athlete can lift the prerequisite weight and exceed the race distance or required repetitions with that weight, the focus shifts to the time needed to complete the distance or reps.
### Strength Training
The HYROX Level 2 course already covers strength training and development with qualified and experienced coaches. The same principles used for general athletes also apply to elite athletes. This section does not replace the previous strength training material. Instead, it offers additional options and guidance on how that information can be blended with the other training demands high-performance athletes face.

chunk.content:
Empathy is a central pillar of coaching high-performance athletes. Connecting and caring about the athlete should be higher in most coaches' repertoire. Working with athletes to develop training that fits their needs, schedule, and consistency is highly valuable.
The unit emphasizes: **Athletes are not robots.** Coaches must learn to be leaders, trustworthy sources, and assets to their athletes. A coach's success is tied to how well they prepare, support, and encourage athletes, both mentally and physically. Coaches should understand the effects a workout will have physically, emotionally, and mentally. Understanding how an athlete feels can inform training, but this takes months to develop and moments to lose.
Sometimes empathy means wanting the best for the athlete even if that means they need someone different to coach them. Coaches need to match the athlete's level of care for what they want to achieve and reflect it back. A determined athlete who cares about the process and their success should see that same care reflected by the coach.
Athletes should be encouraged to log training, keep records of what was performed, how they felt, what they supplemented with, and their nutrition. What is tracked is measured and can be optimized. Coaches should always learn and strive to understand the athlete completely. Coaches can learn from other coaches, athletes, and experts.
There will be moments when the coach needs to push athletes and suggest that they can go further than they currently believe. There will also be times when the coach's unwavering belief is needed to push an athlete to new heights. The coach is not simply a cheerleader, but being a source of support rather than an additional stressor matters. Stress is stress, and removing unnecessary stress allows the athlete to allocate stress elsewhere or recover. Many high-performing athletes do not lack motivation. More often, they need someone to act as their brakes and prevent them from going overboard.
The old model of the hardcore, no-nonsense, robot coach who simply makes athletes do hard things every day is fading. Smarter recovery approaches and body metrics are becoming more normal. Coaches who combine programming knowledge, continuous education, and strong athlete connection will be better suited to work with elite athletes.
### Not a Robot

chunk.content:
A common athlete phrase is "I am not a robot." This may arise when coaches expect athletes to hit times or progressions because they make sense on paper and in theory. Coaches are the engineers of fitness. Without engineers, science is philosophy; without coaches who develop programs and apply sport science theories, information remains conjecture without application. Coaches apply evolving theories in sport science to real athletes. If everything were as easy as writing it on paper, athletes would not need to run the race.
The standalone course will explore how sport science theories apply to athletes not being robots and what to do when a training plan fails.
### Connecting with Athletes
Coaches should be friendly with athletes while maintaining discipline and structure. They should not degrade or put athletes down. The unit frames a coach's role as someone who speaks highly of athletes, supports them, has their back, and is willing to tell hard truths when required, such as addressing deserved no reps that need to be worked on in practice.
### Identifying When to Move On
Sometimes the connection between coach and athlete is not there. Coaches may hang on to athletes longer than they should when the athlete really needs a new approach or a new coach. Athletes may also shy away from switching coaches because of the relationship they have built, even when performance or fitness has suffered.
The standalone course will discuss when it is appropriate to fire athletes or end the coaching relationship.
### Trustworthy Leader
Forcing athletes to immediately adapt to a rigid system is one of the quickest ways to lose trust, burn an athlete out, or get them injured. Elite athletes may come from different systems, may be self-coached, or may have no prior system. Demanding that they complete something or forcing a single system without considering their current level or emotional state can push the athlete toward another coach or away from the sport.
Empathy includes understanding that athletes are complex humans with complex lives. This is vital to maintaining a healthy and positive coach-athlete relationship. The standalone module will cover this topic further, but there is no substitute for experience and culture. Coaches need to choose to listen, understand, and be prepared to adapt to the athlete.

chunk.content:
The expert-in-the-sport pillar is vital for coaches of elite-level athletes. Athletes already experience major training stress, so coaches should avoid adding unnecessary mental or emotional stress. One way to reduce stress is to become an encyclopedia of the rulebook. Coaches should understand the rulebook, movement standards, nuances, penalties, and more so they can prepare athletes properly in training and on race day.
Coaches should understand body mechanics, movement quality, and how to progress or scale back movements so athletes can move more efficiently and use less energy at high intensities. Coaches should be experts in the foundation of fitness, learn how to optimize movement, use legal and sport-compliant supplements, challenge assumptions, know the rulebook and its changes, get involved in the community, learn what is and is not allowed under WADA, and study film to understand the nuances of other high-performing athletes.
Coaches need to know the anti-doping code as well as, or better than, their athletes. Every athlete is responsible for what they put into their body, and it is the coach's job to help athletes understand whether something is acceptable when they ask. Movement quality - safety, efficacy, and efficiency - is part of this pillar. Coaches need to help athletes move through space, with or without load, safely to their own end ranges of motion. Then coaches help safely extend those end ranges until athletes can meet movement standards under the rulebook, before finally optimizing and speeding up the movement pattern. Skipping directly to efficiency can lead to injury or excessive no reps in competition.
Race strategy is part of being an expert coach. Athletes trying to break into the elite field should first be able to time trial their races and hit standard paces they hope to achieve during racing. This helps them optimize strengths and downplay weaknesses. Once an athlete is on the elite start line, they must understand how to race opponents and use razor-thin margins. Most athletes do not have additional capacity to study every opponent, so the coach can contribute by analyzing splits and identifying where the athlete can apply pressure within the race.
The course states that this unit is only a taste of what is to come in the standalone course on coaching high-performance athletes.
### Movement Quality
Movement quality is held paramount. Module 4 of the Level 2 course covered Safety-Efficacy-Efficiency and basic movement demonstrations. The Level 2 course also provided demonstrations of HYROX stations and race movements. An elite coach must understand biomechanics to know how the body should move and to identify imbalances in the athlete.

chunk.content:
Once an athlete has proper mechanics and can safely perform the full required range of motion, attention can shift toward efficiency and moving with speed.
### Rulebook
Coaches must be experts in the rules. They should know what equipment is allowed, what equipment is not allowed, which points of performance judges will look for, how to launch an appeal or challenge, and what is allowed to be appealed or challenged. Coaches should be involved in the sport's evolution, whether through contact with the Elite Working Group or board-level involvement. Coaches should conduct themselves respectfully with race directors, head judges, and HYROX staff.
Coaches should also be fluent in qualification systems. They should understand how to advise athletes on the best route to qualification and avoid mistakes that could require athletes to run unnecessary races. Coaches should stay up to date on point or time requirements for qualification.
### Anti-Doping
Every coach should be aware of the anti-doping code, how to determine if a supplement is allowed under WADA regulations, means of delivery such as IV injection restrictions, and whether an athlete needs to submit a TUE after a hospital or urgent care visit. Coaches should educate athletes on the anti-doping testing process and the rules around where athletes may go after a race if selected for testing.
Coaches must uphold fairness and equal competition. If a coach is aware that an athlete is violating the anti-doping code and cheating, the coach should report or whistleblow the athlete to HYROX or WADA. An athlete who violates the anti-doping code for competitive advantage violates the coach's trust and can damage the coach's reputation. If an athlete violates the code while training on a coach's program, the coach also loses valuable information because it becomes unclear whether performance came from the training plan or the performance enhancer.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: The Complete High Performance Coach
chunk.content:
Once a coach understands the pillars of coaching high-performance athletes, they can focus on improving themselves through those lenses.
| Pillar lens | What the coach develops through this lens | | Programming and science | Balancing intensity with recovery, managing marginal gains, and building data-informed training plans. | | Empathy | Guiding high performers through the full performance cycle. | | Expert in the sport | Preparing athletes for training blocks, tapering, and proper post-race analysis. |
### Balancing Intensity and Recovery
Training approaches vary, but most methods agree that easy work or active recovery work should make up the largest volume of any training plan. Preparing an athlete to hit big workouts can be guided by how the athlete feels, recovery metrics such as resting heart rate, HRV, sleep scores, wearable training readiness scores, or muscle tone. These are indirect measures of readiness.
The coach's role is to plan and prepare a good balance of intensity and easy/recovery days so that, when done properly, the athlete feels ready to work when needed. Athlete feedback and workout logging or journaling are essential.
The unit presents a preference for starting with an elite athlete using only two quality half-days per week, where intensity is moderate to high and all other days are active recovery or easy days. Some athletes may progress up to three full quality days, but it takes time to develop and understand the athlete before making that jump.
#### Example: Starting Week With Two Quality Half-Days

chunk.content:
The unit recommends spending about 4-6 weeks at each stage before adding additional quality work. If the athlete indicates that they are approaching overwork or consistently performs poorly on quality days, the coach should reduce training to the last level of volume the athlete handled well.
Once the coach knows the level of volume the athlete can handle, training can be polarized between very easy days and gradual progression on harder days.
### Additional Structured Unit Content
The High Performance Athlete Programming/Science Most coaches will spend a lot of time here, trying to find some kind of edge in human ability by just having the most perfectly planned out, progressive, and polarized training. Looking for the small percentages in how the human body functions by adapting science into practice. The truth is that while using data and testing to determine an athlete's lactate threshold, Velocity at VO2Max, Critical Power, muscle oxygenation or whatever else you might measure is very valuable and can inform training in a myriad of ways, it is just ⅓ of what the total Elite coach should be able to provide to their athlete. The best made program will not matter if the athlete cannot complete it, or if it does not fit the athlete's training schedule, or if it is inconsistently followed. Programming should not just be what you can put on paper in front of your athletes. The reality is that almost any level coach or trainer can get someone relatively fit and healthy, they can write hard workouts, and develop sound training plans. What sets you apart as an Elite coach will be understanding the time constraints, ability level, identifying areas of strength, and needed improvement of the high performing athletes. Knowing how much time the athlete can devote to recovery so you can optimize the training and recovery balance is vital. This pillar is very important to the development of Elite athletes and needs to be taken seriously. Structured, evidence-based training is vital to progress. Coaches need to be continually learning and keeping up with the most up-to-date science based research. Coaches should have their training philosophy fleshed out but allow room for adapting as you grow and learn. Knowing how to perform scientific testing from Velocity at

They can learn as much from other coaches as you can from athletes and other experts! There will be moments to push athletes and suggest that they can push further than where they currently are. There will be times where your unwavering belief in them is needed to push them to new heights. It is not your job to be their cheerleader, but being someone of support and not an additional stressor is important. Stress is stress and as much stress as you can eliminate from them will allow them to take on that stress in a different aspect (physically, mentally, emotionally) or recover. Most high performing athletes that I have encountered do not have a problem with motivation or need encouragement to train, they more likely than not, need someone to be their brakes to prevent them from going overboard or doing too much. The days of the hardcore, no nonsense, robot coach that just makes the athlete do hard things everyday is fading and will one day be gone as smarter approaches to recovery and body metrics become more normal. The coaches that have a firm grasp on the programming pillar, continually educate themselves, and connect with their athletes will be far better to work with than those lacking the connections. You should understand the rulebook, movement standards, nuances, penalties, and more so you can prepare them properly in training and on race day. This means that you need to help your athlete move through space with or without load safely to their own end ranges of motion. Then you need to extend those end ranges of motion for them safely, until they can meet the efficacy of the movement standards, per the rulebook, before finally finding ways to optimize and speed up that movement pattern. A lot of coaches and athletes want to short cut this route by going to straight to efficiency but this commonly can lead to injury or excessive no reps in competition. Strategizing for the race is part of being an expert coach. When athletes are trying to break into the Elite field, they should be able to firstly time trial their races and hit standard paces that they hope to achieve during the race. This way they can find ways to optimize their strengths and downplay their weaknesses. Once an athlete is on that Elite start line, they need to understand how to race their opponents to take advantage of the razor thin margins between them. Most athletes do not have additional capacity to study each opponent and find certain nuances, this is where they would rely on the expertise of their coach. The coach should be able to analyze splits and find the areas where their athlete can best pressure others within the race. chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: The Complete High Performance Coach
chunk.content:
Lactate Threshold Blood Lactate is measured, usually in lab settings, but can also be done at home with specialized equipment. This test measures the lactate accumulation in the athlete's blood at certain exercise intensities. Lactate threshold (LT 1 and LT 2) are the exercise intensities at which lactate begin accumulating in the bloodstream faster than it can be cleared, signaling a shift toward rapid fatigue. LT2 indicates the maximum, sustainable pace for high-intensity, anaerobic-aerobic hybrid endurance, making it a key metric in endurance performance, with direct correlation of this parameter indicating higher thresholds allow for faster, longer efforts. LT1 indicates the body's shift in lactate accumulation above resting levels. This is the first point where a slow steady accumulation begins. The standalone course will go into more depth on how to measure blood lactate levels, what information is needed, and how to integrate the results of a blood lactate test into your training. In the course you will learn the fundamentals of what Double Threshold training and Threshold Singles program structures are. How to work these in, not only with running, but with machine work and the HYROX movements. In this, we will also cover functional threshold power (FTP) tests and how/if they should be used in HYROX training for elite athletes.
Velocity at VO2Max VVO2Max is the speed at which your body reaches its maximum capacity to consume oxygen. This parameter combines VO2Max with running economy, making it a highly accurate predictor of aerobic endurance. This widely used parameter is another topic we will cover in the stand alone course. We will cover its significance, how to test for it, and how to use it when it is known for your Elite athlete. We will also go over why we do not train to increase any certain parameter but instead treat the race itself, HYROX, like a metric we are constantly testing. It is been shown that at certain levels in elite athletes that measure parameters like VO2Max cannot predict performance. While someone with a VO2Max of 70 and well-trained will more likely than not beat someone with a VO2Max of 50, when the values are within range of each other, usually +/- 8 points, there is not a strong correlation between VO2Max and performance.
