chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: The Complete High Performance Coach
chunk.content:
Critical Power Critical Power is the highest, sustainable metabolic rate or power output an athlete can maintain without entering a state of rapid fatigue. It represents the dividing line between heavy and severe exercise intensities, typically lasting 30-40 minutes. It acts as an, often more accurate, alternative to FTP for guiding training, pacing, and measuring metabolic capacity. This parameter is generally just above the intensity that Elite HYROX athletes would want to train at, but understanding what this level is to stay just below it fits within a comprehensive coaching protocol. Critical Power is paired with W' (W-Prime), a finite anaerobic batter of energy you can spend for efforts exceeding your critical power. We will dive more in-depth on this topic in the stand alone course. We will cover how it can be tested for, how it can be translated into your athlete's training, and what the information from this test tells you.
Building Volume For Elite athletes, the best ability is availability. Building aerobic capacity and not risking injury takes meaningful precise loading waves in the increase in work volume that an athlete can complete. Smart loading can build an athlete able to withstand the amount of training needed (even low volume/high intensity programs need to be built into). Athletes should focus on where their starting point is in terms of hours per week, then look to increase that amount by about 30-60 minutes for 3-4 consecutive weeks before taking a slight deload and then rebuilding up again until they reach their desired volume. From there they can focus on increasing the percentage of that volume that is intensity. This topic will be more thoroughly covered in the stand alone course on coaching high performance athletes.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: The Complete High Performance Coach
chunk.content:
Movement Development (Strength/Volume- Capacity - Intensity) Movement quality is something paramount for athletes to learn and practice. The quality of movements will be covered in the "Expert in the Sport" section. For movement development, the athlete needs to have good movement quality and then transition that along the spectrum from ability/strength to perform to the ability to add intensity in that performance. Coaches need to be able to identify the issues or weaknesses that athletes have in certain movements. If an athlete can perform a weighted lunge but they cannot do more than a couple, then the issue lies in capacity or because it is too high of a percentage of their 1 rep max. For this, a coach needs to increase the volume of the reps that the athlete can do and the total weight that the athlete can lift in the lunge. The intensity portion, which in this case would be adding the component of time, is not currently needed. Once an athlete has demonstrated they can lift the prerequisite amount of weight and they can exceed the distance or reps required in the race with that weight, then the focus turns to the amount of time it takes to complete the distance or reps. This topic will be covered in depth in the stand alone course on coaching high performance athletes.
Strength Training The HYROX Level 2 course has covered strength training and development with several qualified and experienced coaches. The principles of the masses also apply to the Elite. This section will not seek to replace that information but to offer other options and guidance on how that information can be blended and used in conjunction with the other training requirements high performing athletes will face. This section will also be explored further in the stand alone course on high performing athletes.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: The Complete High Performance Coach
chunk.content:
Not a Robot One of the most common phrases I heard from athletes when I started coaching and trying to understand them was "I am not a robot". This was in reference to expected times or progressions that I had built where I thought they should be hitting certain times or weights, because that is what made sense on paper and in theory. Coaches are the Engineers of fitness. Just like in civil, mechanical, or computer engineering disciplines, without engineers, science is just philosophy. Without coaches who develop programs and put into practice the theories of sport scientists, the information would just be conjecture without application. Luckily, the coaches are here to use the lessons and constantly evolving theories in sports sciences to apply to athletes! If everything was as easy as writing it on paper, then we would never have to run the race though! We will be diving into the theories and application of those theories and how they relate to athletes not being robots (though some can be close) and what to do when a training plan fails.
Connecting with Athletes Be a friend. You can have discipline and structure without degrading or putting your athlete down. I like to tell my athletes they do not need to have an ego or boast about themselves, because I will speak so highly of them they would never be able to match it! The greatest athletes never need to tell people how great they are, because those around them that see their character everyday will tell others how great they are! Let your performance do the talking. Be friendly with your athletes, let them know you are there for them reliably and that you have their back and will go to bat for them, but will also be willing to tell them hard truths (like they did deserve those several no reps they got and you will need to work on it in practice)!
Identifying when to move on Sometimes the connection between a coach and athlete is just not there and coaches will tend to hang on to athletes longer than they should when what the athlete really needs is a new approach or a new coach. Athletes will sometimes shy away from switching coaches as well because of the relationship they have built with the one they currently have, even when their fitness or performance has suffered. In the stand alone course on high performance athletes, we will delve into when it is appropriate to fire your athletes or break up the relationship.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: The Complete High Performance Coach
chunk.content:
Trustworthy Leader Forcing athletes to immediately adapt to your system and being rigid in your approach is one of the quickest ways to lose trust and burn an athlete out or get them injured. Coaches of Elite athletes should understand that a lot of them have come from different systems or have an innate talent and were self-coached or had no system previously. Demanding that an athlete complete something or forcing only your system on them without consideration of their current level or emotional state is a quick way to see that athlete move on to another coach or leave the sport. Having empathy and understanding that they are a complex human that leads their own complex life is vital to maintaining a healthy and positive relationship of coach and athlete. This topic will be covered in the stand alone module but there is really no substitute for experience and culture within this piece. Coaches need to choose to listen, understand, and be prepared to adapt to the athlete.
Movement Quality Held paramount. The Level 2 course went over Safety-Efficacy-Efficiency in module 4. The Level 2 course in Module 4 then went over demonstrations of several basic movements of fitness with their points of performance. Additionally, in the Level 2 course you were given demonstrations of the stations and how to perform the movements within the race. It is vital for an elite coach to understand biomechanics to know how the body is supposed to move and identify any imbalances within their athlete. Once an athlete has proper mechanics and can safely perform the full required range of motion, they then should turn their attention to efficiency and how to move with speed.
Rulebook Be an expert in the rules. Know what equipment is allowed and not allowed. Know what points of performance the judges are going to be looking for. Know how to launch an appeal or challenge. Know what is allowed to be appealed and challenged. Be involved in the evolution of the sport, whether by being in contact with the Elite Working Group or being on the board itself. Conduct yourself in a respectful manner when dealing with race directors, head judges, and any staff of HYROX. Coaches should also be fluent in any qualification system, understand how you can advise your athletes to earn the best route for them to get qualified and not making mistakes that could require your athlete to have to run more races than necessary. Stay up-to-date on all the points or time requirements for qualification.

chunk.content:
Anti-Doping Every coach should be aware of the anti-doping code, how to determine if a supplement is allowed per the WADA regulations, its means of delivery (IV injections are disallowed per WADA without cause or a TUE), and if the athlete needs to submit a TUE after a hospital or urgent care visit. Coaches should be able to educate their athletes on the process of anti-doping testing and the rules around what and where athletes are allowed to go after a race if they are selected for testing. Finally, coaches need to uphold the standard of fairness and equal competition, if you are aware of an athlete violating the anti-doping code and cheating (yes, it is straight up cheating), then coaches should be the ones reporting (whistleblowing) the athlete to HYROX or WADA. An athlete violating the anti-doping code to gain a competitive advantage by used a performance enhancer also violates the trust of the coach and can destroy the coach's reputation. When athletes violate the code while training on your program, you also lose a lot of valuable information because now you have no way of knowing if it was a good training plan that increased their fitness or just the performance enhancer.
The Complete High Performance Coach Once a coach understands the pillars to coaching high performance athletes, they can focus on improving themselves through those lenses. From the programming and science pillar, we will go over balancing intensity with recovery, managing marginal gains, and building data-informed training plans. From the Empathy pillar, you will learn how to guide high-performers through the full performance cycle. From the Expert pillar, coaches will know how to prepare athletes for training blocks, how to taper, and how to do proper post-race analysis. Balancing intensity and recovery There are a lot of different ways this has been approached, but almost every training method agrees that "easy" work or active recovery work will be the biggest volume of any training plan. Preparing an athlete to hit big workouts can be done by how they feel, recovery metrics like resting heart rate, HRV, or sleep scores, several wearable companies like to have a training readiness score, or you can use things like muscle tone. All of these are indirect ways of measuring if an athlete is ready to take on a workout. athlete should feel ready to work when needed. Athlete feedback and workout logging (journaling) is very essential to this. My preference for starting with an elite athlete is to only begin with 2 "quality" half days per week where the intensity is on the moderate to high end of the spectrum and all other days are active recovery or easy days. Some athletes will progress up to 3 full quality days, but it takes time to develop and understand the athlete before being able to make that jump. A starting 2 half quality day week would look like (this is just a broad example of an elite athlete's training week with 2 quality ½ days): Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday AM AM AM AM AM AM AM 60 minute easy run 15 min easy warm-up 6x5 min Threshold Run 1 min rest 15 min easy warm- down 45 min easy bike Into… 45 min easy run 60 min easy run Into… 20 min easy row 15 min easy warm-up 8x4 min Threshold Run 48-sec rest 15 min easy warm- down 45-60 min swim or bike 90 min long easy run
20 reps DB Snatch, alt 15 reps DB Thruster 10 reps Burpee Box Jump Over 5 reps pull-up 10 reps Ring Dip 30 reps Walking Lunge steps 250m Ski Erg 25m Sled Pull 100m KB Farmer carry 20m Sled Push 10m Heavy Sled Push 200m Run 2 min rest 60-sec weighted plank 30 reps DB Russian Twist This plan would progress to a single half day of quality with a full day of quality, then two full days of quality in the week, then 2 full days and an "X" workout day, before eventually getting to 3 full quality days within the week. You should want to spend about 4-6 weeks at each stage before adding the additional quality work. If an athlete ever give an indication that they are approaching over-worked or consistently poor workouts on quality days then reducing to the last level of volume they could handle well is what should be focused on. Once you know the level of volume they can handle, then polarizing the training between very easy days and gradual progression on the harder days can be explored.

It uses the ICF biopsychosocial model to distinguish health condition, impairment, and disability, emphasizing that performance is shaped by the interaction between athlete, task, equipment, and environment. The unit covers adapted equipment as a performance interface, environme

chunk.content: [0:00:00] Participation in adapted and inclusive sport has grown rapidly over the past two decades, driven by increased visibility and the expansion of competitive opportunities beyond traditional Paralympic pathways. In functional fitness environments such as HYROX, athletes with impairments are now [0:00:16] competing in structured, high-intensity events that place substantial physiological, mechanical, and psychological demands on performance. This growth brings an important responsibility for coaches. Adapted athletes represent a highly diverse population, encompassing a wide range [0:00:34] of physical, neurological, sensory, and functional presentations. These differences influence how athletes produce force, tolerate fatigue, regulate intensity, recover from training, and respond to competitive stress. Research in adapted sport shows that impairment type, movement mechanics, and [0:00:53] functional constraints can affect energy cost, neuromuscular performance, and sport-specific skill execution. Highlighting that impairment interacts uniquely with performance demands in different sports contexts. Much of the evidence that informs contemporary training prescription, load management, and [0:01:09] injury prevention has historically been derived from able-bodied sport or elite Paralympic cohorts. While this research has advanced understanding of high-performance sport, it does not always translate cleanly to functional fitness settings such as HYROX, where athletes present [0:01:25] with highly variable impairments, training backgrounds, and competitive goals. In fact, previous peer-reviewed analysis characterizing HYROX athlete profiles, examining training habits, physical capacities, and recovery strategies did not include athletes with [0:01:41] impairments, underscoring how adapted athletes remain underrepresented in HYROX research. To address this gap, this module introduces the adapted athlete through a performance-focused lens, drawing on contemporary models of disability, including the International Classification [0:01:57] of Functioning, Disability, and Health, ICF, expanded later. The module explores how impairment, environment, and task demand interact to shape athletic performance. The ICF framework recognizes disability as a multidimensional construct, [0:02:13] integrating biological, psychological, and social factors, rather than reducing disability solely to medical diagnosis. Coaches will be introduced to the range of sporting contexts in which adapted athletes compete, including the Paralympic movement, adapted CrossFit, the Invictus Games, [0:02:31] and HYROX. Particular attention is given to HYROX adaptive divisions, where classification is based on functional impact rather than medical diagnosis, and where performance outcomes are influenced by pacing strategy, movement efficiency, and the ability to sustain work under [0:02:47] fatigue. Scientific analysis of HYROX performance shows that the event places sustained cardiovascular and metabolic load on participants, and requires balanced development of aerobic capacity, anaerobic power, and muscular endurance. These core demands remain central even when adaptations are applied, and they [0:03:06] provide a vital reference for how functional activity patterns and energy system engagement should be understood by coaches working with adapted athletes. Importantly, this module does not attempt to provide exhaustive medical or clinical detail. Instead, it focuses on developing coaching awareness, confidence, and decision-making [0:03:25] capability. Coaches will gain an understanding of how different impairments may influence movement strategies, fatigue profiles, and training response, and how these factors should inform safe, effective, and inclusive coaching practice. This performance-informed perspective reflects broader calls in adapted sport [0:03:44] research for evidence-based approaches that bridge clinical, biomechanical, and coaching knowledge.

chunk.section_title: Audio: Translating Impairment into Effective HYROX Programming
chunk.content: [0:00:00] In HYROX, adaptation does not mean reducing challenge, it means preserving training intent while accounting for how an athlete interacts with the task. The core performance demands of HYROX remain consistent across all divisions, sustained aerobic output, repeated high force efforts, efficient movement under fatigue, and [0:00:19] the ability to manage transitions with minimal performance decay. For adapted athletes, these demands are met through thoughtful manipulation of training variables rather than simplification of workload. The role of the coach is to identify which elements of a task drive the desired physiological [0:00:35] or mechanical stimulus and then adjust how that stimulus is achieved based on the athlete's physiological and functional presentation. Effective programming, therefore, begins with intent, not exercise selection. If the goal of a session is aerobic durability, the coach should preserve time [0:00:51] under tension and cardiovascular strain, even if the mode of locomotion differs. If the goal is strength endurance, the focus remains on repeated force production under fatigue, regardless of whether that load is expressed through bilateral lifting, unilateral work, pushing, pulling, or seated tasks. [0:01:09] This approach ensures that training adaptations align with race demands while respecting individual movement constraints. Importantly, adaptation should not be effort. It should remove unnecessary barriers that do not contribute to performance development. From a practical standpoint, this means coaches should prioritize 1. [0:01:28] Effective intensity over absolute load, using methods such as perceived exertion, repeatability, and fatigue accumulation as key markers. 2. Consistency of stimulus, ensuring that energy system demands, work-to-rest ratios, and session density remain aligned with HYROX competition. [0:01:46] 3. Movement efficiency over movement uniformity, allowing technical variation while maintaining output and safety. 4. Fatigue management across the week, recognizing that daily mobility and equipment use contribute to total training load. [0:02:02] Coaches should also recognize that small inefficiencies compound across HYROX-style training, irrespective of impairment. An athlete who expends slightly more energy per repetition, or per kilometer, may accumulate significantly greater fatigue across a race or training block. [0:02:18] Programming decisions should therefore consider not only what the athlete can do in isolation, but how repeatable that output is under fatigue. Strategic use of pacing, recovery intervals, session ordering, and technical consistency become central to long-term performance progression. [0:02:34] In athletes with impairments, these inefficiencies are often magnified by altered movement mechanics slash increased physiological cost, or impairment-related physiological or biomechanical deficits, making an understanding of how impairment influences energy expenditure critical for maintaining [0:02:50] performance consistency across training and competition. Ultimately, effective programming for adapted athletes mirrors best practice in all high-performance settings. The quality of intent, individualization, and respect for individualized, impairment-specific load management. [0:03:07] When adaptations preserve training purpose rather than reduce challenge, athletes are able to develop the same relative performance qualities as their able-bodied peers-strength, endurance, resilience, and race readiness-within a framework that is safe, equitable, and performance-driven.

### Stoke Mandeville & The Mandeville Legacy
In 1944, Dr. Ludwig Guttmann established the National Spinal Injuries center at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, pioneering the use of wheelchair sport as rehabilitation. This approach emphasized competition, dignity, and inclusion. On July 29, 1948, deliberately coinciding with the London Olympic opening, Guttmann hosted an archery competition for wheelchair athletes-marking the birth of the Stoke Mandeville Games and laying the groundwork for the Paralympic Movement. The Mandeville Legacy video, available via the International Paralympic Committee's YouTube channel, highlights these foundational moments and underscores the Games' transformation into a global symbol of adaptive sport and social change.
### The Paralympic Movement
Origins and Expansion:
In 1952, Dutch ex-servicemen joined the Stoke Mandeville Games, marking the start of international participation and the foundation of the International Stoke Mandeville Games. These Games evolved into the Paralympic Games, first held in Rome, 1960, featuring 400 athletes from 23 countries. Since then, the Summer Games have occurred every four years.
Winter Paralympics
The first Winter Paralympic Games took place in Sweden, 1976, also held every four years, complete with opening and closing ceremonies. Integration with the Olympics Since 1988 (Seoul) for Summer and 1992 (Albertville) for Winter, Paralympic Games have shared cities and venues with the Olympics, thanks to an agreement between the IPC and IOC. Growth of the Paralympic Family Early efforts to include athletes with diverse impairments led to the creation of organizations such as ISOD (1964), CPISRA (1978), and IBSA (1980). These groups coordinated through the International Coordinating Committee (ICC) in 1982, later joined by federations for athletes with intellectual disabilities and deaf athletes. Birth of the IPC On 22 September 1989, the International Paralympic Committee (IPC) was founded in Düsseldorf, Germany, as the global governing body of the Paralympic Movement.
The term "Paralympic" combines para (beside) and Olympic, symbolizing the Games' parallel status to the Olympics. Impact and Legacy Today, the Paralympic Movement represents elite sport, inclusion, and advocacy for athletes with impairments worldwide. It has driven research, innovation, and policy changes that influence adapted sport globally including functional fitness contexts like HYROX. Rise of Sports Medicine in Adaptive Sports Until the Paralympic Games were formalized (1960), research into athlete-specific injury prevention and performance was limited. Practitioner knowledge was adapted from non-disabled sport. Since the Games began, scientific interest has surged: PubMed data show near-zero sports medicine publications before 1992, with steady

rises throughout the 1990s and 2000s, reflecting a growing evidence base dedicated to para-athletes. Early experts, such as Prof. Nick Webborn, pioneered a specialized medical approach that acknowledges the complexity of adapted- athlete care. His model includes 12 core specialty areas These focus areas underscore a shift from generalized medical practice to a deeply nuanced, athlete-centered approaches in Paralympic care and research. From Rehabilitation to Elite Adaptive Performance What began as therapeutic sport for veterans has transformed into elite global competition-currently embodying scientific rigor, athlete development, and performance optimization akin to Olympic models. Academic milestones reflect this: foundational journals (e.g., The Lancet, British Journal of Sports Medicine) now feature peer-reviewed
research on athlete injury epidemiology, metabolic responses, classification effects, and equipment adaptation in Paralympic populations. Functional Fitness and Emerging Adapted Sports While the Paralympic Movement shaped the early decades of adapted sport, recent years have seen a surge in functional fitness adaptations. Events like Adaptive CrossFit divisions and HYROX Adaptive competitions have created new spaces for athletes with impairments to engage in high-intensity, community-driven formats. These sports emphasize versatility, strength, and endurance, offering inclusive pathways outside traditional Paralympic disciplines. Similarly, initiatives such as the Invictus Games and adaptive fitness leagues reflect a growing trend: sport as a tool for empowerment, performance, and social connection in diverse environments.
### Societal Implications
Adapted sport has transformed perceptions of disability worldwide. From its origins as rehabilitation, it evolved into a platform for visibility, inclusion, and equality. The Paralympic Movement challenged stereotypes, proving that athletes with impairments can achieve elite performance. These Games have influenced policy, accessibility standards, and public attitudes-shifting the narrative from limitation to capability.
Beyond competition, adapted sport fosters social integration, inspires innovation in equipment and training, and drives research into health and performance. Implications for HYROX coaching today Understanding the evolution of adapted sport and the Paralympic Movement is not just about knowing where it all began-it shapes how we coach today. The journey from rehabilitation at Stoke Mandeville to elite global competition demonstrates that adapted athletes are not defined by limitations but by performance potential. This perspective challenges outdated assumptions and reinforces the need for evidence-based, individualized coaching. The rise of Paralympic sports medicine and research highlights the complexity of working with adapted athletes. Impairment-specific considerations-such as cardiovascular risk, bone health, equipment ergonomics, and injury prevention-show that coaching adapted athletes requires more than simply modifying non- disabled programs. It demands curiosity, respect, and a willingness to learn from decades of progress in inclusion and performance science. chunk.section_title: Chapter 03: Who is the Adapted Athlete?
chunk.content:
Adapted athletes participate across diverse sporting environments, each guided by unique philosophies, eligibility criteria, and performance demands. This section explores key contexts-Paralympics, Adapted CrossFit, Special Olympics, Invictus Games, and HYROX Adaptive-highlighting their distinct focuses and what they mean for coaching.
### The Biopsychosocial Model of Disability
The International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF) frames disability as a multidimensional concept, moving beyond a purely medical perspective. It integrates biological, psychological, and social factors to explain how health conditions interact with personal and environmental contexts. Health Condition: An umbrella term for disease, disorder, injury, or trauma. This is the starting point for understanding functional limitations.
Impairment: Problems in body function or structure, such as a significant deviation or loss (e.g., muscle weakness, limb deficiency, sensory loss). Disability: A complex phenomenon that reflects the interaction between health conditions and contextual factors-biological, social, and individual. Disability is not solely about impairment; it includes participation restrictions and environmental barriers.
### Why This Matters for Coaching
Coaches must recognize that performance is influenced by more than physical ability. Social attitudes, psychological readiness, and environmental accessibility all shape an athlete's experience. Effective coaching for adapted athletes requires addressing these dimensions holistically.
### Terminology Matters
Using correct language is essential for respect and clarity. Terms like impairment, disability, and health condition have specific meanings within the ICF framework. Avoid outdated or stigmatising language (e.g., "handicapped") and instead use athlete-first or person-first language (e.g., "athlete with a lower limb impairment"). To compete in HYROX Adaptive Divisions, an individual must have a "recognized impairment" as defined in the rulebook. This ensures adaptations are applied appropriately and maintains fairness across divisions.
### The Paralympic Athlete
The Paralympic Games represent the largest elite adaptive sport movement, featuring global, high-performance competition across summer and winter sports. To be eligible to compete at the Paralympics, athletes must have an eligible impairment type, outlined by the International Paralympic Committee (IPC). The impairment must be severe enough to affect sports performance and therefore this will determine which sport an individual is eligible to compete within. Eligible Impairment Types (IPC-defined) Impaired muscle power Impaired passive range of motion Limb deficiency Leg length difference Short stature
Hypertonia
Ataxia
Athetosis
Vision impairment Intellectual impairment
Sports Examples
Summer: Athletics, Swimming, Wheelchair Basketball, Para-Powerlifting
Winter: Alpine Skiing, Para-Nordic Skiing, Ice Sledge Hockey
### Adapted CrossFit
Adaptive CrossFit divisions have been incorporated into major functional fitness events (e.g., CrossFit Games) to support inclusivity. Demonstrates that functional fitness can be made competitive and inclusive through creative programming-without diluting challenge or athletic growth potential.
Impairment Categories
• Upper limb
• Lower limb
• Seated
• Neurological impairments
Adaptations in Practice
• Exercise modifications-e.g., single-arm lifts, seated rows, grip
assistance

### Special Olympics
Focused on athletes with intellectual disabilities, Special Olympics emphasizes participation, social inclusion, and lifelong sports engagement rather than elite performance. Special Olympics reframes what success means: achievement, fitness, confidence, community belonging. It highlights coaching approaches centered on empowerment and supportive environments.
Eligibility
Intellectual disabilities or developmental conditions
Sports Examples
Athletics
Swimming
Basketball
Football
Gymnastics
### Invictus Games
The Invictus Games are a high-profile, adaptive multi-sport event for wounded, injured, and sick service personnel and veterans. emphasizes sport's role in rehabilitation and resilience. Coaching must be trauma- informed, adaptive, and sensitive to both physical and mental health needs-a valuable mindset for HYROX contexts.
Eligibility:
Physical and psychological injuries resulting from military service
Sports Examples
Wheelchair Rugby
Sitting Volleyball
Indoor Rowing
Cycling
### Why HYROX Uses Divisions and How Coaches Should Use Them
HYROX Adaptive divisions exist to promote fairness and comparability by grouping athletes according to the functional impact of impairment and applying task-specific modifications that aim to preserve the core demands of the sport. In other words, the goal is not to make the event "easier," but to maintain a consistent challenge across athletes with different functional constraints so that performance reflects preparation, pacing, and execution rather than impairment severity alone. At the same time, a division label is not a performance descriptor. It does not fully explain an athlete's movement capacity, fatigue profile, equipment interaction, training history, or competition readiness. Two athletes in the same division may present very differently in how they tolerate load, regulate intensity, or execute key tasks under fatigue. For coaches, the practical value of division information is therefore to support planning, not prediction. Coaches should use division guidance to: Confirm eligibility and competition requirements Understand permitted adaptations and equipment considerations Identify likely task constraints (e.g., locomotion demands, gripping/strapping needs, shoulder loading)
### HYROX Adaptive Divisions
HYROX has introduced adaptive divisions guided by its 2025 Adaptive Athlete Rulebook. These divisions are designed to maintain the sport's demands while accommodating diverse impairments.
Divisions
Lower Limb Impairment
Upper Limb Impairment
Short Stature Impairment
Visual/Hearing Impairment
Neurological Impairment (Major & Minor)
Seated Impairment:
Seated With Hip Function (SWHF) Seated Without Hip Function (SWOHF) Seated Without Core Function (SWOC)
### Adaptations and Principles
Consistency of challenge: All athletes complete eight 1-km runs (or pushes) between workouts, preserving HYROX's foundational endurance requirement.
Division-specific modifications: Repetition counts, weights, adapted equipment and distances are adjusted to accommodate each impairment. For example: Seated divisions use wrist straps or hooks to secure equipment during movements like sled push/pull. Short Stature and Neurological divisions complete ~350 m laps instead of 1 km while maintaining workout completion.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 04: Equipment in Adapted Sports Performance
chunk.content:
For many adapted athletes, interaction with equipment begins long before training or competition. Wheelchairs, prosthetic limbs, orthoses, and assistive devices are often essential for daily mobility and independence. Unlike non-disabled athletes, whose equipment use is largely confined to sport-specific contexts, adapted athletes may rely on their equipment continuously throughout the day. As a result, the biomechanical and physiological demands placed on the body are often cumulative rather than limited to training sessions alone. This distinction is critical for coaches to understand. Research has consistently shown that the use of adaptive equipment significantly alters the energetic cost of movement, fatigue development, and mechanical loading of the body. For example, individuals using lower-limb prostheses demonstrate higher oxygen consumption and energy expenditure during walking and exercise compared with non-disabled individuals. These demands increase further with rising task intensity, suboptimal prosthetic fit
or alignment, and at more proximal levels of amputation (Gailey et al., 2008). Similarly, wheelchair propulsion has been shown to increase upper-body loading, shoulder stress, and overall metabolic demand, particularly when equipment configuration is not optimized (Salzman et al., 2025; Mason et al., 2013). Within the biopsychosocial model of disability, equipment represents a critical environmental factor that shapes how impairment translates into function and performance. It acts as the interface between the athlete and the task, influencing how force is generated, transferred, and absorbed. In many cases, performance limitations arise not solely from the impairment itself, but from how effectively the athlete can interact with their equipment under increasing biomechanical and physiological stress. From a coaching perspective, the interaction between the athlete and their equipment is central to performance (figure below), demonstrating performance is influence by the interaction between the athlete, the equipment, and the task demands. Rather than viewing the wheelchair or prosthesis as a passive aid, the model highlights that performance emerges from how effectively the athlete and their equipment function as a single system. This interaction influences the physiological and biomechanical demands of performance capacity.
Mason, B. S., van der Woude, L. H. V., & Goosey-Tolfrey, V. L. (2013). The ergonomics of wheelchair configuration for optimal performance in the wheelchair court sports. In Sports Medicine (Vol. 43, Issue 1, pp. 23-38). https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-012-0005-x As a result, two athletes with the same impairment may demonstrate markedly different performance capabilities depending on:

chunk.section_title: Chapter 04: Equipment in Adapted Sports Performance
chunk.content:
The type, fit, and configuration of their wheelchair, prosthesis, or assistive equipment How efficiently force is generated and transferred through that equipment Their movement strategies and technical proficiency within the constraints of their impairment Their exposure to cumulative fatigue associated with daily equipment use This interaction becomes particularly important in functional fitness environments such as HYROX. Athletes are required to repeatedly engage with external loads-including sleds, wall balls, carries, and rowing or pushing tasks-often with minimal recovery between efforts. When combined with the baseline physical demands of daily ambulation, these requirements can significantly influence fatigue accumulation, movement quality, and injury risk across a training cycle or race. Importantly, equipment in adapted sport should not be viewed as a means of reducing challenge or compensating for performance. Instead, it enables fair and meaningful expression of physical capacity within the constraints of an athlete's impairment. When
appropriately selected and integrated, equipment allows athletes to express strength, endurance, and technical skill in a way that aligns with the demands of the sport. For coaches, this reinforces the need to: Consider daily equipment use as part of total training load Understand how equipment configuration influences movement efficiency and fatigue Monitor how athletes interact with equipment under increasing intensity Integrate equipment considerations into programming, pacing, and recovery strategies "Performance in adapted sport is not determined by the athlete or the equipment alone, but by the quality of interaction between the two."

The conceptual model shows that sports wheelchair performance is influenced by the wheelchair user, the wheelchair, the wheelchair-user interface, and the wheelchair-user combination. chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: Sport Environment and Accessibility in HYROX
chunk.content:
Why the Environment Matters for Performance In adapted sport, performance is shaped not only by the athlete and the task, but by the environment in which training and competition occur. Within the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF), the environment is recognized as a key determinant of participation and performance. For adapted athletes, environmental factors can either enable performance or create unnecessary barriers that increase fatigue, limit execution, or elevate injury risk. In HYROX, the competition and training environment is uniquely demanding. Events are held indoors, often with high ambient temperatures, large crowds, loud noise, constrained space, and complex movement transitions. Athletes must navigate repeated running or pushing efforts, congested workout zones, changing surfaces, and time- pressured transitions. For adapted athletes, these environmental demands interact directly with impairment, equipment use, sensory processing, and fatigue accumulation. From a coaching perspective, understanding the environment is therefore not secondary to programming-it is part of performance preparation.
### Environmental Load as a Performance Variable
The physical environment contributes to total training and competition load in ways that are often underestimated. Heat, noise, visual complexity, floor surfaces, lighting, and spatial layout all influence physiological stress and movement efficiency. #### Indoor HYROX Environmental Load Factors
| Environmental factor | Performance relevance | | Elevated ambient temperatures and limited airflow | May increase cardiovascular strain and heat load. | | High humidity and restricted cooling opportunities | May impair cooling and increase perceived exertion. | | Dense athlete traffic and auditory overload | May increase cognitive and sensory load. | | Variable lighting and visual contrast | May affect visual processing, spatial awareness, and movement confidence. | | Fixed competition layouts with minimal flexibility | May constrain setup, equipment movement, and station transitions. |
For some adapted athletes, these conditions increase cardiovascular strain, impair thermoregulation, or elevate cognitive load. For others, environmental unpredictability may disrupt pacing, spatial awareness, or movement confidence. These factors can amplify fatigue independently of workload and should be considered when planning training density, recovery, and race simulation sessions. Effective coaching recognises that environmental stress adds to physiological stress. Training that appears appropriate on paper may become excessive once environmental load is factored in.
### Accessibility
Accessibility in sport is often misunderstood as a logistical or administrative issue. In practice, accessibility directly influences an athlete's ability to perform, recover, and compete safely.
In HYROX settings, accessibility considerations may include:• Venue layout and travel distance between stations
• Surface consistency and grip
• Entry and exit points for athletes using mobility aids
• Space for equipment setup and adjustment
• Clear sightlines and predictable movement patterns
• Access to quiet areas for preparation or recovery

chunk.section_title: Chapter 05: Sport Environment and Accessibility in HYROX
chunk.content:
Barriers in any of these areas can increase energy expenditure, elevate stress, and reduce performance capacity before the race or training session has even begun. For athletes using wheelchairs, prostheses, or assistive devices, small environmental inefficiencies can accumulate rapidly across a race. From a coaching standpoint, this means viewing accessibility not as accommodation, but as part of performance optimization.
### Sensory and Cognitive Load in Competition Environments
For athletes with neurological, visual, or hearing impairments, the sensory environment can significantly influence performance. HYROX events involve loud music, crowd noise, rapid transitions, and high visual complexity. These factors increase cognitive demand and may impair focus, reaction time, or movement efficiency in line with impairment. Even for athletes without sensory impairment, cognitive fatigue can influence pacing and technical execution. For adapted athletes, the effect may be amplified due to increased reliance on visual cues, proprioception, or structured routines. #### Coach Actions to Reduce Sensory and Cognitive Load
| Coaching action | Purpose | | Maintain consistent training environments where possible | Reduces unnecessary variability. | | Use clear, repeatable cues and task structures | Reduces cognitive load and improves execution. | | Minimize unnecessary variability in warm-ups and transitions | Preserves attention for performance. | | Prepare athletes for competition environments through simulation | Builds tolerance to noise, crowds, transitions, and visual complexity. | | Establish predictable race-day routines | Supports confidence and repeatable execution. |
Consistency reduces cognitive load and allows athletes to direct effort toward performance rather than environmental management.
### Environmental Planning as Part of Coaching Practice
Effective coaches anticipate environmental challenges rather than reacting to them during training or on race days. This includes preparing athletes for:
• Heat and indoor conditions
• Crowded or noisy spaces through exposure and rehearsal
• Equipment transitions under fatigue
• Variability in surface traction and spatial constraints
Importantly, environmental preparation should be integrated into training rather than treated as an afterthought. Just as pacing or fueling is practiced, navigating space, managing equipment, and maintaining composure under sensory load should be trained deliberately. Where possible, coaches should also advocate for athletes by engaging with event organisers, understanding venue layouts in advance, and ensuring that adaptive needs are communicated clearly and early.
### Key Takeaways for Coaches
• The sport environment directly influences performance, fatigue,
and safety
• Environmental stress adds to physiological load and should be
accounted for in programming
• Accessibility is a performance factor, not an administrative detail
• Sensory and spatial demands can affect execution, pacing, and
confidence
• Preparing athletes for environmental challenges is a core coaching

chunk.section_title: Chapter 06: Understanding Impairment in a Functional Fitness Context
chunk.content:
HYROX Performance Demands: A Practical Anchor for
Understanding Impairment
Before considering how different impairments influence performance, it is important to briefly revisit the core demands of HYROX competition. HYROX events are characterised by: Repeated bouts of locomotion (running or pushing) Heavy external loading (e.g. sleds, carries, wall balls) High repetition volumes Minimal recovery between efforts Sustained cardiovascular and metabolic stress
Recent performance analyses of HYROX have demonstrated that the event places a prolonged demand on both aerobic and anaerobic energy systems, with performance influenced by the ability to sustain work rate under accumulating fatigue and maintain movement efficiency across repeated stations (Brandt et al. 2025). These demands create an environment in which small inefficiencies are likely magnified over time, particularly when athletes are required to transition repeatedly between locomotion and loaded functional tasks. Understanding impairment through a performance lens While competition in HYROX currently operates within defined adaptive divisions, it is important for coaches to understand that classification systems are administrative tools, not performance descriptors. Classification exists to promote fairness in competition, but it does not fully explain how an individual athlete moves or responds to training/competition.
Effective coaching requires an understanding of the physiological and biomechanical mechanisms that underpin performance. These mechanisms influence how athletes generate force, regulate effort, tolerate fatigue, and interact with their environment and equipment.
Rather than viewing impairments as discrete diagnostic labels, coaches should consider how different impairments influence key physiological and biomechanical factors that underpin performance in functional fitness. In practice, this includes understanding how impairment may affect:
#### Performance Mechanisms Affected by Impairment
| Mechanism | Coaching meaning | | Neuromuscular control and movement efficiency | Impairments may alter motor control, coordination, or muscle activation patterns, increasing energy cost during repeated tasks. | | Cardiovascular and metabolic responses | Impairment may influence oxygen delivery, heart rate regulation, and sustained output during prolonged or high-intensity efforts. | | Thermoregulation | Some impairments affect heat dissipation through sweating or blood flow regulation. | | Force production and mechanical efficiency | Altered biomechanics, asymmetry, or equipment reliance can influence movement economy and physical cost. | | Fatigue development and recovery capacity | Fatigue may accumulate faster and recovery may be slower, especially when daily mobility already loads the body. | | Technical execution under load | Fatigue can amplify impairment-related coordination, stability, and movement quality challenges. |
Neuromuscular control and movement efficiency Impairments may alter motor control, coordination, or muscle activation patterns, reduce the efficiency of repeated movements and increase the energy cost of tasks such as running, pushing, or lifting.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 06: Understanding Impairment in a Functional Fitness Context
chunk.content:
Cardiovascular and metabolic responses Impairment can influence how effectively an athlete delivers and utilises oxygen, regulates heart rate, and sustains work output during prolonged or high-intensity efforts. In some conditions, autonomic dysfunction or altered muscle mass distribution may limit aerobic capacity or accelerate fatigue.
### Thermoregulation
Certain impairments affect the body's ability to dissipate heat through sweating or blood flow regulation. During high-intensity or prolonged exercise, this can lead to greater heat strain and earlier performance decline if not appropriately managed.
Force production and mechanical efficiency Altered biomechanics, muscle impairment, asymmetry, or reliance on assistive equipment can affect how force is generated and transferred, influencing movement economy and increasing the physical cost of work.
Fatigue development and recovery capacity Impairment may influence how quickly fatigue accumulates and how effectively an athlete recovers between efforts or training sessions, particularly when daily mobility already places a significant load on the body.
Technical execution under load As fatigue increases, impairments may have a greater impact on coordination, stability, and movement quality, affecting the athlete's ability to maintain efficient technique across repeated HYROX stations.
### Summary
This perspective aligns with contemporary models of disability, including the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF), which emphasizes that performance emerges from the interaction between the individual, the task, and the environment-not impairment alone. While knowledge of an athlete's competitive category remains important for eligibility and competition planning, coaching decisions should be guided primarily by how an athlete functions within training and race conditions.
Neurological Impairments
Neurological impairments such as spinal cord injury (SCI), cerebral palsy (CP), multiple sclerosis, or acquired brain injury primarily affect the nervous system's ability to regulate movement and physiological function.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 06: Understanding Impairment in a Functional Fitness Context
chunk.content:
In individuals with spinal cord injury, disruption to autonomic nervous system control significantly alters cardiovascular and thermoregulatory function. Reduced sympathetic outflow below the level of injury limits heart rate response, stroke volume, and peripheral vasoconstriction, resulting in a reduced ability to increase cardiac output during exercise (West et al., 2015; Price, 2006). This places an upper limit on aerobic capacity and contributes to earlier fatigue during sustained or high-intensity activity. Thermoregulation is also markedly affected. Individuals with SCI often have impaired sweating and vasomotor control below the lesion level, reducing their ability to dissipate heat during exercise. During high-intensity efforts, such as those required in HYROX, metabolic heat production increases substantially, while heat loss mechanisms are compromised-placing athletes at increased risk of heat strain and performance decline (Griggs et al., 2017). In athletes with cerebral palsy, impaired motor control, spasticity, and co-contraction increase the metabolic cost of movement. Inefficient muscle activation patterns elevate oxygen consumption and accelerate fatigue during locomotion and repetitive tasks (Bar- Or, 1983; Maltais et al., 2004). Behavioural thermoregulation may also be altered, with reduced ability to modulate pace or adjust effort in response to rising thermal strain.
Implications for performance include: Reduced exercise tolerance Earlier onset of fatigue Higher energy cost for given workloads Increased susceptibility to heat stress Coaching considerations Careful pacing and workload management Knowledge and understanding of individuals physiological/thermoregulatory disfunction Environmental monitoring (temperature, hydration) and effective cooling/heat management strategies Close observation of fatigue and movement quality
### Lower Limb Impairments
Lower limb impairments, including limb deficiency or neurological impairment affecting gait, alter force production and locomotion mechanics. Reduced propulsion from the lower limbs increases reliance on the upper body and trunk, leading to higher cardiovascular and metabolic cost during walking or running tasks. Research demonstrates that individuals using lower-limb prostheses exhibit significantly greater oxygen consumption and energy expenditure during locomotion compared with non-disabled individuals, with demands increasing as walking speed increases, prosthetic fit becomes suboptimal, or the level of amputation rises (Gailey et al., 2008). In addition, reduced active muscle mass and decreased skin surface area available for heat dissipation may impair thermoregulation, increasing susceptibility to heat strain during sustained or high-intensity exercise. These altered mechanics and physiological demands lead to: Increased cardiovascular strain Greater asymmetry and compensatory movement patterns reducing efficiency and increasing injury risk
Higher cumulative fatigue during endurance-based tasks In functional fitness environments such as HYROX, this can result in disproportionate fatigue during running or sled-based stations and increased reliance on upper-body musculature to maintain performance. Coaching considerations: Emphasis on pacing and movement efficiency Targeted conditioning programs Monitoring for asymmetrical loading Managing cumulative training volume Effective cooling/heat management strategies
### Upper Limb Impairments

chunk.section_title: Chapter 06: Understanding Impairment in a Functional Fitness Context
chunk.content:
Upper limb impairments influence force production, grip strength, and load transfer during pushing, pulling, and carrying tasks. When upper-limb function is reduced-due to weakness, limb deficiency, or neurological impairment-athletes often adopt compensatory movement strategies that increase reliance on the trunk and remaining limbs. While these strategies allow task completion, they typically do so at a greater relative physiological cost. When the upper limbs are the primary or limiting contributors to force production, relative muscular effort increases, and fatigue develops more rapidly during repetitive or high-load tasks. Individuals with upper-limb impairment show altered muscle activation patterns, and earlier onset of neuromuscular fatigue during sustained or repeated upper-body work compared with non- disabled controls. These effects are amplified when grip strength is limited or when asymmetrical loading strategies are required due to impairment. From a physiological perspective, this results in: Earlier local muscular fatigue, particularly in the shoulder girdle and forearm musculature Increased whole-body energy expenditure due to reduced mechanical efficiency
Greater reliance on compensatory trunk and lower- limb strategies Potential thermoregulatory challenges due to reduced effective skin surface area for heat dissipation In functional fitness environments such as HYROX, these factors can significantly influence performance during sled pushes and pulls, carries, wall balls, and other upper-body-dominant tasks, particularly when repeated under fatigue. Coaching considerations include: Emphasising grip endurance and trunk stability (where possible) Optimising movement sequencing to reduce unnecessary energy cost Carefully managing training volume and intensity Avoiding excessive repetitive loading without adequate recovery
These strategies help preserve performance quality while reducing the risk of excessive fatigue and overuse injury in athletes with upper-limb impairments.
### Seated Athletes
Seated athletes rely predominantly on the upper body for both daily mobility and sporting performance. As a result, a smaller active muscle mass is responsible for generating force and sustaining cardiovascular work. Research demonstrates that wheelchair propulsion significantly increases shoulder joint loading, with greater forces and moments observed during higher-intensity or prolonged propulsion tasks, reflecting elevated mechanical and metabolic demand on the upper limb musculature (Gil-Agudo et al. 2014). Combined with daily wheelchair use, this places seated athletes at elevated risk of overuse injury, particularly at the shoulder complex. In functional fitness settings, repeated upper-body dominant tasks with minimal rest further increase fatigue and injury risk.
Coaching considerations: Holistic progression of volume and intensity considering external factors Close monitoring of shoulder health Emphasis on movement efficiency and technique Equipment setup to optimize biomechanics
### Short Stature and Sensory Impairments

Reliance on external cues, spatial awareness, and consistent environments becomes critical for safe and efficient movement execution.

chunk.section_title: Chapter 08: Coach Scope, Boundaries, and Referral Considerations
chunk.content:
Coaches play a critical role in observing, supporting, and adapting training for athletes with impairments, but they are not responsible for diagnosis or clinical management. Effective coaching begins with recognizing patterns rather than interpreting pathology. Changes in movement quality, unexpected drops in performance, altered fatigue responses, unusual pain, or declining tolerance to training loads may indicate that an athlete's current training demands exceed their capacity to adapt. Similarly, warning signs such as unexplained reductions in strength or coordination, persistent pain, recurrent skin breakdown, excessive fatigue, dizziness, or marked changes in thermoregulation should prompt further discussion and, where appropriate, referral to a qualified healthcare professional. Coaches should also be alert to equipment-related issues - such as changes in prosthetic fit, wheelchair discomfort, or altered movement mechanics - as these can significantly influence performance and injury risk.
Coaches should also be aware that certain impairment-related conditions can present with acute or serious symptoms that require immediate attention. For example, athletes with spinal cord injury above T6 may be at risk of autonomic dysreflexia-a potentially life-threatening condition characterised by sudden increases in blood pressure, headache, flushing, sweating, or dizziness, often triggered by pain, pressure, or equipment issues. While coaches are not expected to diagnose medical conditions, awareness of these risks and prompt referral or cessation of activity when abnormal symptoms arise is essential for athlete safety. The coach's role is to observe, document, communicate, and adjust training accordingly, while maintaining clear referral pathways to medical, physiotherapy, or allied health professionals when concerns extend beyond normal training responses. Establishing these boundaries protects both athlete wellbeing and coaching integrity, and ensures that performance development remains safe, ethical, and sustainable.

Effective coaching begins with recognizing patterns rather than interpreting pathology.

Changes in movement quality, unexpected drops in performance, altered fatigue responses, unusual pain, or declining tolerance to training loads may indicate that an athlete's current training demands exceed their capacity to adapt.

chunk.content:
This module has introduced the adapted athlete through a performance-focused lens, emphasising that adaptation in HYROX is not about reducing challenge, but about understanding how impairment, environment, and task demand interact to shape performance. Adapted athletes compete within the same fundamental physiological and mechanical demands as all HYROX athletes-sustained aerobic output, repeated high-force efforts, efficient movement under fatigue, and the ability to manage transitions effectively. What differs is how these demands are expressed and experienced across individuals. Throughout this module, the central message has been that performance in adapted sport is not determined by impairment alone, but by the interaction between the athlete, their equipment, and the environment in which they train and compete. By understanding these interactions, coaches are better equipped to make informed decisions about training structure, load management, pacing, and progression. This approach supports
safe, effective, and equitable coaching while preserving the competitive integrity of HYROX.
### What this means for your practice
As a HYROX coach, your role is to recognize how impairment influences movement efficiency, fatigue development, and recovery
-without allowing impairment to define an athlete's potential.
Effective coaching begins with understanding how an athlete functions in real training and race conditions, rather than relying solely on classification labels or assumptions about ability. This means viewing equipment as part of the performance system, considering environmental and accessibility factors as contributors to training load, and recognizing that small inefficiencies, specifically impairment related, can compound across repeated efforts. Programming should preserve intent while allowing flexibility in how that intent is achieved. Consistency of stimulus, intelligent pacing, and appropriate performance strategies are central to long-term performance development in adapted athletes.
Just as importantly, coaches must understand the boundaries of their role. Observing trends, communicating clearly, adapting training where needed, and referring appropriately when concerns arise are all part of responsible, athlete-centered practice.
### Linking back to learning objectives
By completing this module, you should now be able to: Understand the evolution of adapted sport and the diverse characteristics of adapted athletes in functional fitness contexts, including how adapted sport has progressed from rehabilitation to high-performance. Understand how athlete classification is approached within HYROX and how different impairments may influence performance demands and training considerations, while recognizing that classification supports fairness rather than defining performance capacity. These learning outcomes provide a foundation for more advanced exploration of impairment-specific physiology, training adaptation, and coaching strategies in later modules. Final message for HYROX coaches

chunk.content:
Coaching adapted athletes effectively, does not require complex rules or prescriptive modifications. It requires curiosity, observation, and a clear understanding of how performance is shaped by the interaction between athlete, task, and environment. When coaches focus on preserving training intent, managing fatigue intelligently, and creating inclusive, well-structured training environments, adapted athletes are able to train with confidence, perform consistently, and progress over time. This is not about lowering standards-it is about applying high-quality coaching principles in a way that allows every athlete to express their full performance potential within HYROX.
